30344.q: Why were the ration coupons printed on special paper?
a: So that they could not be forged
So that they could be eaten
So that they glowed in the dark
30344.e: The coupons were printed on special paper made under strict control. This was meant to prevent forgeries.
30344.m: Special paper protected the ration coupons from forgery.

30345.q: What did the “J stamp” in German passports mean from 1938?
a: The holder was a young person
30345.e: Germany stamped a red “J” in the passports of Jewish people. This let Swiss border officials recognise them at once and turn them away.
30345.m: The J stamp marked the passports of Jewish people.

30346.q: Between which two states was the J stamp agreed in 1938?
30346.e: On 29 September 1938 Switzerland and Germany agreed on the marking. Switzerland wanted to be able to recognise Jewish refugees at the border.
30346.m: The J stamp goes back to an agreement between Switzerland and Germany.

30347.q: What was the phrase “The boat is full” from 1942 meant to say?
a: Switzerland would take in no more refugees
30347.e: Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger compared Switzerland to a full lifeboat. He used this to justify turning many refugees away.
30347.m: “The boat is full” justified turning refugees away.

30348.q: What did Switzerland decide about Jewish refugees in August 1942?
a: It closed the border to them
It took them all in at once
It paid for their onward journey
30348.e: On 13 August 1942 the border was closed. People fleeing only on “racial grounds” did not count as political refugees.
30348.m: In August 1942 Switzerland closed the border to Jewish refugees.

30349.q: Why did many Jewish people flee Germany from 1933?
a: They were persecuted by the Nazis
They were looking for farm work
They wanted to go on holiday
They had to join the army
30349.e: The Nazis took away Jewish people's rights, their property and later their lives. Many tried to flee abroad, including to Switzerland.
30349.m: Jewish people fled persecution by the Nazis.

30350.q: What did the Bergier Commission investigate in the 1990s?
a: Switzerland's role in the Second World War
The building of the Gotthard Tunnel
30350.e: Historians examined Switzerland's refugee policy and business dealings during the Second World War. They criticised the fact that many persecuted people had been turned away.
30350.m: The Bergier Commission investigated Switzerland in the Second World War.

30351.q: What did the Federal Council publicly apologise for in 1995?
30351.e: On the 50th anniversary of the end of the war, President Kaspar Villiger apologised for the J stamp. Switzerland had agreed on it with Germany in 1938.
30351.m: In 1995 the Federal Council apologised for the J stamp.

30352.q: How many people found protection in Switzerland for shorter or longer periods during the Second World War?
30352.e: They included civilian refugees, interned soldiers and children on recovery holidays. At the same time, however, many persecuted people were turned away at the border.
30352.m: In the Second World War almost 300,000 people found protection in Switzerland.

30353.q: What job did Paul Grüninger have when he helped Jewish refugees in 1938?
30353.e: Grüninger commanded the St Gallen cantonal police. At the border with Austria he decided whether many refugees could enter.
30353.m: Paul Grüninger was police commander in St Gallen.

30354.q: According to what we know today, how many refugees did Paul Grüninger save?
30354.e: In 1938 and 1939 he let several hundred Jewish refugees enter. Without him they would have been sent back.
30354.m: Paul Grüninger saved the lives of several hundred people.

30355.q: What happened to Paul Grüninger in 1939 after his help became known?
30355.e: Grüninger lost his job and his pension in 1939. In 1940 he was convicted of breach of official duty and then lived in poverty.
30355.m: Paul Grüninger was dismissed for his help.

30356.q: Which honour did Paul Grüninger receive from the Yad Vashem memorial in 1971?
30356.e: Yad Vashem in Jerusalem honours people who saved Jews at the risk of their lives or at great personal cost. Grüninger received this title in 1971.
30356.m: Paul Grüninger is one of the Righteous Among the Nations.

30357.q: How was Paul Grüninger honoured after his death?
30357.e: Grüninger died in poverty in 1972. In 1995 a court acquitted him, and today he is honoured as a rescuer of refugees.
30357.m: Paul Grüninger's name was cleared after his death.

30358.q: What in St Gallen has carried Paul Grüninger's name since 2006?
30358.e: FC Brühl's stadium has been called the Paul Grüninger Stadium since 2006. Grüninger himself had played football for FC Brühl.
30358.m: In St Gallen a stadium remembers Paul Grüninger.

30359.q: From which country did most of the refugees Paul Grüninger helped in 1938 flee?
30359.e: After Austria was annexed by the German Reich in March 1938, many Jews fled to Switzerland. Near St Gallen they tried to get across the Rhine.
30359.m: Grüninger mainly helped refugees from Austria.

30360.q: In which city did the Swiss diplomat Carl Lutz save Jews from deportation?
30360.e: From 1942 Carl Lutz was vice-consul at the Swiss legation in Budapest. In 1944 the deportations of Hungarian Jews began there.
30360.m: Carl Lutz saved thousands of Jews in Budapest.

30361.q: With which documents did Carl Lutz protect the Jews in Budapest?
30361.e: Lutz issued letters of protection that placed their holders under Swiss protection. The authorities often respected them and did not deport these people.
30361.m: Carl Lutz saved people with letters of protection.

30362.q: What was the building in Budapest called where Carl Lutz sheltered persecuted Jews?
30362.e: The “Glass House” had been the headquarters of a glass company, and the Swiss mission used it in 1944. Thousands of people found refuge there.
30362.m: Thousands found protection in the Glass House in Budapest.

30363.q: Roughly how many people did Carl Lutz help in Budapest?
30363.e: With letters of protection and safe houses, Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of Jews. It ranks among the biggest rescue operations of the Second World War.
30363.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of people.

30364.q: Why is Carl Lutz honoured as a hero today?
a: He saved many Jews from death
30364.e: In 1944 in Budapest Carl Lutz protected many Jews from deportation. Later other diplomats such as Raoul Wallenberg copied his method.
30364.m: Carl Lutz is honoured for saving many Jews.

30365.q: How did the Swiss authorities first react to Carl Lutz's rescue operation after the war?
a: They criticised him for overstepping his authority
They elected him to the Federal Council
They gave him a monument in Bern
30365.e: The authorities saw part of his independent action as overstepping his authority. Only in 1995 did Switzerland clear his name after his death.
30365.m: Carl Lutz received recognition for his deeds in Switzerland only late.

30366.q: During which war did Carl Lutz save people in Budapest?
30366.e: Carl Lutz worked in Budapest from 1942 to 1945. In 1944 the deportations of Hungarian Jews began there.
30366.m: Carl Lutz helped people in Budapest in the Second World War.

30367.q: What does the abbreviation AHV stand for?
30367.e: AHV stands for old-age and survivors' insurance. It pays pensions to retired people and to surviving dependants such as widows and orphans.
30367.m: AHV protects old people and surviving dependants.

30368.q: Which pillar of the pension system is AHV?
30368.e: Switzerland has three pillars: AHV (1st pillar), pension fund (2nd pillar) and private savings (3rd pillar). AHV is meant to cover basic living costs.
30368.m: AHV is the first pillar of the pension system.

30369.q: What did the “magic formula” in Switzerland settle?
a: How the Federal Council seats are shared among the parties
30369.e: From 1959 the four biggest parties shared the seven seats on the Federal Council according to a fixed formula.
30369.m: The magic formula shared out the Federal Council seats among the big parties.

30370.q: Which party got a second seat on the Federal Council with the magic formula in 1959?
30370.e: In 1959 two Social Democrats, including Hans-Peter Tschudi, were elected. This gave the SP two seats for the first time.
30370.m: Since 1959 the SP has had two Federal Council seats.

30371.q: What is the principle called that all the big parties sit in government together?
30371.e: In concordance, the main parties share responsibility for government. The magic formula counted as the best-known form of this concordance.
30371.m: Concordance means the big parties govern together.

30372.q: Which event ended the 1959 magic formula in 2003?
a: The election of Christoph Blocher to the Federal Council
The introduction of women's right to vote
The resignation of all SP Federal Councillors
The founding of the canton of Jura
30372.e: In 2003 Christoph Blocher (SVP) was elected and Ruth Metzler (CVP) voted out. From then on the SVP had two seats and the CVP only one.
30372.m: The old magic formula ended with Blocher's election in 2003.

30373.q: What took place all over Switzerland on 14 June 1991?
a: The opening of the Federal Palace
The founding of the first women's party
30373.e: On 14 June 1991 hundreds of thousands of women stopped work. They demanded that equality between women and men finally be put into practice.
30373.m: On 14 June 1991 women went on strike for equality.

30374.q: What were foreign workers called who were only allowed to work in Switzerland for a few months a year?
30374.e: Seasonal workers got a permit for one season, for example in building, hotels and restaurants, or farming. After that they had to leave Switzerland.
30374.m: Seasonal workers only worked in Switzerland during one season.

30375.q: Which country did most seasonal workers come from in the 1950s and 1960s?
30375.e: In 1948 Switzerland signed a recruitment agreement with Italy. In the post-war years especially many workers came from Italy, later also from Spain, Portugal and Yugoslavia.
30375.m: Most of the early seasonal workers came from Italy.

30376.q: Which Swiss writer wrote the sentence “We asked for workers, and human beings came”?
30376.e: Max Frisch wrote the famous sentence in 1965 in the foreword to a book about Italian workers. He criticised the fact that people were seen only as workers.
30376.m: Max Frisch reminded people that guest workers are human beings.

30377.q: In which sectors did seasonal workers work especially often?
a: Watch sales and the stock exchange
30377.e: These sectors need many workers depending on the season. On building sites and in hotels there was especially a lot of work in summer.
30377.m: Seasonal workers often worked on building sites and in hotels.

30378.q: In which year did Switzerland vote on the Schwarzenbach initiative?
30378.e: The vote took place on 7 June 1970. At that time only men were allowed to vote.
30378.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative went to the vote in 1970.

30379.q: What did the Schwarzenbach initiative of 1970 want to limit?
30379.e: James Schwarzenbach's initiative wanted to cut the proportion of foreigners in almost all cantons to no more than 10 per cent. The people and the cantons rejected it.
30379.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative wanted fewer foreigners in Switzerland.

30381.q: What stood out particularly in the vote on the Schwarzenbach initiative?
a: That it took place twice on the same day
30381.e: Turnout reached its highest level since 1947. This shows how strongly the issue moved the population.
30381.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative got very many voters to the polls.

30382.q: In which year did the secret files scandal (Fichenskandal) come to light?
30382.e: At the end of 1989 a parliamentary inquiry published its report. It had discovered that the state had kept watch on hundreds of thousands of people.
30382.m: The secret files scandal became known in 1989.

a: An index card with notes about a person
30383.e: Fiche is the French word for index card. On the fiches, the police noted observations about people and organisations.
30383.m: A fiche is an index card with surveillance notes.

30384.q: Roughly how many fiches had been created by 1990?
30384.e: By 1990 the federal government and the cantons had created about 900,000 fiches. They covered over 700,000 people and organisations.

30385.q: What could many people ask for after the secret files scandal?
a: Money from the state for each fiche
30385.e: Over 300,000 people wanted to know what the state had noted about them. They could look at their fiche, often with parts blacked out.
30385.m: After the scandal you could see your own fiche.

30386.q: Which resignation led to the inquiry in which the secret files scandal came to light?
a: The resignation of Federal Councillor Elisabeth Kopp
The resignation of Federal Councillor Walther Stampfli
The resignation of the whole government
The resignation of the head of Swissair
30386.e: Elisabeth Kopp resigned because she had warned her husband about an investigation. The parliamentary inquiry then examined the Justice Department and came across the fiches.
30386.m: The Kopp affair led to the discovery of the fiches.

30387.q: During which period were most people put on file because communists were feared?
30387.e: In the Cold War, anything that looked like left-wing politics counted as suspicious. Trade unionists, peace activists and foreigners, for example, were watched.
30387.m: The fiches came about mainly out of fear of communism.

30388.q: What happened in Bern on 3 March 1990?
a: A big demonstration against the snooping state
The election of the first woman Federal Councillor
The signing of the bilateral agreements
30388.e: About 30,000 people demonstrated in Bern against the surveillance. Afterwards many asked to see their own fiche.
30388.m: In 1990 thousands protested in Bern against the snooping state.

30389.q: What does the abbreviation EEA stand for?
30389.e: EEA stands for European Economic Area. It links the EU's single market with some EFTA states.
30389.m: EEA stands for European Economic Area.

30390.q: On which day did Switzerland reject joining the EEA?
30390.e: On 6 December 1992 the people and the cantons said no to the EEA. The day counts among the most important in recent Swiss history.
30390.m: On 6 December 1992 Switzerland said no to the EEA.

30391.q: Which politician led the campaign against joining the EEA?
30391.e: Christoph Blocher, SVP National Councillor from Zurich, became the best-known opponent. The vote made him famous across the country.
30391.m: Christoph Blocher led the opposition to the EEA.

30392.q: How many agreements make up the Bilateral Agreements I?
30392.e: The Bilateral Agreements I consist of seven agreements, for example on the free movement of persons, land transport and research. They were signed in 1999.
30392.m: The Bilateral Agreements I consist of seven agreements.

30393.q: How did the people decide on the Bilateral Agreements I in 2000?
a: They were not allowed to vote
30393.e: On 21 May 2000 about 67 per cent said yes to the Bilateral Agreements I. They came into force in 2002.
30393.m: The people clearly accepted the Bilateral Agreements I in 2000.

30394.q: What does the so-called guillotine clause of the Bilateral Agreements I do?
a: If one agreement ends, all seven end
Each agreement expires after one year
The EU may change Swiss laws
Only one agreement applies for ever
30394.e: The seven agreements are linked together. If one side cancels one of them, the others also become invalid.
30394.m: The guillotine clause links all the Bilateral Agreements I together.

30395.q: Which agreement of the Bilateral Agreements I allows EU citizens to work and live in Switzerland?
a: The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons
30395.e: Free movement of persons allows citizens of Switzerland and the EU to live and work in each other's territory. It is the best known of the seven agreements.
30395.m: Free movement of persons allows people to live and work freely.

30396.q: Which popular initiative of 2014 called the free movement of persons into question?
30396.e: On 9 February 2014 the people narrowly accepted the mass immigration initiative. It demanded that Switzerland control immigration itself.
30396.m: The mass immigration initiative of 2014 concerned immigration.

30397.q: What did the Federal Council decide about the framework agreement with the EU in May 2021?
a: It signed the agreement at once
It cancelled all the bilateral agreements
30397.e: In May 2021 the Federal Council ended the negotiations on the institutional framework agreement. After that, new talks began on a package of treaties.
30397.m: In 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations on the framework agreement.

30398.q: On which day did all Swissair planes stay on the ground?
30398.e: On 2 October 2001 Swissair had to stop all its flights. This event is called the grounding.
30398.m: The Swissair grounding happened on 2 October 2001.

30399.q: Why could the Swissair planes no longer take off on 2 October 2001?
a: The company could no longer pay for fuel
The pilots went on strike for more pay
30399.e: Swissair had huge debts and no money left. Suppliers demanded cash payment and stopped refuelling the planes.
30399.m: Swissair ran out of money in 2001.

30400.q: What did Swissair buy in large numbers before the grounding?
30400.e: Swissair bought shares in many airlines, most of them small. These made heavy losses and helped cause the collapse.
30400.m: Expensive purchases of other airlines drove Swissair into debt.

30401.q: Which nickname showed how rich Swissair was in the 1980s?
30401.e: Swissair had so much money in reserve that people called it the “flying bank”. That made the shock of the grounding all the greater.
30401.m: Swissair used to be seen as a flying bank.

30402.q: Which group took over the airline Swiss in 2005?
30402.e: The German airline Lufthansa took over Swiss from 2005. But Swiss still flies under its own name.
30402.m: Swiss has belonged to Lufthansa since 2005.

30403.q: What is the assembly called in which all UN members are represented?
30403.e: In the General Assembly every member has one vote. It admitted Switzerland in New York in 2002.
30403.m: In the UN General Assembly every country has one vote.

30404.q: What does the Schengen Agreement abolish at the borders?
a: The need to have a passport
30404.e: In the Schengen Area, people are no longer systematically checked at the internal borders. But spot checks are still possible.
30404.m: Schengen abolishes systematic checks on people at the borders.

30405.q: How did the Swiss people vote on joining Schengen in 2005?
30405.e: On 5 June 2005, 54.6 per cent voted yes to Schengen and Dublin. The agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements II.

30406.q: Do you still need to carry a passport or identity card when travelling in the Schengen Area?
a: Yes, because checks are still possible
No, ID documents have been abolished
30406.e: There are no longer systematic checks at the borders, but there are still spot checks. That is why you always need a valid ID.
30406.m: You need ID even in the Schengen Area.

30407.q: Why are there still customs checks at the Swiss border despite Schengen?
a: Because Switzerland is not part of the EU customs union
Because Schengen only applies to aeroplanes
Because customs duties must be in the constitution
30407.e: Schengen only concerns checks on people. As Switzerland is not in the EU customs union, goods are still checked.
30407.m: Despite Schengen, customs still check goods.

30408.q: Where does the Schengen Agreement get its name from?
30408.e: The agreement was signed in 1985 in the wine-growing village of Schengen in Luxembourg. The village lies near the borders with Germany and France.
30408.m: Schengen is a village in Luxembourg.

30409.q: What is the Dublin Agreement, which applies together with Schengen, about?
a: Which country is responsible for asylum applications
30409.e: Dublin sets out which country has to examine an asylum application. Usually it is the country a person entered first.
30409.m: Dublin decides who is responsible for asylum applications.

30410.q: What is the shared police search database of the Schengen countries called?
30410.e: In the Schengen Information System (SIS), police forces share information on wanted people and objects. It replaces part of the old border checks.
30410.m: The Schengen Information System helps the police find wanted people.

30411.e: Expo.02 was Switzerland’s sixth national exhibition. It took place in 2002.

30412.q: In which region did Expo.02 take place?
30412.e: Expo.02 took place around Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Murten. This area is called the Three Lakes region.
30412.m: Expo.02 took place in the Three Lakes region.

30413.q: What were the exhibition sites of Expo.02 called?
30413.e: The four exhibition sites on the lake shores were called Arteplages. They were in Biel, Neuchâtel, Murten and Yverdon-les-Bains; there was also a floating Arteplage of the canton of Jura.
30413.m: The exhibition sites of Expo.02 were called Arteplages.

30414.q: Which town was NOT the site of an Arteplage at Expo.02?
30414.e: The Arteplages were in Biel, Neuchâtel, Murten and Yverdon-les-Bains. Bern was not an exhibition site.
30414.m: Bern had no Arteplage at Expo.02.

30415.q: What was the “Monolith” in Lake Murten at Expo.02?
30415.e: The Monolith was a large, rusty steel cube floating in Lake Murten. It was one of the best-known structures of Expo.02.
30415.m: The Monolith was a steel cube in Lake Murten.

30416.q: Under which name was the national exhibition originally planned?
30416.e: The exhibition was first planned for 2001. Because of problems with the planning, it was postponed by a year.
30416.m: Expo.02 was originally going to be called Expo.01.

30417.q: Roughly how many visits did Expo.02 count?
30417.e: Expo.02 counted 10.3 million visits. The record day was the last day of the exhibition, 20 October 2002.
30417.m: Expo.02 had around ten million visits.

30418.q: Roughly how long is the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
30418.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long. That makes it the longest railway tunnel in the world.
30418.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long.

30419.q: Which two cantons does the Gotthard Base Tunnel connect?
30419.e: The north portal is in Erstfeld in the canton of Uri, the south portal in Bodio in Ticino.
30419.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel connects Uri and Ticino.

30420.q: Which major rail project does the Gotthard Base Tunnel belong to?
30420.e: NRLA stands for New Rail Link through the Alps (in German NEAT). It also includes the Lötschberg and Ceneri base tunnels.
30420.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is the centrepiece of the NRLA.

30421.q: How many tubes does the Gotthard Base Tunnel have?
a: Two tubes with one track each
Three tubes with two tracks each
Four tubes with one track each
30421.e: The tunnel has two single-track tubes about 40 metres apart. They are linked at regular intervals by cross-passages.
30421.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel has two single-track tubes.

30422.q: What was mainly used to dig the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
30422.e: Big tunnel boring machines ate their way through the rock. In October 2010 one of them broke through the last metres of rock.
30422.m: The base tunnel was built with tunnel boring machines.

30423.q: What is the Gotthard Base Tunnel mainly meant to achieve?
a: More freight by rail instead of by road
30423.e: Flat base tunnels allow long, heavy freight trains. This is meant to move more freight through the Alps onto the railway.
30423.m: The base tunnel moves freight from road to rail.

30424.q: Where, for example, can you find your AHV (old-age insurance) number?
30424.e: Everyone in Switzerland has an AHV number, children too. It is printed, for example, on the health insurance card.
30424.m: The AHV number is on the health insurance card.

30425.q: What did the “AHV 21” reform change about the retirement age for women?
a: It rises step by step from 64 to 65
30425.e: With AHV 21, the retirement age for women is being raised step by step to 65. That makes it the same as for men.
30425.m: With AHV 21, women and men receive their pension at 65.

30426.q: Whom does the invalidity insurance (IV) help?
a: People who cannot work fully because of illness or disability
30426.e: The IV has existed since 1960. It supports people who can no longer work fully because of an illness or disability.
30426.m: The IV helps people with an illness or disability.

30427.q: Do all pensioners receive the same AHV pension?
a: No, the highest is twice as much as the lowest
Yes, everyone gets exactly the same
No, rich people get ten times more
No, only men get a pension
30427.e: The pension depends on income and years of contributions. But the maximum pension is only twice as high as the minimum pension.
30427.m: The largest AHV pension is twice as high as the smallest.

30428.q: What do pensioners receive if their AHV pension is not enough to live on?
a: A tax bonus from the municipality
30428.e: Supplementary benefits help when pension and income do not cover the cost of living. They have been paid since 1966.
30428.m: Supplementary benefits help when the pension is not enough.

30429.q: What is the money that working people pay into the AHV today used for?
a: For each person’s own savings account
30429.e: The AHV passes the money straight on: the contributions of working people pay the pensions of today’s retired people.
30429.m: Working people’s contributions pay today’s AHV pensions.

30430.q: Roughly how long did the magic formula of 1959 last?
30430.e: The magic formula for sharing the Federal Council seats lasted from 1959 to 2003, so 44 years. Then the SVP got a second seat.
30430.m: The magic formula lasted over 40 years.

30431.q: Since 1971, what has the BGB, which had a Federal Council seat under the magic formula, been called?
30431.e: In 1971 the Farmers’, Traders’ and Citizens’ Party (BGB) merged with other parties to form the Swiss People’s Party. Since then it has been called the SVP.
30431.m: In 1971 the BGB became the SVP.

30433.q: What did the women in the Valais village of Unterbäch do in 1957?
a: They took part in a vote as a symbolic act
They elected a female Federal Councillor
They went on strike for a week
30433.e: In 1957 the municipality let the women take part in a federal vote. Their votes did not officially count, but the action became famous.
30433.m: In Unterbäch in 1957, women voted for the first time as a symbolic act.

30434.q: What did the voters accept on 14 June 1981?
a: The equality article in the constitution
30434.e: Since 1981 the Federal Constitution has stated that men and women have equal rights. It also requires equal pay for work of equal value.
30434.m: Since 1981 equality has been part of the constitution.

30435.q: What was the big demonstration for women’s suffrage on 1 March 1969 called?
30435.e: In 1969 around 5,000 women and men marched to the Federal Palace. The demonstration increased the pressure to introduce women’s suffrage quickly.
30435.m: The March on Bern in 1969 demanded votes for women.

30436.q: Since when have women been able to be elected to the National Council?
30436.e: With women’s suffrage in 1971, women could also be elected. In the same year, the first female National Councillors entered the Federal Palace.
30436.m: Women have sat in the National Council since 1971.

30437.q: Who was allowed to vote at federal level in Switzerland before 1971?
30437.e: Until 1971 only men had the right to vote and be elected at federal level. Women fought for it for decades.
30437.m: Before 1971 only men were allowed to vote.

30438.q: Which neighbouring country introduced women’s suffrage only in 1984, even later than Switzerland?
30438.e: Liechtenstein introduced women’s suffrage in 1984, the last country in Europe to do so. Switzerland in 1971 was also one of the last.
30438.m: Liechtenstein only introduced votes for women in 1984.

30439.q: In which year did the second big women’s strike take place in Switzerland?
30439.e: On 14 June 2019 hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets. As in the first women’s strike, they demanded real equality, for example in pay.
30439.m: The second big women’s strike took place in 2019.

30440.q: Which church principality did the Jura region belong to until the French Revolution?
30440.e: For centuries the Jura was part of the Prince-Bishopric of Basel. The Bishop of Basel ruled the area as a worldly prince.
30440.m: The Jura used to belong to the Prince-Bishopric of Basel.

30441.q: Why did the Bishop of Basel leave the city of Basel after the Reformation and move to the Jura?
a: Because the climate was better in the Jura
30441.e: Basel became Protestant in 1529. The Catholic bishop moved to Porrentruy and lived in the castle there.
30441.m: After the Reformation, the prince-bishops of Basel lived in Porrentruy.

30442.q: Which breed of horse comes from the canton of Jura?
30442.e: The Franches-Montagnes is considered the last native Swiss horse breed. It is named after the Franches-Montagnes area (Freiberge in German).
30442.m: The Franches-Montagnes is a horse from the Jura.

30443.q: What is the centre of attention every year at the Marché-Concours in Saignelégier?
30443.e: At the Marché-Concours in August, Franches-Montagnes horses are shown and there are horse races. It is a big festival of the Franches-Montagnes region.
30443.m: The Marché-Concours is the horse festival in Saignelégier.

30444.q: Which language does the large majority speak in the canton of Jura?
30444.e: The canton of Jura is French-speaking. Only the small municipality of Ederswiler is German-speaking.
30444.m: People in the canton of Jura speak French.

30445.q: What did the Jura separatists want?
30445.e: The separatists wanted to separate the northern Jura from the canton of Bern. Their youth group, the Béliers, drew attention with their actions. The canton of Jura was created in 1979.
30445.m: The separatists fought for a separate canton of Jura.

30446.q: Which river flows through the little town of Saint-Ursanne in the canton of Jura?
30446.e: In the Jura, the Doubs makes a big loop through Switzerland. The bridge over the Doubs at Saint-Ursanne is a popular photo spot.

30447.q: What were seasonal workers (Saisonniers) not allowed to do in Switzerland?
a: Bring their families to live with them
30447.e: Seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their families. Husbands, wives and children usually had to stay in their home country.
30447.m: Seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their families to Switzerland.

30448.q: What did many children of seasonal workers who came to Switzerland secretly have to go through?
a: They lived in hiding and could not be noticed
They had to serve in the army
They went to special seasonal workers’ schools
They got a Swiss passport straight away
30448.e: Because families were not allowed to join the workers, thousands of children lived hidden in flats. Often they could neither play outside nor go to school.
30448.m: Many children of seasonal workers lived in hiding.

30449.q: What did seasonal workers often have to do when entering Switzerland?
30449.e: Seasonal workers were given a medical examination at the border. Anyone considered ill was sent back.
30449.m: Seasonal workers were medically examined at the border.

30451.q: Which slogan did the supporters of the Schwarzenbach initiative use?
30451.e: The supporters spoke of Switzerland being “overrun by foreigners” (“Überfremdung”). The word had a strong influence on politics in the 1960s and 1970s.

30452.q: What did business and the Federal Council fear if the Schwarzenbach initiative were accepted?
a: That many businesses would have to close
That wages would double at once
That Switzerland would have to join the EU
That the AHV would be abolished
30452.e: Without foreign workers, many companies could not have carried on. People feared that businesses would close and jobs would be lost.
30452.m: Business feared that companies would have to close.

30453.q: Which part of the country mostly voted for the EEA in 1992?
30453.e: Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Jura and Fribourg said yes, as did the two Basels. The rest of German-speaking Switzerland and Ticino said no.
30453.m: In the EEA vote, it was mainly French-speaking Switzerland that said yes.

30454.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland is in the EEA but not in the EU?
30454.e: Liechtenstein joined the EEA in 1995 but is not an EU member. Switzerland is in neither the EEA nor the EU.
30454.m: Liechtenstein is in the EEA, Switzerland is not.

30455.q: After the no to the EEA, how does Switzerland mainly organise its relations with the EU?
a: As a member of the EU
With the euro as its currency
30455.e: After the no in 1992, Switzerland made separate agreements with the EU, the Bilaterals. They cover things such as trade and travel.
30455.m: Switzerland organises its relations with the EU through bilateral agreements.

30456.q: What was unusually high in the EEA vote of 1992?
30456.e: Almost 79 per cent of those entitled to vote took part. That has rarely happened in a vote.
30456.m: Almost 79 per cent took part in the EEA vote.

30457.q: With whom did Switzerland make the Bilateral Agreements?
30457.e: The Bilateral Agreements set out relations between Switzerland and the EU. There are the Bilaterals I from 1999 and the Bilaterals II from 2004.
30457.m: The Bilaterals are agreements between Switzerland and the EU.

30458.q: What is the title of the person who runs the UN’s administration?
30458.e: The Secretary-General runs the UN’s administration and represents it around the world.
30458.m: The UN is led by a Secretary-General.

30459.q: Roughly how many countries are members of the UN?
30459.e: Today 193 countries belong to the UN. Switzerland has been a member since 2002.
30459.m: Almost every country in the world is in the UN.

30460.q: In which city does the UN have its headquarters?
30460.e: The headquarters of the United Nations is in New York. The General Assembly also meets there.
30460.m: The UN has its headquarters in New York.

30461.q: Which organisation that came before the UN had Switzerland already joined in 1920?
30461.e: Switzerland joined the League of Nations in 1920 after a referendum. Its headquarters were in Geneva.
30461.m: Switzerland was in the League of Nations from 1920.

30462.q: Which UN body was founded in 2006 and meets in Geneva?
30462.e: The UN Human Rights Council was created in 2006 and is based in Geneva. Switzerland had campaigned hard for it.
30462.m: The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva.

30463.q: What could many travellers not do on the day of the Swissair grounding?
a: Take off on the flight they had booked
30463.e: All Swissair planes stayed on the ground. Thousands of passengers were stuck at airports all over the world.
30463.m: During the grounding, all Swissair flights were cancelled.

30464.q: Which regional airline did the new Swiss build on in 2002?
30464.e: Crossair from Basel was a subsidiary of Swissair. It was renamed and took over Swissair’s most important routes.

30465.q: Which other NRLA base tunnel opened as early as 2007?
30465.e: The Lötschberg Base Tunnel between Frutigen and Raron went into service in 2007. It was the first completed base tunnel of the NRLA.
30465.m: The Lötschberg Base Tunnel opened in 2007.

30467.q: In which country was Lucy's skeleton found in 1974?
30467.e: A team led by Donald Johanson found Lucy near Hadar in the Afar region of Ethiopia. Kenya, South Africa and Tanzania are also important countries for finds of early human ancestors.

30468.q: Where does the name “Lucy” for the famous fossil come from?
a: From the name of the woman who found it
30468.e: On the evening after the find, the Beatles song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds” was playing in the camp. That gave the skeleton its nickname.
30468.m: Lucy was named after a Beatles song.

30469.q: What name was given to the collection of bones from several individuals of Australopithecus afarensis found near Hadar in 1975?
30469.e: At site AL 333 there were bones from at least 13 individuals, adults and children. Experts call the find the “First Family”.
30469.m: The First Family shows a whole group of Australopithecus afarensis.

30470.q: Where is the original Lucy kept?
a: In the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa
In the Natural History Museum in London
In the Musée de l'Homme in Paris
In the Smithsonian museum in Washington
30470.e: The original belongs to Ethiopia and is kept in the National Museum in Addis Ababa. Usually a cast is on display; the original toured the USA from 2007 to 2013.
30470.m: Lucy is kept in the National Museum in Addis Ababa.

30471.q: Which way of moving does the pelvis and leg skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis mainly show?
a: Swinging from branches like a gibbon
30471.e: The pelvis, thigh bone and knee joint are adapted to walking on two legs. Long arms and curved fingers also suggest climbing in trees.
30471.m: Australopithecus afarensis already walked upright on two legs.

30472.q: Roughly how large was the brain volume of Australopithecus afarensis?
30472.e: At about 400 to 500 cm³, the brain was hardly bigger than a chimpanzee's. So walking upright developed before the brain grew much larger.
30472.m: Walking upright came before the large brain.

30473.q: Which find of Australopithecus afarensis was discovered in Dikika (Ethiopia) in 2000?
a: The skeleton of a child about three years old
30473.e: The Dikika child, also called “Selam”, is about 3.3 million years old. It is one of the most complete child skeletons of an early human ancestor.
30473.m: Selam is the famous child of the species Australopithecus afarensis.

30474.q: Roughly what percentage of Lucy's skeleton has survived?
30474.e: Several hundred bone fragments of Lucy were found, making up about 40 per cent of a skeleton. For such an old fossil, that is an exceptional amount.
30474.m: About 40 per cent of Lucy's skeleton has survived.

30475.q: What does the species name “Homo habilis” mean?
30475.e: The scientists who first described it thought the species had made the oldest stone tools. “Habilis” is Latin and means skilful or handy.

30476.q: In which region of Africa have most fossils of Homo habilis been found?
30476.e: The most important finds come from Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania and from Koobi Fora in Kenya. There are also some finds from South Africa.
30476.m: Homo habilis is known mainly from East Africa.

30477.q: Roughly how many years ago did Homo habilis live?
30477.e: Homo habilis is one of the earliest members of the genus Homo. In East Africa it partly lived at the same time as other early humans.
30477.m: Homo habilis lived over 1.5 million years ago.

30478.q: Roughly how big was the brain of Homo habilis compared with that of a modern human?
a: About a tenth of the size
30478.e: Homo habilis had a brain volume of about 550 to 700 cm³, while modern humans have about 1350 cm³. That is still more than the australopithecines had.
30478.m: The brain of Homo habilis was about half the size of ours.

30479.q: Which tool culture is traditionally linked with Homo habilis?
30479.e: The Oldowan culture includes simple pebble tools and flakes. For a long time it was credited to Homo habilis; the Acheulean with hand axes came later.
30479.m: The simple Oldowan pebble tools are considered the tools of Homo habilis.

30480.q: Why was Homo habilis placed in the genus Homo and not with Australopithecus in 1964?
a: Because of the larger brain and the link with stone tools
Because remains of clothing were found
Because it was almost two metres tall
30480.e: The researchers saw a larger brain than in Australopithecus and thought the species had made stone tools. The australopithecines already walked upright too.
30480.m: Brain size and tools made Homo habilis a Homo.

30481.q: What debate is there among researchers about Homo habilis?
a: Whether the species really belongs to Australopithecus
Whether it died out in Europe
30481.e: Because of its small body, long arms and small brain, some researchers suggest classifying the species as Australopithecus habilis. Which genus it belongs to is still disputed today.
30481.m: The place of Homo habilis in the genus Homo is disputed.

30482.q: What did the hand bones of OH 7 show, according to John Napier?
a: A hand with a precision grip
A hand used only for knuckle-walking
30482.e: Napier interpreted the hand as able to make a precision grip between thumb and fingers. This supported the idea that this species made tools.
30482.m: The hand of Homo habilis could grip finely.

30483.q: Who found the first fossils on Java in 1891 that are now counted as Homo erectus?
30483.e: The Dutch doctor Eugène Dubois found a skullcap and later a thigh bone near Trinil. At first he called the species Pithecanthropus erectus.

30484.q: Which researcher predicted a missing link between ape and human called “Pithecanthropus” even before the find on Java?
30484.e: The German zoologist Ernst Haeckel coined the name “Pithecanthropus” for a supposed intermediate form. Dubois then searched for it specifically in South-East Asia.
30484.m: Ernst Haeckel invented the name Pithecanthropus.

30485.q: What happened to the original fossils of Peking Man in 1941?
a: They were put on display in Beijing
30485.e: Because of the war, the bones were to be taken to the USA, but they vanished without a trace. Today only casts and descriptions remain.
30485.m: The originals of Peking Man have been missing since 1941.

30486.q: Where have the oldest human fossils outside Africa found so far, about 1.8 million years old, been discovered?
30486.e: The skulls from Dmanisi in the Caucasus are about 1.8 million years old. They show that early forms of Homo left Africa very early.
30486.m: Dmanisi in Georgia proves the early spread of humans out of Africa.

30487.q: What is the early African form of Homo erectus, often listed as a separate species, called?
30487.e: Many researchers call the early African finds Homo ergaster, “working man”. Others simply count them as Homo erectus in the broader sense.
30487.m: Homo ergaster is considered the African form of Homo erectus.

30488.q: Which innovation is often linked with Homo erectus?
30488.e: The first hand axes appear with Homo erectus about 1.7 million years ago. This tool culture is called the Acheulean.
30488.m: Homo erectus was one of the first to make hand axes.

30489.q: In the view of many researchers, what do the finds of Peking Man at Zhoukoudian prove?
30489.e: Ash and burnt bones were found at Zhoukoudian. However, whether the people there controlled fire themselves is still debated today.
30489.m: Homo erectus probably already used fire.

30490.q: Which body proportions characterise Homo erectus compared with the australopithecines?
a: Short legs and very long arms
A grasping foot with a toe sticking out
30490.e: Homo erectus already had largely modern body proportions with long legs. This made it a good long-distance runner and walker.
30490.m: With its long legs, Homo erectus was a good endurance runner.

30492.q: Which country does the island of Flores, where Homo floresiensis lived, belong to?
30492.e: Flores is one of the Lesser Sunda Islands in Indonesia. Even during the Ice Age, the island was separated from the mainland by deep sea.
30492.m: Homo floresiensis lived on Flores in Indonesia.

30493.q: In which cave was the skeleton LB1 of Homo floresiensis found?
30493.e: An Indonesian-Australian team found LB1 in Liang Bua in 2003. The description was published in the journal “Nature” in 2004.
30493.m: The hobbit skeleton LB1 comes from the Liang Bua cave.

30494.q: Roughly how tall was the individual LB1?
30494.e: LB1 was an adult woman about 1.06 metres tall. That made her smaller than most children of primary school age today.
30494.m: The hobbit of Flores was only just over a metre tall.

30495.q: Which explanation is often suggested for the small size of Homo floresiensis?
30495.e: On islands with little food, large animal species often become smaller over generations. The dwarf elephant Stegodon on Flores also shows this effect.
30495.m: Island dwarfism can explain the hobbit's small size.

30496.q: According to today's dating, until roughly when did Homo floresiensis live?
30496.e: The first dates suggested only 12,000 years. Newer studies show that the species disappeared about 50,000 years ago, roughly when modern humans reached the region.
30496.m: Homo floresiensis disappeared about 50,000 years ago.

30497.q: According to the finds at Liang Bua, which animals did Homo floresiensis hunt or butcher, among others?
a: Dwarf elephants of the genus Stegodon
30497.e: Many bones of young Stegodon animals with marks from stone tools were found at Liang Bua. There were no mammoths or reindeer on Flores.
30497.m: The hobbit used dwarf elephants as food.

30498.q: Which other small human species was described on an island in the Philippines in 2019?
30498.e: Homo luzonensis was found in Callao Cave on Luzon. Like Homo floresiensis, it shows that separate human forms developed on islands in South-East Asia.
30498.m: Besides the hobbit, there was another small human species on Luzon.

30499.q: In which year was the finger bone found in Denisova Cave whose DNA revealed a new form of human?
30499.e: Russian archaeologists found the tiny piece of finger bone in 2008. The DNA results were only published afterwards.
30499.m: The Denisova finger bone came to light in 2008.

30500.q: How was Denisovan man recognised as a separate form of human in 2010?
30500.e: The DNA from a finger bone was clearly different from that of Neanderthals and modern humans. It was the first form of human to become known mainly through its genome.
30500.m: Denisovans were discovered through their genome.

30501.q: According to a 2018 study, what was the ancestry of the girl “Denny” (Denisova 11)?
30501.e: Genome analysis of a bone fragment showed that the girl was a first-generation descendant of a mix. Her mother was a Neanderthal and her father a Denisovan.
30501.m: Denny was the child of a Neanderthal woman and a Denisovan man.

30502.q: In which adaptation of many Tibetans does a variant of the EPAS1 gene, probably inherited from Denisovans, play a part?
a: Living at high altitude with little oxygen
30502.e: A 2014 study showed that a variant of the EPAS1 gene common among Tibetans is very similar to the Denisovan genome. It helps people cope with the low oxygen levels in the highlands.
30502.m: A Denisovan inheritance helps Tibetans live in the highlands.

30503.q: According to the finds, which forms of human lived in Denisova Cave at different times?
30503.e: Bones and DNA from the sediments show that the cave was used by different forms of human over a long period.
30503.m: Several forms of human lived in Denisova Cave.

30504.q: Who is Denisova Cave named after?
30504.e: According to tradition, a hermit named Denis (Dionisy) lived in the cave in the 18th century. The cave, and later the type of human, bear his name.
30504.m: Denisova Cave owes its name to a hermit.

30505.q: How was the Xiahe jawbone from the Tibetan Plateau assigned to the Denisovans in 2019?
a: Through ancient proteins from the teeth
30505.e: No DNA had survived in the jawbone, but proteins from the tooth enamel had. Their analysis pointed to the Denisovans; the jaw is at least 160,000 years old.
30505.m: Ancient proteins can also reveal which form of human a fossil belongs to.

30506.q: Which well-known skull from China was assigned to the Denisovans in 2025 with the help of proteins and DNA?
30506.e: In 2025, researchers led by Qiaomei Fu obtained proteins and mitochondrial DNA from the Harbin skull. This gave scientists an almost complete Denisovan skull for the first time.
30506.m: The Harbin skull shows what a Denisovan looked like.

30507.q: What does the Out of Africa theory say about the origin of modern humans?
a: Homo sapiens arose in Africa and spread out from there
Homo sapiens arose on all continents at the same time
Homo sapiens descends directly from Peking Man
30507.e: According to this theory, modern humans developed in Africa and then settled the other continents. In doing so, they largely replaced the forms of human living there.

30508.q: What is the rival hypothesis called, according to which Homo sapiens developed from Homo erectus in several regions of the world in parallel?
30508.e: The multiregional hypothesis was put forward mainly by Milford Wolpoff. Genetic data today mostly support an African origin with some mixing.
30508.m: The multiregional hypothesis is the main counter-theory to Out of Africa.

30509.q: In which region of Africa were the Omo skulls, some of the oldest fossils of Homo sapiens, found?
a: In South Africa at the Cape
30509.e: The skulls Omo I and Omo II come from the Omo River in Ethiopia and are about 230,000 years old. They are among the oldest evidence of modern humans.
30509.m: East Africa is an important region for early Homo sapiens finds.

30510.q: What does the upper jaw from Misliya Cave in Israel, about 180,000 years old, prove?
a: An early venture of Homo sapiens out of Africa
The arrival of Homo erectus in Europe
30510.e: The jaw belongs to Homo sapiens and is much older than the great migration. However, such early ventures left hardly any traces in today's genome.
30510.m: Homo sapiens made early ventures into the Levant.

30511.q: Which other English term is also used for the Out of Africa theory?
30511.e: “Recent African Origin” stresses that modern humans arose in Africa only a relatively short time ago. Multiregional Evolution, on the other hand, is the opposing hypothesis.
30511.m: Out of Africa is also called Recent African Origin.

30512.q: According to current knowledge, roughly when did the ancestors of most of today's non-Africans leave Africa?
30512.e: Genetic data show a large migration about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. Earlier ventures, for example into the Levant, left hardly any traces in today's genome.
30512.m: The great migration out of Africa took place about 60,000 years ago.

30513.q: Across which strait might modern humans have reached Arabia from Africa on the so-called southern route?
30513.e: The Bab al-Mandab strait separates the Horn of Africa from Yemen. When sea levels were low during the Ice Ages, it was much narrower.
30513.m: The southern route led to Arabia via Bab al-Mandab.

30514.q: What do experts mean by “Out of Africa I”?
a: The first spread of Homo erectus out of Africa
30514.e: “Out of Africa I” means the spread of early forms of Homo about 2 million years ago. “Out of Africa II” refers to the later spread of Homo sapiens.
30514.m: Out of Africa I concerns Homo erectus, Out of Africa II concerns Homo sapiens.

30515.q: According to current knowledge, which continent was one of the last to be settled by Homo sapiens?
30515.e: Australia was reached at least 50,000 years ago and Europe over 40,000 years ago. People only came to the Americas about 20,000 to 15,000 years ago via Beringia.
30515.m: The Americas were settled late via the Beringia land bridge.

30517.q: In which country is the site where the Turkana Boy was found?
30517.e: The Nariokotome site lies west of Lake Turkana in northern Kenya. That is where the name Turkana Boy comes from.
30517.m: The Turkana Boy comes from northern Kenya.

30519.q: Which species is the Turkana Boy assigned to?
30519.e: The skeleton shows typical features of Homo erectus in the broader sense. Those who separate out the African finds call the species Homo ergaster.
30519.m: The Turkana Boy belongs to Homo erectus in the broader sense.

30520.q: What does the build of the Turkana Boy show about Homo erectus?
a: It had long legs and was a good endurance runner
It still walked on all fours
It was hardly bigger than a chimpanzee
30520.e: Long legs and a slim body resemble those of modern people in hot regions. Homo erectus was well adapted to walking and running in the open savannah.
30520.m: Homo erectus was a good runner.

30521.q: According to today's analysis of his teeth, roughly how old was the Turkana Boy when he died?
30521.e: He used to be estimated at 11 to 13 years old. Microscopic studies of tooth development showed that he grew faster than children today and was only about 8 to 9 years old.
30521.m: The Turkana Boy was a child of about eight.

30522.q: What was Lake Turkana called in colonial times?
30522.e: In 1888, the Austro-Hungarian explorer Count Teleki named the lake after Crown Prince Rudolf. After Kenya's independence, it was renamed Lake Turkana.
30522.m: Lake Turkana used to be called Lake Rudolf.

30523.q: Roughly how tall was the Turkana Boy when he died?
30523.e: Older estimates were about 1.6 metres, newer ones more like 1.4 to 1.5 metres. His slim body with long legs already resembled that of modern people in hot regions.
30523.m: The Turkana Boy was already quite tall for his age.

30524.q: During what activity did researchers in Laetoli find the first fossil animal tracks by chance in 1976?
a: During a playful fight with dried elephant dung
30524.e: During the fight, Andrew Hill dodged a lump of dung, fell over and noticed prints in the ground. That is how the search for more tracks began.
30524.m: The Laetoli tracks were discovered by chance.

30525.q: Which special tracks were discovered at Laetoli in Tanzania in 1978?
30525.e: Footprints about 3.6 million years old were preserved in hardened volcanic ash. They show that human ancestors already walked upright on two legs.
30525.m: The Laetoli tracks show early upright walking.

30526.q: From how many individuals do the tracks at site G in Laetoli come?
30526.e: There are two parallel trails; in one of them, a third individual probably walked in the prints of another. So the tracks come from at least two human ancestors.
30526.m: At Laetoli, at least two human ancestors walked side by side.

30527.q: Which researcher led the excavations in which the Laetoli tracks of human ancestors were discovered in 1978?
30527.e: Mary Leakey's team found animal tracks from 1976 and the tracks of human ancestors in 1978. Jane Goodall and Dian Fossey studied living great apes.
30527.m: Mary Leakey led the work at Laetoli.

30528.q: Which species are the Laetoli footprints usually attributed to?
30528.e: Fossils of Australopithecus afarensis are known from the same time and region. The tracks match the size and foot structure of this species.
30528.m: The Laetoli tracks probably come from Lucy's species.

30529.q: What do the Laetoli footprints show about the feet of the human ancestors?
a: The big toe lay parallel to the others
The big toe stuck out like a thumb
The foot had only four toes
30529.e: The prints show a heel, an arch and a big toe lying close to the others. This matches a foot built for walking on two legs.
30529.m: At Laetoli, the foot already shows a big toe lying alongside the others.

30530.q: What did the study of the tracks at site S in Laetoli, described in 2016, reveal?
a: One individual was unusually tall at about 1.65 metres
The tracks came from children under five
The human ancestors wore leather shoes
The tracks came from four-legged animals
30530.e: From the length of the prints, one individual was estimated to be about 1.65 metres tall. So some of the Laetoli human ancestors were taller than expected.
30530.m: Some of the Laetoli human ancestors were surprisingly tall.

30531.q: What did a 2021 study of the tracks at site A in Laetoli reveal?
a: They come from another two-legged human ancestor
They come from a young bear
They come from an ape walking on four legs
30531.e: The tracks at site A were long thought to be bear tracks. New studies point to a two-legged human ancestor, possibly of a different species from the one at site G.
30531.m: Perhaps two different species of human ancestor walked at Laetoli.

30532.q: In which country is Olduvai Gorge?
30532.e: The gorge lies in northern Tanzania on the edge of the Serengeti. It is part of the East African Rift.

30533.q: Which skull found in Olduvai Gorge became world-famous in 1959?
30533.e: In 1959, Mary Leakey found the skull of a robust human ancestor, now called Paranthropus boisei. Because of its massive molars, it was nicknamed “Nutcracker Man”.
30533.m: Nutcracker Man comes from Olduvai Gorge.

30534.q: Which couple of researchers made Olduvai Gorge world-famous from the 1930s?
30534.e: Louis and Mary Leakey did research at Olduvai for decades. Their finds shaped the picture of early human history in East Africa.
30534.m: Louis and Mary Leakey made Olduvai famous.

30535.q: Apart from fossils, what has been found in large numbers in Olduvai Gorge?
30535.e: The layers of the gorge contain countless pebble tools and flakes. This early tool culture is named Oldowan after the site.
30535.m: Olduvai is rich in early stone tools.

30536.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Site does Olduvai Gorge belong to?
30536.e: Olduvai Gorge lies in the Ngorongoro protected area, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. The area is both natural and cultural heritage.
30536.m: Olduvai Gorge is part of the Ngorongoro World Heritage Site.

30537.q: Why is Olduvai Gorge so valuable for dating fossils?
a: Its walls show layers lying on top of each other that can be dated
It consists of a single block of rock
30537.e: A river has cut the gorge into layers of rock and ash spanning about two million years. Volcanic layers can be dated radiometrically.
30537.m: In Olduvai Gorge, the layers of time lie open like a book.

30538.q: Roughly how long is Olduvai Gorge?
30538.e: The steep-sided gorge is about 48 kilometres long and up to about 90 metres deep. It has a main branch and a side branch.
30538.m: Olduvai Gorge is about 48 kilometres long.

30539.q: Roughly what percentage of their genome do people outside Africa today have from Neanderthals?
30539.e: Genome comparisons show that non-Africans carry about 1 to 2 per cent Neanderthal DNA. This proves gene flow between the two forms of human.
30539.m: Non-Africans carry one to two per cent Neanderthal genome.

30540.q: What does the term “gene flow” mean in genetics?
a: The passing of genes between populations
The loss of genes through mutation
The movement of genes within a cell
Random loss of genes through disease
30540.e: Gene flow means that genetic material passes from one population into another. That is how Neanderthal genes got into the gene pool of Homo sapiens.
30540.m: Gene flow means the exchange of genes between populations.

30541.q: According to recent studies, roughly when did the main mixing between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens take place?
30541.e: Studies of the genomes of ancient and modern humans date the main gene flow to about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. It probably lasted several thousand years.
30541.m: Neanderthals and Sapiens mixed about 47,000 years ago.

30542.q: How were researchers able to prove that Neanderthals and Homo sapiens mixed?
a: By comparing ancient and modern genomes
30542.e: The Neanderthal genome was decoded in 2010. Comparing it with the genome of people today showed shared sections that can only be explained by mixing. Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize for this in 2022.
30542.m: Ancient DNA proves that Neanderthals and Sapiens mixed.

30543.q: In which part of the body do many Neanderthal gene variants that are still common today have an effect?
a: In the lens of the eye
30543.e: Variants of genes for defence receptors often come from Neanderthals. They probably helped modern humans cope with pathogens outside Africa.
30543.m: Neanderthal genes strengthened the immune system of modern humans.

30544.q: What link did Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo find in 2020 for a Neanderthal gene section on chromosome 3?
a: A higher risk of severe Covid-19
30544.e: A section inherited from Neanderthals was linked to a higher risk of severe Covid-19 illness. It is especially common in South Asia.
30544.m: A Neanderthal inheritance affects the risk from Covid-19.

30545.q: How did some Neanderthal genetic material also get into today's African populations?
a: Through people migrating back to Africa
Through Neanderthals who arose in Africa
30545.e: Some modern humans who already carried Neanderthal DNA migrated back to Africa. That is why small amounts of this genetic material are also found in Africans.
30545.m: People migrating back also brought Neanderthal genes to Africa.

30546.q: Which place is the Neanderthal named after?
30546.e: In 1856, bones were found in the Feldhofer Grotto in the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf. This form of human was named after the valley.
30546.m: The Neanderthal is named after the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf.

30547.q: Added up across all people alive today, roughly what share of the Neanderthal genome still survives?
30547.e: Each person carries different Neanderthal sections. Added together, at least about 20 per cent of the Neanderthal genome still survives in humanity today.
30547.m: Spread across all people, a large part of the Neanderthal genome lives on.

30548.q: For what achievement did Svante Pääbo receive the Nobel Prize in 2022?
a: Discoveries about the genomes of extinct forms of human
30548.e: Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the genomes of extinct hominins and on human evolution.
30548.m: Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in 2022 for researching ancient human DNA.

30549.q: Which country does Svante Pääbo come from?
30549.e: Svante Pääbo was born in Stockholm in 1955. He has been doing research in Germany for decades.
30549.m: Svante Pääbo is a Swedish researcher.

30550.q: At which institute did Svante Pääbo become founding director of a department of genetics in 1997?
a: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig
30550.e: Pääbo is a founding director at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. The genomes of the Neanderthals and Denisovans were decoded there.
30550.m: Svante Pääbo does research at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig.

30551.q: Which field of research is Svante Pääbo considered to have played a key part in founding?
30551.e: Palaeogenetics studies genetic material from old bones and sediments. Pääbo developed methods to detect contamination with modern DNA.
30551.m: Svante Pääbo is a pioneer of palaeogenetics.

30552.q: In which material did Svante Pääbo detect ancient human DNA in a paper published in 1985?
a: In a mammoth in the ice
In hair from a bog body
30552.e: As a doctoral student in Uppsala, Pääbo cloned DNA from an Egyptian mummy about 2400 years old. He published the results in “Nature” in 1985.
30552.m: Pääbo's first work with ancient DNA was on an Egyptian mummy.

30553.q: What did Svante Pääbo's team achieve in 1997?
a: Sequencing the mitochondrial DNA of a Neanderthal
30553.e: The team obtained a piece of mitochondrial DNA from the type specimen from the Neander Valley. It was clearly different from the DNA of people today.
30553.m: In 1997, Neanderthal DNA was read for the first time.

30554.q: In which year did Pääbo's team publish the first draft of the Neanderthal genome?
30554.e: In May of that year, the draft of the Neanderthal genome appeared in “Science”. It showed gene flow between Neanderthals and modern humans for the first time.
30554.m: The Neanderthal genome has been known since 2010.

30555.q: What is special about Svante Pääbo's family?
a: His father also received a Nobel Prize in Medicine
30555.e: His father Sune Bergström received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1982. Father and son were therefore honoured in the same category.
30555.m: Svante Pääbo and his father both received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

30556.q: Which particularly big problem in analysing ancient DNA did Pääbo fight with strict laboratory methods?
a: Too much genetic material being present
30556.e: Ancient DNA is badly broken down and only present in traces. Even tiny amounts of DNA from excavators or lab staff can distort the results, so work is done in clean rooms.
30556.m: Ancient DNA must be protected from contamination in clean rooms.

30557.q: In which German state were the Schöningen spears found?
30557.e: The spears come from the open-cast lignite mine near Schöningen in the district of Helmstedt in Lower Saxony. They were excavated from 1994 to 1998.
30557.m: The Schöningen spears come from Lower Saxony.

30558.q: Where were the Schöningen spears discovered?
30558.e: The spears came to light from 1994 to 1998 in the open-cast lignite mine near Schöningen in Lower Saxony. The diggers there uncovered old lake deposits.
30558.m: The Schöningen spears come from an open-cast lignite mine.

30559.q: Which wood are most of the Schöningen spears made of?
30559.e: Most of the spears are made of spruce wood, and one of pine. The makers placed the point in the harder, lower part of the trunk.
30559.m: The Schöningen spears are mostly made of spruce wood.

30560.q: According to a new dating published in 2025, roughly how old are the Schöningen spears?
30560.e: For a long time they were thought to be about 300,000 years old. A 2025 study using improved methods found about 200,000 years.
30560.m: According to new dating, the Schöningen spears are about 200,000 years old.

30561.q: According to the new dating of 2025, which form of human probably made the Schöningen spears?
30561.e: With the younger age of about 200,000 years, the spears fit into the time of early Neanderthals. Before that, Homo heidelbergensis was often named as their maker.
30561.m: The Schöningen spears probably come from early Neanderthals.

30562.q: Which animals were found in large numbers together with the spears at Schöningen?
30562.e: At the site lay the bones of numerous wild horses with cut marks. This points to a planned group hunt on the lake shore.
30562.m: At Schöningen, mainly wild horses were hunted.

30563.q: What do the Schöningen spears prove about the people of that time?
a: They hunted big game deliberately and with planning
They could not yet work wood
They already knew the bow and arrow
30563.e: The carefully carved spears are balanced like modern javelins. They show that people planned ahead and worked together as hunters.
30563.m: The Schöningen spears prove planned big-game hunting.

30564.q: Why did the wooden spears at Schöningen survive for so long?
a: They lay in damp lake deposits low in oxygen
They lay in a dry desert
30564.e: The spears were buried in waterlogged layers of mud at the edge of a former lake. Without oxygen, fungi and bacteria could hardly break down the wood.
30564.m: Lake mud low in oxygen preserved the wooden spears.

30565.q: Why has the original Lascaux cave been closed to visitors since 1963?
a: The visitors' breath and moisture damaged the paintings
The cave was in danger of collapsing
The paintings were taken to a museum
30565.e: The many visitors brought warmth, carbon dioxide and germs into the cave. Algae and mould threatened the paintings, so copies are shown today.
30565.m: Lascaux is closed to protect the paintings.

30566.q: Where do the red, orange and yellow shades at Lascaux come from?
30566.e: Ochre and other iron-containing minerals provided the warm shades. Depending on the iron compound, yellow, orange or red is produced.
30566.m: The warm colours at Lascaux come from iron oxides.

30567.q: What did analyses reveal about how the paints at Lascaux were prepared?
a: They were applied without mixing or heating
They were always burnt with lime
They were boiled with resin to make varnish
They were pressed from plant sap
30567.e: At Lascaux, the mineral pigments were used directly, without mixing or heating them. This sets Lascaux apart from sites where pigments were burnt.
30567.m: At Lascaux, the paints were used without mixing or heating.

30568.q: What is the almost complete replica of the Lascaux cave that opened in Montignac in 2016 called?
30568.e: Lascaux IV at the Centre International d'Art Pariétal reproduces almost the entire cave system. Lascaux II shows only the Hall of the Bulls and the Axial Gallery, and Lascaux III was a touring exhibition.
30568.m: Lascaux IV is the walk-in copy of the whole cave.

30569.q: Which figure in the Hall of the Bulls at Lascaux is called the “Licorne”?
a: A human with a bird's head
A wild horse with a foal
30569.e: At the start of the Hall of the Bulls stands a puzzling animal figure with long, straight horns. Because of its mythical shape, it is called the “Licorne”, meaning unicorn.
30569.m: The “Licorne” is a puzzling mythical animal at Lascaux.

30570.q: Apart from painting, which technique did the artists of Lascaux also use often?
a: They scratched pictures into the rock
They burnt pictures in with fire
30570.e: Besides the paintings, there are about 1500 engravings at Lascaux. Many are so fine that you can hardly see them with the naked eye.
30570.m: There are also many engravings at Lascaux.

30571.q: On which river is the Lascaux cave?
30571.e: Lascaux lies on the left bank of the Vézère, about 2 kilometres south of Montignac. The valley is rich in sites and has been a World Heritage Site since 1979.
30571.m: Lascaux lies in the Vézère valley.

30572.q: How was the Lascaux cave discovered in 1940?
a: Teenagers climbed in through a hole in the woods
Soldiers came across it while building a bunker
A farmer fell in while ploughing
Archaeologists found it with ground radar
30572.e: In September 1940, four teenagers including Marcel Ravidat discovered an opening in the woods near Montignac. They crawled in and found the magnificent animal pictures.
30572.m: Lascaux was discovered by teenagers in 1940.

30573.q: In which area of France is the Chauvet Cave?
a: In the Ardèche valley in southern France
30573.e: The cave lies near Vallon-Pont-d'Arc in the Ardèche. It was discovered in 1994 by three cave explorers and named after Jean-Marie Chauvet.
30573.m: The Chauvet Cave is in the Ardèche.

30574.q: Roughly how old are the oldest paintings in the Chauvet Cave?
30574.e: Dating gives the oldest pictures an age of about 36,000 years. That makes them about twice as old as the pictures at Lascaux.
30574.m: The pictures in the Chauvet Cave are among the oldest cave paintings in the world.

30575.q: Why are the paintings in the Chauvet Cave so well preserved?
a: A rockfall sealed the entrance for thousands of years
The cave lay under a glacier
They were restored in the Middle Ages
30575.e: Over 20,000 years ago, a rockfall buried the original entrance. As a result, the climate in the cave stayed stable and nobody disturbed the pictures.
30575.m: A rockfall sealed the Chauvet Cave for a long time.

30576.q: Which trick did the painters of the Chauvet Cave use to show movement?
a: Sequences of pictures on wooden boards
30576.e: Some animals have doubled legs or heads, which looks like movement. The artists also used bulges in the rock to create a three-dimensional effect.
30576.m: In Chauvet, multiple outlines create the impression of movement.

30577.q: How old is the charcoal from the torch with which a child walked through the Chauvet Cave?
30577.e: The child kept wiping the torch on the wall to make it burn brighter. The charcoal marks were dated to about 26,000 years, so they are younger than the paintings.
30577.m: A child visited the Chauvet Cave long after the first painters.

30578.q: Why did the Chauvet Cave shake the idea of a steady development of cave art?
a: Its very old pictures are already highly developed
Its pictures are younger than those at Lascaux
30578.e: It was assumed that art grew from simple to complex forms. But Chauvet already shows perspective, shading and movement at a very early time.
30578.m: Chauvet proves that art was masterly very early on.

30579.q: Which rare big cat is shown in the Chauvet Cave alongside many cave lions?
30579.e: Among the predators in the Chauvet Cave, besides lions, bears and hyenas, there is also a panther. Such pictures are extremely rare in Ice Age art.
30579.m: A panther is also one of the predators in the Chauvet Cave.

30580.q: Which animals are mainly shown on the famous ceiling of the Altamira cave?
30580.e: The ceiling of the great hall shows mainly bison in red and black. The artists used bulges in the rock so that the animals look almost three-dimensional.
30580.m: Altamira is famous for its bison.

30581.q: Who was the first to notice the ceiling paintings of Altamira in 1879?
a: Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola's little daughter
A shepherd looking for a sheep
30581.e: Sautuola was digging in the cave floor when his daughter María, aged about eight, looked up at the ceiling and spotted animals. The cave itself had been found a few years earlier.
30581.m: A child discovered the ceiling paintings of Altamira.

30582.q: Which cultural stage do the famous ceiling paintings of Altamira belong to?
30582.e: The ceiling paintings with the bison were made around 16,500 to 13,000 BC. This period is the Magdalenian, the last stage of the Upper Palaeolithic.
30582.m: The bison of Altamira date from the Magdalenian.

30583.q: What ended the use of the Altamira cave around 11,000 BC?
a: A volcanic eruption filled it with ash
Ice blocked the way in for ever
30583.e: The cave was used from about 33,600 BC until its entrance collapsed. This kept the pictures protected for a long time.
30583.m: A collapse sealed Altamira for thousands of years.

30584.q: Near which town in Cantabria is the Altamira cave?
30584.e: Altamira lies near Santillana del Mar, about 32 kilometres south-west of Santander. A museum nearby shows a replica.
30584.m: Altamira lies near Santillana del Mar.

30585.q: How was the World Heritage listing of the Altamira cave changed in 2008?
a: It was extended to include other painted caves in northern Spain
It was removed because of damage
It was transferred to the replica
30585.e: Altamira has been a World Heritage Site since 1985. In 2008, further caves with Palaeolithic art in northern Spain were added.
30585.m: Since 2008, the Altamira World Heritage Site has included several caves in northern Spain.

30586.q: Why did Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola not live to see his discovery recognised?
a: He died in 1888, long before his critic took back his doubts
30586.e: Experts suspected Sautuola of forgery, and he died in 1888. Only in 1902 did Cartailhac publicly withdraw his doubts.
30586.m: Sautuola died before he was proved right.

30587.q: In which present-day country was the Venus of Willendorf found?
30587.e: The figure was discovered in 1908 in Willendorf in the Wachau on the Danube. Today it is on display in the Natural History Museum in Vienna.
30587.m: The Venus of Willendorf comes from Austria.

30588.q: What does the fact that the stone of the Venus of Willendorf does not come from the Wachau show?
a: People or materials travelled long distances at that time
The figure was only carved in the Middle Ages
The figure is a modern fake
There were no people in the Wachau
30588.e: According to analyses from 2022, the oolite probably comes from the area around Lake Garda. This proves long journeys or trading links in the Ice Age.
30588.m: The stone of the Venus of Willendorf came from far away.

30589.q: How was the navel of the Venus of Willendorf made?
a: From a natural hollow that was enlarged
30589.e: The carver used a natural hollow in the stone as the navel and deepened it. So he cleverly adapted the figure to the stone.
30589.m: The Venus's navel uses a natural hollow in the stone.

30590.q: With which tool was the Venus of Willendorf probably worked?
30590.e: Fine lines, such as those on the head, were probably engraved with a flint burin. Such tools were found in the same layers.
30590.m: A flint burin shaped the details of the Venus.

30591.q: What do the notches on the thin arms of the Venus of Willendorf probably represent?
30591.e: The arms rest on the chest and have notched lines. They are interpreted as arm jewellery.
30591.m: The Venus of Willendorf probably wears bracelets.

30592.q: Which body parts are missing on the Venus of Willendorf?
30592.e: The figure ends below the knees, and no feet are carved. The face is not shown either.
30592.m: The Venus of Willendorf has no feet.

30593.q: According to newer dating, since when was the Willendorf site inhabited?
30593.e: The site in the Wachau has many layers. The oldest traces go back about 43,500 years, well before the time of the figure.
30593.m: Willendorf was inhabited long before the Venus.

30596.q: Why was the excavation at Hohlenstein-Stadel suddenly stopped in 1939?
a: Because the Second World War broke out
Because the university ran out of money
30596.e: The fragments were recovered on 25 August 1939. Shortly afterwards the war began and the excavation stopped; the pieces were ignored for decades.
30596.m: The start of the war interrupted the excavation of the Lion Man in 1939.

30597.q: What did the new restoration of the Lion Man in 2013 achieve?
a: About 80 more pieces were fitted in
The figure was exposed as a fake
The figure was copied in stone
30597.e: Newly found fragments of the neck and back were fitted in under Nicole Ebinger-Rist. The figure grew from 29.6 to 31.1 centimetres.
30597.m: Since 2013, the Lion Man has been more complete than before.

30598.q: In which valley is the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave?
30598.e: Hohlenstein-Stadel lies in the Lone valley near Asselfingen in the Swabian Jura. Vogelherd and Bockstein are also there.
30598.m: The Lion Man comes from the Lone valley.

30599.q: Why is the Lion Man considered important for the history of ideas?
a: It is one of the oldest images of a mythical creature
It is the oldest tool made of ivory
30599.e: A creature that is part human and part lion does not exist in nature. The figure therefore shows imagination, perhaps myths or rituals.
30599.m: The Lion Man proves early thinking about mythical creatures.

30600.q: In which museum is the Lion Man on display today?
a: In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich
In the British Museum in London
30600.e: The figure has belonged to the city of Ulm since 1956 and is the most important exhibit of the Museum Ulm. It was found in a cave in the nearby Swabian Jura.
30600.m: The Lion Man can be seen in the Museum Ulm.

30601.q: What might the fine notches on the Lion Man's left upper arm show?
30601.e: The parallel grooves are interpreted as showing tattoos or scars. The left ear also has fine cuts.
30601.m: The Lion Man may have body decoration on its arm.

30602.q: How did a flute made of mammoth ivory have to be made?
a: Split lengthways, hollowed out and joined back together
Softened in fire and drilled out
Pressed into a tube from powder
Soaked in water and rolled up
30602.e: Unlike bird bones, ivory is not hollow. The piece had to be split, both halves hollowed out and tightly joined together.
30602.m: An ivory flute required great craftsmanship.

30603.q: What is the famous flute from Hohle Fels made of?
a: The bone of a griffon vulture
30603.e: The flute was made from the wing bone of a griffon vulture and has five finger holes. It was found in the Swabian Jura in 2008.
30603.m: The flute from Hohle Fels is made from a vulture bone.

30604.q: Roughly how old are the oldest flutes from the caves of the Swabian Jura?
30604.e: The flutes from Hohle Fels and Geissenklösterle are about 35,000 to 43,000 years old. They are among the oldest known musical instruments.
30604.m: The oldest flutes in the world are about 40,000 years old.

30605.q: What did replicas of Stone Age flutes, for example by Friedrich Seeberger, show?
