30832.e: The survey in the Petén lowlands revealed houses, causeways, fields and roads under the rainforest. It changed the picture of how densely populated the Maya culture was.
30832.m: LIDAR revealed huge Maya settlements in the rainforest of Guatemala.

30833.q: In which country did researchers use LIDAR to discover extensive medieval urban landscapes around a famous temple complex?
30833.e: From 2012, the laser data around Angkor revealed street grids, waterworks and settlements of the Khmer. The city of Mahendraparvata on Phnom Kulen was also mapped in more detail in this way.
30833.m: LIDAR revealed the urban landscape around Angkor in Cambodia.

30834.q: What did Thor Heyerdahl want to show with the voyage of the Kon-Tiki in 1947?
a: That people from South America could have reached Polynesia by raft
That the Egyptians crossed the Atlantic
That skin boats crossed the English Channel
30834.e: Heyerdahl sailed on a balsa raft from Peru to the Tuamotu Islands. The experiment proved that it was possible, but not that the islands were actually settled that way.
30834.m: The Kon-Tiki showed that a raft voyage to Polynesia was possible.

30835.q: What can an archaeological experiment basically prove?
a: That something was possible in a certain way
That it happened exactly like that in the past
30835.e: A successful experiment only shows that a technique can work. Whether people really did it that way at the time must be checked against finds and features.
30835.m: Experiments show possibilities, not certain facts.

30836.q: What was the 2007 Swiss television programme called in which two families lived as in the New Stone Age in Thurgau?
30836.e: For the programme, two families and two young men lived for several weeks in a reconstructed pile-dwelling village at the Hinderrietweiher pond near Pfyn. The project was accompanied by archaeologists.
30836.m: The programme “Pfahlbauer von Pfyn” (The Pile Dwellers of Pfyn) showed life in the New Stone Age.

30837.q: What has been researched at Butser Ancient Farm in England since 1972?
a: How house building and farming worked in the Iron Age
30837.e: At Butser Ancient Farm, Iron Age houses are rebuilt and cereals are grown as they were then. Long-term experiments test things such as harvest yields and storage in pits in the ground.
30837.m: Butser Ancient Farm researches Iron Age farming.

30838.q: In which country is the Lejre experimental centre, one of the oldest of its kind?
30838.e: The centre in Lejre was founded in 1964 and is now called Sagnlandet Lejre. Prehistoric houses and techniques are rebuilt and tested there.
30838.m: The Lejre experimental centre is in Denmark.

30839.q: Which type of furnace is rebuilt in experiments to understand early iron production?
30839.e: In the bloomery furnace, iron ore is reduced with charcoal without the iron melting. This produces a spongy bloom that has to be forged.
30839.m: In the bloomery furnace, early smiths obtained iron without melting it.

30840.q: Why do experimental archaeologists make copies of stone tools and use them?
a: To compare the wear marks with those on originals
To add finds to sites artificially
To measure the age of the originals
30840.e: Cutting wood, meat or cereals leaves different polish and notches on the blade. The comparison shows what a find was used for.
30840.m: Replica tools help to interpret wear marks on finds.

30841.q: What does the typological method do in archaeology?
a: It puts objects in time order according to how their form developed
It determines the sex of skeletons
It counts tree rings in wood
30841.e: The shapes of axes, brooches or pots change over time. If you put them in series, you get a chronology. The Swede Oscar Montelius founded this method.
30841.m: Typology orders finds by their form.

30842.q: What is a type fossil (index type) in archaeology?
a: A type of find that is typical of a particular period
The shape of an excavation area
A vessel used as a unit of measurement
The oldest piece in a collection
30842.e: Type fossils were in use only for a short time and were widespread. If you find them, you can place the site in time.
30842.m: A type fossil dates a site to a particular period.

30843.q: Which type of find is especially often used as a type fossil in the Iron Age?
30843.e: Brooches for fastening clothes changed their shape quickly according to fashion. That is why they are excellent for dividing the Hallstatt and La Tène periods into fine stages.
30843.m: Brooches are important type fossils of the Iron Age.

30844.q: How is the La Tène period often divided?
a: Into Early, Middle and Late La Tène
Into Stone, Bronze and Iron La Tène
Into Roman, Celtic and Germanic La Tène
Into Summer and Winter La Tène
30844.e: The three-part division is based mainly on how brooches developed in form. It was introduced in the 19th century and is still used today.
30844.m: The La Tène period has three stages.

30845.q: Which site in Austria is the early Iron Age named after?
30845.e: In the salt-mining town of Hallstatt, a huge cemetery with rich grave goods was found. The early Iron Age is called the Hallstatt period after it.
30845.m: The early Iron Age is named after Hallstatt.

30846.q: What kind of chronology does a seriation provide?
a: A relative sequence without calendar years
A date accurate to the year
30846.e: Seriation puts graves or groups of finds into a series according to how similar their contents are. When this series begins and ends has to be determined with other methods.
30846.m: A seriation gives a relative sequence.

30847.q: In which country did Flinders Petrie first put graves into a sequence according to their grave goods around 1900?
30847.e: Petrie compared the pottery of prehistoric graves in Upper Egypt. He arranged them so that similar grave contents stood next to each other, and so founded seriation.
30847.m: Flinders Petrie founded seriation in Egypt.

30848.q: What shape does the popularity of a type over time form in a typical seriation chart?
a: A battleship curve that first gets wider and then narrower
30848.e: A new type appears, becomes common and then disappears again. In the chart, the bar therefore looks like a ship's hull seen from above.
30848.m: The frequency of a type usually follows a battleship curve.

30849.q: How is the seriation of large cemeteries mostly carried out today?
30849.e: With hundreds of graves and types, sorting by hand is hardly possible. Statistical methods on the computer order graves and types by how similar they are.
30849.m: Large seriations are calculated by computer today.

30850.q: Why are closed finds such as single graves particularly suitable for seriation?
a: Because their grave goods went into the ground at the same time
Because they do not have to be excavated
30850.e: A grave is made and closed at one moment. So the grave goods were in use at the same time and can be compared as a combination.
30850.m: Closed finds show which objects were used at the same time.

30851.q: By which feature did Christian Jürgensen Thomsen divide prehistory into three periods?
a: By the material of tools and weapons
By the climate of the time
30851.e: Thomsen sorted the finds of the Copenhagen collection into stone, bronze and iron. He published his system in 1836.
30851.m: Thomsen ordered prehistory by the material of the tools.

30852.q: Which three periods does the three-age system distinguish?
a: Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age
Stone Age, Copper Age, Bronze Age
Old Stone Age, Middle Stone Age, New Stone Age
30852.e: Christian Jürgensen Thomsen divided prehistory into the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages according to the most important material. The division is still used today.
30852.m: The three-age system has the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age.

30853.q: Which observation did Thomsen particularly base the order of his three periods on?
a: On closed finds whose objects were found together
On written sources of the Vikings
On tree-ring dates of oak coffins
30853.e: Thomsen paid attention to which objects regularly lay together in graves and hoards. This allowed him to form groups and justify their order.
30853.m: Thomsen used objects found together for his system.

30854.q: How was the sequence of stone, bronze and iron confirmed in excavations?
a: The finds lay in layers on top of each other in this order
The finds had dates scratched into them
The iron finds always lay at the bottom
30854.e: Jens Jacob Asmussen Worsaae showed in the field that stone finds lay at the bottom, bronze above them and iron at the top. Deeper layers are usually older.
30854.m: The order of layers confirmed the three-age system.

30855.q: What distinguishes the New Stone Age from the Old Stone Age?
a: The first tools made of iron
30855.e: In the Old Stone Age, people lived as hunter-gatherers with chipped stone tools. In the New Stone Age, farming, livestock keeping and polished stone axes were added.
30855.m: The New Stone Age brought farming and polished stone tools.

30856.q: Which sequence of materials did the Roman poet Lucretius already describe, long before the three-age system?
30856.e: In his didactic poem “De rerum natura”, Lucretius wrote that people first used hands, stones and branches, then bronze and finally iron. Thomsen turned this into a scientific system.
30856.m: Lucretius already sensed the sequence of stone, bronze and iron in ancient times.

30857.q: Why can the three-age system not be applied to all regions of the world?
a: Because some regions went straight from stone to iron
Because bronze was used everywhere before stone
Because iron does not occur anywhere outside Europe
Because stone tools were only known in Europe
30857.e: In many parts of Africa south of the Sahara, the Stone Age was followed directly by the Iron Age. In the Americas there was no iron smelting before the Europeans arrived.
30857.m: The three-age system fits mainly Europe and the Middle East.

a: An excavation before a site is destroyed by building work
A dig to rescue buried people
A dig that only recovers treasure
A repeat of an old excavation
30858.e: When a site is in danger of being lost through building projects, erosion or farming, it is excavated and recorded beforehand. Today most excavations in Central Europe are rescue excavations.
30858.m: Rescue excavations record sites before they are destroyed.

30859.q: Which European agreement of 1992 regulates the protection of the archaeological heritage and the polluter-pays principle?
30859.e: The European Convention on the Protection of the Archaeological Heritage was signed in Valletta in 1992. It requires archaeological concerns to be included early in spatial planning.
30859.m: The Malta Convention protects Europe's archaeological heritage.

30860.q: What does the polluter-pays principle mean in archaeology?
a: Whoever destroys a site by building contributes to the cost of excavating it
Whoever finds something may keep it
The state pays for all excavations alone
30860.e: Developers whose projects endanger sites pay part of the costs of investigation and recording. This is how rescue excavations are financed.
30860.m: Under the polluter-pays principle, whoever destroys a site helps pay.

30861.q: Under the Swiss Civil Code, who owns ownerless archaeological finds of scientific value in Switzerland?
a: The canton in which they were found
30861.e: Under Article 724 of the Civil Code, such antiquities become the property of the canton. That is why the cantonal archaeology services are responsible for excavations in Switzerland.
30861.m: In Switzerland, archaeological finds belong to the canton.

30862.q: During which building project in Zurich were Neolithic lakeside settlements excavated over a large area in 2010 and 2011?
a: The building of the Opéra car park
The building of the Prime Tower
The conversion of the main railway station
The building of the Letzigrund stadium
30862.e: A car park was built under the Sechseläutenplatz, which meant the pile-dwelling remains underground were lost. Before construction, the city's archaeologists investigated the layers with great effort.
30862.m: Pile dwellings were excavated in Zurich before the Opéra car park was built.

30863.q: Why were there large rescue excavations on Lake Neuchâtel in the 1980s?
a: Because the A5 motorway was being built
Because an airport was being built
30863.e: The lake shore near Hauterive was filled in for the motorway. Before that, reindeer hunters' camps and Bronze Age settlements were excavated.
30863.m: Motorway building led to large excavations on Lake Neuchâtel.

30864.q: Which principle does the Malta Convention prefer to excavation?
a: Preserving the site in the ground (in situ)
Building over sites without recording them
30864.e: Every excavation destroys the features, even if it records them. That is why a site should stay untouched in the ground if possible, for example by changing building plans.
30864.m: It is best for a site to stay untouched in the ground.

30865.q: What did a police officer damage Ötzi's hip with during the first recovery?
30865.e: On the day of the discovery, people tried to free the body from the ice with an ice axe and a pneumatic drill. At the time, nobody suspected how old the dead man was.
30865.m: Ötzi was accidentally damaged during the first recovery.

30866.q: Which metal is the blade of Ötzi's axe made of?
30866.e: The blade is about 99 % copper and not bronze. Ötzi lived in the Copper Age, long before the Iron Age.
30866.m: Ötzi's axe blade is made of almost pure copper.

30867.q: What do cut injuries on Ötzi's hands point to?
a: A hand-to-hand fight shortly before his death
A fall into a glacier crevasse
30867.e: Cuts on his hands and arm and scratches on his back are seen as signs of a fight. It took place at least about a day before the fatal attack.
30867.m: Ötzi had already been in a fight before his death.

a: Charcoal dust rubbed into small puncture wounds
Plant juice injected under the nails
30868.e: The marks were made by tiny puncture wounds in the skin into which charcoal dust was rubbed. This kept the lines permanently visible.
30868.m: Ötzi's tattoos consist of rubbed-in charcoal dust.

30869.q: According to a 2023 genome study, from which group was over 90 % of Ötzi's ancestry?
30869.e: His genome is very similar to that of the farmers who brought agriculture to Europe from about 7000 BC. Traces of the steppe herders who arrived later are missing.
30869.m: Most of Ötzi's ancestors were early farmers from Anatolia.

30870.q: How was Ötzi's body mainly preserved in the ice?
a: By drying out in hot sand
30870.e: Cold and wind drew water out of the body, similar to freeze-drying. At times it probably also lay in meltwater.
30870.m: Ötzi is a natural glacier mummy.

30871.q: According to a 2016 DNA analysis, from which animal's skin were Ötzi's leggings made?
30871.e: The study of his clothing showed that Ötzi used skins from both domestic and wild animals. The leggings were sewn together from many pieces of goatskin.
30871.m: Ötzi wore clothing made from the skins of domestic animals.

30872.q: Where were many of Ötzi's tattoos?
a: Over joints and on the back
30872.e: The roughly 60 lines and crosses are often in places where Ötzi had joint wear. Many researchers interpret them as a treatment for pain.
30872.m: Ötzi's tattoos were probably meant to heal.

30873.q: What does the technical term “Chalcolithic” literally mean?
30873.e: The word is made up of Greek “chalkós” (copper) and “líthos” (stone). Alongside the first copper tools, stone tools remained important.
30873.m: In the Copper Age, copper and stone were used side by side.

30874.q: Which of Ötzi's objects shows that he lived in the Copper Age?
a: An axe with a copper blade
30874.e: Ötzi lived around 3300 BC. His axe had a blade of almost pure copper, but he also carried tools made of flint.
30874.m: Ötzi's copper axe shows the Copper Age.

30875.q: Around when does the Copper Age end in Central Europe with the start of the Bronze Age?
30875.e: With the Early Bronze Age, tin bronze became established around 2200 BC. The late Copper Age is shaped by the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker cultures.
30875.m: The Bronze Age begins in Central Europe around 2200 BC.

30876.q: What did the archaeologist Andrew Sherratt call the widespread use of milk, wool and animal pulling power?
30876.e: Sherratt argued that animals were increasingly kept not just for meat, but also for milk, wool and as draught animals. He placed this development mainly in the Copper Age.
30876.m: In the Copper Age, animals were used in more ways than before.

30877.q: How do you make copper that has become hard and brittle from hammering workable again?
a: By soaking it in salt water
30877.e: Hammering hardens the structure of the metal. Annealing makes it soft again so that you can keep working it.
30877.m: Hammered copper becomes soft again through annealing.

30878.q: Which copper alloy was widespread before tin bronze?
30878.e: Copper containing arsenic is harder than pure copper. However, melting it produces poisonous fumes, which is why it was later replaced.
30878.m: Before tin bronze, copper containing arsenic was often used.

30879.q: Which innovation in Europe is proven by wooden finds from the Ljubljana Marshes around 3150 BC?
30879.e: A wooden wheel with an axle was found in the marshes near Ljubljana; it is one of the oldest in the world. The wheel and the wagon spread in Europe in the Copper Age.
30879.m: The wheel was already spreading in Europe in the Copper Age.

30880.q: Roughly how much does the Nebra sky disc weigh?
30880.e: The bronze disc weighs about 2050 grams. It is about 4.5 millimetres thick in the middle and gets thinner towards the edge.
30880.m: The sky disc is heavier than it looks.

30881.q: What does the group of seven closely spaced gold dots on the Nebra sky disc probably represent?
a: The seven days of the week
30881.e: The group of dots is interpreted as the Pleiades star cluster. Its appearance in the sky was an important sign for farmers for sowing and harvesting.
30881.m: The sky disc probably shows the Pleiades.

30882.q: How was the sky disc found in 1999?
a: By illegal treasure hunters with a metal detector
30882.e: Two illegal treasure hunters came across the disc with a metal detector on the Mittelberg near Nebra and sold it on illegally. The find was damaged in the process.
30882.m: The sky disc was dug up illegally.

30883.q: Roughly when was the Nebra sky disc buried?
30883.e: The disc was buried in the early Bronze Age together with swords, axes and arm spirals. These accompanying finds make it possible to date it.
30883.m: The sky disc is about 3600 years old.

30884.q: Why is the Nebra sky disc so important for science?
a: It is considered the oldest known concrete depiction of the sky
It is the oldest piece of gold in the world
It proves that there were telescopes in the Bronze Age
It is the oldest map of the world
30884.e: The disc shows the sun or a full moon, a crescent moon and stars. It has been part of UNESCO's Memory of the World since 2013.
30884.m: The sky disc is the oldest known concrete depiction of the sky.

30885.q: How is the golden, feathered arc on the lower edge of the disc often interpreted?
30885.e: Many researchers see it as a ship carrying the sun across the sky or through the night. Such sun ships are also known from Egypt.
30885.m: One gold arc on the sky disc is seen as a sun ship.

30886.q: What is the Nebra sky disc made of?
30886.e: The disc was forged from bronze, an alloy of copper and tin. The sun, moon and stars are made of gold sheet laid on top.
30886.m: The sky disc is a bronze disc with gold overlays.

30887.q: Roughly what mixing ratio does classic tin bronze have?
30887.e: Classic bronze consists of about nine parts copper and one part tin. More tin makes it harder, but also more brittle.
30887.m: Bronze is mostly copper with a little tin.

30888.q: Why was tin so sought after in the Bronze Age?
a: It was found in only a few places
It was used as a spice
30888.e: Tin ore is found in only a few places in Europe, such as Cornwall, Brittany and the Ore Mountains. But without tin there was no bronze.
30888.m: Tin was rare and therefore valuable.

30889.q: How much tin do you need for 45 kg of bronze with a tin content of 10 %?
30889.e: 10 % of 45 kg is 45 kg times 0.1, which is 4.5 kg. The remaining 40.5 kg is copper.
30889.m: Bronze needs only a small share of tin.

30890.q: Which region was one of Europe's most important sources of tin in the Bronze Age?
30890.e: Cornwall in south-west England had rich tin deposits. Because tin was rare, wide trading networks grew up right across Europe.
30890.m: Much Bronze Age tin came from south-west England.

30891.q: Which metals made up the main cargo of the Uluburun ship, which sank around 1300 BC?
30891.e: The wreck off the Turkish coast carried about ten tonnes of copper and about one tonne of tin. That is exactly the ratio for bronze.
30891.m: The Uluburun ship carried raw materials for bronze.

30892.q: In what typical form was copper traded in the eastern Mediterranean in the Bronze Age?
30892.e: The flat ingots with inward-curving sides look like a stretched animal hide. They were easy to stack and carry.
30892.m: Copper was often traded in ingots shaped like animal hides.

30893.q: Why is every piece made by lost-wax bronze casting unique?
a: Because the clay mould has to be broken
Because bronze can only melt once
Because every cast needs different metals
Because every figure is painted afterwards
30893.e: The wax model is wrapped in clay and melted out, then bronze is poured into the hollow space. To get the figure out, the clay mould has to be smashed.
30893.m: In lost-wax casting, the mould is lost.

30894.q: Which burial custom gave the Urnfield culture its name?
a: Ashes of the dead in urns in flat graves
Burial of bodies in large stone tombs
Burial in tall mounds with wagons
Laying the dead to rest in rock caves
30894.e: The dead were cremated and their ashes buried in clay vessels in large cemeteries. These fields of urns gave the culture its name.
30894.m: In the Urnfield culture the dead were cremated.

30895.q: Roughly when did the Urnfield culture exist in Central Europe?
30895.e: The Urnfield culture forms the late Bronze Age in Central Europe. It was followed by the early Iron Age.
30895.m: The Urnfield culture belongs to the late Bronze Age.

30896.q: Which period followed the Urnfield culture in Central Europe?
30896.e: The Urnfield culture is the late Bronze Age. Around 800 BC it was followed by the early Iron Age, the Hallstatt period.
30896.m: After the Urnfield period came the Iron Age.

30897.q: Which type of settlement was again widespread on the lakes of Switzerland in the Urnfield period?
30897.e: After a gap, the lakeshores were densely settled again in the late Bronze Age, for example in Zurich at the Alpenquai or in Hauterive-Champréveyres. These settlements ended around 800 BC.
30897.m: In the late Bronze Age many people lived on the lakeshores again.

30898.q: Which cone-shaped objects made of gold sheet are interpreted as cult objects with a calendar function?
30898.e: Golden hats such as the Berlin Gold Hat bear patterns interpreted as lunar and solar calendars. They date from the late Bronze Age.
30898.m: Golden hats are seen as ritual calendars of the Bronze Age.

30899.q: Which religious symbol is typical of the Urnfield culture?
a: The stag with the tree of life
30899.e: The bird-sun barque shows a boat with bird heads carrying a sun disc. It probably stands for the journey of the sun.
30899.m: The bird-sun barque is a sun symbol of the Urnfield period.

30900.q: Which east-central European culture, with the settlement of Biskupin, belongs to the group of Urnfield cultures?
30900.e: The Lusatian culture in Poland and eastern Germany also practised cremation burial in urns. Biskupin is a fortified wooden settlement on a lake island.
30900.m: The Lusatian culture is an eastern Urnfield culture.

30901.q: Roughly when did the Hallstatt culture exist as the early Iron Age?
30901.e: The Hallstatt period in the narrow sense covers the phases Hallstatt C and D. It was followed by the La Tène period.
30901.m: The Hallstatt period is the early Iron Age.

30902.q: What is the Hallstatt culture named after?
a: A cemetery near Hallstatt in Austria
30902.e: In the 19th century almost 1000 graves with rich grave goods were excavated near Hallstatt in the Salzkammergut. The site gave the early Iron Age its name.
30902.m: The Hallstatt culture is named after Hallstatt in Austria.

30903.q: Which raw material made Hallstatt rich in the Iron Age?
30903.e: Salt was already mined at Hallstatt in the Bronze Age. Salt was very valuable for preserving meat and was traded far and wide.
30903.m: Hallstatt grew rich from salt mining.

30904.q: How were members of the upper class often buried in the late Hallstatt period?
a: In burial mounds with wagons and rich grave goods
In rock tombs on the sea coast
30904.e: Princely graves such as the one at Hochdorf contained four-wheeled wagons, drinking vessels and gold jewellery under large earth mounds.
30904.m: Hallstatt princes were buried in mounds with wagons.

30905.q: The grave of Vix in Burgundy contained the largest surviving bronze vessel of antiquity. What was this type of vessel used for?
30905.e: The Greek krater of Vix holds about 1100 litres. The Greeks used such mixing bowls to dilute wine with water at feasts.
30905.m: The Vix krater is a huge Greek mixing bowl.

30906.q: What is meant by a “princely seat” of the late Hallstatt period?
a: A fortified hilltop settlement of a rich elite
A stone throne inside a burial mound
30906.e: Princely seats such as the Heuneburg lay on hilltops, were fortified and had contacts as far as the Mediterranean. Rich burial mounds often lie nearby.
30906.m: Princely seats were fortified centres of the Hallstatt elite.

30907.q: Through which Greek colony did wine in amphorae reach the elites of the Hallstatt culture?
30907.e: Massalia, today's Marseille, was founded by Greeks around 600 BC. Wine and luxury goods travelled north along the Rhône.
30907.m: Greek wine reached the Hallstatt princes via Marseille.

30908.q: According to research, what effect did the spread of iron have on long-distance trade?
a: The copper and tin trade became less important
The salt trade came to a complete stop
30908.e: Iron ore is found in many places, whereas copper and tin occur in only a few. As a result, old trading networks collapsed and new elites emerged.
30908.m: With iron, the old bronze trade routes lost importance.

30909.q: Roughly when was the La Tène period in Central Europe?
a: From about 450 BC to about the birth of Christ
30909.e: The La Tène period is the later pre-Roman Iron Age. It ends with Rome's conquest of the Celtic lands.
30909.m: The La Tène period is the later Iron Age of the Celts.

30910.q: Which Greek sanctuary did Celtic bands attack in 279 BC?
30910.e: After invading Macedonia, Celtic groups advanced as far as Delphi. The attack was fought off.
30910.m: Celtic warriors pushed as far as Greece.

30911.q: Which style is typical of La Tène art?
a: Curving tendrils, spirals and grotesque faces
30911.e: La Tène artists took motifs from the Mediterranean and turned them into intertwined, often abstract ornaments. Human and animal faces merge with plant patterns.
30911.m: La Tène art is full of curving lines and mythical creatures.

30912.q: What were the Celts called who settled in Asia Minor in the 3rd century BC?
30912.e: The Galatians settled in the interior of Anatolia. Paul's Letter to the Galatians was later addressed to them.
30912.m: The Galatians were Celts in Asia Minor.

30913.q: From which cultures did Celtic artists of the early La Tène period adopt many patterns?
a: From the Vikings and Germanic peoples
30913.e: Celtic artists adopted tendrils and palmettes from Greek and Etruscan models. They reshaped them into their own intertwined patterns.
30913.m: La Tène art reworks models from Greece and Etruria.

30914.q: What are the rectangular enclosures surrounded by a bank and ditch from the late La Tène period in southern Germany called?
30914.e: Viereckschanzen used to be interpreted mostly as places of worship. Today many are also seen as enclosed farmsteads.
30914.m: Viereckschanzen are typical sites of the late Celts.

30915.q: Which site in Hesse is known for a life-size sandstone statue of a warrior with a leaf crown?
30915.e: The statue was found in 1996 near a burial mound at the Glauberg. It shows a warrior with a shield, a neck ring and a leaf-shaped headdress.
30915.m: A Celtic warrior statue was found at the Glauberg.

30916.q: Why is the site of La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel known internationally?
a: It gave its name to a whole period of the Iron Age
The oldest pile dwellings were found there
The first hand axe was discovered there
30916.e: The later Iron Age in Europe, the La Tène period, is named after La Tène. Scholars such as Édouard Desor made the site famous in the 19th century.
30916.m: La Tène gave its name to the later Iron Age.

30917.q: How was the site of La Tène discovered in 1857?
a: Iron objects were recovered from the lake at low water
A farmer ploughed up a gold treasure
A grave was found while building a tunnel
30917.e: In 1857 Hans Kopp searched the shallow water near the shore for antiquities on behalf of a collector. He immediately found many iron swords and spearheads.
30917.m: La Tène was discovered in 1857 in shallow lake water.

30918.q: By roughly how much did the first Jura water correction lower the level of Lake Neuchâtel?
30918.e: The lowering in the late 19th century left large shore areas dry. This made the site of La Tène easier to reach.
30918.m: The Jura water correction uncovered many archaeological sites.

30919.q: When did the first Jura water correction take place?
30919.e: The first correction diverted the Aare into Lake Biel and regulated the lakes. Lowering the water levels uncovered many archaeological sites.
30919.m: The first Jura water correction took place in the 19th century.

30920.q: Roughly how many finds did the investigations at La Tène produce in total?
30920.e: The finds include weapons, tools, horse harness, pottery and coins. Today they are spread across many museums.
30920.m: Thousands of objects were found at La Tène.

30921.q: How do many researchers interpret the numerous weapons and skeletons at La Tène?
a: Possibly as a place of worship or sacrifice
As the workshop of a Roman smith
As the camp of a trading fleet
30921.e: Many weapons were apparently bent or broken on purpose, which may point to offerings. Because the circumstances of the finds are uncertain, the interpretation remains disputed.
30921.m: La Tène may have been a Celtic place of sacrifice.

30922.q: Why are many questions about the site of La Tène still open today?
a: The finds were recovered early without exact records
The site now lies under a glacier
All the finds were destroyed in a fire
30922.e: In the 19th century many people collected objects without recording where or in which layer they were found. The finds were also sold to many museums and scattered.
30922.m: Without exact records, a find loses much of what it can tell us.

30923.q: What did Caesar call the Celtic fortification wall made of timber beams, earth and stones?
30923.e: Caesar described the walls of the Gallic oppida as “murus gallicus”. A framework of timber beams was filled with earth and stones and faced with stones at the front.
30923.m: Many oppida were fortified with a murus gallicus.

30924.q: In which work does Caesar write about the oppida and the war against the Gauls?
30924.e: In “De bello Gallico” Caesar describes his campaigns in Gaul from 58 to 50 BC. He also describes the fortified towns of the Celts.
30924.m: Caesar described the Gallic oppida in “De bello Gallico”.

30925.q: Which economic activity is recorded in many Celtic oppida?
30925.e: Workshops and tools for making coins have been found in many oppida. The oppida were centres of craft, trade and a money economy.
30925.m: Coins were minted in the oppida.

30926.q: When were most Celtic oppida built?
30926.e: The oppida belong to the late La Tène period. With the Roman conquest most of them lost their importance.
30926.m: Oppida are the towns of the late Celts.

30927.q: Apart from its ramparts, what protected the Celtic oppidum of Altenburg-Rheinau particularly well?
a: Its location in loops of the Rhine
Its location on a sea island
30927.e: The two parts of the oppidum lay on the Swiss and German sides in loops of the Rhine. Water surrounded the settlement on several sides, and ramparts closed off the open side.
30927.m: A Celtic oppidum lay on the Rhine near Rheinau.

30928.q: At which oppidum did Vercingetorix surrender to the Romans in 52 BC?
30928.e: Caesar surrounded Alesia with a double ring of siege works. After the relief army failed, Vercingetorix surrendered.
30928.m: The great Gallic revolt ended at Alesia.

30929.q: On which hill in Basel was there a fortified oppidum in the late Celtic period?
30929.e: At first there was a large open Celtic settlement on the Rhine. Later the settlement moved to the protected Münsterhügel, where the Romans also built.
30929.m: Basel was already an important place in Celtic times.

30930.q: Why do we know little for certain about the teachings of the druids?
a: They passed on their knowledge only by word of mouth
They wrote only in a secret script
They existed for only a few decades
They banned the Romans from entering Gaul
30930.e: According to Caesar, druid pupils spent years learning their knowledge by heart and did not write it down. What we know comes mainly from Greek and Roman authors.
30930.m: The druids did not write down their teachings.

30931.q: How did the Roman Empire deal with the druids in Gaul?
a: It made them priests in Rome
30931.e: The druids were already restricted under Augustus and Tiberius. According to Suetonius, Emperor Claudius finally abolished their religion altogether.
30931.m: Rome acted deliberately against the druids.

30932.q: Which three respected groups among the Gauls does the geographer Strabo distinguish?
30932.e: According to Strabo, the bards were singers and poets, the vates were seers and experts in sacrifice, and the druids were scholars of nature and morals. All three were highly respected.
30932.m: Besides the druids, the Gauls had bards and seers.

30933.q: According to Caesar, which worldly task did the druids carry out in Gaul?
a: They led the army into battle
30933.e: According to Caesar, druids ruled on murder, inheritance and boundary disputes. Anyone who did not accept their judgement was punished.

30934.q: According to Caesar, which script did the Gauls use for accounts and lists?
30934.e: Caesar reports that lists in Greek script were found in the camp of the Helvetii. The teachings of the druids themselves were not written down.
30934.m: The Gauls wrote lists in Greek letters.

30935.q: Which bronze find is regarded as a Gallic calendar and is often linked with the knowledge of the druids?
30935.e: The bronze tablet found in 1897 shows a lunisolar calendar in the Gaulish language. It dates from the Roman imperial period.
30935.m: The Coligny calendar shows how the Gauls counted time.

30936.q: How is the name “druid” often explained linguistically?
a: As “one who knows the oak” or “very knowing one”
30936.e: The word is often traced back to Celtic roots for oak or strength and for knowledge. Its exact origin is not certain.
30936.m: The name druid has to do with knowledge.

30937.q: What made the Celtic princely grave of Hochdorf so special when it was excavated in 1978?
a: It was the oldest grave in the world
30937.e: Most princely graves were already looted in ancient times. At Hochdorf all the grave goods were still in place, including gold jewellery, a bronze cauldron and a wagon.
30937.m: The princely grave of Hochdorf was untouched.

30938.q: Roughly how much did the Greek bronze cauldron in the princely grave of Hochdorf hold?
30938.e: The cauldron measures about one metre across. It stood ready in the burial chamber for a feast in the afterlife.

30939.q: According to analysis of the residue, which drink was in the large bronze cauldron of Hochdorf?
30939.e: Pollen remains show that the cauldron was filled with honey mead. The cauldron itself was made in a Greek workshop.
30939.m: The Hochdorf cauldron once held honey mead.

30940.q: How many drinking horns hung in the burial chamber at Hochdorf?
30940.e: Eight horns come from aurochs, and a large ninth one is made of iron. They are decorated with gold bands and point to feasting.
30940.m: A whole set of drinking vessels lay in the Hochdorf grave.

30941.q: Roughly how tall was the dead man in the princely grave of Hochdorf?
30941.e: Depending on the study, his height is given as about 1.80 to 1.87 m. That made him very tall for his time, which could also point to good nutrition in the upper class.
30941.m: The prince of Hochdorf was a tall man.

30942.q: Roughly what diameter did the burial mound of Hochdorf have?
30942.e: The mound was surrounded by a ring of stones and was about six metres high. Today it has been reconstructed.
30942.m: The Hochdorf burial mound was very large.

30943.q: What is special about one of the three lions on the rim of the Hochdorf cauldron?
a: It was remade in a different style
It is made of solid gold
30943.e: Two lions come from the Greek workshop. The third was probably cast as a replacement by a local craftsman.
30943.m: One cauldron lion from Hochdorf is a Celtic copy.

30944.q: On which river does the Heuneburg lie?
30944.e: The Heuneburg lies near Herbertingen-Hundersingen on a spur of land above the Danube. The river was an important transport route.
30944.m: The Heuneburg towers above the young Danube.

30945.q: What was unusual about the fortification wall of the Heuneburg around 600 BC?
a: It was made of mud bricks on a stone base
It was made entirely of marble blocks
It was built from iron plates
It was just an earth bank with a hedge
30945.e: Air-dried mud bricks were common in the Mediterranean, but unique north of the Alps. The wall shows the influence of Mediterranean building methods.
30945.m: The Heuneburg had a wall based on Mediterranean models.

30946.q: Why is the Heuneburg so important for research into the Celts?
a: It is regarded as one of the oldest town-like settlements north of the Alps
It was a capital of the Roman Empire
The oldest Celtic writing was found there
30946.e: Around 600 BC thousands of people lived on and around the Heuneburg. Some even think it was the Celtic town of Pyrene mentioned by the Greek Herodotus.
30946.m: The Heuneburg was an early Celtic town.

30947.q: At its peak, roughly how many people lived in the centre of the Heuneburg?
30947.e: With its castle, outer bailey and outer settlement, the Heuneburg was one of the earliest town-like settlements north of the Alps. Including the surrounding area, about 17,000 people are estimated.
30947.m: The Heuneburg was an early large Celtic settlement.

30948.q: Roughly how large was the outer settlement of the Heuneburg?
30948.e: The actual castle on the plateau covered only about three hectares. A much larger settlement stretched out beyond it.
30948.m: A large outer settlement lay around the Heuneburg.

30949.q: What lies in the area around the Heuneburg and shows the wealth of its upper class?
30949.e: Mighty burial mounds such as the Hohmichele lie around the Heuneburg. They held burials with wagons, jewellery and goods from the south.
30949.m: Large burial mounds surround the princely seat of the Heuneburg.

30950.q: How was the princess's grave at Bettelbühl near the Heuneburg, discovered in 2010, recovered?
a: In one piece as a block of earth weighing many tonnes
Bit by bit with a brush on site
30950.e: The burial chamber was taken to the laboratory as a huge block on a heavy transporter. This allowed experts to uncover the woman's jewellery carefully.
30950.m: The Bettelbühl grave was excavated in the laboratory.

30951.q: Which motifs appear on the neck rings of the Erstfeld gold treasure?
a: Intertwined hybrid creatures of human and animal
Hunting scenes with horses and dogs
30951.e: Mythical creatures, birds and snakes wind around the rings, including a “master of animals”. The arm rings show the running dog pattern.
30951.m: The Erstfeld rings are decorated with mythical creatures.

30952.q: On what occasion was the Erstfeld gold treasure discovered in 1962?
a: During building work on the slope above the village
While building the Gotthard road tunnel
30952.e: Italian building workers were clearing scree from the slope above Erstfeld. Between rocks they came across seven gold rings stacked inside each other.
30952.m: Building workers found the gold in Erstfeld by chance.

30953.q: Why can the exact find spot of the Erstfeld gold treasure no longer be investigated today?
a: It was buried by a rockslide
It is now a closed military zone
30953.e: The large rock was blasted and the ground levelled before experts could examine the site. So the find spot was lost.
30953.m: The find spot of the Erstfeld gold has been destroyed.

30954.q: Roughly when was the Erstfeld gold treasure made?
30954.e: Their style and decoration date the rings to the La Tène period. That makes them over 2000 years old.
30954.m: The Erstfeld rings date from the Celtic La Tène period.

30955.q: How are the rings of the Erstfeld gold treasure made?
a: Solid, cast from a gold bar
From bronze with a gold coating
30955.e: The goldsmiths joined thin shells of hammered gold together. The gold is up to 95 per cent pure.

30956.q: What is striking about the condition of the rings of the Erstfeld gold treasure?
a: They show hardly any signs of wear
30956.e: The rings look almost new. This suggests that they were not worn for long but were soon deposited.
30956.m: The Erstfeld jewellery was hardly worn.

30957.q: The Erstfeld gold treasure was found in 1962 during building work in the canton of Uri. Which people are the gold rings attributed to?
30957.e: The neck and arm rings of almost pure gold date from the La Tène period and are regarded as Celtic work. They were probably hidden on the route to the Gotthard as an offering or a hoard.
30957.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure is Celtic gold jewellery.

30958.q: Which Celtic people lived on the Swiss Plateau at the time of the oppidum on Mont Vully?
30958.e: The oppidum on Mont Vully lay in the territory of the Helvetii. In the 2nd and 1st centuries BC they built several fortified centres on the Plateau.
30958.m: Mont Vully lay in the land of the Helvetii.

30960.q: Roughly what area did the later rampart of the oppidum on Mont Vully protect?
30960.e: The rampart ran right across the hill and closed off the ground leading to the summit. This made the oppidum one of the larger sites in the territory of the Helvetii.
30960.m: The oppidum on Mont Vully protected a large area.

30961.q: Roughly when was the later rampart on Mont Vully built?
30961.e: The finds date the rampart with its post-slot wall to the late La Tène period, around 124 to 120 BC. The front was made of oak posts, with a bank of earth behind.
30961.m: The large rampart on Mont Vully dates from the late Celtic period.

30962.q: According to the excavation findings, what happened to the rampart on Mont Vully around 80 to 70 BC?
a: The Romans turned it into a fort
30962.e: A thick layer of charcoal shows a fire that destroyed parts of the rampart. Afterwards the fortification was not rebuilt.
30962.m: After a fire the oppidum on Mont Vully was abandoned.

30963.q: What type of gate was partly uncovered during the excavations on the rampart of Mont Vully?
a: A pincer gate with two towers
30963.e: In a pincer gate the ends of the rampart bend inwards and form a narrow gateway. Two flanking towers gave the entrance extra protection.
30963.m: The oppidum on Mont Vully had a pincer gate with towers.

30964.q: To which period is the first building phase of the older rampart on Mont Vully dated?
30964.e: Traces of a late Bronze Age fortification were found on the western slope of the hill. Much later the Celts built their oppidum here.
30964.m: Mont Vully was already fortified in the Bronze Age.

30965.q: Why was the stele of the Code of Hammurabi found not in Babylon but in Susa in present-day Iran?
a: An Elamite king had taken it there as war booty
The Persians had made a new copy there
30965.e: In the 12th century BC, a king of Elam took the stele to Susa as booty. French archaeologists found it there in 1901/02.
30965.m: The Hammurabi stele was discovered in Susa as Elamite war booty.

30966.q: In which museum is the original stele of the Code of Hammurabi displayed today?
30966.e: Since the stele came from a French excavation, it went to Paris. It is one of the best-known objects in the Louvre’s Near Eastern department.
30966.m: The original stele of the Code of Hammurabi is in the Louvre.

30967.q: Which legal principle in the Code of Hammurabi is often summed up as ‘an eye for an eye’?
30967.e: Under the law of retaliation, the punishment should match the harm done. In the Code, however, it did not apply equally to all classes.
30967.m: The law of retaliation demands a punishment that matches the harm.

30968.q: How is the text on the stele of the Code of Hammurabi structured?
30968.e: In the prologue, Hammurabi presents himself as a king appointed by the gods. Then come the laws, and the epilogue curses anyone who disregards them.
30968.m: The Code of Hammurabi is divided into prologue, laws and epilogue.

30969.q: What do older collections of laws from Mesopotamia such as the Code of Ur-Nammu show?
a: The Code of Hammurabi was not the first collection of laws
The Sumerians did not yet have punishments
Written laws existed before only in Egypt
30969.e: The Code of Ur-Nammu was written around 2100 BC in Sumerian, about 300 years before Hammurabi. It already set fines for many offences.
30969.m: The Code of Ur-Nammu is older than the Code of Hammurabi.

30970.q: Which trial by ordeal did the Code of Hammurabi lay down for an unproven accusation of sorcery?
30970.e: The accused had to jump into the river. If he survived, he was considered innocent, and the accuser was punished.
30970.m: In the river ordeal, the river decided guilt as a judgement of the gods.

30971.q: From which city did Hammurabi unite large parts of Mesopotamia?
30971.e: Hammurabi ruled in the 18th century BC. He defeated rivals such as Rim-Sin of Larsa and made Babylon the centre of a great empire.
30971.m: Hammurabi made Babylon the capital of a great empire.

30972.q: In which script and language is the Code of Hammurabi written on the stele?
30972.e: The text is carved in the Akkadian language and cuneiform script. A first translation appeared as early as 1902, so the Code quickly became known internationally.
30972.m: The Code of Hammurabi is written in Akkadian in cuneiform.

30973.q: How many tablets does the well-known later version of the Epic of Gilgamesh consist of?
30973.e: The later version is called the twelve-tablet epic. The flood story is on the eleventh tablet.
30973.m: The later version of the Epic of Gilgamesh has twelve clay tablets.

30974.q: On what has the later standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh mainly come down to us?
a: On bamboo strips in Chinese script
30974.e: Many tablets come from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in Nineveh. The version is attributed to a scholar named Sin-leqi-unninni.
30974.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh has survived on clay tablets in cuneiform.

30975.q: What changes for the wild Enkidu after the temple servant Shamhat has introduced him to human civilisation?
a: The animals of the steppe avoid him
He can talk to the animals
30975.e: Shamhat teaches Enkidu to eat bread, drink beer and behave like a human. Afterwards, the animals he used to live with flee from him.
30975.m: Shamhat turned the wild Enkidu into a man of the city.

30976.q: What does the tavern keeper Siduri advise Gilgamesh on his search for immortality?
a: To enjoy life instead of running from death
To make a great sacrifice to the gods
To build a wall around his city
To fight Humbaba in the Cedar Forest
30976.e: Siduri recommends that he eat, celebrate and cherish his wife and child, because the gods kept immortality for themselves. The passage is seen as an early form of the idea ‘seize the day’.
30976.m: The tavern keeper Siduri advises Gilgamesh to enjoy life.

30977.q: Whom does Gilgamesh seek out to learn the secret of immortality?
a: Utnapishtim, the survivor of the flood
Humbaba, the guardian of the Cedar Forest
Enlil, the lord of the gods
30977.e: Utnapishtim had survived the flood in a boat and been given eternal life by the gods. The ferryman Urshanabi takes Gilgamesh across the waters of death to him.
30977.m: Gilgamesh looked to Utnapishtim for the secret of eternal life.

30978.q: What happens to Enkidu after he and Gilgamesh have killed Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven?
a: The gods decide that he must die
30978.e: As punishment for the two friends’ deeds, one of them must die, and the gods choose Enkidu. His death drives Gilgamesh to search for immortality.
30978.m: Enkidu’s death set off Gilgamesh’s search for eternal life.

30979.q: Which bird does not return to the boat in the flood story of the Epic of Gilgamesh?
30979.e: First the dove and the swallow return because they find no land. The raven stays away, which shows that the water has gone down.
30979.m: In the flood story, the raven showed that land had appeared again.

30980.q: With which words does the later version of the Epic of Gilgamesh begin, after which it is also named?
30980.e: Mesopotamian works were named after their opening words. The standard version is therefore called ‘Sha naqba imuru’ in Akkadian.
30980.m: The standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh is named after its first words, ‘He who saw the deep’.

30981.q: Which language family does Akkadian belong to?
30981.e: Akkadian is the oldest Semitic language recorded in writing. It is therefore distantly related to Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic.
30981.m: Akkadian is the oldest recorded Semitic language.

30982.q: How is the Akkadian Empire often described by historians?
a: As the first great empire in history
As the first sea empire in the Mediterranean
As the first city-state of Sumer
30982.e: The empire for the first time united many cities and peoples under one central rule. It stretched from the Persian Gulf to Syria.
30982.m: The Akkadian Empire is often regarded as the world’s first great empire.

30983.q: What does the birth legend of Sargon tell about his childhood?
a: He was abandoned in a basket
He was suckled by a she-wolf
He grew up in a temple
He was born a prince in Ur
30983.e: According to the legend, his mother set him adrift on the river in a basket of reeds. A water drawer found and raised him.
30983.m: Sargon is said to have been set adrift on the river in a basket as a baby.

30984.q: According to tradition, how did Sargon of Akkad come to power?
a: He rose from court servant to king
He inherited the throne from his father
He was elected king by the people
He was appointed by the pharaoh
30984.e: Sargon came from a humble background and served at the court of the king of Kish. Later he overthrew the old order and founded the Akkadian Empire.
30984.m: Sargon rose from humble origins to found an empire.

30985.q: What was new about how Sargon’s grandson Naram-Sin presented himself as ruler?
a: He had himself worshipped as a god
He shared power with a council
He gave up the title of king
30985.e: Naram-Sin called himself ‘King of the Four Quarters’ and put the sign for a god in front of his name. His victory stele shows him with a horned crown, a sign of the gods.
30985.m: Naram-Sin was the first Mesopotamian king to have himself deified.

30986.q: Which daughter of Sargon is regarded as the first author in world history known by name?
30986.e: Enheduanna was high priestess in Ur and wrote temple hymns. She is the oldest poet whose name has come down to us.
30986.m: Enheduanna is the first known author in history.

30987.q: Which causes are discussed today for the fall of the Akkadian Empire?
a: Invasions by mountain peoples, revolts and drought
30987.e: Tradition names the invasions of the Gutians from the Zagros Mountains. Today internal revolts and a long period of drought are also discussed as causes.
30987.m: The Akkadian Empire fell apart through attacks from outside, revolts and drought.

30988.q: What is known today about the location of the capital Akkad?
a: Its location is not known for certain
It was on the coast of Syria
30988.e: Although the city is mentioned in many texts, it has not yet been clearly found by archaeologists. It is thought to lie in the area of the middle Tigris or Euphrates.
30988.m: The capital Akkad has still not been found for certain.

30989.q: Which city did the Assyrian king Sennacherib besiege in vain in 701 BC, as the Bible also reports?
30989.e: Sennacherib marched against King Hezekiah of Judah. Jerusalem was besieged but remained unconquered in return for high tribute payments.
30989.m: Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem without success in 701 BC.

30990.q: Which language became the common language in the late Assyrian Empire?
30990.e: Through deportations and trade, Aramaic spread throughout the empire. It later remained the language of administration under the Persians too.
30990.m: Aramaic became the most important common language of the ancient Near East.

30991.q: By what means did the Assyrians often secure their rule over conquered areas?
a: They gave citizenship to all the defeated
They paid tribute to the defeated
30991.e: The Assyrians resettled conquered peoples in other parts of the empire. This was meant to prevent revolts. The northern kingdom of Israel also suffered this fate in 722 BC.
30991.m: The Assyrians secured their power through mass deportations.

30992.q: Where was the heartland of the Assyrian Empire?
a: On the Tigris in the north of present-day Iraq
In the Nile Valley in Egypt
30992.e: The Assyrian heartland lay on the upper Tigris, with cities such as Ashur, Kalhu and Nineveh. From there, the kings conquered an empire that at times reached as far as Egypt.
30992.m: Assyria’s heartland lay on the Tigris in the north of present-day Iraq.

30993.q: Why are Assyrian inscriptions and reliefs important for the history of Israel?
a: They name Israelite kings and add to biblical accounts
They were made by Israelite priests
They prove that Israel conquered Assyria
30993.e: The Black Obelisk from Kalhu, for example, shows King Jehu bowing before Shalmaneser III. Such sources make it possible to compare biblical accounts with evidence from outside the Bible.
30993.m: Assyrian sources also mention kings of Israel and Judah.

30994.q: Which subject do the famous reliefs from Ashurbanipal’s North Palace in Nineveh show?
a: The building of the Royal Road
30994.e: The reliefs show the king killing lions with bow, spear and sword. The hunt was meant to show that the king defends order against chaos.
30994.m: The lion hunt reliefs celebrate the power of the Assyrian king.

30995.q: Which Assyrian capital was destroyed by the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC?
30995.e: Babylonians and Medes conquered Nineveh in 612 BC. A last Assyrian remnant held out in Harran until 609 BC.
30995.m: With the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC, the Assyrian Empire collapsed.

30996.q: What did Assyrian merchants trade in Anatolia in the 19th century BC?
a: Tin and textiles for silver and gold
30996.e: In the trading colony of Kanesh, Assyrian merchants exchanged tin and textiles for precious metals. Tin was needed to make bronze. Thousands of business letters on clay tablets have survived.
30996.m: Assyrian traders brought tin and textiles to Anatolia.

30998.q: What kind of building was the temple tower of Babylon that is linked with the Tower of Babel?
a: An obelisk made of one stone
30998.e: The ziggurat Etemenanki was a mighty stepped tower in the sanctuary of the god Marduk. It is thought to be the model for the biblical story of the Tower of Babel.
30998.m: The ziggurat of Babylon is thought to be the model for the Tower of Babel.

30999.q: After which people is the dynasty of the Neo-Babylonian kings often named?
30999.e: The ruling family probably descended from the Chaldeans in the south of Mesopotamia. That is why it is also called the Chaldean Empire.
30999.m: The Neo-Babylonian Empire is also called the Chaldean Empire.

31000.q: Which Babylonian crown prince sees the mysterious writing ‘Mene, mene, tekel’ on the wall in the Book of Daniel?
31000.e: Belshazzar was the son of the last king and represented him in Babylon. Daniel interprets the writing as announcing the end of his rule.
31000.m: In the Book of Daniel, the writing on the wall appears to Belshazzar.

31001.q: Why was the Phoenician city of Tyre so hard for besiegers to capture?
a: It lay on an island off the coast
It lay on a high mountain
31001.e: The island city of Tyre could be supplied by sea. Nebuchadnezzar II therefore besieged it for years without capturing it.
31001.m: As an island city, Tyre withstood long sieges.

31002.q: How did Nebuchadnezzar II have his name recorded on his buildings in Babylon?
31002.e: Many bricks from Babylon bear a stamp with Nebuchadnezzar’s name and titles. They show how much he had built.
31002.m: Nebuchadnezzar II had his name stamped into the bricks of his buildings.

31003.q: How long did the Neo-Babylonian Empire last, from 626 to 539 BC?
31003.e: With years BC, you subtract the smaller number from the larger one: 626 minus 539 equals 87. So the empire lasted less than 90 years.
31003.m: The Neo-Babylonian Empire lasted less than a century.

31004.q: What followed for many inhabitants of Judah after Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem?
a: The building of the First Temple
31004.e: After the destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC, many Judeans were taken away to Babylon. Only after the victory of the Persian king Cyrus were they allowed to return.
31004.m: After the destruction of Jerusalem, the Babylonian captivity began.

31005.q: Which city did the Hittite king Mursili I plunder around 1595 BC?
31005.e: Mursili I marched as far as Mesopotamia and plundered the city. This ended the dynasty to which Hammurabi had once belonged.
31005.m: With his campaign, Mursili I ended the Old Babylonian dynasty.

31006.q: Because of its many adopted gods, what is the Hittite kingdom often called?
31006.e: The Hittites took gods of conquered and neighbouring peoples into their pantheon. That is why they themselves spoke of the ‘thousand gods’ of the land.
31006.m: The Hittites worshipped so many gods that people speak of the land of a thousand gods.

31007.q: What was the capital of the Hittite kingdom in Anatolia called?
31007.e: Hattusa lay in what is now central Turkey and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Nearby is the rock sanctuary of Yazılıkaya with reliefs of processions of gods.
31007.m: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittites.

31008.q: On which writing materials have most Hittite texts come down to us?
31008.e: Tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments were found in the archives of Hattusa. The Hittites had adopted cuneiform from Mesopotamia.
31008.m: The Hittites wrote their archives in cuneiform on clay.

31009.q: In a famous letter, what did a widowed Egyptian queen ask the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I for?
31009.e: The queen, probably Tutankhamun’s widow, wanted to marry a Hittite prince. However, the prince who was sent was killed on the way to Egypt.
31009.m: An Egyptian queen asked Suppiluliuma I for a son as her husband.

31010.q: What did the edict of the Hittite king Telipinu around 1500 BC mainly regulate?
31010.e: After many murders in the royal family, Telipinu laid down which son should inherit the throne. The edict was meant to prevent bloody power struggles.
31010.m: The Edict of Telipinu regulated the Hittite succession.

31011.q: What makes Hittite laws stand out compared with other ancient Near Eastern collections of laws?
a: More often fines instead of bodily punishment
31011.e: Many Hittite laws demand compensation in silver or livestock. Later versions even explicitly softened older punishments.
31011.m: Hittite law often relied on fines instead of bodily punishment.

31012.q: What is the Hittite queen Puduhepa known for?
a: She wrote letters to Ramesses II herself
She founded the city of Babylon
She led the army at the Battle of Kadesh
31012.e: Puduhepa, the wife of Hattusili III, was politically very influential. She sealed state documents and corresponded with the pharaoh herself.
31012.m: Queen Puduhepa was a powerful Hittite politician.

31013.q: Around which year did the Battle of Kadesh take place?
31013.e: The battle is usually dated to 1274 BC, in the fifth year of the reign of Ramesses II. It took place in what is now Syria.
31013.m: The Battle of Kadesh is dated to around 1274 BC.

31014.q: Which Hittite great king faced Ramesses II at Kadesh?
31014.e: Muwatalli II led the Hittite army and its allies. He lured the Egyptians into an ambush with false information.
31014.m: At Kadesh, Muwatalli II fought against Ramesses II.

31015.q: On which river was the city of Kadesh?
31015.e: Kadesh lay on the Orontes in the west of present-day Syria. The city was fought over in the border area between Egyptian and Hittite influence.
31015.m: The Battle of Kadesh was fought on the Orontes.

31016.q: What is the Battle of Kadesh particularly known for in military history?
a: As probably the largest chariot battle
As the first great sea battle
As the first use of war elephants
As the first siege with cannons
31016.e: Probably several thousand chariots fought on each side. It is regarded as the largest known chariot battle in history.
31016.m: Kadesh is regarded as the largest chariot battle of antiquity.

31017.q: How do historians judge the outcome of the Battle of Kadesh?
31017.e: Ramesses II celebrated the battle in inscriptions as a great victory. In fact, Kadesh remained Hittite, and neither side could prevail.
31017.m: The Battle of Kadesh ended without a clear winner.

31018.q: How did the Hittite chariots at Kadesh differ from the Egyptian ones?
a: They carried three men instead of two
They had four wheels instead of two
They were made entirely of iron
31018.e: The heavier Hittite chariots carried a driver, a fighter and a shield bearer. The Egyptian chariots were lighter and carried two men.
31018.m: Hittite chariots were heavier and carried three men.

31019.q: Where did Ramesses II have his version of the Battle of Kadesh shown in pictures and text?
a: In temples such as Abu Simbel
31019.e: Ramesses II had the battle depicted on temple walls at Abu Simbel, Karnak, Luxor and in the Ramesseum. The images celebrate him as a victorious hero.
31019.m: Ramesses II glorified Kadesh on many temple walls.

31020.q: In which present-day country is the ziggurat of Ur?
31020.e: Ur lies in the south of Iraq, near the city of Nasiriyah. In the past the city lay close to the Euphrates and the coast of the Persian Gulf.
31020.m: The ziggurat of Ur stands in the south of Iraq.

31021.q: To which god was the ziggurat of Ur dedicated?
31021.e: Nanna, Sin in Akkadian, was the city god of Ur. His temple stood on top of the ziggurat.
31021.m: The ziggurat of Ur was dedicated to the moon god Nanna.

31022.q: What was the ziggurat of Ur built from?
31022.e: There was hardly any stone in Mesopotamia. The core consists of sun-dried mud bricks, the outer shell of fired bricks with bitumen as mortar.
31022.m: The ziggurat of Ur is made of mud bricks.

31023.q: How does a ziggurat differ from an Egyptian pyramid?
a: It is a stepped building with a temple on top
It contains a burial chamber for the king
It is carved from a single rock
31023.e: The ziggurat had a shrine for the god on top and could be reached by stairs. Egyptian pyramids, by contrast, were royal tombs.
31023.m: A ziggurat is a stepped temple, not a tomb.

31024.q: According to estimates, how high was the ziggurat of Ur originally?
31024.e: Since only the lower parts have survived, the height is estimated. It is thought to have been about 30 metres, roughly the height of a ten-storey building.
31024.m: The ziggurat of Ur was probably about 30 metres high originally.

31025.q: Which famous find from the Royal Cemetery of Ur shows war and peace on its two sides?
31025.e: The Standard is a wooden box decorated with shell, lapis lazuli and red limestone. One side shows an army with chariots, the other a banquet.
31025.m: The Standard of Ur shows the war and peace of the Sumerians.

31026.q: According to the Book of Genesis, which biblical figure came from ‘Ur of the Chaldees’?
31026.e: According to the Bible, Abraham moved with his family from Ur to Haran and on to Canaan. Whether this means the Ur in southern Iraq is disputed among historians.
31026.m: The Bible names Ur of the Chaldees as Abraham’s place of origin.

31027.q: Where are the most important pictorial and written sources about the Sea Peoples?
a: In the mortuary temple of Medinet Habu
31027.e: The reliefs of the mortuary temple of Ramesses III in western Thebes show a sea battle against the Sea Peoples. Accompanying texts name individual groups.
31027.m: The reliefs of Medinet Habu are the main source on the Sea Peoples.

31028.q: Which people probably goes back to the Peleset mentioned in Egyptian sources?
31028.e: The Peleset settled on the southern coast of the Levant. The name Palestine is also derived from them.
31028.m: The Philistines were among the Sea Peoples.

31029.q: Which trading city on the Syrian coast was destroyed around 1185 BC and left behind calls for help on clay tablets?
31029.e: In Ugarit, letters were found reporting enemy ships off the coast. The city was destroyed shortly afterwards and never rebuilt.
31029.m: Ugarit fell during the onslaught of the Sea Peoples.

31030.q: With which Mediterranean island are the Sherden among the Sea Peoples often associated?
31030.e: Because of the similar name, a link between the Sherden and Sardinia is suspected. Whether they came from there or only settled there later is disputed.
31030.m: The Sherden are linked with Sardinia because of their name.

31031.q: How do historians today usually explain the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BC?
31031.e: Droughts, famines, earthquakes, revolts, migrations and the breakdown of long-distance trade are discussed. The Sea Peoples are seen more as one part of it than as the only cause.
31031.m: The Bronze Age collapse had many causes working together.

31032.q: Which Greek palace culture came to an end in the course of the Bronze Age collapse?
31032.e: Around 1200 BC, many Mycenaean palaces were destroyed. With them the Linear B script disappeared, and the so-called Dark Ages followed.
31032.m: With the end of the Bronze Age, the Mycenaean palace culture disappeared.

31033.q: What did the Egyptians themselves call the groups that are known today as the ‘Sea Peoples’?
a: Each group by its own name
31033.e: The collective term ‘Sea Peoples’ comes from Egyptologists of the 19th century. The Egyptian texts name groups such as the Peleset, Sherden or Shekelesh individually.
31033.m: The term Sea Peoples is a modern name.

31034.q: Which pharaoh fought against Libyans and their allies among the Sea Peoples as early as around 1208 BC?
31034.e: Merneptah, a son of Ramesses II, fought off an attack from the west. His inscriptions name several groups that are later counted among the Sea Peoples.
31034.m: As early as around 1208 BC, Merneptah defeated a coalition including Sea Peoples.

31035.q: Which oracle is Croesus said to have received before the war against Cyrus?
a: He would destroy a great empire
31035.e: According to Herodotus, the Oracle of Delphi said that he would destroy a great empire if he attacked. He did indeed destroy one: his own.
31035.m: The ambiguous oracle cost Croesus his own empire.

31036.q: Which city did Cyrus take almost without a fight in 539 BC?
31036.e: Cyrus entered the city without having to besiege it. With this, the last great Mesopotamian empire fell to Persia.

31037.q: Where is the Cyrus Cylinder kept today?
a: In the British Museum in London
In the National Museum in Tehran
31037.e: The clay cylinder was found in Babylon in 1879 and came to London. It is sometimes called an early declaration of human rights, but experts see this as an over-interpretation.
31037.m: The Cyrus Cylinder is in the British Museum.

31038.q: Which son succeeded Cyrus II on the throne and conquered Egypt in 525 BC?
31038.e: Cambyses II defeated the Egyptian army at Pelusium. With this, Egypt became part of the Persian Empire.
31038.m: Cambyses II made Egypt part of the Persian Empire.

31039.q: Which people did Cyrus allow to return to their homeland after conquering Babylon?
31039.e: Nebuchadnezzar II had taken many Jews away to Babylon. Cyrus let them return home and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. That is why the Bible calls him one anointed by God.
31039.m: Cyrus ended the Babylonian exile of the Jews.

31040.q: Which region with many Greek cities did Cyrus conquer around 545 BC?
a: Ionia on the coast of Asia Minor
31040.e: After the victory over Croesus of Lydia, the general Harpagus conquered the Greek coastal cities of Ionia for Cyrus. Their later revolt led to the Persian Wars.
31040.m: Harpagus conquered the Greeks of Ionia for Cyrus.

31041.q: Which Greek author wrote the ‘Cyropaedia’, an idealised work about the education of Cyrus?
31041.e: Xenophon presented Cyrus as a model of a just ruler. The work is more a teaching text than an accurate historical source.
31041.m: In the Cyropaedia, Xenophon described Cyrus as an ideal ruler.

31042.q: According to ancient accounts, what did Alexander the Great have done with the tomb of Cyrus when he found it plundered?
31042.e: Arrian reports that Alexander had the tomb robbers punished and the tomb put back in order. He wanted to show himself as a worthy successor of the Persian kings.
31042.m: Alexander the Great had the plundered tomb of Cyrus restored.

31043.q: How did Darius I come to the Persian throne in 522 BC?
a: With conspirators he overthrew an alleged usurper
He inherited the throne from his father Cyrus
He was appointed by Alexander the Great
He was elected by the people
31043.e: Darius claimed that the magus Gaumata had pretended to be the brother of Cambyses. With six conspirators he killed him and became king.
31043.m: Darius I came to power through a coup.

31044.q: Why was Darius’s trilingual Behistun Inscription so important for research?
a: It contains the world’s oldest laws
It shows the first map of Persia
31044.e: The rock inscription tells of Darius’s rise to power in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. In the 19th century Henry Rawlinson used it to decipher cuneiform.
31044.m: The trilingual Behistun Inscription became the key to cuneiform.

31045.q: What were the provinces into which Darius I divided the Persian Empire called?
31045.e: Each satrapy was run by a satrap and had to pay taxes to the king. Herodotus names twenty such tax districts.
31045.m: Darius divided his empire into satrapies.

31046.q: What were the royal inspectors called who kept watch over the satraps in the Persian Empire?
a: The eyes and ears of the king
31046.e: Greek sources report inspectors who travelled on the king’s behalf. They were meant to stop satraps becoming too powerful.
31046.m: The eyes and ears of the king kept watch over the satraps.

31047.q: Which city did the Persians destroy in 494 BC at the end of the Ionian Revolt?
31047.e: Miletus had led the revolt of the Ionian Greeks. After the naval Battle of Lade, the city was captured and destroyed.
31047.m: The Ionian Revolt ended in 494 BC with the destruction of Miletus.

31048.q: Against which people did Darius I lead a campaign across the Bosporus and the Danube around 513 BC?
31048.e: Darius had a bridge of boats built across the Bosporus. However, the mobile Scythians avoided a decisive battle.
31048.m: Darius’s Scythian campaign brought no decisive victory.

31049.q: Which magnificent royal city did Darius I have built in the Persian heartland?
31049.e: Darius began building Persepolis around 518 BC. A few kilometres away is his rock tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam.

31050.q: As far as which river did Darius I extend Persian rule in the east?
31050.e: Darius had the Indus explored by the Greek seafarer Scylax. He then extended his rule to the Indus Valley.
31050.m: Under Darius I, the Persian Empire reached the Indus.

31051.q: What was the Persian Royal Road mainly used for?
a: For the silk trade with China
For pilgrims on their way to Mecca
31051.e: The road linked Susa with Sardis in Asia Minor. Messengers and troops could thus cross the huge empire quickly.
31051.m: The Royal Road held the Persian Empire together.

31052.q: How did messages travel so fast on the Persian Royal Road?
a: Riders took over from one another at stations
One runner carried them the whole way
31052.e: At each station, a rider handed the message to a rested messenger with a fresh horse. In this way messages moved on day and night.
31052.m: Persian messengers took over from one another at the stations.

31053.q: Where is Herodotus’s praise of the Persian couriers (‘Neither snow nor rain ...’) found today as an inscription?
a: On a post office building in New York
31053.e: The quotation is carved on the James Farley Post Office building in New York. It is often seen as the unofficial motto of the US Postal Service.
31053.m: Herodotus’s praise of the Persian messengers decorates a post office building in New York.

31054.q: In which Persian unit of length did Herodotus give the length of the Royal Road?
31054.e: Herodotus gives about 450 parasangs. A parasang is about five to six kilometres, roughly the distance you walk in an hour.
31054.m: The parasang was the Persian measure for long distances.

31055.q: In which present-day country was the western end of the Persian Royal Road?
31055.e: The road ended in western Asia Minor, that is, in what is now Turkey. From there, routes continued to the Aegean coast.
31055.m: In the west, the Royal Road ended in what is now Turkey.

31056.q: What did travellers on the king’s business need in order to receive food at the stations?
31056.e: Administrative tablets from Persepolis record rations for travellers who showed a sealed document. In this way supplies were closely controlled.
31056.m: A sealed travel pass secured food at the stations.

31057.q: Who set Persepolis on fire in 330 BC?
31057.e: Alexander the Great captured Persepolis and had the palace burnt down. Ancient authors saw this as revenge for Xerxes’ destruction of Athens.
31057.m: Alexander the Great destroyed Persepolis by fire.

31058.q: Which Persian king began the building of Persepolis?
31058.e: Darius I began building the palace terrace around 518 BC. His son Xerxes I and later kings continued the work.
31058.m: Persepolis was begun under Darius I.

31059.q: What is carved into the rock above the terrace of Persepolis?
31059.e: The rock tombs are usually attributed to Artaxerxes II and Artaxerxes III. Their facades show the king in front of a fire altar.
31059.m: Above Persepolis lie rock tombs of Persian kings.

31060.q: In which present-day country is Persepolis?
31060.e: The ruins of Persepolis lie in the province of Fars in southern Iran, north-east of Shiraz. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

31061.q: Which material was mainly used for the buildings of Persepolis?
31061.e: For stairs, columns and reliefs, mainly grey limestone from the area was used. Roofs and ceilings were made of wood such as cedar.
31061.m: Persepolis was built mainly of grey limestone.

31062.q: How are many column capitals in Persepolis designed?
a: With the front halves of two animals back to back
31062.e: Capitals with the front parts of two bulls or other animals are typical. The roof beams rested on their backs.
31062.m: Double-animal capitals are typical of the columns of Persepolis.

31063.q: Which celebration did the Shah of Iran hold near Persepolis in 1971?
a: The 2,500-year celebration of the Persian monarchy
31063.e: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi invited state guests from all over the world to a lavish celebration. It was strongly criticised for its high cost.
31063.m: In 1971 the Shah celebrated 2,500 years of Persian monarchy near Persepolis.

31064.q: Roughly how large is the terrace of Persepolis?
31064.e: The platform covers about 125,000 square metres. That is roughly the area of 17 football pitches.
31064.m: The terrace of Persepolis is about 125,000 square metres in size.

31065.q: Which buildings were built in Egypt during the Old Kingdom?
a: The tombs in the Valley of the Kings
31065.e: The pyramids of Giza were built in the 26th century BC for Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. Abu Simbel and the Valley of the Kings date from the New Kingdom, the lighthouse from the Ptolemaic period.
31065.m: The great pyramids of Giza date from the Old Kingdom.

31066.q: Who is regarded as the architect of the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara?
31066.e: Imhotep was a high official of Djoser in the 3rd Dynasty. The Step Pyramid is regarded as Egypt’s oldest monumental stone building.
31066.m: Imhotep designed the first step pyramid for King Djoser.

31067.q: Which city was the capital of Egypt in the Old Kingdom?
31067.e: Memphis lay on the border between Upper and Lower Egypt near present-day Cairo. The kings of the Old Kingdom ruled from there.
31067.m: Memphis was the residence of the kings of the Old Kingdom.

31068.q: Why does the Bent Pyramid at Dahshur have its unusual shape?
a: The angle of the slope was reduced during building
It was put together from two pyramids
31068.e: King Sneferu had the pyramid built. Probably because of stability problems, the angle was made flatter halfway up. Sneferu was experimenting with the shape of the pyramid.
31068.m: With the Bent Pyramid, the angle of the slope was reduced during building.

31069.q: What were the Pyramid Texts in the burial chambers of Egyptian kings for?
a: They were meant to secure the king’s way into the afterlife
They listed the builders and their pay
They contained the laws of the kingdom
They explained how the pyramid was built
31069.e: From the end of the 5th Dynasty, the spells were carved into the walls of the burial chambers, first in the pyramid of Unas. They are among the oldest religious texts of Egypt.
31069.m: The Pyramid Texts were meant to secure the king’s rise into the afterlife.

31070.q: Which period came immediately after the Old Kingdom?
31070.e: After the end of the 6th Dynasty, central royal power broke down. In the First Intermediate Period, regional rulers gained influence.
31070.m: The Old Kingdom was followed by the First Intermediate Period.

31071.q: Which sun god did the kings of the Old Kingdom increasingly worship, building him his own sanctuaries?
31071.e: The kings of the 5th Dynasty in particular built sun temples with a large obelisk at Abusir. They also called themselves ‘Son of Ra’.
31071.m: In the Old Kingdom, the sun god Ra became more and more important.

31072.q: What is the period of decline between the Old and Middle Kingdoms in Egypt called?
31072.e: After the Old Kingdom, Egypt split into several centres of power. Around 2000 BC a king from Thebes reunited the country, and so the Middle Kingdom began.
31072.m: The First Intermediate Period was followed by the Middle Kingdom.
