31073.q: Which region south of Egypt did the pharaohs of the Middle Kingdom secure with fortresses on the Nile?
31073.e: At the second cataract of the Nile, a chain of fortresses such as Semna was built. They secured the southern border against Nubia and controlled trade.
31073.m: In the Middle Kingdom, fortresses on the Nile secured the border with Nubia.

31074.q: Which area west of the Nile did the kings of the 12th Dynasty especially develop for farming?
31074.e: Especially under Amenemhat III, the Faiyum was turned into fertile farmland with canals and dams. His pyramid at Hawara was also built there.
31074.m: In the Middle Kingdom, the Faiyum became a breadbasket.

31075.q: Which story about a court official who fled is regarded as a classic of Middle Kingdom literature?
31075.e: After the death of Amenemhat I, Sinuhe flees to the Near East and returns in old age. The Egyptians themselves read the text as a model work.
31075.m: The Story of Sinuhe is the best-known work of the Middle Kingdom.

31076.q: What was new about the Coffin Texts of the Middle Kingdom?
a: High officials now also used spells for the afterlife
They were written in Greek script
They were found only in royal pyramids
They were passed on only by word of mouth
31076.e: In the Old Kingdom, such spells were found only in royal pyramids. In the Middle Kingdom, they were also written on the coffins of high officials.
31076.m: The Coffin Texts made spells for the afterlife available to officials too.

31077.q: In the Middle Kingdom, what was the border fortification on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta meant to protect against?
31077.e: Amenemhat I had the ‘Walls of the Ruler’ built. They were meant to keep nomads from Sinai and Canaan away from the fertile Delta.
31077.m: In the Middle Kingdom, a fortification protected the eastern border of the Delta.

31078.q: Which type of tomb did the kings of the 12th Dynasty choose in the Middle Kingdom?
a: Pyramids, often with a mud-brick core
Rock tombs in the Valley of the Kings
31078.e: The kings of the 12th Dynasty built pyramids again, usually with a mud-brick core and a stone casing. The rock tombs in the Valley of the Kings only came in the New Kingdom.
31078.m: The kings also built pyramids in the Middle Kingdom.

31079.q: What are the foreign rulers called who controlled the Nile Delta before the New Kingdom?
31079.e: The Hyksos came from the Near East and ruled from Avaris. Ahmose I drove them out around 1550 BC and so opened the New Kingdom.
31079.m: The New Kingdom began with the expulsion of the Hyksos.

31080.q: Which pharaoh of the Amarna Period placed the sun god Aten above all other gods?
31080.e: Akhenaten worshipped almost only the sun disc Aten and founded the new capital Amarna. After his death, Egypt returned to the old gods.
31080.m: In the Amarna Period, Akhenaten worshipped the sun god Aten.

31081.q: Which woman had herself crowned pharaoh during the childhood of Thutmose III?
31081.e: Hatshepsut first ruled on behalf of the young Thutmose III and then had herself crowned pharaoh. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari is famous.
31081.m: Hatshepsut was a woman on the pharaoh’s throne.

31082.q: Which pharaoh fought off the attack of the Sea Peoples around 1177 BC?
31082.e: Ramesses III had his victory over the Sea Peoples shown on the walls of his mortuary temple Medinet Habu. At that time the Sea Peoples threatened many kingdoms around the Mediterranean.
31082.m: Ramesses III defeated the Sea Peoples and recorded it at Medinet Habu.

31083.q: Roughly which period did the New Kingdom cover?
31083.e: The New Kingdom covers the 18th to 20th Dynasties. It was the time of Egypt’s greatest extent.
31083.m: The New Kingdom lasted from about 1550 to 1070 BC.

31084.q: Which pharaoh do the Colossi of Memnon in western Thebes depict?
31084.e: The two colossal statues stood in front of the mortuary temple of Amenhotep III. The Greeks later linked them with the hero Memnon.
31084.m: The Colossi of Memnon show Amenhotep III.

31085.q: At the end of the New Kingdom, who gained so much power in Thebes that they effectively ruled independently?
31085.e: Under the last Ramesside kings, the monarchy lost power. In Thebes, the high priests of Amun ruled largely independently, and then the Third Intermediate Period began.
31085.m: At the end of the New Kingdom, the priests of Amun ruled in Thebes.

31086.q: In which museum is the famous bust of Nefertiti displayed today?
31086.e: The bust was found in Amarna in 1912 during a German excavation led by Ludwig Borchardt and came to Berlin. Egypt still demands its return.
31086.m: The bust of Nefertiti is in the Neues Museum in Berlin.

31087.q: Roughly how long did Akhenaten reign?
31087.e: Akhenaten ruled from about 1351 to 1334 BC. His reform did not last long after his death.

31088.q: How was the god Aten typically shown in the art of the Amarna Period?
a: As a sun disc with rays ending in hands
As a man with a falcon’s head
As a ram with twisted horns
As a woman with cow horns
31088.e: Aten had no human or animal form. His ray hands often hold out the ankh, the sign of life, to the royal family.
31088.m: Aten appears as a sun disc with ray hands.

31089.q: In which script are most of the Amarna letters written?
31089.e: The Amarna letters are clay tablets of diplomatic correspondence. Most are written in Akkadian, the language of diplomats at the time, in cuneiform.
31089.m: The Amarna letters are clay tablets in cuneiform.

31090.q: What does the Great Hymn to the Aten, attributed to Akhenaten, praise?
a: The sun as the giver of all life
The power of the god Amun
The judgement of the dead in the underworld
31090.e: The hymn describes how Aten, as the sun, keeps people, animals and plants alive. It is often compared with Psalm 104 in the Bible.
31090.m: The Hymn to the Aten praises the sun as the source of all life.

31091.q: What did the boy king Tutankhaten call himself after the Amarna reform was reversed?
31091.e: With the return to the old faith, he replaced Aten in his name with Amun. The court left Amarna again.
31091.m: Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun when Amun returned.

31092.q: What is Akhenaten’s religion often called because it recognised only a single god?
31092.e: Akhenaten had images and names of other gods partly erased. Many researchers see this as an early form of monotheism, but how to classify it is still debated.
31092.m: Akhenaten’s belief in the Aten is regarded as an early form of monotheism.

31093.q: Roughly how long did Hatshepsut reign as pharaoh?
31093.e: Hatshepsut ruled from about 1479 to 1458 BC. Her reign is regarded as a peaceful time with large building projects.

31094.q: What happened to many of Hatshepsut’s images and names some time after her death?
31094.e: Many statues were smashed and names chiselled out of inscriptions. The reasons are disputed; it may have been about securing the succession.
31094.m: Hatshepsut’s memory was later partly wiped out.

31095.q: Which legend did Hatshepsut have depicted at Deir el-Bahari to justify her claim to the throne?
a: Her conception by the god Amun
31095.e: The reliefs show how Amun, in the form of her father, visits the queen. In this way Hatshepsut appeared as a ruler chosen by the gods.
31095.m: Hatshepsut claimed divine descent from Amun.

31096.q: How was Hatshepsut’s mummy identified in 2007?
a: By a gold mask with her name
By an inscription on the coffin
31096.e: A box bearing her name contained a molar. It fitted exactly into a gap in the jaw of a mummy from tomb KV60.
31096.m: In 2007 a tooth helped to identify Hatshepsut’s mummy.

31097.e: Hatshepsut was the daughter of Thutmose I. She married her half-brother Thutmose II.

31098.q: What was the Red Chapel, which Hatshepsut had built in the temple of Karnak, used for?
a: As a resting place for the sacred boat of Amun
As a palace for the royal family
As a treasury for gold from Nubia
31098.e: The chapel of red quartzite held the boat with the god’s image of Amun during festivals. Its blocks were later reused in other buildings and put back together in the 20th century.
31098.m: Hatshepsut’s Red Chapel stands rebuilt in Karnak today.

31099.q: What did Hatshepsut have set up in the temple of Karnak, one of which still stands today?
31099.e: She had huge granite obelisks brought from Aswan to Karnak. At almost 30 metres, one of them is among the tallest obelisks still standing in Egypt.
31099.m: Hatshepsut’s obelisk still towers over Karnak today.

31100.q: What is the literary account of the Battle of Kadesh called that Ramesses II had carved in several temples?
31100.e: The Kadesh Poem describes how Ramesses drives back the enemy alone with divine help. It appears at Karnak, Luxor, Abydos and Abu Simbel, among other places.
31100.m: With the Kadesh Poem, Ramesses II presented the battle as a heroic deed.

31101.q: In which region did Ramesses II have the rock temples of Abu Simbel built?
31101.e: Abu Simbel lies in the south of Egypt in Nubia. There the temples displayed the pharaoh’s power to the neighbours in the south.
31101.m: Ramesses II had huge rock temples built in Nubia.

31102.q: Why were two rock temples of Ramesses II taken apart in the 1960s and rebuilt higher up?
a: Because of the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam
Because the Suez Canal was moved
Because of damage from desert sand
31102.e: The reservoir of the Aswan High Dam would have flooded the temples. In an international UNESCO rescue campaign, they were moved between 1964 and 1968.
31102.m: The temples were saved from the water of the Aswan reservoir.

31103.q: What makes the treaty between Ramesses II and the Hittites around 1259 BC famous?
a: It is one of the oldest surviving peace treaties
It divided Egypt into two kingdoms
It made Egypt a Hittite province
31103.e: The treaty has survived in an Egyptian and a Hittite version. A copy now hangs as a symbol in the UN building in New York.
31103.m: Ramesses II and the Hittites made a famous peace treaty.

31104.q: Roughly how long did Ramesses II reign?
31104.e: Ramesses II reigned from about 1279 to 1213 BC. He outlived many of his children, and his successor was his 13th son Merneptah.
31104.m: Ramesses II reigned for about 66 years.

31105.q: Where is the splendidly painted tomb of Nefertari, the chief wife of Ramesses II?
a: In the Valley of the Queens
In the Valley of the Kings
31105.e: Tomb QV66 is regarded as one of the most beautiful tombs in Egypt. Its paintings have been carefully restored.
31105.m: Nefertari rests in the Valley of the Queens.

31106.q: Where does one of the two obelisks that Ramesses II had set up in front of Luxor Temple stand today?
a: On the Place de la Concorde in Paris
In St Peter’s Square in Rome
On the Thames Embankment in London
In Central Park in New York
31106.e: Egypt gave the obelisk to France, and it was put up in Paris in 1836. Its partner still stands in Luxor.
31106.m: An obelisk of Ramesses II stands on the Place de la Concorde.

31107.q: Which part of the inscription on the Rosetta Stone is the most incomplete?
31107.e: The top part of the stone has broken off. That is why only 14 lines of the hieroglyphic text have survived.
31107.m: Most is missing from the hieroglyphic text on the Rosetta Stone.

31108.q: Which of the scripts on the Rosetta Stone was the everyday script of the Egyptians at the time?
31108.e: Demotic was a greatly simplified cursive script for administration and contracts. Hieroglyphs were used mainly for temples and monuments.
31108.m: Demotic was the everyday script in late Egypt.

31109.q: Why was the Rosetta Stone so important for deciphering hieroglyphs?
a: It carries the same text in three scripts, including Greek
It contains a dictionary of hieroglyphs
It shows labelled pictures for each sign
It was translated by Napoleon himself
31109.e: Since people could read Ancient Greek, the Greek text could be compared with the hieroglyphic and Demotic ones. This provided the key to the hieroglyphs.
31109.m: The Rosetta Stone shows one text in three scripts.

31110.q: What kind of text is on the Rosetta Stone?
a: A decree by priests in honour of the king
A love poem by a pharaoh
A letter to the Roman emperor
31110.e: With it, an assembly of priests in Memphis confirmed the royal cult for the young Ptolemy V. The text also grants tax relief to the temples.
31110.m: The Rosetta Stone carries a priestly decree.

31111.q: Who deciphered hieroglyphs in 1822 with the help of the Rosetta Stone?
31111.e: Champollion compared the royal names in the texts and realised that hieroglyphs represent partly sounds and partly ideas. Earlier researchers such as Åkerblad and Young had done some groundwork.

31112.q: How did the Rosetta Stone come to Great Britain?
a: Through a purchase in Cairo in 1820
31112.e: After their defeat in Egypt, the French had to hand over finds under the Capitulation of Alexandria. So the stone came to England as war booty.
31112.m: The Rosetta Stone came to Great Britain as war booty.

31113.q: From which period of Egyptian history does the Rosetta Stone date?
a: From the time of the Ptolemies
From the time of the pyramid builders
From the time of Ramesses II
From the time of the Arabs
31113.e: The decree was passed in 196 BC, about 130 years after Alexander conquered Egypt. At that time the Greek Ptolemaic dynasty ruled, which is why part of it is in Greek.
31113.m: The Rosetta Stone dates from the time of the Ptolemies.

31114.q: What did Champollion do on his journey to Egypt in 1828 to 1829?
a: He copied inscriptions and tested his method on site
He discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun
He led the building of the Suez Canal
31114.e: With the Italian Ippolito Rosellini, he copied numerous inscriptions from real monuments. The Rosetta Stone had already been found in 1799, and Tutankhamun’s tomb was only found in 1922.
31114.m: Champollion travelled to Egypt with Rosellini in 1828.

31115.q: Which language particularly helped Champollion to decipher the hieroglyphs?
31115.e: Coptic is the latest form of the Egyptian language and was written with Greek letters. Champollion learnt it in his youth and so recognised the sounds behind the hieroglyphs.
31115.m: For Champollion, Coptic was the key to the language of the pharaohs.

31116.q: What did Champollion show in his famous letter to the Paris Academy in 1822?
a: That hieroglyphs are only pictures of objects
That the Rosetta Stone is a fake
31116.e: In the ‘Lettre à M. Dacier’, Champollion explained the sound signs of the hieroglyphs, first using royal names. The letter is regarded as the birth certificate of Egyptology.
31116.m: Champollion’s letter of 1822 proved that hieroglyphs represent sounds.

31117.q: Which find with the same text in three scripts was the starting point for Champollion’s decipherment?
31117.e: The Rosetta Stone carries a decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek script. Through the Greek text, Champollion was able to work out the hieroglyphs. In 1824 he set out his system in detail in the ‘Précis’.
31117.m: The Rosetta Stone was the key to the hieroglyphs.

31118.q: Which professorship did Champollion receive in Paris in 1831?
a: The first chair of Egyptology at the Collège de France
The chair of Greek at the Sorbonne
The headship of the École Polytechnique
The chair of Arabic in Grenoble
31118.e: The chair was created especially for him. Because of his illness, he could give only a few lectures.
31118.m: In 1831 Champollion became the first professor of Egyptology.

31119.q: Which royal name did Champollion read in a cartouche from Abu Simbel in 1822, confirming his method?
31119.e: He recognised the sun sign for ‘Ra’ and the signs for ‘mes’ and ‘s’. This showed that purely Egyptian names were also written with sound signs.
31119.m: In 1822 Champollion read the name Ramesses in hieroglyphs.

31120.q: Which collection did Champollion look after as curator from 1826?
a: The Egyptian collection of the Louvre
The collection of the British Museum
31120.e: King Charles X appointed him curator of the Egyptian department of the Louvre. There he arranged the collection according to his new findings.
31120.m: From 1826 Champollion ran the Egyptian collection of the Louvre.

31121.q: Why was a heart scarab placed on the chest of a mummy?
a: So that the heart would not testify against the dead person at the judgement
So that the mummy would not decay
So that the dead person could see in the afterlife
31121.e: The scarab bore a spell from the Book of the Dead. It asks the heart not to bear witness against its owner at the judgement of the dead.
31121.m: The heart scarab protected the dead person at the judgement.

31122.q: What was the Book of the Dead usually written on?
31122.e: The scrolls were filled with texts and coloured pictures and placed in the tomb with the dead person. Some are more than 20 metres long.
31122.m: The Book of the Dead was placed in the tomb on papyrus scrolls.

31123.q: At the Egyptian judgement of the dead, against what was the dead person’s heart weighed?
a: Against the heart of a bull
31123.e: The feather stands for Maat, truth and world order. If the heart was heavier, it was eaten by Ammit, the devourer of the dead.
31123.m: The heart was weighed against the feather of Maat.

31124.q: According to Egyptian belief, which god presided over the judgement of the dead?
31124.e: Osiris, the ruler of the underworld, presided over the court. Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead describes the test of the dead person with the weighing of the heart.
31124.m: Osiris was the judge at the Egyptian judgement of the dead.

31125.q: In the scene of the judgement of the dead, which god records the result of the weighing?
31125.e: Thoth, the god of scribes, is often shown with the head of an ibis. He records the verdict with palette and reed pen.
31125.m: Thoth writes down the verdict of the judgement of the dead.

31126.q: According to Spell 6 of the Book of the Dead, which figures were meant to work for the dead person in the afterlife?
31126.e: The spell calls on the small figures to do field work instead of the dead person. Some tombs contained one figure for every day of the year.
31126.m: Shabtis were meant to do the work for the dead person in the afterlife.

31127.q: What is the list of wrongdoings called that the dead person denies before the judges of the dead?
31127.e: The dead person declares, for example, that he has not stolen and not lied. In this way he proves that he has led an upright life.
31127.m: In the negative confession, the dead person denies wrongdoing.

31128.q: What does the ancient Egyptian concept of Maat stand for?
31128.e: Maat refers to the right order of nature, society and the cosmos. It was also worshipped as a goddess.
31128.m: Maat stands for the just order of the world.

31129.q: According to ancient Egyptian belief, what constantly threatened Maat?
a: The daily course of the sun
31129.e: The Egyptians called chaos Isfet. It included lies, violence and disorder. The world was seen as a constant struggle of Maat against Isfet.
31129.m: Isfet is the chaos that threatens Maat.

31130.q: What was the pharaoh’s task with regard to Maat?
a: He was to bring it about and ward off chaos
He was to reinvent it every year
He was completely exempt from it
He had to leave it to the priests
31130.e: The king was seen as the guarantor of world order. On temple reliefs he symbolically offers Maat to the gods.
31130.m: The pharaoh was to establish Maat on Earth.

31131.q: The goddess Maat was regarded as the daughter of which god?
31131.e: Maat was the daughter of the sun god Ra. She accompanies him on his journey in the sun boat.
31131.m: The goddess Maat is the daughter of the sun god Ra.

31132.q: Which type of text passed on the rules of Maat for daily life?
31132.e: Teachings such as those of Ptahhotep give advice on right behaviour. They stress modesty, justice and speaking with moderation.
31132.m: Wisdom literature explained how to live according to Maat.

31134.q: What do the wall paintings in many royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings show?
a: The night journey of the sun through the underworld
The king’s battles against the Hittites
The building of the pyramids of Giza
The everyday life of farmers on the Nile
31134.e: Texts such as the Amduat describe the twelve hours of the night in which the sun god crosses the underworld. The king hoped to take part in this journey.
31134.m: The royal tombs show the sun’s night journey through the underworld.

31135.q: Why did priests later move many royal mummies from their tombs to a shared hiding place?
a: To protect them from tomb robbers
To make room for new kings
31135.e: Many tombs had been robbed. Priests of the 21st Dynasty gathered the mummies and reburied them in a shaft tomb near Deir el-Bahari, which was only discovered in 1881.
31135.m: Priests hid royal mummies to protect them from tomb robbers.

31136.q: Whose almost untouched tomb did Howard Carter discover in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
31136.e: The young king’s tomb had hardly been robbed and contained thousands of grave goods, including the golden death mask. Khufu, by contrast, lies in a pyramid at Giza.
31136.m: In 1922 Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun.

31137.q: Where did the craftsmen who built the royal tombs live?
a: In tents right in the valley
31137.e: The tomb workers lived with their families in the village of Deir el-Medina on the west side of the Nile. Finds from there give insight into their everyday life.
31137.m: The tomb workers lived in their own village.

31138.q: On what did the tomb workers of the valley often note everyday things such as absences or deliveries?
31138.e: Ostraca are flakes of limestone or pieces of pottery used as cheap writing material. Thousands of them give insight into everyday working life.
31138.m: The tomb workers wrote their notes on ostraca.

31140.q: Who was Ptolemy I before he became king of Egypt?
a: A general of Alexander the Great
31140.e: After Alexander’s death in 323 BC, his general Ptolemy took over the administration of Egypt. Later he made himself king and founded the Ptolemaic dynasty.
31140.m: The Ptolemaic kingdom grew out of the legacy of Alexander the Great.

31141.q: Which god did the Ptolemies promote as a shared deity for Greeks and Egyptians?
31141.e: Serapis combined features of Osiris and Apis with Greek gods. His sanctuary in Alexandria was the Serapeum.
31141.m: Serapis was meant to unite Greeks and Egyptians in religion.

31142.q: Which scholar in Alexandria calculated the Earth’s circumference astonishingly accurately in the 3rd century BC?
31142.e: Eratosthenes compared the position of the sun in Syene and Alexandria. From the difference in angle and the distance, he calculated the Earth’s circumference.
31142.m: Eratosthenes measured the Earth’s circumference from Alexandria.

31143.q: Which famous ruler was the last Ptolemy on the throne of Egypt?
31143.e: Cleopatra VII allied herself with Caesar and later with Mark Antony. After her death in 30 BC, Egypt became a Roman province.
31143.m: The Ptolemaic kingdom ended with Cleopatra VII.

31144.q: Which translation of the Hebrew Bible was made in Alexandria at the time of the Ptolemies?
31144.e: The Septuagint translated the holy scriptures of the Jews into Greek. Many Jews in Alexandria spoke Greek as their everyday language.
31144.m: The Septuagint is the Greek Bible translation from Alexandria.

31145.q: Against which Hellenistic kingdom did the Ptolemies fight the Syrian Wars?
31145.e: For generations both kingdoms fought for control of Coele-Syria and Palestine. A well-known battle took place at Raphia in 217 BC.
31145.m: In the Syrian Wars, the Ptolemies fought against the Seleucids.

31146.q: Which city at the third cataract of the Nile was the centre of an early Kushite culture in the 2nd millennium BC?
31146.e: The Kerma culture was a powerful opponent of the Middle Kingdom. Huge mud-brick buildings, the deffufas, come from it.
31146.m: Kerma was the first great centre of Kush.

31147.q: Which Egyptian dynasty was formed by the kings of Kush?
31147.e: In the 8th and 7th centuries BC, Kushite kings ruled over all of Egypt. They are also called the ‘black pharaohs’.
31147.m: The kings of Kush formed Egypt’s 25th Dynasty.

31148.q: What did the kings of Kush build for their tombs, similar to the Egyptians before them?
31148.e: Hundreds of small, steep pyramids stand at Nuri and Meroe. That is why present-day Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.
31148.m: The kings of Kush were buried in pyramids.

31149.q: Which empire drove the Kushites out of Egypt in the 7th century BC?
31149.e: Assyrian armies under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal pushed as far as Memphis and Thebes. The Kushite kings withdrew to Nubia.
31149.m: The Assyrians ended the rule of the Kushites in Egypt.

31150.q: Which Kushite pharaoh is mentioned in the Bible as Tirhakah?
31150.e: Taharqa reigned in the 7th century BC and built a great deal in Egypt and Nubia. He was buried in a pyramid at Nuri.
31150.m: Taharqa is the Tirhakah of the Bible.

31151.q: Which bronze sculpture did Kushite troops seize in Egypt around 25 BC and bury in Meroe?
31151.e: The head lay under the steps of a victory temple, so that people would tread on the enemy. Today it is in the British Museum.
31151.m: The Meroe Head of Augustus recalls Kush’s fight against Rome.

31152.q: Which kingdom contributed to the end of Meroe in the 4th century AD?
31152.e: King Ezana of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, led a campaign to the Nile. Meroe had already lost power before this.
31152.m: Aksum ended the golden age of Meroe.

31153.q: Whom did Caesar support in the Egyptian dispute over the throne in 48 BC?
31153.e: Cleopatra had been driven out by her brother Ptolemy XIII. With Caesar’s help she won the Alexandrian War and became queen again.
31153.m: Caesar decided the dispute over the throne for Cleopatra against Ptolemy XIII.

31155.q: With which Roman general did Cleopatra ally herself after Caesar’s death?
31155.e: In 41 BC Antony summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus in Asia Minor. She arrived on a magnificent barge dressed as Aphrodite. This led to a political and personal alliance.
31155.m: The alliance between Cleopatra and Antony began in Tarsus.

31156.q: What did Octavian use in Rome as propaganda against Mark Antony?
a: That Antony was giving Roman eastern territories to Cleopatra’s children
That Antony wanted to abolish the Senate
That Antony had defected to the Parthians
31156.e: In the Donations of Alexandria in 34 BC, Antony granted eastern territories to Cleopatra and her children. Octavian therefore portrayed him as the servant of a foreign queen.
31156.m: The Donations of Alexandria sharpened the conflict with Rome.

31157.q: Where was Cleopatra when Caesar was murdered in 44 BC?
31157.e: From 46 BC Cleopatra lived in Caesar’s gardens across the Tiber. After the assassination she returned to Egypt.
31157.m: Cleopatra was in Rome when Caesar died.

31158.q: What became of Egypt after Cleopatra’s death in 30 BC?
a: An independent kingdom of her children
31158.e: Octavian made Egypt a province and placed it directly under his own control. Cleopatra’s daughter Cleopatra Selene grew up in Rome and later became queen of Mauretania.
31158.m: With Cleopatra’s death, Egypt became Roman.

31159.q: What position did the vizier hold in ancient Egypt?
31159.e: The vizier ran the administration, the courts and taxation. He was directly responsible to the king.
31159.m: The vizier was the most powerful official after the pharaoh.

31160.q: How many viziers were there at the same time in the New Kingdom?
31160.e: One vizier was responsible for Upper Egypt, based in Thebes, the other for Lower Egypt. In this way the long country could be governed better.
31160.m: In the New Kingdom, two viziers shared the administration.

31161.q: What task did the Egyptian vizier have besides administration?
a: He administered justice as chief judge
He carried out the temple offerings
He built the ships of the fleet
He brought up the king’s children
31161.e: The vizier held court sessions and supervised taxes. A well-known set of instructions for the vizier has survived in the tomb of Rekhmire in Thebes.
31161.m: The vizier was also Egypt’s chief judge.

31162.q: What were the administrative districts of ancient Egypt called?
31162.e: Egypt was divided into about 42 nomes. Each was headed by a governor, whom the Greeks called a nomarch.
31162.m: Ancient Egypt was divided into nomes.

31163.q: Which professional group formed the backbone of pharaonic administration?
31163.e: Scribes kept lists, counted harvests and wrote documents. Only a small minority could read and write.
31163.m: Without scribes, the Egyptian administration could not work.

31164.q: What were Nilometers used for in the administration of ancient Egypt?
31164.e: A Nilometer showed the height of the yearly flood. From this, people could estimate the size of the harvest and therefore the level of taxes.
31164.m: Nilometers were used to estimate the harvest and the taxes.

31165.q: After which legendary king did Arthur Evans name the Bronze Age civilisation of Crete?
31165.e: Evans coined the term “Minoan” after the mythical King Minos, who was said to have ruled at Knossos. What the Minoans called themselves is unknown.
31165.m: The Minoan civilisation is named after the legendary King Minos.

31166.q: Which British archaeologist began the great excavation of the palace of Knossos in 1900?
31166.e: From 1900 Arthur Evans uncovered the palace of Knossos and rebuilt parts of it with concrete. These reconstructions are still controversial today.
31166.m: Arthur Evans excavated the palace of Knossos from 1900.

31167.q: What is the name of the Minoan syllabic script that has still not been deciphered?
31167.e: Linear A was used on Crete, mainly on clay tablets. The signs can partly be read as sounds, but the language behind them is not understood.
31167.m: The Minoan script Linear A has still not been deciphered.

31168.q: Which Bronze Age natural event is often linked with the decline of Minoan civilisation?
31168.e: The huge eruption of the volcano on Thera (Santorini) in the 2nd millennium BC devastated the Aegean. Whether it directly caused the Minoan decline is disputed among researchers.
31168.m: The volcanic eruption on Thera shook the Minoan world.

31169.q: Which dangerous activity is shown on a famous fresco from the palace of Knossos?
31169.e: The so-called Bull-Leaping Fresco shows young people jumping over a charging bull. The bull played an important role in Minoan religion.
31169.m: A fresco from Knossos shows Minoan bull-leaping.

31170.q: Which Greek myth is linked with the maze-like palace of Knossos?
a: The abduction of Europa on Cyprus
31170.e: According to legend, the Minotaur lived in a labyrinth on Crete, from which Theseus found his way out with Ariadne’s thread. The many rooms and corridors of the palace may have inspired the myth.
31170.m: The myth of the Minotaur’s Labyrinth is linked with Knossos.

31171.q: What clearly distinguishes Minoan palaces such as Knossos from the later Mycenaean citadels?
31171.e: The Minoan palaces were open complexes around a central courtyard and hardly fortified. The Mycenaeans, by contrast, built mighty citadel walls.
31171.m: Unlike Mycenaean citadels, Minoan palaces were hardly fortified.

31172.q: Which merchant and archaeologist excavated the shaft graves of Mycenae from 1876?
31172.e: Heinrich Schliemann, who had already dug at Troy, found richly furnished shaft graves at Mycenae. He wanted to prove Homer’s epics true.
31172.m: Heinrich Schliemann excavated at Mycenae from 1876.

31173.q: What is the name of the golden death mask from Mycenae that Schliemann attributed to a Homeric king?
31173.e: Schliemann believed he had found the face of Agamemnon. Today we know that the mask is about 300 years older than the supposed Trojan War.
31173.m: The Mask of Agamemnon is older than the king whose name it bears.

31174.q: Which script did Michael Ventris decipher in 1952 as an early form of Greek?
31174.e: In 1952 Michael Ventris showed that the Linear B clay tablets record Greek. This proved that the Mycenaeans were Greeks.
31174.m: Linear B is the oldest known script for the Greek language.

31175.q: Why have many Linear B clay tablets survived to this day?
a: A palace fire hardened the clay
They had been set in gold
They were buried in sealed jars
31175.e: The tablets of unfired clay were really only meant for a short time. When palaces such as Pylos burned down, they were fired and so became durable.
31175.m: Palace fires made the Linear B tablets durable.

31176.q: What are the huge stone walls of Mycenaean citadels called, which later Greeks believed were built by one-eyed giants?
31176.e: The blocks were so large that the Greeks believed only the Cyclopes could have moved them. Such walls can be found at Mycenae and Tiryns, for example.
31176.m: Cyclopean walls are made of enormous, barely worked stone blocks.

31177.q: What do the Linear B tablets of the Mycenaean palaces mainly record?
a: Administrative lists of supplies and dues
Heroic poems such as the Iliad
31177.e: The tablets are the palaces’ bookkeeping: lists of grain, oil, livestock, weapons and workers. No literature or letters have been found on them.
31177.m: The Mycenaean palaces used Linear B for bookkeeping.

31178.q: Around what time did the Mycenaean palace centres collapse?
31178.e: Around 1200 BC many palaces were destroyed or abandoned; the causes are disputed. The so-called Dark Ages followed.
31178.m: Mycenaean palace culture came to an end around 1200 BC.

31179.q: In which period did the great Greek colonisation take place?
31179.e: In the Archaic period, Greek cities founded many daughter cities around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. That is why Plato compared the Greeks to frogs around a pond.
31179.m: The great colonisation took place in the Archaic period.

31180.q: Which modern French city did Greeks from Phocaea found around 600 BC?
31180.e: Greeks from Phocaea in Asia Minor founded Massalia around 600 BC. The city became an important trading centre, including for goods that travelled north along the Rhône.
31180.m: Marseille goes back to the Greek colony of Massalia.

31181.q: What did the Romans call southern Italy, which was shaped by Greek colonies?
31181.e: Magna Graecia means “Greater Greece”. It included cities such as Taras, Croton and Neapolis, today’s Naples.
31181.m: Southern Italy was called Magna Graecia because of its many Greek cities.

31182.q: Which oracle did Greeks consult especially often before founding a colony?
31182.e: The oracle of Apollo at Delphi gave advice on the destination and timing of a foundation. In this way it gained great influence throughout the Greek world.
31182.m: Before founding a colony, people usually consulted the oracle of Delphi.

31183.q: What were the tasks of the oikistes, the founder of a Greek colony?
a: He led the settlers and divided up the land
He collected taxes for the mother city
He ran the oracle of Delphi
He commanded the mother city’s fleet
31183.e: The oikistes led the emigrants to the new site, divided up the land and gave the city its order. After his death he was often honoured as a hero.
31183.m: The founder of a colony was called the oikistes.

31184.q: Which colony of the city of Megara on the Bosporus later became Constantinople?
31184.e: Byzantion was founded from Megara in the 7th century BC. Emperor Constantine made the city his new capital in AD 330.
31184.m: Today’s Istanbul goes back to the Greek colony of Byzantion.

31185.q: What was the main purpose of the Greek settlement of Naukratis in the Nile Delta?
a: A trading post between Greeks and Egyptians
A prison for Greek prisoners of war
A pilgrimage site for the pyramids
31185.e: In the 6th century BC Pharaoh Amasis allowed Greek traders to settle in Naukratis and build their own sanctuaries. For a long time the city was Greece’s gateway to Egypt.
31185.m: Naukratis was the Greek trading post in Egypt.

31186.q: In which century BC did Solon carry out his reforms in Athens?
31186.e: In 594 BC Solon became archon with special powers to solve Athens’ severe social crisis. His reforms are seen as an important step on the way to Athenian democracy.
31186.m: Solon reformed Athens in the 6th century BC.

31187.q: How did Solon help the indebted small farmers of Athens?
a: He freed them from military service
31187.e: With the Seisachtheia, the “shaking off of burdens”, Solon cancelled debts and removed the debt stones from the fields.
31187.m: Solon freed the small farmers from their debts.

31188.q: By which criterion did Solon divide the citizens of Athens into four classes?
a: By the size of their harvest
31188.e: A citizen’s class depended on his yearly yield of grain, wine or oil. This system is called timocracy, because property decided political rights.
31188.m: Solon divided the citizens into four classes by their yield.

31189.q: What right did the poorest citizens have in Solon’s system?
a: They could take part in the Assembly
They could sit on the council of nobles
They had no political rights at all
31189.e: The poorest class, the thetes, owned little or no land. They could take part in the Assembly, but could not hold high office.
31189.m: Under Solon, even the poorest citizens could attend the Assembly.

31190.q: Which practice did Solon abolish for Athenian citizens?
31190.e: After Solon, anyone who could not pay their debts could no longer be enslaved. He even had Athenians who had already been sold brought back.
31190.m: Solon banned Athenians from being enslaved because of debt.

31191.q: Whose proverbially harsh laws did Solon largely replace?
31191.e: Draco’s laws from around 621 BC prescribed the death penalty for many offences. Solon kept only the laws on homicide.
31191.m: Solon replaced most of Draco’s laws.

31192.q: According to tradition, what did Solon do immediately after his reforms?
a: He went travelling for ten years
He went to war against Sparta
31192.e: Solon left Athens so that nobody could force him to change his laws. The Athenians had sworn to leave them unchanged for a certain time.
31192.m: After his reforms Solon travelled abroad to protect his laws.

31193.q: Around which year did Cleisthenes carry out his reforms in Athens?
31193.e: After the fall of the tyrant Hippias, Cleisthenes pushed through a reorganisation of the citizen body around 508/507 BC. It is seen as the foundation of Athenian democracy.
31193.m: The reforms of Cleisthenes around 508 BC laid the foundation of democracy.

31194.q: Into how many new tribes (phylai) did Cleisthenes divide the citizens of Attica?
31194.e: Each of the ten tribes was made up of parts of the city, the coast and the inland area. This weakened the old ties to noble families.
31194.m: Cleisthenes created ten tribes from all parts of the country.

31195.q: How many members did the Council (Boule) have after Cleisthenes’ reform?
31195.e: Each of the tribes provided 50 councillors, chosen by lot. The Council prepared the decisions of the Assembly.
31195.m: The Council of Cleisthenes had 500 members.

31196.q: What were the local communities called that Cleisthenes made the smallest political unit of Attica?
31196.e: Every citizen was registered in a deme and from then on added its name to his own. The demes were grouped via the trittyes into the tribes.
31196.m: The demes were the basic units of Cleisthenes’ system.

31197.q: In which square in Athens did the vote for ostracism take place?
31197.e: For an ostracism, an area of the Agora was fenced off. Citizens cast their votes separately by tribe.
31197.m: Ostracism took place in the Agora.

31198.q: For how many years did someone banished by ostracism have to leave Athens?
31198.e: The banished person had to leave Attica for ten years. After that he could return and exercise his rights again.
31198.m: Ostracism meant banishment for ten years.

31199.q: According to tradition, how many votes at least were needed for an ostracism to be valid?
31199.e: Ancient sources mention a quorum of 6000 votes. It is disputed whether this number had to be reached in total or for one single person.
31199.m: An ostracism needed at least 6000 votes.

31200.q: Which politician, who had earlier pushed for the expansion of the Athenian fleet, was ostracised around 471 BC?
31200.e: Themistocles had made Athens a sea power, but was later seen as too powerful. In the end he fled to the Persian Empire.
31200.m: Even Themistocles was banished by ostracism.

31201.q: What did the Athenians write on the pieces of pottery during an ostracism?
a: Their preferred candidate for an office
31201.e: Each citizen scratched the name of the man he wanted to banish. The shards are called “ostraka” in Greek, hence the name ostracism.
31201.m: In an ostracism, people scratched names on pottery shards.

31202.q: Which temple on the Acropolis was built from 447 BC under the leadership of Pericles?
31202.e: The Parthenon was dedicated to the goddess Athena Parthenos and paid for with funds of the Delian League. It is seen as the high point of classical architecture.
31202.m: The Parthenon was built in the time of Pericles.

31203.q: What innovation did Pericles introduce for the jurors of the people’s courts?
31203.e: With jury pay, poorer citizens could also take part in the courts without losing wages. This strengthened the participation of ordinary citizens.
31203.m: Pericles paid the jurors a daily allowance.

31204.q: What did Pericles’ citizenship law of 451/450 BC lay down?
a: Both parents had to be Athenian
31204.e: Only someone with an Athenian father and an Athenian mother counted as a citizen. The law therefore clearly restricted citizenship.
31204.m: From Pericles on, an Athenian needed two Athenian parents.

31205.q: Which office did Pericles hold for many years through annual re-election?
31205.e: The ten strategoi (generals) were elected every year and could be re-elected. Pericles used this office as the basis of his leading role.
31205.m: Pericles led Athens as a strategos who was elected again and again.

31206.q: Which roofed building for musical performances did Pericles have built on the southern slope of the Acropolis?
31206.e: According to tradition, the roof of the Odeon of Pericles was reminiscent of Xerxes’ tent. Musical competitions were held there.
31206.m: Pericles had an Odeon built for music competitions.

31207.q: What was the name of Pericles’ partner, who came from Miletus?
31207.e: Aspasia was considered highly educated and was often mocked by the comic poets. Because she was not Athenian, Pericles could not legally marry her.
31207.m: Aspasia of Miletus was Pericles’ partner.

31208.q: Which sculptor directed the design of the buildings on the Acropolis under Pericles?
31208.e: Phidias created the gold and ivory statue of Athena in the Parthenon. Later he also made the statue of Zeus at Olympia.
31208.m: Phidias was the leading artist on Pericles’ Acropolis.

31209.q: Where did the Athenians defeat the Persian landing army in 490 BC?
31209.e: The Athenian army under Miltiades beat the Persians on the plain of Marathon. Salamis, Thermopylae and Plataea came only later, during Xerxes’ campaign of 480/479 BC.
31209.m: At Marathon the Athenians defeated the Persians in 490 BC.

31210.q: Which polis led the Hellenic League against Xerxes in 481 BC?
31210.e: Sparta was considered the strongest land power and was therefore given supreme command on land and at sea. Thebes, by contrast, later sided with the Persians.
31210.m: Sparta led the Hellenic League against Xerxes.

31211.q: In which battle in 479 BC did the Greeks destroy the rest of the Persian fleet on the coast of Asia Minor?
31211.e: At Mycale the Greeks attacked the Persian camp on land and burned the ships. Afterwards the Ionian cities rose up again.
31211.m: With the victory at Mycale the war moved to Asia Minor.

31212.q: According to Herodotus, who betrayed to the Persians the mountain path they used to get round the Greeks at Thermopylae?
31212.e: Ephialtes of Trachis led the Persians along a path to the rear of the Greeks. His name is still a byword for a traitor today.
31212.m: Ephialtes betrayed the way round Thermopylae to the Persians.

31213.q: Which Persian king watched his fleet’s defeat at Salamis from the shore in 480 BC?
31213.e: According to Herodotus, Xerxes had a throne set up on the coast to watch the battle. After the defeat he returned to Asia.
31213.m: Xerxes witnessed the defeat of his fleet at Salamis.

31214.q: Which revolt is seen as the trigger of the Persian Wars?
31214.e: From 500/499 BC the Greek cities of Asia Minor rose up against the Persians and were supported by Athens. Darius wanted to punish Athens for this.
31214.m: The Ionian Revolt led to the Persian Wars.

31215.q: In which land battle in 479 BC was the Persian army in Greece finally defeated?
31215.e: At Plataea a Greek army under the Spartan Pausanias won. This meant the Persian invasion of mainland Greece had failed.
31215.m: The Battle of Plataea ended the Persian invasion of Greece.

31216.q: According to Herodotus, which runner is said to have run from Athens to Sparta before the Battle of Marathon to get help?
31216.e: Herodotus reports that Pheidippides covered the distance of about 240 kilometres in about two days. The later legend of the run to Athens inspired the modern marathon.
31216.m: According to Herodotus, Pheidippides ran from Athens to Sparta.

31217.q: With the income from which silver mines did Athens expand its war fleet before 480 BC?
31217.e: A rich silver find at Laurion in southern Attica paid for about 200 triremes. This fleet later decided the naval Battle of Salamis.
31217.m: Silver from Laurion paid for the Athenian fleet.

31218.q: When was the Delian League founded?
31218.e: After the victory over the Persians, many islands and coastal cities joined together under the leadership of Athens. The aim was continued protection against Persia.
31218.m: The Delian League was founded in 478/477 BC.

31219.q: On which island was the treasury of the Delian League originally kept?
31219.e: The island of Delos was a sacred place of Apollo and therefore a neutral seat for the treasury and meetings. That is why it is called the Delian League.
31219.m: The League treasury was at first on the island of Delos.

31220.q: Under Pericles, what did Athens also use money from the treasury of the Delian League for?
a: For buildings such as the Parthenon
31220.e: In 454 BC Athens moved the League treasury from Delos to its own city. The money was also used to pay for splendid buildings on the Acropolis such as the Parthenon.
31220.m: From 454 BC Athens managed the League treasury itself.

31221.q: Which Athenian, known as “the Just”, fixed the first contributions of the allies?
31221.e: Aristides assessed the contributions so fairly that he kept the nickname “the Just” for it.
31221.m: Aristides the Just fixed the first contributions of the League.

31222.q: What did members of the Delian League have to provide if they did not supply their own warships?
a: They paid yearly contributions to the treasury
They supplied slaves for the silver mines
31222.e: These contributions were called phoros. Many members preferred to pay money rather than supply ships. This mainly benefited the Athenian fleet.
31222.m: The members of the League paid the phoros.

31223.q: What happened to members who wanted to leave the Delian League?
a: Athens forced them to stay by force
They had to emigrate to Persia
31223.e: When Naxos wanted to leave around 470 BC, the island was besieged and subdued by Athens. In this way the alliance increasingly turned into Athenian rule.
31223.m: Athens prevented members leaving the League by force.

31224.q: Which great war followed Athens’ growing claim to power in the Delian League?
31224.e: Sparta and its allies feared the growing power of Athens. In 431 BC the Peloponnesian War began, which Athens lost in 404 BC. This also ended the League.
31224.m: The Peloponnesian War ended the first Delian League.

31225.q: In which period did the Peloponnesian War take place?
31225.e: The war between Athens and Sparta and their allies lasted, with interruptions, 27 years. It ended with the surrender of Athens.
31225.m: The Peloponnesian War lasted from 431 to 404 BC.

31226.q: What is the first phase of the Peloponnesian War, from 431 to 421 BC, called?
31226.e: It is named after the Spartan king Archidamus II, who invaded Attica every year.
31226.m: The first phase of the war is called the Archidamian War after Archidamus.

31227.q: What is the peace called that ended the first phase of the Peloponnesian War in 421 BC?
31227.e: The Athenian politician Nicias negotiated it. It was meant to last 50 years, but held for only a few years.
31227.m: The Peace of Nicias of 421 BC brought only a short pause.

31228.q: Which Athenian politician pushed for the Sicilian Expedition and then defected to Sparta?
31228.e: During the expedition in 415 BC Alcibiades was recalled because of a religious offence. He fled and then advised the Spartans.
31228.m: Alcibiades changed sides several times in the Peloponnesian War.

31229.q: In which naval battle in 405 BC did Athens lose almost its entire fleet?
31229.e: The Spartans surprised the Athenian ships at the Hellespont while the crews were on land. After that Athens could no longer be supplied and surrendered.
31229.m: The defeat at Aegospotami decided the Peloponnesian War.

31230.q: Why did the surrender of Spartan hoplites at Pylos in 425 BC shock the Greek world?
a: Spartans were seen as warriors who never give up
Sparta had never fought a war before
It was the first naval battle in history
31230.e: On the island of Sphacteria almost 300 hoplites surrendered, including about 120 Spartiates. Until then people had believed Spartans would rather die than surrender.
31230.m: The surrender at Pylos destroyed the myth of the invincible Spartans.

31231.q: Which neutral island did Athens conquer in 416 BC, after which the men were killed and the women and children enslaved?
31231.e: The inhabitants wanted to remain neutral, but Athens demanded submission. The event is seen as an example of ruthless power politics.
31231.m: Athens acted brutally against the island of Melos in 416 BC.

31232.q: What is the oligarchic government called that was installed after Athens’ defeat in 404 BC?
31232.e: The Thirty ruled with Sparta’s support and had many opponents killed. As early as 403 BC democracy was restored.
31232.m: After the war the Thirty Tyrants briefly ruled Athens.

31233.q: Why did Thucydides have plenty of time to collect material for his history?
a: He was banished from Athens for 20 years
He was bedridden after an injury
He spent years in prison in Sparta
He lived as a priest at Delphi
31233.e: After a failure as a general in 424 BC, Thucydides was banished. This also let him talk to Spartans and their allies.
31233.m: Thucydides wrote his work in exile.

31234.q: What is striking about Thucydides’ work on the Peloponnesian War?
a: It breaks off before the end of the war
It tells the war from the gods’ point of view
31234.e: The work ends in the middle of the events of 411 BC, but the war lasted until 404 BC. The rest was described by other authors such as Xenophon.

31235.q: Which historian continued Thucydides’ work with his “Hellenica”?
31235.e: Xenophon picked up exactly where Thucydides had stopped. His Hellenica goes up to 362 BC.

31236.q: How did Thucydides himself describe his history?
a: As a possession for all time
As a song of the Muses
As a mirror of the gods
31236.e: Thucydides wrote that his work was not a showpiece for the moment, but “a possession for all time”. It was meant to help people understand future events.
31236.m: Thucydides wanted his work to be a possession for all time.

31237.q: What does Thucydides give as the “truest cause” of the Peloponnesian War?
a: The abduction of a king’s daughter
31237.e: Thucydides distinguished between the outward occasions and the deeper cause. He saw the latter in the growth of Athens, which frightened Sparta.
31237.m: Thucydides distinguished between the occasion and the deeper cause of a war.

31238.q: What is a modern term for the danger of war between a rising and an established power?
31238.e: The political scientist Graham Allison coined the term, based on the cause of war described by Thucydides. It is often applied to the relationship between the USA and China.
31238.m: The Thucydides Trap describes the rivalry between an old and a new great power.

31239.q: Which city in Asia Minor did Herodotus come from?
31239.e: Herodotus was born in Halicarnassus, today’s Bodrum in Turkey. Later he lived for a long time in Athens, among other places.

31240.q: Which horse-riding people north of the Black Sea does Herodotus describe in detail in his fourth book?
31240.e: Herodotus describes the customs, burials and warfare of the Scythians. He also reports on Darius’ unsuccessful campaign against them.
31240.m: Herodotus described the Scythians in the fourth book of his Histories.

31241.q: After which figures were the nine books of Herodotus’ “Histories” later named?
31241.e: Ancient scholars divided the work into nine books and gave each one the name of one of the nine Muses. The first book is called Clio.
31241.m: The nine books of Herodotus bear the names of the Muses.

31242.q: To which country does Herodotus devote the entire second book of his Histories?
31242.e: Herodotus describes the landscape, customs and history of Egypt in detail. The saying that the country is a gift of the Nile comes from him.
31242.m: Herodotus described Egypt as a gift of the Nile.

31243.q: In Herodotus, which rich king talks with Solon about who the happiest person is?
31243.e: The Lydian king Croesus thinks he is the happiest person, but Solon warns that nobody should be called happy before his death. Later Croesus loses his kingdom.
31243.m: In Herodotus, Solon warns the rich Croesus against arrogance.

31244.q: Which war is at the centre of Herodotus’ “Histories”?
31244.e: Herodotus wanted to explain how the war between Greeks and Persians came about. The Peloponnesian War was later described by Thucydides. Herodotus spent his last years in the colony of Thurii in southern Italy.
31244.m: Herodotus wrote the history of the Persian Wars.

31245.q: With which event is the Hellenistic period usually said to begin?
a: The death of Alexander the Great
31245.e: After Alexander’s death in 323 BC, Greek culture spread throughout his huge former empire. This period is called the Hellenistic Age.
31245.m: The Hellenistic Age begins with the death of Alexander the Great.

31246.q: With which event in 30 BC does the Hellenistic period usually end?
a: Egypt’s incorporation into the Roman Empire
31246.e: After the death of Cleopatra VII, Egypt became a Roman province. With that the last great Hellenistic kingdom had disappeared.
31246.m: The Hellenistic Age ends in 30 BC with the Roman conquest of Egypt.

31247.q: What mainly characterises the Hellenistic period?
a: The spread of Greek culture as far as Egypt and Asia
The golden age of Athenian democracy
The Greeks’ retreat to their peninsula
31247.e: After Alexander’s conquests, the Greek language, art and science spread across the whole East. The term was coined in the 19th century by the historian Johann Gustav Droysen.
31247.m: In the Hellenistic Age, Greek culture spread across the whole East.

31248.q: What is the common Greek language called that spread across the whole eastern Mediterranean in the Hellenistic period?
31248.e: Koine developed mainly from the Attic dialect. The New Testament is also written in Koine.
31248.m: Koine was the world language of the Hellenistic period.

31249.q: What was the name of the school that the philosopher Epicurus founded in Athens around 306 BC?
31249.e: Epicurus taught in a garden, in Greek Kepos, where women and slaves were also welcome. The aim of his teaching was a life without fear and pain.
31249.m: Epicurus founded the school of the Garden in Athens.

31250.q: Which Hellenistic sculpture in the Louvre shows a winged goddess of victory on the prow of a ship?
31250.e: The statue was probably made in the 2nd century BC and was found on the island of Samothrace in 1863. Its flowing robe is typical of Hellenistic art.
31250.m: The Winged Victory of Samothrace is a masterpiece of Hellenistic sculpture.

31251.q: Which of Alexander’s generals founded the royal dynasty that ruled Egypt until 30 BC?
31251.e: After Alexander’s death Ptolemy secured Egypt and took the title of king in 305/304 BC. All male rulers of the dynasty bore the name Ptolemy.
31251.m: Ptolemy I founded the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt.

31252.q: Which successor kingdom at times covered most of the former Persian Empire?
31252.e: Seleucus I at times ruled from Asia Minor to the border of India. The empire, however, shrank greatly over time.
31252.m: The Seleucid Empire was the largest successor kingdom by area.

31253.q: What happened to the empire of Alexander the Great after his death in 323 BC?
a: His generals fought over it and divided it up
It stayed united under his son
It was immediately conquered by Rome
It went back to the Persian Empire
31253.e: The generals were called the Diadochi, meaning successors. At the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BC the last attempt to unite the empire under one ruler failed.
31253.m: Alexander’s empire broke up into the successor kingdoms.

31254.q: Which power in the end conquered the Hellenistic kingdoms one after the other?
31254.e: Rome defeated the Antigonids in Macedonia in 168 BC, inherited Pergamon in 133 BC and made Egypt a province in 30 BC.
31254.m: The successor kingdoms fell to Rome one by one.

31255.q: How did the Hellenistic kingdom of Pergamon pass to Rome in 133 BC?
a: The last king left it to Rome in his will
Rome conquered it in a naval battle
It joined by a popular vote
31255.e: King Attalus III of the Attalid dynasty died without heirs and left his kingdom to the Romans. It became the province of Asia.
31255.m: Pergamon passed to Rome by inheritance in 133 BC.

31256.q: Which city on the River Orontes, later capital of the Seleucid Empire, did Seleucus I found around 300 BC?
31256.e: Seleucus named the city after his father Antiochus. Antioch became one of the largest cities of the ancient world.
31256.m: Seleucus I founded Antioch on the Orontes.

31257.q: Which culture spread through the successor kingdoms in the eastern Mediterranean and the Orient?
31257.e: In the successor kingdoms, Greek became the language of administration, trade and education. This period is called the Hellenistic Age.
31257.m: In the Hellenistic Age, Greek culture spread across the whole East.

31258.q: What work were the scholars at the Library of Alexandria particularly known for?
a: They compared copies and produced reliable editions of texts
They printed books in large numbers
They translated all the books into Latin
31258.e: Scholars such as Aristophanes of Byzantium examined different copies of old works. He is also said to have introduced the Greek accent marks to preserve pronunciation.
31258.m: Reliable editions of old texts were produced in Alexandria.

31259.q: What is believed today about the end of the Library of Alexandria?
a: It was probably lost gradually over centuries
It was moved to Rome and preserved there
31259.e: A fire during Caesar’s fighting in 48 BC is said to have destroyed books. Later came wars and, in AD 391, the destruction of the daughter library in the Serapeum. There was probably no single end.
31259.m: The Library of Alexandria did not disappear all at once.

31260.q: Which poet did the scholars of the Library of Alexandria study particularly intensively?
31260.e: Scholars such as Aristarchus of Samothrace examined which lines in the Iliad and the Odyssey had been added later. Their work still shapes editions of Homer today.
31260.m: The scholars of Alexandria studied Homer above all.

31261.q: According to ancient tradition, how did the kings of Egypt obtain new writings for the library?
a: By copying books on ships in the harbour
By exchanging books only for gold
31261.e: Books on arriving ships were confiscated and copied. The owners often got only the copy back.
31261.m: The Library of Alexandria even had books from ships copied.

31262.q: According to legend, which writing material came about because Egypt stopped supplying papyrus to a rival library?
31262.e: According to legend, a Ptolemaic king banned the export of papyrus to Pergamon, whereupon people there improved animal skins. The name parchment recalls this city.
31262.m: The name parchment goes back to the city of Pergamon.

31263.q: Which international organisation supported Egypt in building the modern Bibliotheca Alexandrina and organised the architecture competition in 1988?
31263.e: UNESCO worked closely with Egypt. The competition was won by the Norwegian architecture firm Snøhetta.
31263.m: UNESCO helped build the Bibliotheca Alexandrina.

31264.q: According to tradition, which translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek was made in Alexandria?
31264.e: According to legend, 72 Jewish scholars translated the scriptures on the orders of an Egyptian king. The name means “seventy”.
31264.m: The Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.

31265.q: Which substance did Thales of Miletus consider the origin (arche) of all things?
31265.e: Thales saw water as the origin of all things. In doing so he was the first to look for a natural rather than a mythical explanation of the world.
31265.m: Thales of Miletus declared water the basic substance of all things.

31266.q: According to Herodotus, which natural event is Thales said to have predicted?
31266.e: According to Herodotus, Thales announced a solar eclipse, usually dated to 585 BC. It is said to have ended a battle between the Lydians and the Medes.
31266.m: Thales is said to have predicted a solar eclipse.

31267.q: Which statement about a river is attributed to Heraclitus?
a: You cannot step into the same river twice.
All rivers flow back into the sea.
The river is the father of all things.
The river mirrors the world of ideas.
31267.e: The image of the river stands for Heraclitus’ teaching of constant change, often summed up as “panta rhei” (everything flows).
31267.m: Heraclitus taught that everything is constantly changing.

31268.q: Which element did Heraclitus regard as the basic principle of the world?
31268.e: For Heraclitus, fire was the symbol of constant change and the basic principle of the cosmos. Because of his puzzling language he was called “the Obscure”.
31268.m: Heraclitus saw fire as the basic principle of the world.

31269.q: Which city in Asia Minor did Heraclitus come from?
31269.e: Heraclitus lived around 500 BC in Ephesus on the west coast of Asia Minor. He came from a noble family of the city.

31270.q: Which term did Anaximander use for the boundless origin of all things?
31270.e: Anaximander, a pupil of Thales, called the origin “apeiron”, the boundless. It was not meant to resemble any known substance.
31270.m: Anaximander called the origin the boundless.

31271.q: Which Presocratic philosopher saw air as the basic substance?
31271.e: Anaximenes of Miletus believed that all other substances came about through the thickening and thinning of air.
31271.m: Anaximenes considered air the basic substance.

31272.q: Which Presocratic philosopher developed, together with Leucippus, the theory of indivisible smallest particles?
31272.e: Democritus assumed that everything consists of indivisible particles (“atomos”) and empty space. The word “atom” comes from this.
31272.m: Democritus is seen as the founder of ancient atomic theory.

31273.q: In which work by Plato is the Allegory of the Cave found?
31273.e: The Allegory of the Cave is in the seventh book of the “Republic”. It shows the soul’s ascent from the shadows to knowledge of the Good.
31273.m: The Allegory of the Cave is in Plato’s Republic.

31274.q: Into which three parts did Plato divide the human soul?
31274.e: Plato distinguished the rational, the spirited and the desiring part. Justice prevails when reason guides the other two parts.
31274.m: Plato divided the soul into reason, spirit and appetite.

31275.q: In which of Plato’s dialogues is the legend of Atlantis told?
31275.e: In the “Timaeus” and the “Critias”, Plato tells of the island power of Atlantis, which is said to have sunk into the sea. Most researchers think Plato invented it.
31275.m: Plato tells of Atlantis in the Timaeus and the Critias.

31276.q: According to Plato’s theory of Forms, what is the actual, true reality?
31276.e: For Plato, the things we perceive with our senses are only imperfect copies of eternal Forms. Only the Forms are truly unchanging.
31276.m: For Plato, the eternal Forms are the true reality.

31277.q: What does Plato call the knowing of the Forms, which he interprets as a recollection by the soul?
31277.e: According to Plato, the immortal soul saw the Forms before birth. Learning is therefore recollection (anamnesis), as shown for example in the “Meno”.
31277.m: Plato understood learning as the soul’s recollection.

31278.q: Which Form holds the highest place in Plato’s theory of Forms?
31278.e: In the “Republic”, Plato compares the Form of the Good to the sun. It makes all the other Forms knowable.
31278.m: For Plato, the highest Form is the Form of the Good.

31279.q: What is the form of reasoning developed by Aristotle, made up of two premises and a conclusion, called?
31279.e: An example is: All humans are mortal; Socrates is a human; therefore Socrates is mortal.
31279.m: Aristotle founded logic with the syllogism.

31280.q: How did Aristotle describe human beings in his “Politics”?
31280.e: Aristotle called the human being a social creature that by nature lives in the polis.
31280.m: For Aristotle, the human being is a social creature.

31281.q: What is the highest goal of human action in Aristotle’s ethics?
31281.e: Eudaimonia means a fulfilled, happy life. It is pursued for its own sake and achieved through virtuous activity.
31281.m: For Aristotle, the highest goal is eudaimonia.

31282.q: In his theory of the four causes, which cause does Aristotle name besides the material, formal and efficient causes?
31282.e: The final cause (causa finalis) asks what a thing is for. A house, for example, exists to provide shelter.
31282.m: Aristotle distinguished material, formal, efficient and final causes.

31283.q: Who founded the Stoa in Athens around 300 BC?
31283.e: Zeno came from Citium on Cyprus and taught in Athens. He should not be confused with the Presocratic Zeno of Elea.
31283.m: The Stoa was founded by Zeno of Citium.

31284.q: Which state of freedom from passions did the Stoics strive for?
31284.e: Apatheia does not mean indifference, but that reason is not ruled by emotions such as anger or fear.
31284.m: The Stoics strove for freedom from passions.

31285.q: Which Roman emperor wrote the Stoic “Meditations”?
31285.e: Marcus Aurelius (emperor from 161 to 180) wrote his notes in Greek, partly during campaigns on the Danube.

31286.q: Which Stoic philosopher was tutor and adviser to Emperor Nero?
31286.e: Seneca helped shape Nero’s early reign. Later he was suspected of conspiracy and forced to commit suicide in AD 65.

31287.q: Which Stoic was originally a slave?
31287.e: Epictetus came from Hierapolis in Phrygia and was a slave in Rome. His pupil Arrian wrote down his teachings in the “Handbook” (Enchiridion).
31287.m: The Stoic Epictetus was once a slave.

31288.q: According to Stoic ethics, how should people live?
a: In harmony with nature and reason
As withdrawn as possible in a garden
By the laws of the gods alone
31288.e: The Stoics saw the world as pervaded by a rational world order (logos). Whoever lives according to reason lives according to nature.
31288.m: The Stoics wanted to live in harmony with nature.

31289.q: In which city did Epicurus found his school of philosophy, “the Garden”?
31289.e: Epicurus was born on Samos and taught in Athens from 306 BC. Because the school met in his garden, it was called “the Garden”.
31289.m: Epicurus’ school in Athens was called the Garden.

31290.q: Which state of peace of mind did Epicurus strive for?
31290.e: Ataraxia means an untroubled soul. It comes about when you live free from fear and unnecessary desires.
31290.m: Epicurus strove for ataraxia, peace of mind.

31291.q: How did Epicurus understand pleasure, which he saw as the goal of life?
a: As the absence of pain and disturbance
As as much enjoyment and luxury as possible
31291.e: Epicurus did not mean excess, but a simple life without bodily pain or mental disturbance.
31291.m: For Epicurus, pleasure is above all freedom from pain.

31292.q: According to Epicurus, why should we not fear death?
a: Because we do not experience death while we exist
Because the soul is rewarded in the afterlife
Because the gods watch over death
31292.e: Epicurus wrote, roughly: where death is, we are not, and where we are, death is not. All sensation ends with death.
31292.m: Epicurus taught that death is nothing to us.

31293.q: Which Roman poet spread Epicurus’ teaching in the didactic poem “De rerum natura”?
31293.e: In the 1st century BC Lucretius wrote a didactic poem in six books on the nature of things, following Epicurus.
31293.m: Lucretius spread Epicurus’ teaching in De rerum natura.

31294.q: What did Epicurus think about the gods?
a: They exist but do not care about humans
They control every event in the world
They punish every sin after death
31294.e: For Epicurus, the gods live in perfect bliss and do not interfere in the world. That is why there is no need to fear them.
31294.m: According to Epicurus, the gods do not interfere in the world.

31295.q: Which statement fits the “fourfold remedy” that sums up Epicurus’ teaching?
a: Gods and death are not to be feared
Only wealth really makes you happy
31295.e: The tetrapharmakos says, roughly: God is not to be feared, death is not to be felt, the good is easy to obtain, the bad is easy to bear.
31295.m: The tetrapharmakos sums up Epicurus’ teaching.

31296.q: Which Sophist said “Man is the measure of all things”?
31296.e: With this, Protagoras of Abdera held a form of relativism: what is true depends on the person who judges.
31296.m: Protagoras called man the measure of all things.

31297.q: What especially distinguished the Sophists of the 5th century BC from Socrates?
a: They charged money for their teaching.
31297.e: The Sophists travelled around as teachers and charged fees. Socrates, by contrast, stressed that he had never taken money for conversations.
31297.m: The Sophists were paid for their teaching.

31298.q: Which skill did the Sophists mainly teach?
31298.e: In Athenian democracy you had to be able to persuade the Assembly and the courts. That is why rhetoric was in great demand.

31299.q: What was the Sophist Gorgias particularly famous for?
31299.e: Gorgias came to Athens from Sicily in 427 BC and impressed the Athenians with his showy speeches. Plato named a dialogue after him.
31299.m: Gorgias was famous for his elaborate speeches.

31300.q: In which comedy did Aristophanes portray Socrates like a Sophist?
31300.e: In “The Clouds” (423 BC), Socrates runs a “Thinkery” where people learn to make weak arguments strong.
31300.m: Aristophanes mocked Socrates in The Clouds.

31301.q: Which claim for the art of speaking was Protagoras accused of making?
a: To make the weaker argument the stronger
To be able to prove the gods
To be able to cure all diseases
31301.e: To critics, this claim was proof that the Sophists sacrificed truth to persuasiveness.
31301.m: Sophists wanted to make the weaker argument stronger with words.

31302.q: What did the Greek word “sophistes” originally mean?
31302.e: The word comes from “sophos” (wise). Only through Plato’s criticism did it get the negative sense of someone who twists words.
31302.m: Sophist originally meant a wise person.

31303.q: How does the Iliad begin, and which theme dominates it?
a: With the building of the Trojan Horse
31303.e: The first word of the Iliad is “menin”, wrath. Achilles is angry with Agamemnon and withdraws from the fighting at Troy.
31303.m: The Iliad tells of the wrath of Achilles.

31304.q: To which island does Odysseus return home after his wanderings?
31304.e: After ten years of war and ten years of wandering, Odysseus reaches his home, Ithaca.

31305.q: Which Cyclops is blinded by Odysseus?
31305.e: Odysseus calls himself “Nobody”, gets Polyphemus drunk and puts out his eye.

31306.q: In the Odyssey, how does Penelope keep the suitors waiting?
a: She unpicks her weaving again at night.
She sends them on a long journey.
31306.e: Penelope promises to marry only once she has finished a shroud for Laertes, and at night she unpicks the day’s weaving.
31306.m: Penelope unpicked her weaving again at night.

31307.q: What does the so-called “Homeric Question” investigate?
a: Who wrote the epics and how they came about
31307.e: Since the 18th century, researchers have argued about whether one poet or several created the epics and what role oral tradition played.
31307.m: The Homeric Question concerns how the epics came about.

31308.q: Which tragedy by Sophocles tells of a king who unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother?
31308.e: Oedipus fulfils the oracle even though he tries to escape it. When he recognises the truth, he blinds himself.
31308.m: Oedipus the King is a major work by Sophocles.

31309.q: In Sophocles’ tragedy, whom does Antigone bury against King Creon’s ban?
31309.e: Antigone puts the divine law of burial above Creon’s order and is sentenced to death for it.
31309.m: Antigone buried her brother despite the ban.

31310.q: Which tragedian wrote “Medea”, in which an abandoned woman kills her children?
31310.e: Euripides put “Medea” on stage in 431 BC. He often showed his characters with strong inner conflicts.

31311.q: At which festival were tragedies performed in Athens?
31311.e: At the Great Dionysia in honour of the god Dionysus, poets competed against each other with tragedies.
31311.m: Tragedies were performed at the Dionysia.

31312.q: According to Aristotle’s “Poetics”, what effect does tragedy have on the audience?
a: A cleansing through pity and fear
31312.e: Aristotle calls this effect catharsis. The audience experiences pity and fear and is thereby inwardly cleansed.
31312.m: According to Aristotle, tragedy brings about catharsis.

31313.q: Which of the three great tragedians is the oldest?
31313.e: Aeschylus (about 525 to 456 BC) fought at Marathon. His “Oresteia” is the only fully surviving trilogy.
31313.m: Aeschylus is the oldest of the three great tragedians.

31314.q: Which innovation does Aristotle attribute to Sophocles?
31314.e: According to the “Poetics”, Aeschylus introduced the second actor and Sophocles the third. This made more complex dialogues possible.

31315.q: Which island did the physician Hippocrates come from?
31315.e: Hippocrates lived from about 460 to 370 BC. On Kos there was an important school of medicine and a sanctuary of Asclepius.
31315.m: Hippocrates came from the island of Kos.

31316.q: What is the collection of about 60 medical writings handed down under the name of Hippocrates called?
31316.e: The writings come from various authors over several generations. Which ones Hippocrates wrote himself is unclear.
31316.m: The Hippocratic Corpus contains the writings of Hippocratic medicine.

31317.q: Which four bodily fluids does the humoral theory of Hippocratic medicine distinguish?
a: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
31317.e: Health was seen as a balance of the four humours, illness as an imbalance. This theory shaped medicine until the 19th century.
31317.m: The theory of the four humours names blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

31318.q: How did the Hippocratic text “On the Sacred Disease” explain epilepsy?
a: Through natural causes rather than divine action
As a punishment from the gods
As the result of a curse
31318.e: The text rejects the idea that epilepsy is more sacred than other diseases. All diseases, it says, have natural causes.
31318.m: Hippocratic medicine looked for natural causes of disease.

31319.q: Which text on professional ethics is named after Hippocrates?
31319.e: In the oath, doctors promise among other things not to harm the sick and to keep confidentiality.
31319.m: The Hippocratic Oath is a basic text of medical ethics.

31320.q: In which Swiss city did the World Medical Association adopt a modern version of the physician’s pledge in 1948?
31320.e: The “Declaration of Geneva” was adopted in 1948 at the General Assembly of the World Medical Association in Geneva and has been revised several times since.
31320.m: The Declaration of Geneva is a modern form of the Hippocratic Oath.

31321.q: What did Hippocratic medicine mainly rely on when treating the sick?
a: Careful observation of the signs of illness
31321.e: Hippocratic doctors carefully observed pulse, breathing, skin and face. For example, they described the typical face of a dying person, still called the facies hippocratica today.
31321.m: Hippocratic medicine was based on careful observation.

31322.q: Which of Euclid’s postulates led to the development of non-Euclidean geometries in the 19th century?
31322.e: The fifth postulate could not be proved from the others. Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky developed geometries in which it does not hold.
31322.m: The parallel postulate is Euclid’s fifth postulate.

31323.q: What does the Euclidean algorithm give as the greatest common divisor of 1071 and 462?
31323.e: 1071 divided by 462 leaves remainder 147, 462 divided by 147 leaves remainder 21, 147 divided by 21 leaves remainder 0. So the GCD is 21.
31323.m: The Euclidean algorithm finds the GCD by repeated division with remainder.

31324.q: Which perfect number does Euclid’s formula 2 to the power (p-1) times (2 to the power p minus 1) give for p equal to 3?
31324.e: For p equal to 3 we get 2 squared times (8 minus 1), so 4 times 7 equals 28. Its proper divisors 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14 add up to 28.
31324.m: A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors.

31325.q: According to tradition, what answer is Euclid said to have given King Ptolemy I?
a: There is no royal road to geometry.
I know that I know nothing.
Give me a place to stand.
31325.e: The king wanted an easier way into geometry than the “Elements”. Euclid replied that there was no shortcut, even for kings.
31325.m: Even for kings there is no royal road to geometry.

31326.q: In which city did Archimedes live?
31326.e: Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in the Greek city of Syracuse in Sicily.
31326.m: Archimedes lived in Syracuse in Sicily.

31327.q: What buoyant force acts on a body with a volume of 2 dm³ fully submerged in water (1 kg per dm³), with g equal to 9.81 N/kg?
31327.e: The body displaces 2 dm³ of water, that is 2 kg. Its weight is 2 kg times 9.81 N/kg equals 19.62 N.
31327.m: Buoyancy equals the weight of the displaced liquid.

31328.q: Which puzzle is Archimedes said to have solved when he cried “Eureka!”?
a: Whether a crown was made of pure gold
31328.e: King Hiero II suspected the goldsmith of cheating. In the bath, Archimedes realised how he could determine the volume of the crown.

31329.q: Which fraction is an approximation of pi that goes back to Archimedes?
31329.e: Using inscribed and circumscribed 96-sided polygons, Archimedes showed that pi is just under 22/7. 22/7 gives about 3.143.
