31329.m: Archimedes showed that pi is just under 22/7.

31330.q: What was the screw named after Archimedes used for?
31330.e: A slanting spiral inside a tube carries water upwards when it is turned. The principle is still used today.

31331.q: How did Archimedes die in 212 BC?
a: A Roman soldier killed him during the capture of Syracuse.
He was banished by the Carthaginians.
31331.e: In the Second Punic War the Romans captured Syracuse. Archimedes is said to have said: “Do not disturb my circles!”
31331.m: Archimedes died during the capture of Syracuse.

31332.q: Which ratio of volumes between a sphere and its circumscribed cylinder did Archimedes prove?
31332.e: Sphere 4/3 pi r³, cylinder pi r² times 2r equals 2 pi r³. The ratio is 4/3 to 2, so 2 to 3. The figure is said to have been on his tomb.
31332.m: A sphere has two thirds of the volume of its circumscribed cylinder.

31333.q: Eratosthenes measured an angle of 1/50 of a full circle and assumed 5000 stadia between Syene and Alexandria. What circumference of the Earth did this give?
31333.e: The distance corresponds to 1/50 of the Earth’s circumference. So 5000 times 50 equals 250,000 stadia.
31333.m: Eratosthenes multiplied the distance by fifty.

31334.q: How many prime numbers up to 30 remain in the Sieve of Eratosthenes?
31334.e: After crossing out the multiples of 2, 3 and 5, you are left with 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29, so 10 numbers.
31334.m: The Sieve of Eratosthenes crosses out all multiples of known primes.

31335.q: What nickname did his contemporaries give Eratosthenes?
31335.e: He was very good in many fields but was never seen as the very best in any, hence “Beta”, the second letter.

31336.q: In which city did Eratosthenes run the famous library?
31336.e: Eratosthenes came from Cyrene in today’s Libya. King Ptolemy III brought him to Alexandria, where he ran the great library.
31336.m: Eratosthenes ran the Library of Alexandria.

31337.q: How was the Antikythera mechanism discovered around 1900/1901?
a: Sponge divers found it in a shipwreck.
Farmers ploughed it up in a field.
Archaeologists dug it up in a temple.
It was lying in a monastery library.
31337.e: Greek sponge divers came across an ancient wreck off the island of Antikythera. Only in 1902 did someone notice the gearwheels in a piece of bronze.
31337.m: The mechanism comes from an ancient shipwreck.

31338.q: What is the Antikythera mechanism considered to be today?
31338.e: Using gearwheels, it calculated the positions of the sun, the moon and probably the planets too. A device of similar complexity is known only from the Middle Ages.
31338.m: The Antikythera mechanism is considered the oldest analogue computer.

31339.q: What material are the gearwheels of the Antikythera mechanism made of?
31339.e: About 30 bronze gearwheels have survived. They are badly corroded by the seawater.
31339.m: The gearwheels of the mechanism are made of bronze.

31340.q: Where is the Antikythera mechanism kept today?
a: In the National Archaeological Museum in Athens
In the British Museum in London
In the Vatican Museums in Rome
31340.e: The fragments are on display in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.
31340.m: The mechanism is in Athens today.

31341.q: Which events in the sky could be predicted with the Antikythera mechanism?
31341.e: The mechanism used the Saros cycle of about 18 years and 11 days. After that, eclipses repeat in a similar sequence.
31341.m: The mechanism predicted eclipses using the Saros cycle.

31342.q: Which competitions does a dial on the Antikythera mechanism show?
a: The Panhellenic Games such as Olympia
The ball games of the Spartans
31342.e: In 2008 researchers discovered a scale with the names of games, including the Olympic Games. So the device also served as a calendar.
31342.m: The mechanism also showed the dates of the games.

31343.q: What was the Antikythera mechanism mainly used for?
a: Calculating the sun, moon and planets
31343.e: The gearing showed the positions of the sun, the moon and the planets, as well as eclipses. It is considered the oldest known analogue computer.
31343.m: The Antikythera mechanism was an ancient sky calculator.

31344.q: Which three orders of columns did the Greeks develop?
31344.e: The three Greek orders differ mainly in their capital, base and proportions.
31344.m: The Greeks had Doric, Ionic and Corinthian columns.

31345.q: What does the Doric column lack compared with the Ionic one?
31345.e: The Doric column stands directly on the stylobate, the top step of the temple platform.
31345.m: The Doric column stands on the stylobate without a base.

31346.q: Which plant decorates the Corinthian capital?
31346.e: The Corinthian capital is decorated with rows of acanthus leaves. It is the youngest and most ornate of the Greek orders.
31346.m: The Corinthian capital is decorated with acanthus leaves.

31347.q: What is the slight swelling of a column shaft called?
31347.e: Entasis makes the column look more alive and corrects an optical illusion in which perfectly straight columns appear pinched in the middle.
31347.m: Entasis is the swelling of the column shaft.

31348.q: Which Roman architect described the orders of columns in his ten books on architecture?
31348.e: Vitruvius wrote “De architectura” in the 1st century BC. In the Renaissance the work became the most important model for architecture.
31348.m: Vitruvius described the ancient orders of columns.

31349.q: What are the speeches in the dialogue “Symposium” about?
a: About the death of the soul
About the origin of the world
31349.e: At a banquet, the guests give speeches in praise of Eros. Socrates describes love as an ascent from a beautiful body to beauty itself.

31350.q: To which city in Sicily did Plato travel several times to win a ruler over to his ideas about the state?
31350.e: Plato visited the court of the tyrants Dionysius I and Dionysius II. His attempts to put philosophical politics into practice there failed.
31350.m: Plato’s political journeys to Sicily failed.

31351.q: In his “Metaphysics”, what does Aristotle call the first cause of all motion in the cosmos?
31351.e: So that there is no endless chain of causes, Aristotle assumes a first cause that is itself not moved. It moves everything by being desired.
31351.m: Aristotle assumed an unmoved mover as the first cause.

31352.q: According to Aristotle, which form of government is the corrupt form of kingship?
31352.e: Aristotle distinguishes good and corrupt constitutions. If one person rules only for his own benefit instead of for the good of all, kingship becomes tyranny.
31352.m: For Aristotle, kingship degenerates into tyranny.

31353.q: Where does the name of Aristotle’s work “Metaphysics” probably come from?
a: It came after the Physics in the edition of his works.
Aristotle named it after a pupil.
It was found in a temple.
It is about numbers and measurements.
31353.e: “Ta meta ta physika” means “the things after the physics”. The title probably goes back to the ordering of the writings by Andronicus of Rhodes.
31353.m: The name Metaphysics originally meant after the Physics.

31354.q: With which event does the Iliad end?
a: With the homecoming of the Greeks
31354.e: In the last book, Priam fetches his son’s body from Achilles. The fall of Troy is not told in the Iliad.
31354.m: The Iliad ends with the burial of Hector.

31355.q: What are the first four books of the Odyssey called, in which Odysseus’ son searches for his father?
31355.e: In these books Telemachus travels to Pylos and Sparta to see Nestor and Menelaus. Odysseus himself appears only afterwards.
31355.m: The Odyssey begins with the Telemachy.

31356.q: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 10 cm long and the segment p of the hypotenuse below leg a is 3.6 cm. How long is a according to Euclid’s leg theorem?
31356.e: The leg theorem states a² equals c times p. So a² equals 10 times 3.6 equals 36, and a equals 6 cm.
31356.m: By the leg theorem, the square of a leg equals the hypotenuse times its segment.

31357.q: The altitude divides the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle into segments of 4 cm and 16 cm. How long is the altitude according to Euclid’s altitude theorem?
31357.e: The altitude theorem states h² equals p times q. So h² equals 4 times 16 equals 64, and h equals 8 cm.
31357.m: By the altitude theorem, the square of the altitude equals the product of the hypotenuse segments.

31358.q: What is the name of Euclid’s main work, which served as a geometry textbook for over 2000 years?
31358.e: The “Elements” consist of 13 books. They begin with definitions, postulates and the construction of an equilateral triangle on a line segment.
31358.m: Euclid’s Elements were the standard work of geometry for over 2000 years.

31359.q: How did people in Syene know that the sun stood directly overhead there at noon on the summer solstice?
a: Its light reached the bottom of a deep well
Shadows were twice as long as usual
The moon could be seen in the sky at the same time
The stars were visible during the day
31359.e: At noon on the summer solstice, upright objects in Syene cast no shadow. In Alexandria, however, a stick cast a short shadow. From this Eratosthenes calculated the Earth’s circumference.
31359.m: In Syene the sun stood directly overhead at noon on the summer solstice.

31360.q: Eratosthenes is seen as the founder of which science because he drew a world map with lines of longitude and latitude?
31360.e: Eratosthenes wrote a work called “Geographika” and drew a world map with a grid of lines. He is therefore seen as one of the founders of scientific geography.
31360.m: Eratosthenes is seen as the father of geography.

31361.q: A cube-shaped altar is to be given double the volume. By what factor must each edge be multiplied?
31361.e: The volume grows with the cube of the edge. For double the volume you therefore need the edge times the cube root of 2, about 1.26. Eratosthenes built a device called the mesolabe for this problem.
31361.m: To double a cube’s volume, multiply the edge by the cube root of 2.

31362.q: Which Roman order of columns combines Ionic volutes with Corinthian acanthus leaves?
31362.e: The Romans created the Composite order as a splendid mixed form. An early example is the Arch of Titus in Rome.
31362.m: The Composite order combines Ionic and Corinthian features.

31363.q: What does the capital of a Doric column look like?
a: Plain, with a cushion and a slab
31363.e: The Doric capital consists of a rounded cushion (echinus) and a square slab on top (abacus). Volutes belong to the Ionic order, acanthus leaves to the Corinthian.

31364.q: Where does the Stoic school of philosophy get its name from?
a: From a painted colonnade in Athens
From an island in the Aegean
From the Greek word for calm
31364.e: Zeno taught in the “Stoa Poikile”, the painted colonnade by the market place of Athens. The whole school was named after it.
31364.m: The Stoa is named after a colonnade in Athens.

31365.q: Which two groups of Roman citizens faced each other in the Conflict of the Orders?
31365.e: The Conflict of the Orders (about 494 to 287 BC) was the struggle between the old hereditary nobility of the patricians and the rest of the citizens, the plebeians, for political equality.
31365.m: In the Conflict of the Orders, the plebeians fought the patricians for equal rights.

31366.q: What is the plebeians’ means of pressure called, in which they left the city together and refused to cooperate?
31366.e: In a secessio plebis the plebeians left Rome, according to tradition for example in 494 BC to the Sacred Mount. Without them there were no soldiers or workers, which forced the patricians to make concessions.
31366.m: With the secessio plebis the plebeians put pressure on the patricians by walking out.

31367.q: Which office came about during the Conflict of the Orders to protect plebeians from the arbitrary actions of patrician magistrates?
31367.e: The tribunes of the plebs were inviolable (sacrosanct) and could protect plebeians against official actions with their right to help and to veto.
31367.m: The tribune of the plebs was the protector of the plebeians.

31368.q: Which highest office was open to plebeians from 367 BC?
31368.e: The Licinian-Sextian laws laid down that plebeians could also become consul. Soon afterwards they regularly provided one of the two consuls.
31368.m: From 367 BC plebeians could become consul.

31369.q: How did the Conflict of the Orders in Rome end in 287 BC?
a: With legal equality for the plebeians
With the expulsion of the patricians
With the abolition of the Senate
31369.e: With the Lex Hortensia, the decisions of the plebeian assembly became law for all citizens. This essentially achieved legal equality.
31369.m: The Conflict of the Orders ended with equality for the plebeians.

31370.q: Which ban was lifted in 445 BC during the Conflict of the Orders?
a: The ban on marriage between patricians and plebeians
31370.e: The Lex Canuleia allowed marriages between patricians and plebeians. This removed an important barrier between the two orders.
31370.m: From 445 BC patricians and plebeians were allowed to marry each other.

31371.q: What is the ruling class of patrician and rich plebeian families that emerged after the Conflict of the Orders called?
31371.e: The nobility included families whose ancestors had reached the consulship, whether patrician or plebeian. This new elite dominated the Senate and the high offices.
31371.m: The nobility emerged from the Conflict of the Orders as the new upper class.

31372.q: According to tradition, around what time was the Law of the Twelve Tables written down?
31372.e: According to tradition, the body of law was created in the years 451 and 450 BC. It is Rome’s oldest written collection of laws.
31372.m: The Law of the Twelve Tables was created around 450 BC.

31373.q: According to tradition, which body drew up the Law of the Twelve Tables?
31373.e: To write down the law, the decemviri, ten men with special powers, were appointed. During their term the regular offices were suspended.
31373.m: The decemviri wrote down the Law of the Twelve Tables.

31374.q: Why was writing down the Law of the Twelve Tables especially important for the plebeians?
a: The law could be checked publicly by everyone.
Plebeians got seats in the Senate for the first time.
Plebeians were freed from military service.
31374.e: Before, it was mainly patrician priests and magistrates who knew and interpreted customary law. A written law, displayed in public, limited this arbitrariness.
31374.m: Written law protects against arbitrary interpretation.

31375.q: How far did the power of the father of a family over his children reach in early Rome?
a: Very far, even over life and death
Only up to the age of 7
It lay entirely with the state
31375.e: Paternal power (patria potestas) was very broad in the Twelve Tables. But it was limited: a son whom his father had sold three times became free.
31375.m: The Roman father had great power over his children.

31376.q: How has the content of the Law of the Twelve Tables come down to us?
a: only in fragments and quotations by later authors
on the fully preserved original tablets
in an inscription in the Colosseum
in an ancient copy held by the Vatican
31376.e: The original tablets are lost. We know the content only from quotations and mentions by writers and jurists such as Cicero or Gaius.
31376.m: We know the Law of the Twelve Tables only from quotations.

31377.q: According to Livy, where did the Romans send a delegation to study foreign laws before writing down the Twelve Tables?
31377.e: Livy reports that three envoys copied the laws of Solon in Athens. Whether this journey really took place is disputed among researchers.
31377.m: According to Livy, the Romans looked to the laws of Athens.

31378.q: Which principle did the Twelve Tables lay down for serious bodily injury if the parties could not agree?
a: A fine paid to the treasury
31378.e: The tables laid down that if a limb was destroyed and no agreement was reached, talio should apply. Usually, however, a payment was agreed.
31378.m: The Twelve Tables knew talio, retaliation in kind.

31379.q: What is the principle called that an office was always held by at least two people with equal rights?
31379.e: Through collegiality, office holders could control and block each other. In this way nobody was supposed to seize power alone.
31379.m: Collegiality shared each office among several people with equal rights.

31380.q: What is the principle called that Roman offices each lasted only one year?
31380.e: Annuality comes from the Latin annus, year. The short term of office was meant to prevent the build-up of power.
31380.m: Annuality limited each office to one year.

31381.q: Which popular assembly elected the consuls?
31381.e: The consuls were elected in the comitia centuriata, which was organised by property classes. Rich citizens had much more weight in it.
31381.m: The Centuriate Assembly elected the consuls.

31382.q: What was the senator called who stood first on the list of senators and was usually allowed to give his opinion first?
31382.e: The place of honour as princeps senatus usually went to a respected former censor from an old family. His vote at the start of a debate carried great weight.
31382.m: The princeps senatus was seen as the first and most respected senator.

31383.q: Formally, what legal character did decisions of the Senate have in the Republic?
31383.e: A senatus consultum was formally only advice. Because of the Senate’s high standing (auctoritas), however, it was usually followed.
31383.m: The Senate gave advice, but its advice carried great weight.

31384.q: What is the highest military and civil power of command that the consuls held called?
31384.e: Imperium allowed its holder to lead armies, judge cases and impose punishments. Auctoritas, by contrast, meant standing, for example that of the Senate.
31384.m: The consuls held imperium, the highest power of command.

31385.q: For what maximum period could a dictator be appointed in an emergency?
31385.e: In a crisis the dictator received sole power of command, but for six months at most. After that he had to step down.
31385.m: A republican dictator held office for half a year at most.

31386.q: What was a former consul called who governed a province with extended power of command after his year in office?
31386.e: A consul’s power was often extended (prorogued) after his year. As proconsul he then led an army or governed a province.
31386.m: A proconsul acted in place of a consul in a province.

31387.q: In which order were the most important offices of the cursus honorum held?
31387.e: The career of offices began with the quaestorship and led via the praetorship to the consulship. The aedileship could be held in between, but was not compulsory.
31387.m: The cursus honorum led from quaestor via praetor to consul.

31388.q: What did a Roman law of 180 BC lay down for the career of offices?
a: A minimum age for each office
A maximum age of 40 for consuls
The election of consuls for life
The admission of women to offices
31388.e: The Lex Villia annalis laid down how old you had to be at least for the quaestorship, praetorship and consulship. Sulla later adjusted the rules.
31388.m: The Lex Villia annalis set the minimum age for offices.

31389.q: Why did you have to spend two years without office between two offices in the cursus honorum?
a: So that nobody gained too much power too quickly
So that you could do military service
Because elections were held only every two years
Because you first had to pay off the office
31389.e: This break was called the biennium. It prevented someone from rising from office to office without a break and so becoming too powerful.
31389.m: The biennium required a two-year break between offices.

31390.q: What were the quaestors mainly responsible for?
31390.e: The quaestors managed the treasury (aerarium) and accompanied governors and generals as finance officials.
31390.m: The quaestors looked after the state’s money.

31391.q: What was the main task of the praetors?
31391.e: The praetors presided over court cases and were therefore responsible for justice. They also held military power of command.
31391.m: Praetors were responsible for the administration of justice.

31392.q: What were the aediles responsible for?
31392.e: The aediles looked after the city of Rome itself, for example streets, markets, the grain supply and the public games. Splendid games helped in later elections.
31392.m: Aediles saw to order, markets and games in Rome.

31393.q: What was the task of the censors?
a: Assessing citizens and drawing up the list of senators
Confirming laws of the popular assembly
31393.e: The censors carried out the census, the registration of citizens according to their property. They also drew up the list of senators and could remove unworthy ones.
31393.m: The censors registered the citizens and checked the senators.

31394.q: Where does the name “Punic Wars” come from?
a: from the Latin name for the Phoenicians
from the name of a Carthaginian king
from a river in North Africa
from the Latin word for punishment
31394.e: The Romans called the Carthaginians Poeni, meaning Phoenicians, because Carthage had been founded by Phoenicians. This became “Punic”.
31394.m: Punic means Phoenician, because Carthage was founded by the Phoenicians.

31395.q: Which island was mainly fought over in the First Punic War (264 to 241 BC)?
31395.e: The trigger was a request for help from the city of Messana. After that, Rome and Carthage fought for decades for control of Sicily.
31395.m: The First Punic War was mainly about Sicily.

31396.q: Which device helped the Romans in the First Punic War to fight sea battles like land battles?
31396.e: With the corvus, a boarding bridge with a hook, the Romans fastened their ships to the enemy’s. Their legionaries could then fight on board, for example in the victory at Mylae in 260 BC.
31396.m: With the corvus the Romans turned sea battles into close combat.

31397.q: What did Sicily become after the First Punic War?
31397.e: After the victory in 241 BC Sicily came under Roman rule and became the first province outside Italy, governed by a governor.
31397.m: Sicily was the first Roman province.

31398.q: Which river in Spain was agreed in 226 BC as the border between the Roman and Carthaginian spheres of influence?
31398.e: In the Ebro Treaty, Carthage promised not to cross the Ebro with warlike intent. The dispute over the area south of it later led to the next war.
31398.m: The Ebro Treaty set a border in Spain.

31399.q: In which battle was the Second Punic War decided in 202 BC?
31399.e: At Zama in North Africa, Scipio, later called Africanus, defeated the Carthaginian army. Carthage then had to accept a harsh peace.
31399.m: The Second Punic War ended with a Roman victory at Zama.

31400.q: Before the Third Punic War, which North African king did Carthage go to war with, which Rome used as a pretext?
31400.e: The Numidian king Masinissa, an ally of Rome, claimed more and more Carthaginian territory. When Carthage defended itself militarily around 150 BC, Rome saw this as a breach of treaty and declared war in 149 BC.
31400.m: The conflict with Masinissa gave Rome the reason for the Third Punic War.

31401.q: Which Roman politician is said to have always ended his speeches by demanding that Carthage must be destroyed?
31401.e: The sentence “Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam” is attributed to Marcus Porcius Cato. He still saw Carthage as a danger to Rome.
31401.m: Cato the Elder repeatedly demanded the destruction of Carthage.

31402.q: In which year did Hannibal cross the Alps with his army and war elephants?
31402.e: In 218 BC Hannibal marched from Spain over the Pyrenees and the Alps into Italy, losing many soldiers on the way. Most of his roughly 37 elephants survived the Alps, but died the following winter.
31402.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BC.

31403.q: Which battle of 216 BC is seen as Rome’s worst defeat against Hannibal?
31403.e: At Cannae Hannibal surrounded the much larger Roman army from both sides. Tens of thousands of Romans died. The encirclement is still a textbook example in military history.
31403.m: At Cannae Rome suffered its worst defeat against Hannibal.

31404.q: Which important city in Campania went over to Hannibal’s side after the Roman disaster of 216 BC?
31404.e: After Rome, Capua was one of the largest cities in Italy. The Romans recaptured it in 211 BC and punished it harshly.
31404.m: Capua defected to Hannibal after Rome’s defeat.

31405.q: Which nickname did Quintus Fabius Maximus receive for his strategy of avoiding open battles against Hannibal?
31405.e: Cunctator means “the Delayer”. Fabius wanted to wear Hannibal down through small skirmishes and supply problems instead of attacking him directly.
31405.m: Fabius Maximus was called Cunctator because he avoided the decisive battle.

31406.e: Hamilcar Barca was a general in the First Punic War and then expanded Carthaginian power in Spain. He is said to have made Hannibal swear eternal hostility to Rome.
31406.m: Hannibal was the son of Hamilcar Barca.

31407.q: Which city in Spain did Hannibal capture in 219 BC after a long siege, which triggered the Second Punic War?
31407.e: Saguntum was allied with Rome. After Hannibal captured it, Rome declared war on Carthage in 218 BC.
31407.m: The fall of Saguntum triggered the Second Punic War.

a: He took poison so as not to be handed over to Rome.
He fell in a battle in Spain.
He died at a great age as ruler of Carthage.
31408.e: After fleeing Carthage, Hannibal lived at royal courts in the East. When Bithynia was about to hand him over around 183 BC, he poisoned himself.
31408.m: Hannibal chose death so as not to fall into Roman hands.

31409.q: Which body was to carry out the distribution of land under the land law of Tiberius Gracchus?
31409.e: At first the commission consisted of Tiberius, his brother Gaius and his father-in-law Appius Claudius Pulcher. It checked which land was public land and assigned it.
31409.m: A commission of three men carried out the land distribution.

31410.q: What was the core of Tiberius Gracchus’ land law?
a: Distributing public land to landless citizens
31410.e: Rich large landowners used large parts of the public land (ager publicus). Tiberius wanted to limit their holdings and give the rest of the land to impoverished citizens, partly to have more farmers fit for military service again.
31410.m: The Gracchi wanted to distribute public land to poor citizens.

31411.q: What did Tiberius Gracchus’ land law lay down for rich large landowners?
a: An upper limit on the use of public land
The confiscation of all their private land
31411.e: One person could use only 500 iugera of public land, with extra allowances for sons. The rest of the land was to go to poor citizens.
31411.m: The law limited the use of public land by the rich.

31412.q: How did Tiberius Gracchus deal with the veto of his fellow tribune Marcus Octavius?
a: He had him removed from office by the popular assembly.
He accused him before the Senate.
He asked the consuls for a ruling.
31412.e: Removing a tribune of the plebs had no precedent and was seen by opponents as a breach of the constitution. This made the conflict with the Senate worse.
31412.m: Removing a fellow tribune was an unheard-of step.

31414.q: What did the grain law of Gaius Gracchus regulate?
a: cheaper grain for citizens in Rome
31414.e: The lex frumentaria of 123 BC guaranteed citizens in Rome grain at a fixed, low price. This strengthened Gaius’ support among the people.
31414.m: Gaius Gracchus provided cheap grain in Rome.

31415.q: Which emergency decree of the Senate was first used in 121 BC against Gaius Gracchus and his followers?
31415.e: With the senatus consultum ultimum, the Senate called on the consuls to protect the state by any means. The consul Lucius Opimius then acted violently against Gaius, who lost his life.
31415.m: The Senate first used the emergency decree against Gaius Gracchus.

31416.q: How many times was Gaius Marius consul?
31416.e: Marius was consul seven times in all, every year from 104 to 100 BC. This went against the usual rules of the Republic.

31417.q: Which citizens did Marius take into the army in large numbers for the first time in 107 BC?
31417.e: Previously, only citizens who owned land served. Marius also recruited people without property (capite censi), who received their equipment from the state.
31417.m: Under Marius, people without property could also become legionaries.

31418.q: What long-term political consequence did Marius’ army reform have?
a: Soldiers felt bound to their general.
The army was led entirely by the Senate.
31418.e: The soldiers expected booty and land from their general for the time after their service. This created army clienteles that powerful generals could use politically.
31418.m: After Marius, soldiers were often more loyal to their general than to the state.

31419.q: Why were legionaries mockingly called “Marius’ mules” after the reform?
31419.e: Marius made the soldiers carry their own weapons, tools and food. The long baggage train became smaller and the army more mobile.
31419.m: Marius’ soldiers carried their own baggage.

31420.q: Which animal became the standard of every legion under Marius?
31420.e: According to Pliny the Elder, in 104 BC Marius made the eagle (aquila) the only legionary standard. Losing it was seen as the greatest disgrace.
31420.m: The eagle became the emblem of the Roman legion.

31421.q: Against which Numidian king did Marius wage war as consul from 107 BC?
31421.e: The Jugurthine War in North Africa dragged on for a long time. Marius brought it to a successful end, and Jugurtha was captured in 105 BC.
31421.m: Marius ended the war against Jugurtha.

31422.q: Which peoples did Marius defeat in 102 and 101 BC at Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae?
31422.e: The migration of the Cimbri and Teutones had brought Rome heavy defeats. With his newly raised army, Marius first beat the Teutones and then the Cimbri.
31422.m: With his reformed army Marius defeated the Teutones and Cimbri.

31423.q: What did Sulla do in 88 BC as the first Roman general to do so?
a: He marched on Rome with his army.
31423.e: When his command in the East was about to be taken away from him, Sulla led his legions against his own city. This made violence with citizen troops a tool of domestic politics.
31423.m: Sulla was the first to lead a Roman army against Rome.

31424.q: Against which king did Sulla wage war in the East?
31424.e: In 88 BC Mithridates had conquered large parts of Asia Minor and had many Romans and Italians killed. Sulla defeated him in the First Mithridatic War.
31424.m: Sulla fought against Mithridates in the East.

31425.q: What are the publicly posted lists called with which Sulla declared opponents outlaws?
31425.e: Anyone on a proscription list could be killed without punishment, and their property went to the state. Murderers and informers received rewards.
31425.m: Sulla had his opponents hunted down with proscriptions.

31426.q: Which office did Sulla take on in 82 BC, but without the usual time limit?
31426.e: Sulla had himself appointed dictator for making laws and reorganising the state. Unlike earlier, no time limit was set.
31426.m: Sulla ruled as dictator without a fixed time limit.

31427.q: Which office did Sulla restrict especially severely in his reforms?
31427.e: Sulla curbed the tribunes’ right to propose laws and made it harder for them to hold further offices. The office was no longer to be used against the Senate.
31427.m: Sulla cut the tribunate of the plebs down to size.

31428.q: Which nickname, meaning “the Lucky”, did Sulla take?
31428.e: Sulla put his successes down to luck and the favour of the gods and therefore called himself Felix.
31428.m: Sulla called himself Felix, the Lucky.

31429.q: What surprising thing did Sulla do after completing his reforms?
a: He gave up power and withdrew.
He named his son as successor.
31429.e: Sulla gave up his dictatorship and lived as a private citizen in Campania until his death in 78 BC.
31429.m: After his reforms Sulla voluntarily gave up power.

31430.q: In which period did the Spartacus revolt take place?
31430.e: The revolt began in 73 BC with the escape of a few gladiators and was crushed in 71 BC. During this time the rebels defeated several Roman armies.
31430.m: The Spartacus revolt lasted from 73 to 71 BC.

31431.q: Which number great slave war of the Roman Republic is the Spartacus revolt counted as?
31431.e: The two earlier great slave wars took place in Sicily. The revolt of Spartacus was the third and took place on the Italian mainland.
31431.m: The Spartacus revolt was the Third Servile War.

31432.q: According to ancient reports, which region did Spartacus come from?
31432.e: Spartacus was a Thracian, from the area of today’s Bulgaria and northern Greece. He is said to have been captured by the Romans as a soldier.

31433.q: On which mountain did the rebels entrench themselves at the start?
31433.e: The group withdrew to Vesuvius. When the Romans surrounded them there, they are said to have climbed down on ropes made of vines and surprised the besiegers.
31433.m: At the start the rebels sought refuge on Vesuvius.

31434.q: Which Roman general decisively defeated Spartacus’ army in 71 BC?
31434.e: Crassus was given a large command and defeated Spartacus in southern Italy in 71 BC. Spartacus fell in the battle.

31435.q: Along which road did the victor have about 6000 captured rebels crucified?
31435.e: The crosses lined the road between Capua and Rome. This deterrent was meant to prevent further slave revolts.
31435.m: About 6000 rebels were crucified along the Via Appia.

31436.q: Which general wiped out a scattered group of rebels and claimed the glory of having ended the war?
31436.e: Pompey returned from Spain and intercepted about 5000 fugitives in northern Italy. Afterwards he presented himself as the real victor over the revolt.
31436.m: Pompey claimed the glory for ending the revolt.

31437.q: What was Cicero called because he was the first in his family to reach the consulship?
31437.e: A homo novus (“new man”) was a politician with no ancestors who had been consul. Cicero came from an equestrian family from Arpinum.
31437.m: Cicero was a homo novus, a newcomer without consular ancestors.

31438.q: Which work on right action did Cicero dedicate to his son Marcus in 44 BC?
31438.e: In “De officiis” (On Duties), Cicero deals with the morally good and the useful. The work had a strong influence on later European ethics.
31438.m: In “De officiis” Cicero wrote for his son about duties.

31439.q: With which words does Cicero’s first speech against Catiline begin?
a: Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?
Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres.
31439.e: The sentence means roughly “How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?”. Cicero gave the speech before the Senate in November 63 BC.
31439.m: Cicero’s first speech against Catiline begins with “Quo usque tandem”.

31440.q: Against which governor of Sicily did Cicero successfully lead the prosecution in 70 BC?
31440.e: Gaius Verres had plundered the province of Sicily. Cicero’s evidence was so overwhelming that Verres went into exile of his own accord.
31440.m: The prosecution of Verres made Cicero famous as a speaker.

31441.q: Why did Cicero have to leave Rome and go into exile in 58 BC?
a: Because he had had followers of Catiline executed without trial
Because he had taken part in Caesar’s murder
Because he had rigged an election
31441.e: The tribune Clodius passed a law outlawing anyone who had had Roman citizens killed without a trial. This was aimed at Cicero’s actions against Catiline’s conspiracy.
31441.m: Because of the execution of the Catilinarians, Cicero had to go into exile in 58 BC.

31442.q: To which close friend is one of Cicero’s great surviving collections of letters addressed?
31442.e: The letters to Titus Pomponius Atticus fill 16 books. They give a very personal insight into the politics of the late Republic.
31442.m: Cicero’s letters to Atticus are an important source on the late Republic.

31443.q: How did Cicero die in 43 BC?
a: He was killed by soldiers while fleeing.
He died in exile in Greece.
He took his own life in Rome.
He was stabbed in the Senate.
31443.e: After the formation of the Second Triumvirate, Cicero was outlawed. In December 43 BC soldiers caught up with him near Formiae and killed him.
31443.m: Cicero was killed while fleeing in 43 BC.

31444.q: What did Pompey mainly want to achieve through the First Triumvirate?
a: confirmation of his settlement in the East and land for his veterans
31444.e: After his return from the East, the Senate had long refused Pompey these demands. With his partners he was able to push them through.
31444.m: Pompey needed the alliance for his eastern settlement and his veterans.

31445.q: Which three politicians formed the First Triumvirate in 60 BC?
31445.e: Caesar wanted the consulship, Pompey land for his veterans and Crassus help for the tax farmers. Together they prevailed against the Senate. Octavian, Antony and Lepidus later formed the Second Triumvirate.
31445.m: The First Triumvirate was formed by Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.

31446.q: What was the legal status of the First Triumvirate?
a: an office created by the Senate
31446.e: Unlike the later Second Triumvirate, the First was not an official office. It was an unofficial alliance of three powerful men.
31446.m: The First Triumvirate was a private power alliance.

31447.q: Thanks to the triumvirate, which command did Caesar receive after his consulship in 59 BC?
31447.e: Through the Lex Vatinia and a decree of the Senate, Caesar received the Gallic provinces and Illyricum. From there he conquered all of Gaul.
31447.m: The triumvirate gave Caesar the command in Gaul.

31448.q: As consul in 59 BC, how did Caesar push his partners’ wishes through against the Senate?
a: He had the laws passed directly by the popular assembly
He dissolved the Senate with his army
He postponed all elections for five years
31448.e: Caesar put the laws before the popular assembly and so bypassed the Senate. His fellow consul Bibulus tried in vain to block him with religious objections.
31448.m: As consul, Caesar pushed laws through by going round the Senate.

31449.q: Which war followed the break-up of the First Triumvirate in 49 BC?
a: The civil war between Caesar and Pompey
31449.e: After the death of Crassus, Pompey moved closer to the Senate, which in 52 BC even made him sole consul. In 49 BC Caesar crossed the Rubicon and the civil war began.
31449.m: The end of the triumvirate led to the civil war between Caesar and Pompey.

31450.q: In which battle against the Parthians did Crassus die in 53 BC?
31450.e: Crassus sought military glory in the East and was beaten and killed by the Parthian horsemen at Carrhae in Mesopotamia. This left the alliance without its third member.
31450.m: Crassus fell against the Parthians at Carrhae in 53 BC.

31451.q: In which period did Caesar wage the Gallic War?
31451.e: As governor, Caesar conquered all of Gaul up to the Rhine in about eight years. The civil war followed.
31451.m: The Gallic War lasted from 58 to 50 BC.

31452.q: Which people from the area of today’s Switzerland triggered the Gallic War in 58 BC by emigrating?
31452.e: The Helvetii wanted to move to the land of the Santones on the Atlantic coast. Caesar refused to let them pass through the Roman province and pursued them.
31452.m: The departure of the Helvetii was the reason for the Gallic War.

31453.q: Which Gallic leader united many tribes in a great revolt against Caesar in 52 BC?
31453.e: Vercingetorix of the Arverni even defeated Caesar at Gergovia. Only at the siege of Alesia did he have to surrender.
31453.m: Vercingetorix led the great revolt of the Gauls in 52 BC.

31454.q: According to his own account, what did Caesar have built in only ten days in 55 BC?
31454.e: The wooden bridge led across the Rhine into the land of the Germanic tribes. After a short stay, Caesar returned and had it taken down again.
31454.m: In 55 BC Caesar crossed the Rhine on a bridge he had built.

31455.q: Which Germanic war leader did Caesar defeat in Alsace in 58 BC?
31455.e: Ariovistus, a leader of the Suebi, had settled in Gaul. Caesar beat him and pushed the Germanic tribes back across the Rhine.
31455.m: In 58 BC Caesar defeated the Germanic leader Ariovistus.

31456.q: At which siege did the Arvernian chieftain Vercingetorix have to surrender in 52 BC?
31456.e: Caesar surrounded Alesia with a double ring of siege works and also beat off a Gallic relief army. Vercingetorix surrendered and the great revolt had failed.
31456.m: With the fall of Alesia, Gallic resistance was broken.

31457.q: In which grammatical person did Caesar write about himself in his accounts of the Gallic War?
31457.e: In the Commentarii de bello Gallico it always says “Caesar” instead of “I”. This seems factual and objective, but also served his self-promotion.
31457.m: Caesar wrote about himself in the third person.

31458.q: Which of Caesar’s wives is said to have begged him after a bad dream not to go to the Senate on the day of his murder?
31458.e: Calpurnia had been married to Caesar since 59 BC. According to ancient authors, Caesar hesitated but went to the meeting after all at the urging of a conspirator.
31458.m: Calpurnia is said to have warned Caesar not to go to the Senate.

31459.q: Which title did Caesar hold from the beginning of 44 BC?
31459.e: As dictator perpetuo, Caesar held lasting, wide-ranging power. For many senators this meant the end of the free Republic.
31459.m: In 44 BC Caesar became dictator for life.

31460.q: Whom did Caesar name as his main heir in his will and adopt?
31460.e: The will was read out after the murder. The young Gaius Octavius then called himself Caesar and later, as Augustus, became the first emperor.
31460.m: Through the will, Caesar’s great-nephew Octavius became his heir.

31461.q: Who were the leading figures in the conspiracy against Caesar?
31461.e: Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus organised the deed with over 60 fellow conspirators, including former supporters of Caesar.
31461.m: Brutus and Cassius led the conspiracy against Caesar.

31462.q: According to the historian Suetonius, how many stab wounds did Caesar receive?
31462.e: Suetonius reports 23 stab wounds. According to the doctor Antistius, only one of them is said to have been fatal.
31462.m: According to Suetonius, Caesar was stabbed 23 times.

31463.q: What did Caesar’s murderers call themselves?
31463.e: They saw themselves as liberatores who were freeing the Republic from a tyrant. The people, however, reacted rather with hostility.
31463.m: Caesar’s murderers saw themselves as liberators of the Republic.

31464.q: In which battle were Caesar’s murderers defeated by the armies of Antony and Octavian in 42 BC?
31464.e: At Philippi in Macedonia, Cassius and Brutus were defeated in two battles and took their own lives.
31464.m: The struggle of Caesar’s murderers ended at Philippi.

31465.q: From which Latin term, which described Augustus as the “first citizen”, does the word “Principate” come?
31465.e: Augustus called himself “princeps”, the first among citizens. In this way he disguised the fact that he was in practice the sole ruler.
31465.m: The Principate is named after the title “princeps”.

31466.q: With special powers, what did Augustus above all secure control over?
31466.e: With an overriding power of command in the provinces with legions, Augustus in practice commanded almost the whole army. This was the basis of his power.
31466.m: Control over the army secured Augustus’ power.

31467.q: Which naval battle in 31 BC made Octavian the undisputed master of the Roman Empire?
31467.e: At Actium in western Greece, Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeated the fleet of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. After that Octavian had no serious rival left.
31467.m: At Actium Octavian decided the last civil war of the Republic.

31468.q: Which power gave Augustus the right of veto and inviolability without his holding the corresponding office?
31468.e: The tribunicia potestas gave Augustus the rights of a tribune of the plebs, such as the veto and inviolability. He even counted the years of his reign by it.
31468.m: Tribunician power was a pillar of imperial power.

31469.q: Which troops served as the imperial bodyguard in Rome from Augustus onwards?
31469.e: Augustus created the Praetorian Guard to protect the emperor. Later it often became a power in its own right in making and murdering emperors.
31469.m: The Praetorians guarded the emperor and sometimes overthrew one.

31470.q: What is the account called in which Augustus himself summed up his achievements?
31470.e: The Res Gestae are Augustus’ own report on his life and work. The best-preserved copy is the inscription on the temple in Ankara, the Monumentum Ancyranum.
31470.m: Augustus wrote down his deeds himself in the Res Gestae.

31471.q: What term do historians use for the late antique form of rule that replaced the Principate?
31471.e: From Diocletian on, the emperor appeared openly as “dominus”, lord, and was honoured with court ceremonial. The republican façade of the Principate disappeared.
31471.m: In late antiquity the Principate was followed by the Dominate.

31472.q: Who succeeded Augustus as emperor in AD 14?
31472.e: Tiberius was the stepson and adopted son of Augustus. He ruled from AD 14 to 37.
31472.m: Tiberius was the second Roman emperor.

31473.q: To which island did Tiberius withdraw in the last years of his reign?
31473.e: From AD 26 Tiberius lived on Capri and ruled from there. In Rome during this time his Praetorian prefect Sejanus gained great influence.
31473.m: In the end Tiberius ruled from the island of Capri.

31474.q: How did Caligula’s rule end in AD 41?
a: He fell fighting the Germanic tribes
31474.e: Caligula was killed in January 41 by officers of the Praetorian Guard. The Guard then proclaimed his uncle Claudius emperor.
31474.m: Caligula fell victim to a conspiracy of the Praetorians.

31475.q: Under which emperor did the lasting conquest of Britain begin in AD 43?
31475.e: In AD 43 Claudius had troops land in Britain and briefly travelled there himself. This became the province of Britannia.
31475.m: Claudius made Britain a Roman province.

31476.q: Under which emperor did Germanic tribes destroy three legions in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9?
31476.e: Arminius lured Varus and three legions into an ambush. Augustus then gave up conquering Germania up to the Elbe.
31476.m: The Varus disaster stopped expansion into Germania under Augustus.

31477.q: Under which emperor did the Great Fire of Rome rage in AD 64?
31477.e: The fire destroyed large parts of the city. Nero blamed the Christians and had many of them executed.
31477.m: After the fire of Rome in 64, Nero persecuted the Christians.

31478.q: What is AD 69, which followed the end of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, called?
31478.e: After Nero’s death in 68, Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian fought for power. Vespasian won and founded the Flavian dynasty.
31478.m: In the Year of the Four Emperors, 69, Vespasian came out on top.

31479.q: What are the emperors from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius called, whose successors were chosen by adoption?
31479.e: The emperors chose a capable man and adopted him as successor. This period is seen as the high point of the Pax Romana.
31479.m: Under the adoptive emperors the empire reached its golden age.

31480.q: In Rome, what traditionally showed that there was peace throughout the empire?
a: The gates of the Temple of Janus were closed
The temples of Vesta were open
The standards hung in the Senate
31480.e: The gates of the Temple of Janus stood open in war and were closed only in times of peace. Augustus boasted that he had closed them three times.
31480.m: A closed Temple of Janus meant peace.

31481.q: Which Roman colony lay on Lake Geneva near today’s Nyon?
31481.e: The colony was founded for veterans around 45 BC. In imperial times it was a prosperous town with a forum and basilica.
31481.m: As Colonia Iulia Equestris, Nyon was a Roman colony.

31482.q: Which Roman colonial town lay near today’s Augst and Kaiseraugst?
31482.e: Augusta Raurica was founded around 44 BC and flourished in imperial times. Today it is a large archaeological park.
31482.m: Augusta Raurica is the Roman town near Augst.

31483.q: Which town was the chief town of the Helvetii in imperial times?
31483.e: Aventicum, today’s Avenches in the canton of Vaud, was raised to the status of a colony under Vespasian. Remains of the amphitheatre and the town wall still survive today.
31483.m: As Aventicum, Avenches was the capital of the Helvetii.

31484.q: Which son of Marcus Aurelius took power in AD 180 and ended the series of adoptive successions?
31484.e: Commodus was the biological son of his predecessor. His rule was marked by arbitrariness, and he was murdered in 192.
31484.m: With Commodus unrest returned to the empire.

31485.q: Which Alpine pass in Valais, as “Summus Poeninus”, was an important Roman route to Italy?
31485.e: Under Claudius the road over the Great St Bernard was improved. At the top of the pass stood a sanctuary for Jupiter Poeninus.
31485.m: The Great St Bernard was a main Roman route over the Alps.

31486.q: What did the Latin word “limes” originally mean?
31486.e: A limes was at first a path or a cleared strip, for example between fields. Only later did the word mean the fortified frontier of the empire.
31486.m: The limes was originally a boundary path.

31487.q: Which reconstructed Limes fort in the Taunus near Bad Homburg is a museum today?
31487.e: The fort was rebuilt at the end of the 19th century at the wish of Emperor Wilhelm II. It shows vividly what a Roman fort looked like.
31487.m: The Saalburg brings the Limes in the Taunus to life.

31488.q: Why did the Romans build a fortified fort right on the Rhine near Kaiseraugst around AD 300?
a: The Rhine was once again the empire’s frontier
There was an important gold mine there
The emperor wanted to live there
It was meant to protect an amphitheatre
31488.e: After the Alamannic invasions of the 3rd century, Rome gave up the land north of the Rhine. The Castrum Rauracense secured the new frontier and was later the seat of a bishop.
31488.m: The late Roman Castrum Rauracense stood near Kaiseraugst.

31489.q: Which emperor had a stone wall built right across the island in northern England from AD 122?
31489.e: Hadrian’s Wall ran about 117 kilometres from coast to coast. Under Antoninus Pius the Antonine Wall was later built further north, but it was soon abandoned.
31489.m: Hadrian’s Wall secured the frontier of Britain.

31490.q: What do local people call the remains of the stone wall of the Raetian Limes?
31490.e: On the Raetian Limes, a stone wall replaced the older wooden palisade in the 3rd century. People later explained the remains as the work of the devil.
31490.m: The Raetian Limes is popularly called the Devil’s Wall.

31491.q: In the 1st century AD, where was the only legionary fortress in the area of today’s Switzerland?
31491.e: Three legions were stationed in Vindonissa one after another, the last being the XI Claudia until AD 101. Aventicum and Augusta Raurica, by contrast, were civilian towns.
31491.m: Vindonissa was the legionary fortress in today’s Switzerland.

31492.q: What changed on the northern frontier when Rome gave up the area behind the Limes in south-west Germany around AD 260?
a: The Rhine and the Danube formed the frontier again
The frontier moved forward to the North Sea
The Alps became the new frontier
Rome gave up frontier defence altogether
31492.e: The abandoned area was called the Agri Decumates. After that Rome secured the frontier on the Rhine and Danube rivers again.
31492.m: The Agri Decumates lay behind the Limes and were lost around 260.

31493.q: From about AD 300, how did the Romans secure the frontier on the High Rhine?
a: With a canal beside the river
31493.e: This frontier line is called the Danube-Iller-Rhine Limes. Remains of late Roman watchtowers can still be seen on the High Rhine in Switzerland today.
31493.m: Late Roman watchtowers of the Danube-Iller-Rhine Limes stood on the High Rhine.

31494.q: Why did Trajan have a large stone bridge built over the Danube?
a: For the war against the Dacians
To escape from the Germanic tribes
31494.e: The bridge near Drobeta, over a kilometre long, made it possible to move troops quickly into Dacia. It was designed by the architect Apollodorus of Damascus.
31494.m: Trajan’s Danube bridge served the war against the Dacians.

31495.q: Which emperor adopted Trajan in AD 97?
31495.e: The elderly Nerva needed the army’s support and adopted the respected general Trajan.
31495.m: Nerva adopted Trajan and began the era of the adoptive emperors.

31496.q: Against which king did Trajan wage the Dacian Wars?
31496.e: Trajan defeated Decebalus in two wars, from 101 to 102 and from 105 to 106. Dacia, in today’s Romania, became a Roman province.
31496.m: Trajan conquered the kingdom of Decebalus.

31497.q: Which monument in Rome shows the Dacian Wars on a spiral band of reliefs?
31497.e: The column was dedicated in AD 113 in Trajan’s Forum. The relief band, about 200 m long, shows hundreds of scenes from the campaigns.
31497.m: Trajan’s Column tells the story of the Dacian Wars in pictures.

31498.q: Which Parthian capital did Trajan capture in 116?
31498.e: Trajan advanced as far as the Persian Gulf and took Ctesiphon on the Tigris. Revolts, however, soon forced him to retreat.
31498.m: In 116 Trajan captured the Parthian capital Ctesiphon.

31499.q: Which famous rock city belonged to the Nabataean kingdom, which Trajan made a Roman province in AD 106?
31499.e: The Nabataean kingdom with Petra and Bostra was annexed without a major war. The new province of Arabia secured trade routes to Arabia.
31499.m: With the Nabataean kingdom, Petra came under Roman rule.

31500.q: With which governor of Bithynia did Trajan exchange famous letters, including about how to deal with Christians?
31500.e: Trajan replied that Christians should not be hunted down and anonymous accusations ignored, but those accused should be punished. The letter is an early source on Christianity.
31500.m: The letters with Pliny show Trajan’s attitude to the Christians.

31501.q: Which successor of Trajan gave up the conquests in Mesopotamia?
31501.e: Hadrian thought the new territories in the East could not be held and withdrew to the Euphrates. He relied on securing the frontiers rather than on conquest.
31501.m: Hadrian gave up Trajan’s conquests in the East.

31502.q: In which year was the Constitutio Antoniniana issued?
31502.e: The decree dates from the year 212. Part of the text survives on a papyrus in Giessen.

31503.q: Which emperor issued the Constitutio Antoniniana?
31503.e: Caracalla ruled from 211 to 217. The decree is his best-known law.

31504.q: What did the Constitutio Antoniniana lay down?
a: Citizenship for almost all free inhabitants of the empire
Freedom for all slaves in the empire
31504.e: Almost all free people in the empire became Roman citizens. This greatly reduced the importance of the difference between citizens and provincials.
31504.m: From 212, almost all free inhabitants of the empire were Roman citizens.

31505.q: Which group did not receive Roman citizenship through the Constitutio Antoniniana in AD 212?
31505.e: Citizenship applied only to free inhabitants of the empire. Slaves remained excluded, as did a small group of subjected people with lower status, the dediticii.
31505.m: Slaves did not receive citizenship in 212.

31506.q: What motive does the historian Cassius Dio give for the Constitutio Antoniniana?
31506.e: Only Roman citizens paid certain taxes such as inheritance tax. More citizens therefore meant more income for the treasury.
31506.m: According to Cassius Dio, Caracalla was mainly after money.

31507.q: Where does the name “Constitutio Antoniniana” come from?
a: From the official imperial name Antoninus
From the town of Antonina in Syria
From the month of Antoninus in the calendar
31507.e: Caracalla’s official name was Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus. “Caracalla” was only a nickname after a Gallic hooded cloak.
31507.m: The name of the decree goes back to the imperial name Antoninus.

31508.q: What are the rulers between 235 and 284, mostly raised to power by the army, called?
31508.e: During this time troops often proclaimed their commanders emperor. Many ruled only briefly and died violently.
31508.m: The soldier emperors marked the crisis of the empire.

31509.q: Why did many soldier emperors rule only for a short time?
a: Their own troops often killed them
They could only be in office for one year
They had to hand the office back to the Senate
Most of them died of the plague
31509.e: The armies proclaimed their commanders emperor and overthrew them if pay or success failed to come. Between 235 and 284 there were over 20 recognised emperors.
31509.m: Many soldier emperors were murdered by their own soldiers.

31510.q: Which emperor was taken prisoner by the Persians in AD 260?
31510.e: Valerian was captured by the Sasanian king Shapur I. A rock relief at Naqsh-e Rostam celebrates this victory.
31510.m: Valerian was the first Roman emperor taken prisoner by an enemy.

31511.q: Which emperor in 251 was the first to fall in battle against a foreign enemy?
31511.e: Decius died at Abritus in today’s Bulgaria fighting the Goths. This was a severe shock for Rome.
31511.m: Decius fell against the Goths in 251.

31512.q: What is the breakaway state called that Postumus founded in the West from 260?
31512.e: Postumus ruled over Gaul, Germania, Britain and at times Hispania. Only Aurelian won these areas back in 274.
31512.m: The Gallic Empire split off the West.

31513.q: Which ruler of Palmyra conquered Egypt and parts of Asia Minor around 270?
31513.e: Zenobia ruled on behalf of her son and greatly extended the power of Palmyra. Aurelian defeated her in 272.
31513.m: Zenobia of Palmyra challenged Rome in the East.

31514.q: Which emperor had a new city wall built around Rome from 271?
31514.e: The Aurelian Walls protected Rome against raids by Germanic groups. Large parts of them still survive today.
31514.m: The Aurelian Walls show that even Rome was no longer safe.

31515.q: What happened to the silver coin called the antoninianus in the 3rd century?
a: It was minted only in the East
31515.e: To be able to pay soldiers, the emperors added less and less silver. In the end the coins were almost just silver-plated copper, which drove inflation.
31515.m: Debasement of the coinage drove prices up in the 3rd century.

31516.q: In which year was Diocletian proclaimed emperor?
31516.e: The army proclaimed Diocletian emperor near Nicomedia in November 284. This ended the era of the soldier emperors.

31517.q: How was the Tetrarchy organised from 293?
31517.e: Each Augustus ruled with a Caesar as assistant and successor. This was meant to protect the frontiers better and avoid fights over the throne.
31517.m: The Tetrarchy was rule by four: two Augusti and two Caesars.

31518.q: Whom did Diocletian appoint as co-emperor in the West?
31518.e: Maximian became Caesar in 285 and Augustus in 286. He ruled the West, Diocletian the East.
31518.m: Maximian was Diocletian’s fellow Augustus in the West.

31519.q: What did Diocletian’s edict of 301 lay down?
a: Maximum prices for goods and wages
31519.e: The Edict on Maximum Prices was meant to slow inflation. It set upper limits for over a thousand goods and services, but had little success.
31519.m: Diocletian tried to stop inflation with maximum prices.

31520.q: Where was the palace built specially for Diocletian, in which he spent his old age after stepping down in 305?
31520.e: The palace was on the Dalmatian coast in today’s Croatia. The old town of Split is built into its walls.
31520.m: Diocletian’s Palace forms the core of the old town of Split.

31521.q: Into which new administrative units did Diocletian group several provinces together?
31521.e: Diocletian made the provinces smaller and grouped them into dioceses under a vicar. The word lives on in church administration today.
31521.m: Diocletian organised the provinces into dioceses.

31522.q: Which place in Valais bears the name of the leader of the Theban Legion, who according to legend was martyred under Maximian?
31522.e: According to legend, Maurice and his Christian soldiers at Agaunum refused to take part in persecuting Christians. The abbey there has existed since 515.

31523.q: In which modern city was Constantine proclaimed emperor by his father’s troops in 306?
31523.e: Constantine’s father Constantius Chlorus died in Roman Eboracum, today’s York. The soldiers immediately raised his son instead.
31523.m: Constantine was proclaimed emperor in York.

31524.q: Whom did Constantine defeat at the Milvian Bridge in 312?
31524.e: Maxentius ruled Rome and Italy and drowned in the Tiber. Constantine put the victory down to the help of the Christian God.
31524.m: At the Milvian Bridge Constantine won Rome.

31525.q: Which sign are Constantine’s soldiers said to have painted on their shields in 312?
31525.e: According to Lactantius, Constantine had the Greek letters chi and rho put on the shields. They are the first letters of “Christ”.

31526.q: By defeating which co-emperor did Constantine become sole ruler in 324?
31526.e: Constantine defeated Licinius at Adrianople and Chrysopolis. After that he ruled the whole empire alone until 337.

31527.q: In which city on the Moselle did Constantine reside for a long time and have a huge palace hall built?
31527.e: Trier was one of the residence cities of the Tetrarchy and, under Constantine, a centre of the West. The palace hall, today called the Basilica of Constantine, still stands.
31527.m: In Trier the Basilica of Constantine bears witness to Constantine’s residence.

31528.q: Which monument next to the Colosseum commemorates Constantine’s victory in 312?
31528.e: The arch was dedicated in 315. Many of its reliefs come from older monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius.
31528.m: The Arch of Constantine celebrates the victory over Maxentius.

31529.e: Constantine was baptised only on his deathbed by Bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia. A late baptism was not unusual at the time.
31529.m: Constantine was baptised only shortly before his death.

31530.q: In which year was the Milan agreement made?
31530.e: The two emperors met in Milan at the beginning of 313. The agreement is often called the “Edict of Milan”.

31531.q: Which two emperors made the Milan agreement?
31531.e: The occasion was the wedding of Licinius to Constantine’s half-sister Constantia. At the time the two ruled the West and part of the East.
31531.m: Constantine and Licinius reached agreement in Milan in 313.

31532.q: What did the Milan agreement grant?
a: Freedom of religion for all, including Christians
Christianity as the only state religion
A ban on all pagan cults
31532.e: Everyone was to be allowed to practise the religion they wanted. Christianity was thus permitted, but not yet the state religion.
31532.m: From 313 Christians could practise their faith freely.

31533.q: What was to happen to confiscated church property?
a: It was to be given back
31533.e: The Christians’ meeting places and goods were to be returned without payment. Those who had bought them could claim compensation from the state.
31533.m: In 313 the Christians got their property back.

31534.q: Why do experts today prefer to speak of the “Milan agreement” rather than the “Edict of Milan”?
a: It was not a formal edict but an agreement between the emperors
The agreement was never put into practice
The text was written by a bishop
It applied only to the city of Milan
31534.e: In 313 Constantine and Licinius agreed on common rules. What has survived is a letter from Licinius, quoted by Lactantius and Eusebius.
31534.m: Lactantius preserves the text of the Milan agreement.

31535.q: Which emperor had already issued an edict of toleration for the Christians in 311?
31535.e: Shortly before his death, Galerius ended the persecution in the East. The Milan agreement two years later went much further.
31535.m: Galerius ended the persecution of Christians as early as 311.

31536.q: In which year did the First Council of Nicaea take place?
31536.e: About 250 to 300 bishops gathered in the summer of 325. It is seen as the first ecumenical council.
31536.m: The Council of Nicaea took place in 325.

31537.q: Who called the First Council of Nicaea?
31537.e: The emperor wanted to secure the unity of the church and thus of the empire. He opened the council in person.
31537.m: An emperor, not the pope, called the Council of Nicaea.

31538.q: Which teaching did the Council of Nicaea condemn?
31538.e: The priest Arius of Alexandria taught that the Son was created by the Father and subordinate to him. The council rejected this teaching.
31538.m: Nicaea condemned the teaching of Arius.

31539.q: What was the main dispute at the Council of Nicaea about?
a: The relationship between God the Father and the Son
The election of a new emperor
The translation of the Bible into Latin
The division of the Roman Empire
31539.e: The Nicene Creed calls the Son “homoousios”, of the same substance as the Father. In this way the council rejected the teaching of Arius.
31539.m: According to Nicaea, the Son is of the same substance as the Father.

31540.q: On which date in the church year did the council make an important ruling?
31540.e: The council decided that all Christians should celebrate Easter on the same Sunday and not follow the Jewish calendar. The exact calculation came later.
31540.m: Nicaea brought about a common date for Easter.

a: A text still used today that sums up the Christian faith
A list of the first popes
A law against the persecution of Christians
31541.e: The creed of 325 was expanded at Constantinople in 381. In this form, Catholic, Orthodox and many Reformed churches still say it today. Athanasius of Alexandria was its leading defender.
31541.m: The Nicene Creed is still prayed today.

31542.q: In which modern country was Nicaea, the site of the first council?
31542.e: Nicaea lay in Bithynia in north-western Asia Minor, not far from Constantinople. Today it is the small town of Iznik in Turkey.
31542.m: Ancient Nicaea is today’s Iznik in Turkey.

31543.q: Which edict made Nicene Christianity the binding religion in 380?
31543.e: Theodosius and his co-emperors demanded that all peoples adopt the faith of Nicaea. In practice this made Christianity the state religion.
31543.m: From 380 Christianity was the state religion.

31544.q: Which bishop forced Theodosius to do penance in church in 390 after a massacre in Thessalonica?
31544.e: After the massacre of thousands of inhabitants, Ambrose refused the emperor communion. Theodosius did public penance.
31544.m: Ambrose showed that even an emperor had to bow to the church.

31545.q: What did laws of Theodosius ban in 391 and 392?
31545.e: Sacrifices and visits to pagan temples were made punishable. Many temples were then closed or destroyed.
31545.m: Theodosius banned the old Roman cults.

31546.q: According to tradition, which long-established competitions came to an end under Theodosius?
31546.e: According to tradition, the last ancient Olympic Games were held in 393. As a pagan festival, they no longer fitted the new religious policy.
31546.m: The ancient Olympic Games came to an end under Theodosius.

31547.q: How did many contemporaries interpret Theodosius’ victory at the Frigidus in 394?
a: As a victory of the Christians over the pagans
As a victory over the Huns
As the end of the Republic
As a victory over the Persians
31547.e: The rival emperor Eugenius was supported by followers of the old cults. Theodosius’ victory was therefore seen as a triumph of Christianity.
31547.m: At the Frigidus the Christian side won in 394.

31548.q: What happened after the death of Theodosius I in 395?
a: The empire was divided between two sons
The empire fell to the Goths
The Senate elected a new emperor
31548.e: Theodosius was the last emperor to rule the whole empire. After that the Western and Eastern empires developed separately.
31548.m: From 395 there was a Western and an Eastern Roman Empire.

31549.q: What question was at stake in the dispute over the teaching of Arius, which Theodosius wanted to end?
a: Whether Christ is of the same substance as God
Whether the pope stands above the emperor
31549.e: Arius taught that Christ was created by God and subordinate to him. The Council of Constantinople in 381, by contrast, confirmed the identity of substance and the doctrine of the Trinity.
31549.m: The Arian dispute was about the relationship of Christ to God.

31550.q: Which event around 375 is seen as the trigger of the Migration Period?
a: The advance of the Huns westwards
The division of the Roman Empire
31550.e: The Huns destroyed the realm of the Greuthungi north of the Black Sea. Many Goths then fled across the Danube into the Roman Empire.
31550.m: The Migration Period began with the onslaught of the Huns around 375.

31551.q: Which emperor fell against the Goths at the Battle of Adrianople in 378?
31551.e: At Adrianople the Goths destroyed a large part of the Eastern Roman army. The defeat showed how vulnerable Rome had become.
31551.m: Adrianople was one of Rome’s worst defeats.

31552.q: Which peoples crossed the Rhine into Gaul around the turn of the year 406/407?
31552.e: The groups moved on through Gaul as far as Hispania. The Rhine frontier was thus broken for good.
31552.m: The Rhine crossing of 406 opened Gaul to Germanic groups.

31553.q: Which Visigothic leader captured and sacked Rome in 410?
31553.e: Rome had not been taken by enemies for almost 800 years. The sack shook the whole Roman world.

31554.q: Which city in North Africa did the Vandals capture in 439 and make their centre?
31554.e: With Carthage, the Western Empire lost its richest province and important grain supplies. Under Gaiseric the Vandals also sacked Rome in 455.
31554.m: With Carthage the Vandals won the heart of North Africa.

31555.q: On which battlefield did a Roman and Germanic army under Aetius face the Huns in 451?
31555.e: Aetius and the Visigoths stopped Attila’s advance in Gaul. Attila then moved on to Italy.
31555.m: Attila was stopped on the Catalaunian Plains in 451.

31556.q: In which area did the Romans settle the Burgundians in 443?
31556.e: After a defeat by the Huns, the Burgundians received land in Sapaudia around Lake Geneva. Their kingdom later shaped western Switzerland.
31556.m: The Burgundians settled on Lake Geneva in 443.

31557.q: Which Germanic group settled large parts of today’s German-speaking Switzerland from the 5th century?
31557.e: The Alamanni spread southwards from the area north of the Rhine. Their language is the origin of the Alemannic dialects, to which Swiss German belongs.
31557.m: Swiss German goes back to the language of the Alamanni.

31558.q: Which emperor did Odoacer depose in 476?
31558.e: Odoacer deposed the young emperor and sent him into retirement. The year 476 is therefore often seen as the end of the Western Roman Empire.
31558.m: With the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 the Western Empire ended.

31559.q: What does “Augustulus”, the mocking name of the last Western Roman emperor, mean?
31559.e: Romulus Augustulus was still a boy when his father Orestes made him emperor in 475. The diminutive ending “-ulus” mocks the child emperor.

31560.q: Which title did Odoacer hold in Italy after 476?
31560.e: Odoacer did without the title of emperor and ruled as king. Formally he recognised the emperor in Constantinople.
31560.m: Odoacer ruled Italy as king, not as emperor.

31561.q: Where did Odoacer send the imperial regalia of the West?
31561.e: He sent the insignia to Emperor Zeno. This was meant to show that the West no longer needed an emperor of its own.
31561.m: Odoacer sent the imperial insignia to the East.

31562.q: How did Odoacer treat the deposed emperor Romulus Augustulus?
a: He let him live on a pension
He sent him to Persia as a hostage
31562.e: Odoacer spared the young emperor and gave him a pension. Romulus Augustulus then lived near Naples.
31562.m: The last Western emperor was not killed but pensioned off.

31563.q: Which ruler defeated and killed Odoacer in Ravenna in 493?
31563.e: The Ostrogothic king marched to Italy on behalf of the Eastern emperor. After a long siege of Ravenna, he killed Odoacer with his own hands.

31564.q: Why do some historians date the end of the Western Empire to 480?
a: A Western emperor recognised by the East lived until 480
31564.e: Julius Nepos had been driven out in 475, but for Constantinople he remained the lawful Western emperor until his murder in 480.
31564.m: Some historians date the end of the Western Empire to 480.

31565.q: Which finds in Mesopotamia prove trade contacts with the Indus civilisation?
a: Seals and beads from the Indus Valley
Iron swords from the Indus Valley
31565.e: In cities such as Ur, seals and carnelian beads from the Indus Valley have been found. Cuneiform texts mention a trading land called Meluhha, which is usually identified with the Indus Valley. The Indus script has still not been deciphered.
31565.m: Mesopotamia traded with the Indus Valley, which it probably called Meluhha.

31566.q: Which is the oldest of the four Vedas?
31566.e: The Rigveda is a collection of over a thousand hymns to the gods. It is seen as the oldest text of Vedic literature.
31566.m: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas.

31567.q: In which language are the Vedas written?
31567.e: The Vedas are written in an ancient form of Sanskrit. It belongs to the Indo-European languages.
31567.m: The Vedas are written in Vedic Sanskrit.

31568.q: How were the Vedic texts mainly passed down over many centuries?
31568.e: Priests learned the texts by heart syllable by syllable using strict recitation techniques. They were only written down much later.
31568.m: The Vedas were passed down orally for a long time.

31569.q: In the Vedic model of society, which varna did the priests belong to?
31569.e: The model has four varnas. The Brahmins were responsible for sacrifices and sacred texts.
31569.m: In the varna system the Brahmins formed the priestly class.

31570.q: To which god is the largest number of hymns in the Rigveda dedicated?
31570.e: About a quarter of the hymns in the Rigveda praise Indra, the god of thunderstorms and war. In them he defeats the serpent Vritra.
31570.m: Indra is the god most often praised in the Rigveda.

31571.q: Which Vedic god embodies the sacrificial fire and is seen as the messenger between humans and gods?
31571.e: Agni is fire itself. He carries the offerings to the gods and is therefore central to the ritual.
31571.m: Agni is the Vedic god of the sacrificial fire.

31572.q: Which writings at the end of the Vedic period deal with the relationship between Atman and Brahman?
31572.e: The Upanishads ask about the innermost self (Atman) and the ground of the world (Brahman). They still shape Indian philosophy today.
31572.m: The Upanishads teach about Atman and Brahman.

31573.q: Who founded the Maurya Empire in India around 320 BC?
31573.e: Chandragupta used the power vacuum after Alexander’s withdrawal from India. The Greek envoy Megasthenes later described his court in the “Indica”.
31573.m: Chandragupta Maurya founded India’s first great empire.

31574.q: Which noble clan did Siddhartha Gautama come from?
31574.e: Siddhartha was the son of a leader of the Shakyas. That is where his title Shakyamuni, “sage of the Shakya clan”, comes from.
31574.m: The Buddha came from the Shakya clan.

31575.q: Why are the exact dates of Siddhartha Gautama’s life disputed among researchers?
a: The texts were written down long after his death
He lived before calendars were invented
His tomb inscription has been destroyed
31575.e: His teachings were passed on orally for centuries before being written down. Dates therefore usually vary between the 6th and the 4th century BC.
31575.m: The Buddha’s dates are uncertain because the sources were written down late.

31576.q: Which path did Siddhartha choose after practising strict asceticism for years?
31576.e: He realised that neither luxury nor extreme fasting leads to liberation. That is why he taught a path between the two extremes.
31576.m: The Buddha taught the Middle Way between indulgence and asceticism.

31577.q: Which dynasty overthrew the Shang dynasty around 1046 BC?
31577.e: At the Battle of Muye, King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king. The Zhou justified their rule with the “Mandate of Heaven”.
31577.m: The Zhou overthrew the Shang around 1046 BC.

31578.q: Which ruined site near today’s city of Anyang was the late capital of the Shang?
31578.e: Yinxu means “Ruins of Yin”. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006 and has yielded many royal tombs.
31578.m: Yinxu near Anyang was the late capital of the Shang.

31579.q: What is the Shang period especially known for archaeologically?
31579.e: The Shang mastered bronze casting with piece moulds. Elaborate vessels such as ding tripods were used in ancestor worship.
31579.m: The Shang created elaborate bronze ritual vessels.

31580.q: Which wife of the Shang king Wu Ding is also known as a military commander?
31580.e: Her tomb, discovered unlooted in 1976, contained hundreds of bronzes and jade objects. Inscriptions report that she led military campaigns.
31580.m: Fu Hao was a Shang queen and general.

31581.q: Which materials did the Shang mainly use as oracle bones?
a: Cattle shoulder blades and turtle shells
31581.e: Mainly the shoulder blades of cattle and the undershells of turtles were used. They were easy to work and to write on.
31581.m: Oracle bones were mostly cattle bones and turtle shells.

31582.q: How was a question answered using oracle bones?
a: The bone was heated and the cracks interpreted
Bones were thrown and the dots counted
Bones were put in water and watched
Bones were broken and the marrow read
31582.e: Heat was applied to prepared hollows until cracks appeared. From their shape people read the ancestors’ answer and carved the question and result into the bone.
31582.m: With oracle bones, cracks caused by heat were interpreted.

31583.q: Before their inscriptions were recognised in 1899, what were oracle bones traded as?
31583.e: Pharmacies sold the bones ground up as a remedy. In 1899 the scholar Wang Yirong recognised the carved signs as ancient writing.
31583.m: Oracle bones used to be sold as dragon bones.

31584.q: What is the importance of oracle bones for the history of writing?
a: They are the oldest extensive evidence of Chinese writing
They prove the origin of cuneiform
They show the first letters of an alphabet
31584.e: The inscriptions from the late Shang period are the earliest larger bodies of text in Chinese writing. Many signs can be linked to modern Chinese characters.
31584.m: The oracle bones are the oldest larger evidence of Chinese writing.

31585.q: What role did the Confucian classics play in imperial China for a long time?
a: They formed the material of the civil service examinations
They were rules only in the army
