31585.e: Anyone who wanted to become an official had to know the Confucian texts thoroughly. The examination system lasted until 1905.
31585.m: The Confucian classics were the basis of the civil service examinations.

31586.q: Which measure was part of the standardisation under Qin Shi Huangdi?
a: Election of officials by the people
31586.e: As well as writing, measures, weights and coins, the gauge of carts was also fixed. That way carts fitted the worn ruts everywhere.
31586.m: Qin Shi Huangdi even standardised the axle width of carts.

31587.q: What does Legalism, the state philosophy under Qin Shi Huangdi, stand for?
31587.e: Legalism relied on clear laws, rewards and harsh punishments to create a strong state. The chancellor Li Si put this teaching into practice under the first emperor.

31588.q: What happened to the older border walls in the north under Qin Shi Huangdi?
a: They were joined into a longer line of defence
They were completely torn down as useless
They were handed over to the Xiongnu
31588.e: General Meng Tian had the existing walls of the earlier states joined and extended. The wall known today, however, dates mostly from the Ming period.
31588.m: Under the Qin, older border walls were joined into one line.

31589.q: Near which modern Chinese city was the Terracotta Army discovered?
31589.e: In 1974 farmers digging a well near Xi’an came across the first clay soldiers. Under the name Chang’an the city was China’s capital for a long time.
31589.m: The Terracotta Army is near Xi’an.

31590.q: According to the historian Sima Qian, what is the unopened tomb of the emperor said to contain?
31590.e: Sima Qian describes a model of the empire with streams of mercury. Soil samples above the burial mound do in fact show raised levels of mercury.
31590.m: Mercury is said to flow in the tomb of the first emperor.

31591.q: Which revolt in AD 184 decisively weakened the Eastern Han dynasty?
31591.e: Peasants influenced by Daoism rose up against hunger and abuses. The generals who crushed the revolt became so powerful that the empire fell apart in AD 220.
31591.m: The Yellow Turban Rebellion began the end of the Han.

31592.q: Which oasis town on the western edge of the Tarim Basin was an important junction?
31592.e: In Kashgar the northern and southern routes around the Taklamakan met. From there, routes led on westwards over the Pamir Mountains.
31592.m: Kashgar was a junction on the edge of the Taklamakan.

31593.q: Which Buddhist cave complex near Dunhuang bears witness to exchange along the Silk Road?
31593.e: The Mogao Caves contain hundreds of painted caves from over a thousand years. In one cave tens of thousands of old manuscripts were also found.
31593.m: The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang are a treasure of the Silk Road.

31594.q: Which people, centred around Samarkand, dominated the caravan trade for a long time?
31594.e: The Sogdians spoke an Iranian language and had trading colonies as far as China. Their language served as a trading language for a long time.
31594.m: The Sogdians were the great traders of the Silk Road.

31595.q: What are the Olmecs especially known for?
31595.e: The Olmecs created colossal heads of basalt, some almost three metres high. They probably show rulers.
31595.m: The colossal heads are the trademark of the Olmecs.

31596.q: Where is the ruined city of Teotihuacán?
a: On the Pacific coast of Peru
31596.e: Teotihuacán is about 40 kilometres north-east of Mexico City. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
31596.m: Teotihuacán lies in the Valley of Mexico.

31597.q: Who gave the city the name Teotihuacán?
31597.e: The name comes from Nahuatl and is often interpreted as “place where one becomes a god”. What the inhabitants called their city themselves is unknown.
31597.m: The name Teotihuacán was given only by the Aztecs.

31598.q: Which is the largest pyramid in Teotihuacán?
31598.e: The Pyramid of the Sun is about 65 metres high and one of the largest pyramids in the Americas. The Pyramid of the Moon stands at the northern end of the main axis.
31598.m: The Pyramid of the Sun is the largest building in Teotihuacán.

31599.q: What is the great main axis of Teotihuacán called?
31599.e: The Aztecs thought the buildings along the axis were tombs. That is where the name Calzada de los Muertos comes from.
31599.m: The main axis of Teotihuacán is called the Avenue of the Dead.

31600.q: About how many people lived in Teotihuacán at its height around AD 450?
31600.e: Estimates range from about 100,000 to 125,000 inhabitants. That made the city one of the largest in the world at the time.
31600.m: At its height Teotihuacán had about 100,000 inhabitants.

31601.q: Which civilisation in today’s Guatemala was strongly influenced by Teotihuacán in the 4th century?
31601.e: Maya inscriptions report how in AD 378 a general linked to Teotihuacán arrived in Tikal. Shortly afterwards a new line of rulers came to power there.

31602.q: What do archaeological traces show about the end of Teotihuacán’s golden age in the 6th century?
a: Great fires in the centre of the city
A move of the city to the coast
31602.e: Above all, temples and palaces along the Avenue of the Dead were burned down. Whether a revolt or an attack was behind it is disputed.
31602.m: Fires in the centre mark the decline of Teotihuacán.

31603.q: Which religion became the king’s religion in the kingdom of Aksum in the 4th century?
31603.e: King Ezana converted to Christianity around 330. Aksum was thus one of the first Christian kingdoms in the world.
31603.m: Aksum became Christian in the 4th century.

31604.q: What is the city of Aksum especially famous for archaeologically?
a: Rock temples with statues of pharaohs
31604.e: The stelae probably marked royal tombs and are decorated with false windows and doors. The largest is over 30 metres long but lies broken on the ground.
31604.m: Aksum is famous for its huge stelae.

31605.q: What at the site of Lothal in Gujarat points to trade by sea?
a: A large brick basin thought to be a dock
A temple to a sea god
31605.e: At Lothal there is a brick-lined basin about 215 metres long next to the settlement. Many researchers see it as a dock for ships, others as a water tank for irrigation.
31605.m: Lothal probably had a brick dock.

31606.q: What do the standardised cube-shaped stone weights found at many Indus sites prove?
a: A uniform system of weights for trade
An early dice game for gambling
A grain tax paid in coins
The worship of a god of numbers
31606.e: Across a wide area the weights follow the same steps, first doubling and then decimal for larger values. This points to regulated trade over long distances.
31606.m: The Indus civilisation used a uniform system of weights.

31607.q: Which explanation for the decline of the Indus cities is especially discussed today?
a: Climate change with a weaker monsoon and shifting rivers
Conquest by an army from Mesopotamia
A great volcanic eruption in the Himalayas
31607.e: From about 1900 BC the cities were gradually abandoned. The main factors discussed are weakening monsoon rains and rivers that shifted or dried up.
31607.m: Climate change probably contributed to the end of the Indus cities.

31608.q: What is the well-known stone figure of a bearded man in a robe with a trefoil pattern from Mohenjo-Daro called?
31608.e: The small soapstone figure was found in 1927. The name “Priest-King” is a modern interpretation, since hardly anything is known about the city’s rulers.
31608.m: The Priest-King is the most famous stone figure from Mohenjo-Daro.

31609.q: How was the layout of Mohenjo-Daro roughly divided?
a: Into a raised citadel and a lower town
Into four quarters around a temple
Into a harbour and a palace quarter
Into a ring of villages without a centre
31609.e: In the west there is an artificially raised mound with public buildings. In the east lies the lower town with houses and workshops.
31609.m: Mohenjo-Daro consisted of a citadel and a lower town.

31610.q: What is the city of Mohenjo-Daro especially known for?
a: Streets in a grid and drains
31610.e: The streets of Mohenjo-Daro cross at right angles, and many houses were connected to covered drains. This was very advanced for the Bronze Age.
31610.m: Mohenjo-Daro was a planned city with drains.

31611.q: What did Seleucus I receive from Chandragupta around 303 BC in exchange for territories in the west?
31611.e: After the war Seleucus gave up territories in today’s Afghanistan and Pakistan. The elephants later helped him at the Battle of Ipsus.
31611.m: Seleucus swapped land for 500 Maurya elephants.

31612.q: According to Jain tradition, which religion did Chandragupta Maurya join at the end of his life?
31612.e: According to this tradition he abdicated and lived as a Jain ascetic in Shravanabelagola. There he is said to have died through ritual fasting.
31612.m: Chandragupta is said to have died as a Jain monk.

31613.q: Which Maurya ruler turned to Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga War?
31613.e: Ashoka, the grandson of Chandragupta and son of Bindusara, regretted the suffering of the war. He had edicts on non-violence and tolerance carved in stone.
31613.m: Ashoka became a Buddhist after the Kalinga War.

31614.q: How did the rule of the Maurya dynasty end around 185 BC?
a: A general killed the last king
The last king stepped down voluntarily
31614.e: The commander Pushyamitra Shunga murdered King Brihadratha at a military parade. He then founded the Shunga dynasty.
31614.m: A military coup ended the Maurya dynasty.

31615.q: What did the Indian ruler Ashoka become known for after the bloody war against Kalinga?
a: He turned to Buddhism and non-violence
He then conquered all of China
He introduced the caste system anew
He banned all religions except one
31615.e: The suffering of the war is said to have shaken Ashoka. Afterwards, in his edicts, he proclaimed the Dhamma: respect for parents, tolerance towards all faiths and kindness to animals.
31615.m: After the Kalinga War Ashoka relied on Buddhism and tolerance.

31616.q: How did Ashoka contribute to the spread of Buddhism?
a: He sent monks as missionaries to other countries
He forced all his subjects to become monks
31616.e: According to tradition, missionaries set off under Ashoka to many countries, for example to Sri Lanka. In this way Buddhism spread far beyond India.
31616.m: Under Ashoka Buddhism spread beyond India.

31617.q: Why did Ashoka have some inscriptions in the north-west of his empire carved in Greek and Aramaic?
a: Because people there understood these languages
Because Greek was the language of Buddhist monks
Because Ashoka himself came from Greece
Because Indian languages were banned at the time
31617.e: Since Alexander the Great, Greek settlers had lived in today’s Afghanistan, and Aramaic was an administrative language there. One example is the inscription of Kandahar.
31617.m: Ashoka spread his messages in the languages of the people.

31618.q: Why could Ashoka’s inscriptions not be read for a long time?
a: The Brahmi script used had been forgotten
The stones were all under water
They were written in a secret code
They were only found in the 21st century
31618.e: Over the centuries the old Brahmi script was no longer understood. Only in 1837 did the Briton James Prinsep decipher it.
31618.m: James Prinsep made Ashoka’s inscriptions readable again in 1837.

31619.q: Which empire did Ashoka rule in the 3rd century BC?
a: The kingdom of Aksum in Africa
31619.e: Ashoka was the third ruler of the Maurya dynasty. His empire covered almost the whole Indian subcontinent. In his inscriptions he called himself “Beloved of the Gods”.
31619.m: Ashoka ruled the Indian Maurya Empire.

31620.q: According to tradition, where did the Buddha die and enter parinirvana?
31620.e: He is said to have died at the age of about 80 in Kushinagar between two sal trees. Today the place is one of the four great pilgrimage sites.

31621.q: According to tradition, under which tree did Siddhartha attain enlightenment?
31621.e: In Bodh Gaya Siddhartha meditated under a sacred fig, the Bodhi tree. According to tradition, there he became the Buddha, the Awakened One.
31621.m: The Buddha attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree.

31622.q: In which language has the oldest complete canon of Buddhist teachings come down to us?
31622.e: According to tradition, the Pali Canon of Theravada Buddhism was written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BC. Pali is a Middle Indian language.
31622.m: The oldest complete Buddhist canon is written in Pali.

31623.q: What is the community of monks and nuns founded by the Buddha called?
31623.e: Sangha means community. Together with the Buddha and his teaching, it forms the “Three Jewels” of Buddhism.
31623.m: The Buddhist monastic community is called the Sangha.

31624.q: Roughly in which period did the Shang dynasty rule?
31624.e: The Shang are seen as the first Chinese dynasty proven by written finds. Around 1046 BC they were overthrown by the Zhou.
31624.m: The Shang ruled in the 2nd millennium BC.

31625.q: Which military innovation appears in China in the late Shang period around 1200 BC?
31625.e: Chariots complete with horses have been found in late Shang tombs. The technology probably came to China from the steppe.
31625.m: Chariots appeared in China in the late Shang period.

31626.q: Which philosopher of the 4th century BC developed Confucius’ teaching further and believed that people are good by nature?
31626.e: Mengzi, in Latin Mencius, is seen as the second most important Confucian. Xunzi, by contrast, held that human nature is bad.
31626.m: Mengzi taught that people are good by nature.

31627.q: Which term does Confucius use for the rites and proper manners?
31627.e: Li covers sacrificial rituals as well as everyday politeness. For Confucius, the rites bring order to the family and the state.
31627.m: For Confucius, li are the rites and good manners.

31628.q: What did Confucius call for with the “rectification of names”?
a: That all children get new names
That officials keep their names secret
31628.e: A ruler should really act like a ruler, a father like a father. Otherwise, according to Confucius, order breaks down.
31628.m: Confucius wanted words and reality to match.

31629.q: Which chronicle, after which a whole era is named, is traditionally attributed to Confucius?
a: The Records of the Three Kingdoms
The Book of the Dao and De
31629.e: The brief chronicle covers the years 722 to 481 BC. This part of the Zhou period is called the Spring and Autumn period after it.
31629.m: The Spring and Autumn Annals are attributed to Confucius.

31630.q: Who created the Latinised form of the name “Confucius”?
31630.e: In the 16th and 17th centuries Jesuits such as Matteo Ricci studied the Chinese classics. They Latinised the honorific title Kong Fuzi as Confucius.
31630.m: Jesuits turned Kong Fuzi into the name Confucius.

31631.q: Near which modern city is the tomb of the first emperor with the Terracotta Army?
31631.e: The Terracotta Army was discovered near Xi’an in 1974. The old Qin capital Xianyang was also nearby.
31631.m: The Terracotta Army is near Xi’an.

31632.q: How did Qin Shi Huangdi organise his empire administratively?
31632.e: Instead of giving principalities to relatives, he first divided the empire into 36 commanderies. They were run by officials whom the emperor could appoint and dismiss.
31632.m: Qin Shi Huangdi ruled through centrally appointed officials.

31633.q: According to tradition, what did Qin Shi Huangdi have done in 213 BC?
31633.e: To suppress criticism, the emperor had many writings burned, especially works by Confucians. Only books on medicine, farming and divination remained allowed.
31633.m: Many books were burned under the first emperor.

31634.q: How long did the Qin dynasty last after the death of the first emperor in 210 BC?
31634.e: After intrigues at court and great revolts, the empire collapsed in 206 BC. Then the Han dynasty began.
31634.m: The Qin dynasty fell apart soon after the death of the first emperor.

31635.q: Which weapons were found with the figures of the Terracotta Army?
31635.e: Thousands of arrowheads were found, as well as swords, lances and crossbow parts made of bronze. Many blades were surprisingly well preserved.
31635.m: The clay soldiers carried real bronze weapons.

31636.q: What does Pit 1, the largest pit of the Terracotta Army, contain?
a: A battle formation mainly of foot soldiers
31636.e: In Pit 1 the figures stand in long columns in corridors. At the front is a vanguard of archers.
31636.m: Pit 1 shows an army of foot soldiers in battle formation.

31637.q: Which find of 1980 near the burial mound is seen as a masterpiece of Qin bronze casting?
a: Two half-size bronze chariots with horses
An imperial throne of solid gold
31637.e: The two chariots consist of thousands of separate parts and are decorated with gold and silver. They copy chariots of the imperial retinue.
31637.m: The bronze chariots show the high level of Qin bronze art.

31638.q: Which figures were found in side pits of the mausoleum besides the soldiers?
a: Gods of heaven and the underworld
31638.e: The side pits show that the emperor also wanted to take his court and entertainment into the afterlife. There are also bronze water birds with figures of musicians.
31638.m: The mausoleum also contains acrobats, officials and musicians.

31639.q: Which goods did Han Wudi make a state monopoly to pay for his campaigns?
31639.e: From about 117 BC the state controlled the production and sale of salt and iron. Officials and scholars argued about this monopoly in a famous debate in 81 BC.
31639.m: The Han financed themselves with the salt and iron monopoly.

31640.q: How did the early Han emperors try to pacify the horse-riding Xiongnu in the north?
a: With marriages of princesses and gifts
By settling the Xiongnu in the imperial palace
With a joint campaign against India
31640.e: This policy was called heqin, roughly “harmony through kinship”. The Han married women of the court to Xiongnu rulers and paid regular gifts.
31640.m: With the heqin policy the Han bought peace from the Xiongnu.

31641.q: Which distant empire did the Han envoy Gan Ying try to reach in AD 97?
31641.e: Gan Ying got as far as a large arm of the sea, probably the Persian Gulf. There he was advised against the long sea voyage and turned back.
31641.m: Gan Ying was the first of the Han to try to reach Rome.

31642.q: What makes the Han-period tomb complex of Mawangdui near Changsha so famous?
a: A very well-preserved body and texts on silk
An army of thousands of clay warriors
A treasure of Roman gold coins
31642.e: In the 1970s the mummy of Lady Xin Zhui and many texts on silk were found at Mawangdui, including early versions of the Daodejing. The clay army, by contrast, belongs to the tomb of the first Qin emperor.
31642.m: Mawangdui is a rich tomb site of the Han period.

31643.q: In what were some Han princes such as Liu Sheng buried?
a: In suits of jade plates with gold wire
31643.e: People believed that jade protected the body from decay. Liu Sheng’s suit consists of over 2000 jade plates.
31643.m: Han princes were buried in jade suits.

31644.q: Which section of the route network was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014?
a: The Amber Road on the Baltic
The Grand Trunk Road in India
31644.e: China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan nominated this section together. It includes dozens of sites, from cities to watchtowers.
31644.m: The Chang’an-Tianshan corridor has been World Heritage since 2014.

31645.q: According to tradition, how did silkworm breeding reach the Byzantine Empire around AD 552?
a: Monks smuggled eggs in hollow canes
A Chinese emperor gave it as a gift
31645.e: According to the historian Procopius, monks secretly brought silkworm eggs from Central Asia for Emperor Justinian. This ended the monopoly of the East.
31645.m: Monks smuggled the silkworm to Byzantium.

31646.q: Which empire controlled the routes between China and Rome as a middleman in Han times?
31646.e: The Parthians ruled Iran and Mesopotamia. They profited from reselling silk and prevented direct contacts between the Han and Rome.
31646.m: The Parthians were middlemen between China and Rome.

31647.q: Which work of 868 found in Dunhuang is seen as the oldest dated printed book?
31647.e: The scroll was printed with wooden blocks and bears an exact date. Today it is in the British Library in London.
31647.m: The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book.

31648.q: What was found at the Olmec offering site of El Manatí?
a: Some of the oldest known rubber balls
The largest of all colossal heads
31648.e: In the oxygen-poor swamp, rubber balls from around 1600 BC were preserved. They are early evidence of the Mesoamerican ballgame.
31648.m: Ancient rubber balls were found at El Manatí.

31649.q: Which stone block, published in 2006, may bear the oldest writing in the Americas?
31649.e: The block from Veracruz shows 62 signs and is dated to the Olmec period. Whether it is real writing is still disputed.
31649.m: The Cascajal Block may show the oldest writing in the Americas.

31650.q: What was the great pyramid of La Venta made of?
31650.e: The pyramid, about 30 metres high, was built up from earth and clay. In the Gulf coast plain there were hardly any quarries nearby.
31650.m: The pyramid of La Venta is built of clay.

31651.q: In which region did the Olmecs live?
a: On the Gulf coast of Mexico
31651.e: The Olmecs lived in the humid lowlands on the Gulf of Mexico, in today’s Veracruz and Tabasco. They are seen as one of the oldest civilisations of Mesoamerica.
31651.m: The Olmecs lived on the Gulf coast of Mexico.

31652.q: Across which sea did the kingdom of Aksum reach out to southern Arabia?
31652.e: Aksum lay near the coast of the Red Sea. Around AD 525 King Kaleb crossed over to southern Arabia with an army.
31652.m: Aksum was a power on the Red Sea.

31653.q: Which Nubian kingdom was decisively weakened by Aksumite campaigns in the 4th century?
31653.e: An inscription of King Ezana tells of a campaign to the Nile. The already weakened kingdom of Meroë then disappears from the sources.
31653.m: Aksum contributed to the end of the kingdom of Meroë.

31654.q: Which Greek trading text of the 1st century AD mentions the kingdom of Aksum?
a: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
31654.e: The Periplus is a handbook for sea traders in the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. It names the city of the Aksumites and their king Zoskales.
31654.m: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea mentions Aksum.

31655.q: With which ruler did early followers of Muhammad find refuge around 615?
31655.e: Islamic tradition calls this the first Hijra. The Christian king of Aksum is said to have protected the refugees from Mecca.
31655.m: The Negus of Aksum took in early Muslims.

31656.q: According to Ethiopian tradition, which object is the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Aksum said to house?
31656.e: According to legend, Menelik, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia. Only one guardian monk may see it, so it cannot be checked.
31656.m: Tradition places the Ark of the Covenant in Aksum.

31657.q: How was Carthage governed at the time of the Punic Wars?
a: By officials elected each year and a council
By a hereditary king without a council
31657.e: At the top were two suffetes elected each year. There was also a council of elders and a popular assembly.
31657.m: Carthage was led by two suffetes.

31658.q: Which Greek philosopher praised the constitution of Carthage in his “Politics”?
31658.e: Aristotle saw in Carthage a well-mixed constitution with royal, aristocratic and democratic elements. He compared it with Sparta and Crete.
31658.m: Aristotle considered the constitution of Carthage exemplary.

31659.q: What is the Tophet of Carthage?
a: A sacred area with urns of small children
The citadel on the Byrsa hill
31659.e: In the Tophet thousands of urns were found with the burned remains of infants and animals. Whether these were sacrifices or burials of children who died young is disputed.
31659.m: The Tophet of Carthage is a disputed sacred burial ground for children.

31660.q: Which goddess was especially worshipped in Carthage as the companion of Baal Hammon?
31660.e: Tanit was the main goddess of Carthage. Her sign, a triangle with a crossbar and a circle, appears on many gravestones.
31660.m: Tanit was the most important goddess of Carthage.

31661.q: Which work from Carthage did the Roman Senate have translated after the city was destroyed?
a: A history of the Punic Wars
A law code of the suffetes
31661.e: The handbook by the Carthaginian Mago filled 28 books. Rome had it translated into Latin because it was considered especially useful.
31661.m: Rome had the farming book of the Carthaginian Mago translated.

31662.q: Which Germanic people made Carthage their capital in AD 439?
31662.e: Under King Gaiseric the Vandals captured the rich Roman city. From there they also sacked Rome in 455.
31662.m: From 439 Carthage was the capital of the Vandals.

31663.q: Over which island did Carthaginians and Greeks fight for centuries?
31663.e: Carthage controlled western Sicily, Greek cities such as Syracuse the east. In 480 BC the Sicilian Greeks defeated a large Carthaginian army at Himera.
31663.m: Carthaginians and Greeks fought over Sicily for a long time.

31664.q: Which war shook Carthage directly after the First Punic War?
31664.e: Unpaid mercenaries and Libyan subjects rose up against Carthage from 241 to 237 BC. Hamilcar Barca finally crushed the revolt.
31664.m: After the First Punic War Carthage’s mercenaries rebelled.

31665.q: Which city did the Merovingian king Clovis I make his capital around 508?
31665.e: Clovis chose Paris as his residence and was also buried there. Paris later lay in the western sub-kingdom of Neustria.
31665.m: Clovis made Paris the capital of the Franks.

31666.q: Which Merovingian king was baptised around 500 and led the Franks to Catholic Christianity?
31666.e: Clovis was baptised in Reims. Because he became Catholic and not Arian, he won the support of the Roman population and the bishops in Gaul.
31666.m: With Clovis's baptism the Franks became Catholic.

31667.q: Who held the real power in the late Merovingian kingdom, while the kings were only shadow kings?
31667.e: The mayors of the palace originally ran the royal household. Over time they took over government and army, until Pepin the Short became king himself in 751.
31667.m: In the late Merovingian kingdom the mayors of the palace ruled.

31668.q: What happened in 751 to Childeric III, the last Merovingian king?
a: He was shorn and sent to a monastery
He was killed in a battle
He fled to the Lombard kingdom
31668.e: With the Pope's approval, Childeric III was deposed. His long royal hair was cut off and he was banished to a monastery.
31668.m: In 751 Childeric III lost his crown and his hair and went to a monastery.

31669.q: Which inheritance rule repeatedly led to divisions of the Merovingian kingdom?
a: Division among all the king's sons
Succession of the eldest son only
Election of the king by the bishops
31669.e: The kingdom was seen as the property of the royal family and was divided among all the sons. This created sub-kingdoms and frequent wars between brothers.
31669.m: The Merovingians divided their kingdom among all their sons.

31670.q: Which grave goods from the tomb of Childeric I served Napoleon as a model for an imperial symbol?
31670.e: Many small golden insects were found in the tomb and were interpreted as bees. Napoleon therefore chose the bee as a symbol of his empire.
31670.m: Napoleon's bees go back to finds from Childeric's tomb.

31671.q: Which people did the Merovingians belong to?
31671.e: The Merovingians were the first royal dynasty of the Franks. Under them, the Frankish kingdom grew into the strongest power in Western Europe.
31671.m: The Merovingians were kings of the Franks.

31672.q: Which people ruled over what is now western Switzerland before the Franks?
31672.e: The Burgundians settled in the area around Lake Geneva from 443. In 534 the sons of Clovis conquered their kingdom, and western Switzerland became Frankish.
31672.m: Before the Franks, the Burgundians ruled western Switzerland.

31673.q: Against which people did Clovis fight around 496 in the battle after which he is said to have vowed to become a Christian?
31673.e: According to Gregory of Tours, Clovis called on his wife's God during a battle against the Alemanni. The battle is traditionally placed near Zülpich. After the victory he was baptised.
31673.m: The victory over the Alemanni led Clovis to baptism.

31674.q: Which bishop baptised Clovis in Reims?
31674.e: Bishop Remigius of Reims baptised Clovis together with many Frankish warriors. The exact year is disputed; dates from 496 to 508 are often given.
31674.m: Remigius of Reims baptised the Frankish king Clovis.

31675.q: Why was it politically important that Clovis was baptised Catholic and not Arian?
a: He won over the Gallo-Roman bishops
It earned him the title of emperor
It made him heir to the Visigothic kingdom
It ended his quarrel with Byzantium
31675.e: Most other Germanic kings were Arians. As a Catholic, Clovis found support among the Roman population and their influential bishops.
31675.m: With his Catholic baptism, Clovis gained the Church of Gaul as an ally.

31676.q: Which honour did Clovis receive from the Eastern Roman emperor in 508 after his victory over the Visigoths?
a: The imperial crown of the West
31676.e: After the victory over the Visigoths, Clovis received the rank of consul from Emperor Anastasius I. This strengthened his standing with the Roman population.
31676.m: Clovis was honoured with the rank of consul by the emperor in Constantinople.

31677.q: Which city did Clovis make the centre of his kingdom towards the end of his reign?
31677.e: Clovis chose Paris as his residence. There he also had a church built, in which he was buried.

31678.q: Which church assembly did Clovis call shortly before his death?
31678.e: The First Council of Orléans in 511 regulated the relationship between king and Church. It shows how closely Clovis worked with the bishops.
31678.m: The Council of Orléans in 511 bound the Church to the Frankish king.

31679.q: Which ruling dynasty did the Frankish king Clovis I belong to?
31679.e: The dynasty is named after Merovech, a legendary ancestor. Clovis's father Childeric I was king of the Salian Franks.
31679.m: Clovis was the most important king of the Merovingians.

31680.e: The nickname comes from the Latin “martellus”, meaning hammer. He was given it because of his military successes.
31680.m: Charles Martel means Charles the Hammer.

31681.q: Which office did Charles Martel hold in the Frankish kingdom?
31681.e: The mayor of the palace was actually only supposed to run the royal court. But as mayor of the palace, Charles Martel had more power than the Merovingian kings.
31681.m: Charles Martel ruled the Frankish kingdom as mayor of the palace.

31682.q: Where did Charles Martel often get the land with which he rewarded his warriors?
31682.e: Charles Martel seized Church property and passed it on to his followers. This later earned him criticism from Church writers.
31682.m: Charles Martel rewarded his warriors with Church land.

31683.q: What did Charles Martel do after the death of King Theuderic IV in 737?
a: He handed the crown to the Pope
31683.e: From 737 Charles Martel continued to rule without a king, but did not take the title himself. Only in 743 was a Merovingian put on the throne again.
31683.m: For a time Charles Martel ruled with no king at all.

31684.q: Who led the Frankish army in the Battle of Tours and Poitiers in 732?
31684.e: The mayor of the palace Charles Martel defeated the army of the governor of al-Andalus, who fell in the battle. Charles was the grandfather of Charlemagne.
31684.m: Charles Martel won at Tours and Poitiers in 732.

31685.q: From where did the Muslim army advance into Gaul in 732?
31685.e: After 711, Arabs and Berbers had conquered almost the whole Iberian Peninsula. From there they crossed the Pyrenees into Aquitaine.
31685.m: The army of 732 came from al-Andalus.

31686.q: Which rich target drew the Muslim army towards Tours?
a: The silver mines on the Loire
The harbour on the Atlantic coast
31686.e: The basilica of Saint Martin of Tours was one of the richest shrines in Gaul. The army was stopped on its way there.
31686.m: The army was heading for the rich church of Saint Martin in Tours.

31687.q: Why was the Battle of Tours and Poitiers often exaggerated later?
a: It was seen as the rescue of Christian Europe from Islam
It was the biggest battle in world history
It led to the conquest of the Frankish kingdom
31687.e: Later historians turned the battle into a turning point of world history. Today it is seen more soberly as a victory against a raid for plunder.
31687.m: The battle of 732 later became a myth.

31688.q: What did the Frankish king Pepin promise the Pope in 754?
a: Areas in Italy that the Lombards had occupied
The imperial crown for the Pope
An army of its own for Rome
Half of the Frankish royal treasure
31688.e: At Quierzy, Pepin promised to hand over to the Pope the areas conquered by the Lombards. This promise is called the Donation of Pepin.
31688.m: In 754 Pepin promised the Pope land in Italy.

31689.q: What did Pepin receive from the Pope in return for his help?
31689.e: Pepin had become king in 751 although he did not come from the royal family. Being anointed by Pope Stephen II in 754 gave his rule the Church's blessing.
31689.m: The Pope anointed Pepin as king.

31690.q: Which people threatened Rome around 750, so that the Pope asked the Frankish king Pepin for help?
31690.e: The Lombard king Aistulf had conquered Ravenna in 751 and was threatening Rome. In two campaigns Pepin forced him to give up the areas.
31690.m: Pepin protected the Pope from the Lombards.

31691.q: Which formerly Byzantine area passed to the Pope through the donation?
31691.e: The Exarchate of Ravenna had once been a Byzantine administrative area. Pepin handed it not to Byzantium but to the Pope.
31691.m: The Exarchate of Ravenna went to the Pope.

31692.q: What grew out of the Donation of Pepin?
31692.e: The areas handed over formed the basis of the Papal States. They lasted until 1870 as the Pope's worldly territory.
31692.m: The Donation of Pepin laid the foundation for the Papal States.

31693.q: What did the title “Patricius Romanorum” oblige the Frankish king Pepin to do?
a: To protect Rome and the Pope
To elect the emperor in Constantinople
31693.e: With the title, Pepin became the protector of Rome in 754. The Franks thus took over a task that Byzantium had once had.
31693.m: As patricius, Pepin became protector of the Romans.

31694.q: Which forged document, supposedly from a Roman emperor, was meant to justify the worldly power of the popes?
31694.e: The Donation of Constantine was probably written in the 8th or 9th century. In 1440 the humanist Lorenzo Valla proved that it is a forgery.
31694.m: The Donation of Constantine is a medieval forgery.

31695.q: Which Frankish ruler conquered the Lombard kingdom in 774 and confirmed the donation to the Pope?
31695.e: Charlemagne, Pepin's son, defeated the Lombard king Desiderius. In Rome he confirmed the Donation of Pepin.
31695.m: Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom in 774.

31696.q: In which battle in 778 was Charlemagne's rearguard wiped out in the Pyrenees?
31696.e: On the retreat from Spain, the rearguard was ambushed in the pass of Roncesvalles. The event later became a heroic legend in the Song of Roland.
31696.m: The defeat at Roncesvalles lives on in the Song of Roland.

31697.q: Which people on the middle Danube did Charlemagne defeat in the 790s, seizing their great treasure?
31697.e: In 795 and 796 Frankish armies captured the “Ring”, the centre of the Avars. The treasure taken was so large that it was carried away in many wagons.
31697.m: Charlemagne seized the treasure of the Avars.

31698.q: Which Duke of Bavaria did Charlemagne depose in 788?
31698.e: Tassilo III was Charlemagne's cousin and wanted to rule as independently as possible. Charlemagne had him deposed and sent to a monastery and brought Bavaria into the empire.
31698.m: With Tassilo's removal, Bavaria came fully under Charlemagne's rule.

31699.q: What is the name of the decree that regulated the running of the royal estates, down to lists of useful plants?
31699.e: The Capitulare de villis laid down how royal estates were to be run. It contains a famous list of plants that were to grow in the gardens.
31699.m: The Capitulare de villis regulated the royal estates right down to the garden.

31700.q: In the Carolingian coin system, how many pennies (denarii) made a pound?
31700.e: A pound of silver was divided into 20 shillings of 12 pennies each. That gives 20 times 12, so 240 pennies.
31700.m: In the Carolingian coin system a pound had 240 pennies.

31701.q: Which animal did Caliph Harun al-Rashid send Charlemagne as a gift?
31701.e: The elephant Abul Abbas arrived in Aachen in 802. It was a sign of the good relations between Charlemagne and the caliph in Baghdad.
31701.m: Charlemagne received an elephant from the caliph.

31702.q: What is the name for the way of ruling in which the king travelled with his court from palace to palace?
a: Rule by mayors of the palace
31702.e: There was no fixed capital with an administration. The king appeared in person in the regions and lived off the produce of the royal estates.
31702.m: In itinerant kingship the king ruled on the move from palace to palace.

31703.q: What was the name of the border area that Charlemagne set up south of the Pyrenees against the Emirate of Córdoba?
31703.e: After the capture of Barcelona in 801, the Spanish March secured the southern border. The County of Barcelona later grew out of it.
31703.m: The Spanish March protected the Frankish kingdom in the south.

31704.q: On which day of the year 800 was Charlemagne crowned emperor?
31704.e: The coronation took place on Christmas Day during Mass. By the reckoning of the time, the new year often began at Christmas.
31704.m: Charlemagne was crowned emperor at Christmas.

31705.q: What does Einhard claim about Charlemagne's attitude to the coronation?
a: He would not have gone to church had he known the plan
He put the crown on his own head
He forced the Pope to crown him
31705.e: Einhard writes that Charlemagne was surprised by the coronation. Many experts think this is a modest portrayal, as the coronation was probably arranged in advance.
31705.m: According to Einhard, Charlemagne was surprised by the coronation.

31706.q: Which Pope crowned Charlemagne emperor in 800?
31706.e: Pope Leo III depended on Charlemagne's protection. At Christmas 800 in Rome he placed the imperial crown on his head.

31707.q: In which city was Charlemagne crowned emperor in 800?
31707.e: The coronation took place in St Peter's Church in Rome. Aachen, on the other hand, was Charlemagne's favourite palace.

31708.q: What is the name of the medieval idea that the Roman imperial title had passed to another people?
31708.e: According to this doctrine, the imperial title passed from the Romans to the Franks and later to the Germans. It justified the Western empire.
31708.m: The translatio imperii explained the transfer of the imperial title.

31709.q: How did Byzantium first react to Charlemagne's coronation as emperor?
a: It chose Charlemagne as its own emperor
31709.e: In Byzantium people saw themselves as the only heirs of Rome. Only in 812, after long negotiations, did Emperor Michael I recognise Charlemagne as emperor.
31709.m: Byzantium only recognised Charlemagne's imperial title after years.

31710.q: Why did Charlemagne avoid the title “Emperor of the Romans”?
a: So as not to provoke the emperor in Byzantium
Because he did not understand Latin
Because the Pope had forbidden it
Because Rome did not belong to his empire
31710.e: Byzantium saw itself as the only Roman Empire. So Charlemagne called himself emperor “governing the Roman Empire”.
31710.m: Charlemagne chose his imperial title with Byzantium in mind.

31711.q: Which capitulary of 789 is seen as the programme of Charlemagne's educational and Church reform?
31711.e: Among other things, the Admonitio generalis called for schools at monasteries and bishops' seats. It aimed to train clergy better and have texts corrected.
31711.m: The Admonitio generalis of 789 called for more education.

31712.q: Which document from the early 9th century shows the ideal ground plan of a whole monastery?
31712.e: The plan was made around 820 to 830 at Reichenau Abbey and is kept in the Abbey Library of St Gallen. It is the earliest surviving drawing of a monastery from the Middle Ages.
31712.m: The Plan of St Gall shows an ideal Carolingian monastery.

31713.q: Which Anglo-Saxon scholar led Charlemagne's palace school?
31713.e: Alcuin came from York to Charlemagne's court and promoted learning and writing. Later he became abbot in Tours.
31713.m: Alcuin was the most important scholar at Charlemagne's court.

31714.q: Which script from the time of Charlemagne is the model for our lowercase letters today?
31714.e: Carolingian minuscule was clear and easy to read. Humanists later took it up again, and our printed letters developed from it.
31714.m: Our lowercase letters go back to Carolingian minuscule.

31715.q: Why is the work of the Carolingian scriptoria so important for our knowledge of antiquity?
a: Many ancient texts survive only in their copies
They translated all ancient texts into German
They kept all the Greek originals
31715.e: Monks copied many works by Roman authors. For many ancient texts, these Carolingian manuscripts are the oldest surviving evidence.
31715.m: Without Carolingian copies, many ancient texts would be lost.

31716.q: From which city did the scholar Alcuin come to Charlemagne's court?
31716.e: Alcuin led the famous cathedral school of York. Charlemagne met him in Italy in 781 and brought him to his court.
31716.m: Alcuin came to Charlemagne from the cathedral school in York.

31717.q: Which monastery did Alcuin lead as abbot from 796?
31717.e: As abbot of Saint-Martin in Tours, Alcuin built up an important writing school there. He died in Tours in 804.
31717.m: Alcuin's last post was as abbot in Tours.

31718.q: Which text did Alcuin revise to create a uniform and error-free wording?
31718.e: Alcuin produced an improved version of the Vulgate. This so-called Alcuin Bible was copied many times in Tours.
31718.m: Alcuin improved the text of the Latin Bible.

31719.q: Which nickname did Charlemagne have among the scholars at his court?
31719.e: In the court circle the scholars gave themselves names from the Bible and antiquity. Charlemagne was named after the biblical King David, and Alcuin called himself Flaccus.
31719.m: At court, Charlemagne was called David.

31720.q: Which part of the empire did Lothair receive in the Treaty of Verdun in 843, together with the imperial title?
31720.e: Lothair received a strip from the North Sea to Italy. Louis the German got East Francia and Charles the Bald got West Francia.
31720.m: In 843 Lothair received Middle Francia and the imperial title.

31721.q: In which languages were the Oaths of Strasbourg of 842 sworn?
a: Old French and Old High German
31721.e: Each king swore in the language of his brother's army so that it would understand him. The text is regarded as the oldest record of the French language.
31721.m: The Oaths of Strasbourg are an early record of French.

31722.q: What did the sons of Louis the Pious keep quarrelling about from 830 onwards?
31722.e: Louis at first wanted to give the empire undivided to Lothair. When he also wanted to give land to his youngest son Charles, the older sons rebelled.
31722.m: The dispute over dividing the empire shaped the time after Charlemagne.

31723.q: Whose son was Charles the Bald?
31723.e: Charles the Bald was the youngest son of Louis the Pious from his marriage to Judith. This made him a grandson of Charlemagne.
31723.m: Charles the Bald was a son of Louis the Pious.

31724.q: What happened to Middle Francia after Lothair's death in 855?
a: It was divided among his three sons
It went undivided to the Pope
It was joined to West Francia
31724.e: Lothair's sons received Italy, the area north of the Alps and Provence. As a result, Middle Francia quickly broke apart.
31724.m: Middle Francia broke apart under Lothair's sons after 855.

31725.e: Verdun lies on the Meuse in north-eastern France. The town also became known in 1916 for a great battle of the First World War.

31726.q: What was the main principle used to draw the borders of the sub-kingdoms in 843?
a: Royal estates of roughly equal value
The borders of old Roman provinces
31726.e: Experts recorded the royal estates so that each brother would get a share of similar value. Language or ethnic origin played hardly any part.
31726.m: In the division of 843, the value of the royal estates mattered most.

31727.q: Which Viking leader received land at the mouth of the Seine from the West Frankish king in 911?
31727.e: In the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, Charles the Simple gave this area to Rollo. In return, Rollo was to defend the land against other Vikings.
31727.m: Rollo received land on the Seine in 911.

31728.q: What was the name of the area in northern and eastern England where Danish law applied?
31728.e: After fighting Alfred the Great, the Danes settled in a large part of England. Their legal customs applied there, hence the name Danelaw.
31728.m: In the Danelaw, Danish law applied.

31729.q: What was the name of the Byzantine emperor's bodyguard in which many Scandinavians served?
31729.e: From the late 10th century, Scandinavians and later also Anglo-Saxons served in this guard. It was considered especially loyal and well paid.
31729.m: Scandinavians served in the Varangian Guard in Constantinople.

31730.q: Which Varangian is regarded by the Primary Chronicle as the founder of the ruling family of Kievan Rus?
31730.e: According to the chronicle, Rurik was called to Novgorod around 862. The Rurikids, named after him, ruled in Russia for a long time.
31730.m: Rurik is regarded as the ancestor of the Rurikids.

31731.q: Which city did Vikings besiege for almost a year from 885 to 886?
31731.e: Count Odo defended Paris successfully. Because Emperor Charles III paid the Vikings off, he lost respect.
31731.m: Paris withstood a long Viking siege in 885 and 886.

31732.q: Which important trading place of the Viking Age lay on the Schlei near Schleswig?
31732.e: Hedeby was one of the most important trading places in Northern Europe. Together with the Danevirke, the settlement is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
31732.m: Hedeby was a great Viking trading town.

31733.q: What is the name of the tribute payments with which English kings tried to keep the Vikings from attacking?
31733.e: English rulers such as Æthelred paid large amounts of silver to the Danes. The payment was later partly continued as a tax.
31733.m: With the Danegeld, the English bought themselves free from attacks.

31734.q: With which battle in 1066 is the Viking Age often said to end?
31734.e: At Stamford Bridge the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada fell fighting an Anglo-Saxon army. After that, the great Viking raids on England ended.
31734.m: The Battle of Stamford Bridge marks the end of the Viking Age.

31735.q: Where in Newfoundland were the remains of a Viking settlement discovered?
31735.e: Excavations in the 1960s proved there was a Norse settlement there around the year 1000. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
31735.m: L'Anse aux Meadows proves Vikings were in America.

31736.q: Which famous 7th century ship burial was discovered in Suffolk in 1939?
31736.e: At Sutton Hoo lay a ship grave with rich grave goods, including a magnificent helmet. It is thought that King Rædwald of East Anglia was buried there.
31736.m: The ship grave of Sutton Hoo is an Anglo-Saxon treasure.

31737.q: What is the most important heroic epic in Old English?
31737.e: The epic tells of the hero Beowulf, who fights the monster Grendel and later a dragon. It survives in a single manuscript.
31737.m: Beowulf is the great heroic epic of the Anglo-Saxons.

31738.q: At which synod in 664 did Northumbria choose Roman rather than Irish church practice?
31738.e: One of the points in dispute was how to calculate the date of Easter. King Oswiu decided in favour of the Roman custom.
31738.m: At Whitby in 664 the Roman church practice won.

31739.q: Which king of Wessex defeated the Danes at Edington in 878?
31739.e: After the victory, Alfred made peace with the Dane Guthrum. He is regarded as one of the most important kings in Anglo-Saxon history.
31739.m: Alfred the Great defeated the Danes in 878.

31740.q: Which king of Mercia had a long border earthwork built against Wales?
31740.e: Offa ruled in the 8th century and was the most powerful Anglo-Saxon king of his time. The earthwork is still called Offa's Dyke today.
31740.m: Offa had the border earthwork against Wales built.

31741.q: According to Bede, which third people came to Britain alongside the Angles and Saxons?
31741.e: The Jutes came from Jutland and settled mainly in Kent. Today it is thought that other groups were involved as well.
31741.m: Along with the Angles and Saxons, the Jutes came to Britain.

31742.q: Which last Anglo-Saxon king fell at the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
31742.e: Harold Godwinson was defeated by the Norman duke William. This ended Anglo-Saxon rule in England.
31742.m: In 1066 the last Anglo-Saxon king, Harold Godwinson, fell.

31743.q: What is special about the roof of the Mausoleum of Theodoric in Ravenna?
a: A dome made from a single block of stone
31743.e: The dome is made from a single block of limestone from Istria. It is estimated to weigh around 230 tonnes.
31743.m: Theodoric's mausoleum has a dome made of one stone.

31744.q: Whom was Theodoric sent to defeat in Italy in 488 on behalf of the Eastern Roman emperor?
31744.e: In 476 Odoacer had deposed the last Western Roman emperor. Theodoric defeated him and then ruled Italy himself.
31744.m: Theodoric drove Odoacer out of Italy.

31745.q: How did Theodoric form alliances with the other Germanic kingdoms?
a: By taking all the kings hostage
31745.e: Theodoric married a sister of the Frankish king Clovis and married his daughters and sister to other kings. This created a network of alliances.
31745.m: Theodoric linked the Germanic kingdoms through marriages.

31746.q: How did Theodoric deal with the Roman administration in Italy?
a: He kept it and appointed Romans as officials
He abolished it and drove out all Romans
He replaced Roman law with Gothic law
He handed it over to the Pope
31746.e: The Goths provided the army, and the Romans continued to run the administration. Scholars such as Cassiodorus served the king as high officials.
31746.m: Under Theodoric, Romans continued to govern Italy.

31747.q: Which Ostrogothic king ruled Italy from 493?
31747.e: Theodoric defeated Odoacer and ruled Italy for over 30 years. He let the Roman administration carry on working and is regarded as one of the most important Germanic kings.
31747.m: Theodoric the Great ruled the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy.

31748.q: Which Byzantine emperor wanted to win back Italy in the 6th century and began the Gothic War?
31748.e: Justinian wanted to restore the old Roman Empire. After around 20 years of war, the Ostrogothic kingdom was defeated in 553.
31748.m: Emperor Justinian waged war against the Ostrogoths.

31749.q: Which city was the capital of the Ostrogoths that Byzantium captured in 540?
31749.e: The general Belisarius took Ravenna and captured King Witiges. The Mausoleum of Theodoric still stands in Ravenna today.
31749.m: Ravenna was the capital of the Ostrogoths.

31750.q: How were the tasks divided between Goths and Romans in the Ostrogothic kingdom?
a: Goths in the army, Romans in the administration
Romans in the army, Goths in the administration
31750.e: The Goths provided the army, while Romans carried on the civil administration. There was also the religious divide between Arian Goths and Catholic Romans.
31750.m: In the Ostrogothic kingdom the Goths fought and the Romans governed.

31751.q: Which region in northern Italy is named after the Lombards?
31751.e: From 568 the Lombards ruled large parts of Italy, with Pavia as their capital. The name Lombardy still recalls them today.
31751.m: Lombardy bears the name of the Lombards.

31752.q: Which crown, into which a nail from Christ's cross is said to have been worked, is kept in Monza Cathedral?
31752.e: According to legend, the inner band contains a piece of a nail from the cross. Several rulers were later crowned kings of Italy with it.
31752.m: The Iron Crown is kept in Monza Cathedral.

31753.q: Which Frankish king conquered the Lombard kingdom in 774?
31753.e: Charlemagne captured Pavia and afterwards also called himself King of the Lombards. His father Pepin had only fought the Lombards before.
31753.m: Charlemagne ended the Lombard kingdom in 774.

31754.q: Which Lombard duchy in southern Italy continued as an independent principality after 774?
31754.e: Charlemagne was never able to fully subdue Benevento. The principality remained an independent Lombard state for a long time.
31754.m: Benevento outlasted the end of the Lombard kingdom.

31755.q: Which Lombard scholar at Charlemagne's court wrote a history of his people?
31755.e: Paul the Deacon wrote the “Historia Langobardorum”. It is the most important source on the history of the Lombards.
31755.m: Paul the Deacon wrote the history of the Lombards.

31756.q: According to Roman sources, on which river did the Lombards live around the beginning of the Common Era?
31756.e: Roman authors such as Tacitus mention the Lombards as a small people on the lower Elbe. Later they moved via Pannonia to Italy.
31756.m: The Lombards originally came from the lower Elbe.

31757.q: Which additional title did Charlemagne bear after conquering the Lombard kingdom?
31757.e: Charlemagne now called himself “Rex Francorum et Langobardorum”. He thus put the Lombard crown on his own head and ruled Italy in personal union.
31757.m: Charlemagne also became King of the Lombards.

31758.q: Which monastery was founded in 744 on behalf of Boniface and later became his burial place?
31758.e: Boniface's pupil Sturm founded Fulda Abbey and became its first abbot. After his death in 754, Boniface was buried there.
31758.m: Boniface is buried at Fulda Abbey.

31760.q: What did Boniface want to achieve with the synods in the Frankish kingdom in the 740s?
a: A reform of the Church with stricter rules for clergy
The election of a Frankish Pope
The separation of the Frankish Church from Rome
31760.e: At the Concilium Germanicum and other synods, Boniface demanded regular assemblies and a stricter way of life for the clergy. He worked closely with the Pope.
31760.m: Boniface reformed the Frankish Church at synods.

31761.q: How did Boniface die on a missionary journey in Frisia in 754?
a: He was killed in an attack
He fell ill with the plague
He drowned in a storm flood
He was executed by the king
31761.e: Boniface and his companions were attacked near Dokkum by robbers or pagan Frisians. A place of pilgrimage there remembers him today.
31761.m: Boniface was killed in Frisia in 754.

31762.q: According to legend, what did Boniface hold over his head for protection during the fatal attack?
31762.e: In Fulda a book with cuts is shown, the so-called Ragyndrudis Codex. It is said to have been damaged by a sword blow during the attack.
31762.m: According to legend, Boniface shielded himself with a book.

31763.q: In which duchy did Boniface organise the dioceses of Salzburg, Freising, Regensburg and Passau in 739?
31763.e: Together with Duke Odilo of Bavaria, Boniface set up a fixed system of dioceses. It still shapes the Church organisation in Bavaria today.
31763.m: Boniface organised the dioceses in Bavaria in 739.

31764.q: Why was the support of the Frankish mayors of the palace so important for Boniface?
a: They gave military protection to his mission
They paid him for every baptism
31764.e: Boniface himself wrote that without the mayor of the palace's protection he could neither guide the people nor prevent paganism. Mission and Frankish rule therefore went hand in hand.
31764.m: Boniface needed the protection of the mayors of the palace for his mission.

31765.q: In which century did Emperor Justinian I rule the Eastern Roman Empire?
31765.e: Justinian ruled from 527 to 565. Under him the Hagia Sophia was built and a great collection of Roman law was made.
31765.m: Justinian I ruled in the 6th century.

31766.q: Which uprising of the circus factions in Constantinople almost cost Justinian his throne in 532?
31766.e: The Blues and the Greens rose up together, shouting “Nika” (Win!). The uprising was bloodily crushed in the Hippodrome.
31766.m: The Nika riots of 532 shook Justinian's rule.

31767.q: Which general conquered the Vandal kingdom in North Africa for Justinian in 533/534?
31767.e: Belisarius defeated the Vandals in a short campaign and then also fought in Italy. Narses later ended the war in Italy.
31767.m: Belisarius was Justinian's most famous general.

31768.q: Which empress from humble beginnings had great political influence as Justinian's wife?
31768.e: Before her marriage Theodora was an actress. As empress she had a major influence on politics and Church matters.
31768.m: Empress Theodora helped shape Justinian's policies.

31769.q: What is the name for Justinian's aim of restoring the Roman Empire to its former borders?
31769.e: Justinian wanted to win back the western areas lost to Germanic kingdoms. Parts of North Africa, Italy and southern Spain were indeed reconquered.
31769.m: Justinian aimed to restore the Roman Empire.

31770.q: Which famous school of philosophy in Athens was closed under Justinian in 529?
31770.e: Justinian banned pagan teachers from teaching. The closure is seen as the symbolic end of ancient philosophy in Athens.
31770.m: Under Justinian, Plato's Academy in Athens came to an end in 529.

31771.q: Against which people did Justinian wage a long war for Italy from 535 to 554?
31771.e: In the Gothic War Italy was reconquered but devastated. The Lombards only invaded Italy in 568.
31771.m: Justinian took Italy from the Ostrogoths in a long war.

31772.q: In which city do famous mosaics in the church of San Vitale show Justinian with his court?
31772.e: The church of San Vitale was consecrated in 547. Its mosaics show the emperor and empress with their followers and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
31772.m: In Ravenna you can see Justinian in the mosaics of San Vitale.

31773.q: Which emperor had Roman law collected in the Corpus iuris civilis in the 6th century?
31773.e: In 528 Emperor Justinian I set up a commission under his lawyer Tribonian. It collected and arranged Roman law.
31773.m: Justinian had Roman law collected in the Corpus iuris civilis.

31774.q: Why is the Corpus iuris civilis still important today?
a: It shaped the civil law of many European countries
It is still valid law in Italy today
It is the basis of Islamic law
It still governs the UN's international law
31774.e: From the Middle Ages, Roman law was taught at universities and adopted. Many terms and principles live on in law codes such as the German Civil Code or the Swiss Code of Obligations.
31774.m: Justinian's Roman law still shapes European civil law today.

31775.q: What were the “Institutes”, a short part of the Corpus iuris civilis, used for?
a: As a textbook for law students
As a prayer book for judges
As a list of all taxes
31775.e: The Institutes of 533 are a short textbook for beginners. Their structure follows the textbook of the lawyer Gaius.
31775.m: The Institutes served as a textbook for law students.

31776.q: From which capital did Justinian have the Corpus iuris civilis drawn up?
31776.e: Justinian ruled the Eastern Roman Empire from Constantinople. His later laws, the Novels, were mostly written there in Greek.
31776.m: The Corpus iuris civilis was made in Constantinople.

31777.q: In which city was the Corpus iuris civilis first taught academically from the late 11th century?
31777.e: The law teacher Irnerius worked on the rediscovered Digest in Bologna. The glossators came out of his school.
31777.m: The rediscovery of Roman law began in Bologna.

31778.q: What does the Latin name “Corpus iuris civilis” mean?
31778.e: Corpus means body or collection, ius civile means civil law. The overall title only became established through a printed edition of 1583; Justinian himself did not use it.
31778.m: The name Corpus iuris civilis dates from the time of humanism.

31779.q: In which language have most of Justinian's Novels come down to us in the original?
31779.e: The other parts were written in Latin, but the Novels were mostly written in Greek for the people of the East. In the West they were known mainly from Latin collections such as the Authenticum.
31779.m: Justinian's Novels survive mainly in Greek.

31780.q: Which building achievement makes the Hagia Sophia especially famous?
a: Its huge dome over a square space
The tallest church tower of its time
Its front made of pure gold
31780.e: The dome is about 31 metres across. Curved triangular surfaces, the pendentives, carry it over onto the square base.
31780.m: The dome of the Hagia Sophia was a masterpiece of building.

31781.q: What role did the Hagia Sophia play for the Byzantine emperors?
31781.e: Many emperors were crowned by the patriarch in the empire's main church. They were mostly buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.
31781.m: The Hagia Sophia was the coronation church of the Byzantine emperors.

31782.q: What is written on the eight large round 19th century panels inside the Hagia Sophia?
a: Names of Allah, Muhammad and early caliphs
31782.e: The calligraphic medallions bear the names of Allah, Muhammad, the first four caliphs and the grandsons Hasan and Husayn.
31782.m: The large medallions of the Hagia Sophia show Islamic names in calligraphy.

31783.q: Which part of the Hagia Sophia collapsed after earthquakes in 558 and had to be rebuilt?
31783.e: The first, flatter dome collapsed after earthquakes. The steeper new dome was consecrated in 562.
31783.m: The dome of the Hagia Sophia was rebuilt after 558.

31784.q: What happened to the Hagia Sophia straight after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople?
31784.e: The church was turned into a main mosque and was given minarets over time. Many mosaics were painted over.
31784.m: After 1453 the Hagia Sophia served as a mosque.

31785.q: What did the Turkish Republic turn the Hagia Sophia into in the 1930s?
31785.e: By decision of the government under Atatürk, the building was secularised and opened as a museum in 1935. Byzantine mosaics were uncovered in the process.
31785.m: Under Atatürk the Hagia Sophia became a museum.

31786.q: In which year was the Hagia Sophia reopened as a mosque for prayer?
31786.e: In 2020 a Turkish court cancelled its status as a museum. Since then Islamic prayers have been held there again.
31786.m: Since 2020 the Hagia Sophia has been a mosque again.

31787.q: Which Byzantine emperor started the Iconoclast Controversy around 726/730?
31787.e: Leo III took action against the veneration of religious images. His son Constantine V made this policy stricter.
31787.m: Leo III began the Byzantine Iconoclast Controversy.

31788.q: What are the opponents of the veneration of images in the Byzantine Iconoclast Controversy called?
31788.e: Iconoclasts literally means “image breakers”. The supporters of images are called iconodules.
31788.m: The opponents of images are called iconoclasts.

31789.q: Which council allowed the veneration of images again in 787?
31789.e: Empress Irene called the council. It distinguished the permitted veneration of images from the worship that is due to God alone.
31789.m: The Second Council of Nicaea allowed the veneration of images in 787.

31790.q: In which year did the Byzantine Iconoclast Controversy finally end?
31790.e: After a second phase hostile to images from 815, a regent ruling for her young son permanently restored the veneration of images in 843.
31790.m: The Iconoclast Controversy finally ended in 843.

31791.q: Which feast of the Eastern Church still commemorates the victory of the friends of images?
a: Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross
31791.e: The Sunday of Orthodoxy is celebrated on the first Sunday of Lent. Believers often carry icons in a procession.
31791.m: The Sunday of Orthodoxy celebrates the return of the icons.

31792.q: Which theologian defended the veneration of images with influential writings in the 8th century?
31792.e: John of Damascus lived under Muslim rule and was therefore safe from the emperor. He argued that Christ becoming human made it possible to depict him.
31792.m: John of Damascus defended the icons.

31793.q: What did the opponents of images mainly appeal to?
31793.e: They saw the veneration of icons as breaking the Old Testament ban on worshipping images. The supporters saw images as aids to devotion.
31793.m: The opponents of images appealed to the biblical ban on images.

31794.q: In which year did the great break between the Eastern and Western Churches happen?
31794.e: In 1054 papal envoys and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other. The year is seen as the start of the East-West Schism.
31794.m: In 1054 the Eastern and Western Churches split.

31795.q: In which church did the papal envoys place the bull of excommunication against the patriarch on the altar in 1054?
31795.e: The delegation under Cardinal Humbert laid the bull down in the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople on 16 July 1054. This is seen as the symbolic start of the split in the Church.
31795.m: The bull of 1054 lay on the altar of the Hagia Sophia.

31796.q: Which addition to the Creed did the Eastern and Western Churches argue about?
31796.e: The West added that the Holy Spirit proceeds “and from the Son”. The Eastern Church rejected this one-sided addition.
31796.m: The Filioque addition was a main point of dispute between East and West.

31797.q: What did the Eastern and Western Churches argue about in celebrating the Eucharist?
31797.e: The West used unleavened bread, the East leavened bread. This so-called azymes controversy played an important part in 1054.
31797.m: East and West also argued about the bread of the Eucharist.

31798.q: In which year were the mutual excommunications of 1054 lifted?
31798.e: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the excommunications at the end of the Second Vatican Council. The split in the Church itself continues, however.
31798.m: The excommunications of 1054 were lifted in 1965.

31799.q: Which event in 1204 especially deepened the split between the Eastern and Western Churches?
a: The sack of Constantinople by crusaders
The fall of the city of Acre
The founding of the Teutonic Order
31799.e: In the Fourth Crusade, Western crusaders captured and plundered Constantinople. Afterwards a Latin Empire was set up.
31799.m: The sack of Constantinople in 1204 poisoned relations between East and West.

31800.q: Why did the Byzantine emperor seek an agreement with the Western Church in 1439?
a: He needed help against the Ottomans
He wanted to become Pope himself
He wanted to convert to Islam
31800.e: A union was agreed at the Council of Ferrara-Florence. It failed because of resistance in the East, and in 1453 Constantinople fell to the Ottomans.
31800.m: In 1439 Byzantium sought Church union to get help against the Ottomans.

31801.q: In which year did the Hijra take place?
31801.e: The emigration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca happened in 622. The Islamic calendar begins with this year.
31801.m: The Hijra of 622 is the start of the Islamic calendar.

31802.q: To which city did Muhammad emigrate in the Hijra?
31802.e: Yathrib was afterwards called “Madinat an-Nabi”, the city of the Prophet. The first Muslim community with its own rules grew up there.
31802.m: In the Hijra Muhammad moved to Yathrib, today's Medina.

31803.q: What is the pilgrimage to Mecca called that every Muslim should make once in their life if they can?
31803.e: The Hajj is one of the five pillars of Islam. Ramadan is the month of fasting, Zakat the duty to give alms and Shahada the declaration of faith.
31803.m: The Hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca.

31804.q: According to Islamic tradition, which angel brought Muhammad the revelations?
31804.e: According to tradition, Gabriel (Jibril in Arabic) appeared to Muhammad around 610 in a cave near Mecca. Gabriel also appears in the Bible as a messenger of God.
31804.m: In Islam the angel Gabriel brought the revelations.

31805.q: In which city was Muhammad born around 570?
31805.e: Muhammad came from the Quraysh tribe, which controlled Mecca. He only emigrated to Medina in 622.

31806.q: Who was Muhammad's first wife and is regarded as the first Muslim woman?
31806.e: Khadija was a wealthy businesswoman and supported Muhammad from the start. Fatima was their daughter.

31807.q: What did Muhammad have done with the Kaaba after entering Mecca in 630?
a: Remove the images of gods from it
Hand it over to the Christians
31807.e: Before Islam, images of many gods stood in the Kaaba. Muhammad had them removed and made the Kaaba the centre of faith in the one God.
31807.m: In 630 Muhammad had the images of gods removed from the Kaaba.

31808.q: Which city did the Umayyads besiege without success in 717/718?
31808.e: Emperor Leo III defended the city successfully, among other things with Greek fire. Afterwards Byzantium held on in Asia Minor.
31808.m: In 717/718 the Umayyad siege of Constantinople failed.

31809.q: Which river did Umayyad armies reach in the east around 711 with the conquest of Sindh?
31809.e: Muhammad ibn Qasim conquered the area in what is now Pakistan. The empire thus expanded into South Asia.
31809.m: Around 711 the Umayyad empire reached the Indus.

31810.q: Which building in Jerusalem did the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik have built?
31810.e: The Dome of the Rock was completed around 691/692 and is regarded as the oldest surviving large building of Islam.
31810.m: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem dates from the time of the Umayyads.

31811.q: In which battle in 732 did Charles Martel stop an advance by an Umayyad army into the Frankish kingdom?
31811.e: An army from Muslim Spain was defeated between two towns in western France. The importance of the battle is judged more cautiously today than it used to be.
31811.m: Charles Martel won at Tours and Poitiers in 732.

31812.q: In which battle in 680 did Husayn, Muhammad's grandson, fall against an Umayyad army?
31812.e: Shia Muslims mourn Husayn's death every year on the day of Ashura. The event deepened the split between Sunnis and Shias.
31812.m: Husayn's death at Karbala still shapes Shia Islam today.

31813.q: Which language did Caliph Abd al-Malik make the administrative language of his empire?
31813.e: Before that, the administration in the conquered areas often worked in Greek or Persian. Abd al-Malik also had coins minted for the first time with only Arabic writing.
31813.m: Under Abd al-Malik, Arabic became the language of administration.

31814.q: What was the poll tax called that Christians and Jews had to pay as protected people in the caliphate?
31814.e: In return for the jizya they received protection and were allowed to practise their religion. Zakat, on the other hand, is the obligatory payment of Muslims, and kharaj is a land tax.
31814.m: Non-Muslims paid the jizya poll tax in the caliphate.

31815.q: According to tradition, which technique reached the Islamic world from China after the Battle of Talas in 751?
31815.e: Chinese prisoners are said to have passed on papermaking in Samarkand. Soon there were paper mills in Baghdad as well.
31815.m: Paper came west from China via the Islamic world.

31816.q: What shape was the original centre of Baghdad?
31816.e: The “Round City” had a ring of walls with four gates and the palace with the mosque in the middle.
31816.m: Baghdad was laid out as a round city.

31817.q: Which Abbasid caliph, known from “One Thousand and One Nights”, ruled from 786 to 809?
31817.e: Under Harun al-Rashid, Baghdad enjoyed a golden age. He often appears as a character in the stories of “One Thousand and One Nights”.
31817.m: Harun al-Rashid is the most famous Abbasid caliph.

31818.q: Which Western ruler was given an elephant called Abul Abbas by the Abbasids around 802?
31818.e: After a long journey the elephant reached Aachen. The gift shows the diplomatic contacts between Baghdad and the Frankish kingdom.
31818.m: Charlemagne got an elephant from Baghdad.

31819.q: In which city did a shadow Abbasid caliphate exist after 1261 under the protection of the Mamluks?
31819.e: The caliphs there only had religious and ceremonial duties. Real power lay with the Mamluk sultans until 1517.
31819.m: After losing Baghdad, Abbasid caliphs lived powerless in Cairo.

31820.q: What is the Great Mosque of Samarra, built in the Abbasid period, famous for?
31820.e: Samarra was the caliphs' residence from 836 to 892. The minaret of the Great Mosque winds upwards in a spiral as a ramp.
31820.m: Samarra is known for its spiral minaret.

31821.q: Whom did the Abbasids trace their name back to?
31821.e: The dynasty was descended from al-Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet. They used this family link to justify their rule.
31821.m: The Abbasids are named after al-Abbas, an uncle of Muhammad.

31822.q: What did scholars working for Caliph al-Ma'mun determine by taking measurements in the desert?
31822.e: They measured the length of one degree along a meridian and used it to calculate the Earth's circumference. The result came quite close to today's value.
31822.m: Under al-Ma'mun, scholars measured the Earth's circumference.

31823.q: In which city was the famous House of Wisdom of the Abbasids?
31823.e: In the 9th century the Abbasid caliphs made Baghdad the centre of science. Scholars from many countries worked in the House of Wisdom.
31823.m: The House of Wisdom was in Baghdad.

31824.q: Which writing material was produced in Baghdad from the late 8th century and made it easier to spread books?
31824.e: The technique came from China and was cheaper than parchment. Baghdad thus became a centre of the book trade.
31824.m: Paper made books cheaper in Baghdad.

31825.q: Which work was at the centre of the House of Wisdom in Baghdad?
31825.e: Scholars translated works by Aristotle, Galen and others into Arabic. So a lot of ancient knowledge was preserved and later reached Europe.
31825.m: In the House of Wisdom, ancient knowledge was translated into Arabic.

31826.q: Which mathematician from Baghdad lives on in the word “algorithm”?
31826.e: The Latin form of his name, “Algorismi”, became the term for step-by-step methods of calculation.
31826.m: The term algorithm goes back to al-Khwarizmi.

31827.q: Which Arabic word does the term “algebra” come from?
31827.e: Al-jabr means “restoring” and comes from the title of a maths textbook from Baghdad. The other words gave us chemistry, alkali and alcohol.
31827.m: The word algebra comes from the Arabic al-jabr.

31828.q: Which number system was passed on by scholars in Baghdad and later reached Europe?
31828.e: The place value system with zero, which came from India, was explained in Arabic writings. In Europe it only became widespread from the late Middle Ages.
31828.m: Our numerals come from India and reached us via the Arab world.

31829.q: Which city was the capital of the caliphate in al-Andalus in the 10th century?
31829.e: Under Abd al-Rahman III, Córdoba became one of the largest and richest cities in Europe. The palace city of Medina Azahara was built outside its gates.
31829.m: Córdoba was the capital of the caliphate in al-Andalus.

31830.q: Which general lives on in the name “Gibraltar”?
31830.e: Gibraltar comes from “Jabal Tariq”, the mountain of Tariq. That is where he landed with his troops.
31830.m: Gibraltar means the mountain of Tariq.

31831.q: Who founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756?
31831.e: He was one of the few Umayyads who escaped the overthrow of his family in the East. In al-Andalus he set up an independent rule.
31831.m: Abd al-Rahman I founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

31832.q: Which dynasty did the caliphs of Córdoba belong to?
31832.e: After his family was overthrown in the East, an Umayyad fled to Spain. His descendant Abd al-Rahman III took the title of caliph in 929.

31833.q: Which building in Córdoba was built as a mosque from 785 and later became a cathedral?
31833.e: The Mezquita is famous for its forest of columns with red and white arches. After the Christian conquest in 1236 it became a church.
31833.m: The Mezquita of Córdoba is both mosque and cathedral.

31834.q: Which city fell to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492 as the last Muslim-ruled territory in Spain?
31834.e: The Nasrid emirate surrendered to Isabella and Ferdinand. This ended the Reconquista.
31834.m: With the fall of Granada in 1492, al-Andalus came to an end.

31835.q: What are the small kingdoms called into which the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up after 1031?
31835.e: Taifa means “party” or “faction”. The quarrelling small kingdoms made it easier for the Christian kingdoms to advance.
31835.m: After 1031 al-Andalus broke up into taifa kingdoms.

31836.q: In which area was Ibn Sina (Avicenna) born around 980?
31836.e: He was born in the village of Afshana near Bukhara in what is now Uzbekistan. At that time the region belonged to the Samanid empire.
31836.m: Ibn Sina was born near Bukhara in Central Asia.

31837.q: What is the name of Ibn Sina's main medical work?
31837.e: The Canon systematically summed up the medical knowledge of Greeks, Persians and Arabs. Colliget is a work by an Andalusian scholar, and Physica is by Hildegard of Bingen.
31837.m: Ibn Sina's main work is the Canon of Medicine.

31838.q: Until when was Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine used as a textbook at European universities?
31838.e: The work was translated into Latin in the 12th century. In Montpellier and Leuven it was still used in teaching until around 1650.
31838.m: The Canon of Medicine was a textbook in Europe for about five centuries.

31839.q: Which fields of knowledge did Ibn Sina cover in his great philosophical collection, “The Book of Healing”?
a: Logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics
Law and interpretation of the Quran
31839.e: The title refers to healing the soul from ignorance. The work covers logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics, summing up almost all the knowledge of its time.
31839.m: Ibn Sina's Book of Healing covers almost all the knowledge of his time.

31840.q: With which thought experiment did Ibn Sina want to show that the soul is aware of itself without sense impressions?
31840.e: A person floats in the air without any sensory perception and still knows that he exists. The allegory of the cave is by Plato.
31840.m: With the floating man, Ibn Sina argued for the soul's self-awareness.

31841.q: In which language did Ibn Sina write most of his scientific works?
31841.e: Arabic was then the language of science in the Islamic world, although Ibn Sina came from the Persian region. His works were only translated into Latin later.
31841.m: Ibn Sina wrote his works mainly in Arabic.
