31842.q: Which title of honour did Ibn Sina receive because of his importance for medicine?
31842.e: His wide medical knowledge made him a model for doctors in East and West. Herodotus was called the “Father of History”.
31842.m: Ibn Sina is regarded as the Prince of Physicians.

31843.q: In which city was Ibn Rushd (Averroes) born in 1126?
31843.e: He came from a respected family of lawyers in the city. His grandfather had already been chief judge there.
31843.m: Averroes was born in Córdoba in 1126.

31844.q: By which nickname was Averroes known in the Latin Middle Ages?
31844.e: His detailed explanations of ancient writings were authoritative at European universities. “The Philosopher”, on the other hand, was the name for the ancient author himself.
31844.m: In the Middle Ages Averroes was simply called the Commentator.

31845.q: Which ancient philosopher did Averroes mainly write commentaries on?
31845.e: He wrote short, middle and long commentaries on almost all the works of this philosopher. They had a strong influence on scholasticism.
31845.m: Averroes mainly explained the works of Aristotle.

31846.q: Which view did Averroes defend against the theologian al-Ghazali?
a: Philosophy and faith do not contradict each other
31846.e: Al-Ghazali had sharply attacked the philosophers in “The Incoherence of the Philosophers”. Averroes replied with “The Incoherence of the Incoherence” and showed that reasoning and faith can go together.
31846.m: Averroes defended philosophy as compatible with faith.

31847.q: Which office did Averroes hold in Seville and Córdoba, among other places?
31847.e: Averroes was a respected legal scholar and worked as a qadi. He was also personal physician to the Almohad caliph.
31847.m: Averroes also worked as a judge.

31848.q: How did the Church react in the 13th century to Paris scholars who adopted the teachings of Averroes?
a: It condemned some of their theses
31848.e: Scholars such as Siger of Brabant represented so-called Latin Averroism. The Bishop of Paris condemned several of their theses in 1270 and 1277, and Thomas Aquinas wrote against them.
31848.m: Latin Averroism was condemned by the Church in Paris.

31849.q: In which city did Averroes die in 1198?
31849.e: After a period of banishment he was called back to the Almohad court in North Africa, where he died shortly afterwards.

31850.q: Which title did the leader of the Seljuks receive from the caliph in Baghdad in 1055?
31850.e: The caliph remained the spiritual head of the Sunnis, while the sultan took over worldly power. This made the Seljuks the leading power in the Middle East.
31850.m: The Seljuks ruled as sultans alongside the caliph.

31851.q: Which battle in 1071 opened Anatolia to settlement by Turkic groups?
31851.e: The Byzantine army suffered a heavy defeat in eastern Anatolia against Sultan Alp Arslan. Afterwards Turkmen groups pushed far into Asia Minor.
31851.m: The Battle of Manzikert in 1071 changed Anatolia.

31852.q: Which empire suffered a heavy defeat against the Seljuks at Manzikert in 1071?
31852.e: The Byzantine army was beaten in eastern Anatolia, and the emperor was even taken prisoner. Afterwards Byzantium lost large parts of Asia Minor.
31852.m: At Manzikert in 1071 Byzantium lost to the Seljuks.

31853.q: What are the Islamic colleges called that were founded in many places in the Seljuk empire?
31853.e: In the madrasas, students learned Islamic law and theology. The vizier Nizam al-Mulk had many of them founded in the 11th century.
31853.m: Madrasas were the colleges of the Islamic world.

31854.q: Which city was the capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum?
31854.e: Konya, ancient Iconium, enjoyed a cultural golden age in the 13th century. The mystic Rumi also worked there.
31854.m: Konya was the capital of the Seljuks of Rum.

31855.q: Which scholar worked on a precise calendar reform for Sultan Malik Shah?
31855.e: Omar Khayyam led a group of astronomers who created the Jalali calendar. Today he is also known as a poet of quatrains.
31855.m: Omar Khayyam created a precise calendar for the Seljuks.

31856.q: Which power made the Seljuks of Rum pay tribute in 1243?
31856.e: After a defeat against a Mongol army, the Seljuks of Rum lost their independence. Their empire then broke up into small principalities.
31856.m: In 1243 the Seljuks of Rum came under Mongol rule.

31857.q: Around which year is the founding of the Ottoman Empire by Osman I traditionally placed?
31857.e: Osman I led a small principality in north-western Anatolia. The year 1299 is a traditional date that is not precisely documented.
31857.m: The Ottoman Empire began around 1299 under Osman I.

31858.q: Which city did the Ottomans conquer in 1453 and make their capital?
31858.e: In 1453 Sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire. Before that, Bursa and Edirne had been Ottoman capitals.
31858.m: In 1453 Constantinople became the capital of the Ottomans.

31859.q: What was special about the location of the Ottoman capital Edirne in the 14th century?
a: It was on the Caspian Sea
31859.e: Edirne, formerly Adrianople, lies in Thrace. By moving the capital there, the centre of the empire shifted to the Balkans.
31859.m: With Edirne the Ottomans had their capital in Europe.

31860.q: In which battle did the Ottomans fight a Serbian army in 1389, in which Sultan Murad I was killed?
31860.e: The battle in what is now Kosovo ended with heavy losses on both sides. Serbia then became dependent on the Ottomans.
31860.m: In 1389 Ottomans and Serbs fought at Kosovo Field.

31861.q: Who defeated Sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara in 1402?
31861.e: Bayezid was taken prisoner and died shortly afterwards. The empire fell into a civil war between brothers over the succession that lasted years.
31861.m: Timur defeated the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402.

31862.q: Whom did the Ottomans defeat at Nicopolis on the Danube in 1396?
31862.e: King Sigismund of Hungary led a large army of knights from many European countries. Sultan Bayezid I crushed it.
31862.m: In 1396 the Ottomans defeated the crusaders at Nicopolis.

31863.q: Which peninsula became the Ottomans' first permanent base in Europe in 1354?
31863.e: After an earthquake, Ottoman troops occupied the fortress of Gallipoli on the Dardanelles. From there they advanced into the Balkans.
31863.m: The Ottomans gained a foothold in Europe at Gallipoli in 1354.

31864.q: What was the name of the Ottoman elite troop formed from Christian boys recruited by force?
31864.e: The boys were chosen through the devshirme (boy levy), converted to Islam and trained. Sipahis, by contrast, were mounted cavalrymen holding land grants.
31864.m: The Janissaries were the sultans' elite troop.

31865.q: What did it mean for a vassal when his fief became hereditary?
a: His son could take over the fief after his death
He no longer had to do military service
He could sell the fief to strangers
The fief went to the Church after his death
31865.e: Originally a fief went back to the lord when the vassal died. With heredity, granted for example by Conrad II in 1037 for Italy, the sons could take it over. This made vassals more independent.
31865.m: Hereditary fiefs stayed in the vassal's family.

31866.q: Which two duties of the vassal did the Latin formula “auxilium et consilium” sum up?
31866.e: The vassal owed his lord military and material aid as well as counsel, for example at court assemblies. In return the lord gave protection and support.
31866.m: The vassal owed his lord counsel and aid.

31867.q: What was the ceremony called in which the vassal placed his folded hands in the hands of his lord?
31867.e: With commendation (the joining of hands) the vassal symbolically placed himself under the lord's protection. This was usually followed by the oath of fealty.
31867.m: In commendation the vassal placed his hands in his lord's.

31868.q: What could happen to a vassal who broke faith with his lord?
a: He could be raised to the nobility
He could be taken into a monastery
He could be banished from the Church by the king
31868.e: A serious breach of faith was called felony. The lord could then take back the fief, since the land had only been granted in exchange for loyalty.
31868.m: If he broke faith, the vassal could lose his fief.

31869.q: What was the difference between a fief and land owned outright?
a: With a fief the lord kept the ultimate ownership
A fief could not be farmed
A fief always belonged to the Church
No one paid dues on a fief
31869.e: A fief was land on loan: the vassal could use it, but ultimate ownership stayed with the lord. Freehold land, the allod, belonged to its owner without any tie to a lord.
31869.m: A fief was land on loan, not free property.

31870.q: What is the name of the picture that shows the ranks of the feudal system from the king down to the peasants?
31870.e: At the top of the feudal pyramid is the king, below him princes and knights, and at the bottom the peasants. In the Middle Ages itself, the order of shields in the Sachsenspiegel, for example, arranged the holders of fiefs in ranks.
31870.m: The feudal pyramid shows the ranks of the feudal system.

31871.q: With what did the king symbolically grant a duchy as a fief to a lay prince?
31871.e: The banner was the sign of military command, so such imperial fiefs were called banner fiefs. Ring and staff, on the other hand, were the signs with which bishops were installed in office.
31871.m: Lay princes received their fief with a banner.

31872.q: Which problem arose when a vassal held fiefs from several lords?
a: He faced conflicting loyalties when the lords fought each other
He could no longer employ peasants
He automatically lost his noble title
He had to give all the lords the same land
31872.e: Many vassals held fiefs from several lords. If these quarrelled, it was unclear whom the vassal had to help. So it was laid down which lord had first claim on his loyalty.
31872.m: Several lords led to conflicting loyalties.

31873.q: What did a polyptych, an estate register of a Carolingian manor, record?
31873.e: A polyptych lists farms, dependent peasants and their dues and services. A well-known one is that of Abbot Irminon of Saint-Germain-des-Prés from the early 9th century.
31873.m: A polyptych records the lands and dues of a manor.

31874.q: How was a manor usually organised in the early Middle Ages?
a: A lord's home farm with dependent peasant farms around it
A village with no lord and an elected council
31874.e: Historians call this form the bipartite manor or villication (from Latin villa). A home farm was the centre, surrounded by dependent peasant farms that paid dues and did labour services.
31874.m: The bipartite manor combined the lord's home farm and dependent peasant holdings.

31875.q: Which payment often had to be made to the lord when a serf died, for example in the form of the best animal?
31875.e: The heriot (in German “Besthaupt”) was a kind of death duty. The heirs had to give the lord the most valuable animal or a best garment.
31875.m: With the heriot the lord received the dead person's best animal.

31876.q: Which decree of Charlemagne regulated the running of the royal estates around 800?
31876.e: The Capitulare de villis laid down how royal estates were to be run, right down to plants and supplies. It is an important source on the Carolingian manorial system.
31876.m: The Capitulare de villis regulated Charlemagne's royal estates.

31877.q: What did the hide (Latin mansus) mean in the medieval manorial system?
a: A peasant holding meant to feed a family
A church district under a priest
31877.e: The hide was the basic unit of peasant property and was meant to feed one family. Its size varied greatly depending on region and soil.
31877.m: A hide was a family's peasant holding.

31878.q: Which law governed the relations between the lord and his dependants within a manor?
31878.e: Manorial law applied to the members of a manor and was often written down in records of customs. It set out dues, services and jurisdiction.
31878.m: Manorial law ordered life on the manor.

31879.q: Which development increasingly shaped the manorial system in the High Middle Ages?
a: Labour services replaced by money and payments in kind
Return to the ancient slave economy
Handing all land over to the towns
31879.e: Many lords gave up farming their own land and leased out the demesne in return for dues. This created the so-called rent-based manor.
31879.m: In the High Middle Ages, dues increasingly replaced labour services.

31880.q: Which monastery in what is now Switzerland was one of the biggest landowners of the region in the early and High Middle Ages?
31880.e: The Abbey of St Gallen owned estates all around Lake Constance, in Thurgau, in the Zürichgau and as far as the Breisgau. Its charters are among the most important sources on the manorial system.
31880.m: The Abbey of St Gallen was an important landowner.

31881.q: Into which three groups did the medieval doctrine of the three orders divide society?
a: Those who pray, those who fight and those who work
31881.e: Bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society like this around 1025. The clergy prayed, the nobility fought, the peasants worked.
31881.m: The three orders were those who pray, those who fight and those who work.

31882.q: What usually decided whether someone belonged to the nobility or the peasantry in the Middle Ages?
31882.e: People were born into an order and usually stayed in it. The society of orders therefore allowed little movement between groups.
31882.m: In the Middle Ages, a person's order was usually decided by birth.

31883.q: How was the order of the three estates mainly justified in the Middle Ages?
a: As an order willed by God
As the result of a popular vote
As a consequence of owning money
31883.e: The orders were seen as part of a divine order in which everyone had a fixed place. This was meant to justify and stabilise existing rule.
31883.m: The order of estates was seen as willed by God.

31884.q: Which order came first according to the doctrine of the three orders?
31884.e: Those who prayed had the highest rank because they cared for the salvation of everyone. Then came the fighting nobility and the working peasants.
31884.m: The clergy formed the first estate.

31885.q: Which path offered a peasant's son the best chance of rising in society in the Middle Ages?
31885.e: The Church also took in sons of humble birth, who could rise as monks or priests. Some even reached high Church offices.
31885.m: The Church offered peasants' sons a way to rise.

31886.q: Which group did not fit well into the order of the three estates in the High Middle Ages?
a: The merchants and craftsmen of the towns
31886.e: The doctrine of the three orders only knew those who prayed, fought and worked on the land. With the growing towns a middle class of townspeople emerged that did not fit this scheme.
31886.m: The urban middle class broke the order of the three estates.

31887.q: In which assembly were the three estates represented in France until the Revolution of 1789?
31887.e: The Estates General (États généraux) consisted of clergy, nobility and Third Estate. Calling them in 1789 helped to set off the French Revolution.
31887.m: The three estates of France sat in the Estates General.

31888.q: In which city was Otto I crowned king in 936?
31888.e: Otto deliberately had himself crowned in Aachen, Charlemagne's palace city. In this way he linked himself to the Carolingian tradition.
31888.m: Otto I was crowned in Aachen in 936.

31889.q: In which year was Otto I crowned emperor in Rome?
31889.e: Pope John XII crowned Otto I emperor on 2 February 962. This renewed the Western empire, linked with the East Frankish kingship.

31890.q: Under the Privilegium Ottonianum of 962, what did a newly elected Pope have to do before his consecration?
a: Swear an oath of loyalty to the emperor
Give the crown back to the emperor
31890.e: In 962 Otto I confirmed the Papal States. At the same time he secured influence over papal elections, because the Pope had to swear loyalty to him.
31890.m: In 962 Otto I secured influence over papal elections.

31891.q: Which king from Saxony founded the rule of the Ottonians in 919?
31891.e: Henry I was Duke of the Saxons and became king in 919. His son Otto I later became emperor.
31891.m: Henry I was the first king of the Ottonian house.

31892.q: Which city did Emperor Otto III want to make the centre of his empire?
31892.e: Otto III dreamed of renewing the Roman Empire and lived in Rome at times. He died in 1002 aged only 21.
31892.m: Otto III wanted to make Rome the centre of his empire.

31893.q: Which monastery on Lake Constance was a centre of Ottonian book illumination?
31893.e: Magnificent manuscripts for Ottonian rulers were made on Reichenau. Several of them are now part of the Memory of the World register.
31893.m: Reichenau was a centre of Ottonian book illumination.

31894.q: Which ruling house followed the Ottonians in 1024?
31894.e: After Henry II died childless, Conrad II, the first Salian, was elected. The Salians were later followed by the Hohenstaufen.
31894.m: The Salians followed the Ottonians in 1024.

31895.q: Which political programme did Otto III pursue with the motto “Renovatio imperii Romanorum”?
a: Division of the empire among his sons
31895.e: Otto III wanted to renew the imperial office on the Roman model and make Rome the centre. That is why he lived in Rome at times.
31895.m: Otto III aimed to renew the Roman Empire.

31896.q: What could a landowner in the early Middle Ages usually decide himself about a church on his land?
31896.e: Under the proprietary church system, the church belonged to the landowner. He appointed the priest and used the income.
31896.m: Under the proprietary church system, the church belonged to the landowner.

31897.q: What services did bishoprics and imperial abbeys provide for the king in the High Middle Ages?
a: They housed the court and provided troops
They elected the king on their own
They minted all the empire's money
They paid the Pope on the king's behalf
31897.e: The king travelled around with his court and was provided for by the imperial Church. Bishops and abbots also supplied him with warriors.
31897.m: The imperial Church served the king with hospitality and troops.

31898.q: Why did the Ottonians like to use bishops rather than counts as pillars of their power?
a: Bishops had no heirs, so their office went back to the king
Bishops were always richer than counts
Bishops were not allowed to demand taxes
Bishops were elected by the people
31898.e: Lay fiefs became hereditary, but bishoprics did not. So after a bishop died, the king could appoint someone he trusted again. One example is Otto's brother Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne.
31898.m: Bishops as office holders could not found dynasties.

31899.q: What did the privilege of immunity mean for a Church estate in the Middle Ages?
a: Royal counts could not hold court there
The estate could not be inherited
The Church had to provide the king with soldiers
31899.e: With immunity, royal officials were not allowed to enter the Church estate. The bishops exercised the rights there themselves or through an advocate.
31899.m: Immunity protected Church estates from the royal counts.

31900.q: Which institution at the royal court served as a training ground for future imperial bishops?
31900.e: In the royal chapel, clergy served the king in the liturgy and the chancery. Many of them were afterwards made bishops.
31900.m: The royal chapel trained future imperial bishops.

31901.q: Which worldly rights did kings often grant to bishops to strengthen them as supporters?
a: The sole right to elect the king
The right of inheritance for sons
31901.e: Bishops received counties, tolls, market and minting rights. This made them powerful territorial lords in the king's service.
31901.m: Bishops received counties and regalia from the king.

31902.q: Why did the Church reformers of the 11th century reject the imperial Church system?
a: Because laymen such as the king appointed bishops
Because the bishops owned too little land
Because the king was not baptised
31902.e: The reformers demanded that only the Church should appoint its office holders. The dispute about this between emperor and Pope is called the Investiture Controversy.
31902.m: The imperial Church system led to the Investiture Controversy.

31903.q: Which group rose up against Henry IV in 1073, partly because of his castle building in the Harz?
31903.e: The Saxons saw Henry's castles, such as the Harzburg, as a threat. The Saxon War weakened the king before his conflict with the Pope.
31903.m: The Saxons rose up against Henry IV in 1073.

31904.q: What did the Church reformers of the 11th century demand of priests?
31904.e: The reformers fought against priests marrying and demanded strict celibacy. They wanted to free the Church from the influence of lay families.
31904.m: The Church reform required priests to stay unmarried.

31905.q: Which group did the papal election decree of 1059 give the decisive role in electing the Pope?
31905.e: Pope Nicholas II wanted to free the election from the influence of the Roman nobility and the emperor. The cardinal bishops were to choose the candidate.
31905.m: The papal election decree of 1059 gave the election of the Pope to the cardinals.

31906.q: At which assembly in January 1076 did Henry IV and the German bishops declare Pope Gregory VII deposed?
31906.e: At Worms, Henry IV and many bishops broke with Gregory and called him simply “Hildebrand”. Gregory replied in February 1076 by excommunicating Henry.
31906.m: At Worms in 1076 Henry IV and bishops declared the Pope deposed.

31907.q: What did Henry IV do in the winter of 1077 to free himself from excommunication?
a: He went to Canossa as a penitent
He marched on Rome with an army
31907.e: Henry crossed the Alps to Canossa Castle, where Pope Gregory VII was staying. After three days of penance, the Pope lifted the excommunication.
31907.m: With the walk to Canossa in 1077, Henry IV freed himself from excommunication.

31908.q: With which agreement was the Investiture Controversy settled in 1122?
31908.e: In the Concordat of Worms the emperor gave up investing bishops with ring and staff. But he was still allowed to grant them worldly rights.
31908.m: The Concordat of Worms ended the Investiture Controversy in 1122.

31909.q: What was the Investiture Controversy really about?
a: Who may install bishops in office
Which language is used at Mass
Who owns the city of Rome
31909.e: Investiture means installation in office. Emperor and Pope argued about who had the right to install bishops and abbots.
31909.m: The Investiture Controversy was about installing bishops.

a: A pope raised up against another pope
The Pope's representative at the emperor's court
A head of the Eastern Church
31910.e: In the Investiture Controversy, Henry IV had his own pope, Clement III, elected against Gregory VII. The Church does not regard antipopes as legitimate.
31910.m: An antipope stood against another pope.

31911.q: In which year did Henry IV make his walk to Canossa?
31911.e: In January 1077 Henry IV appeared as a penitent in front of Canossa Castle. He wanted to be freed from excommunication.
31911.m: The walk to Canossa took place in 1077.

31912.q: Why did Henry IV cross the Alps into Italy in the winter of 1076/77?
a: He wanted to be freed from excommunication
He wanted to be crowned emperor
31912.e: Pope Gregory VII had excommunicated Henry in 1076. The princes threatened to stop recognising him as king if he was not soon freed from it. He was accompanied by his wife Bertha of Savoy.
31912.m: Henry IV went to Canossa to be freed from excommunication.

31913.q: Why did Henry's appearance as a penitent at Canossa put Pope Gregory VII in a difficult position?
a: As a priest he had to forgive a repentant sinner
He had no army to defend the castle
He did not recognise the king
He was not allowed to leave the castle
31913.e: Gregory had actually wanted to travel to an assembly of princes in Augsburg to sit in judgement on Henry. When the king appeared as a penitent outside the castle, the Pope could hardly refuse him absolution.
31913.m: With his penance, Henry IV forced the Pope to absolve him.

31914.q: Why is the most famous account of the penance at Canossa seen today as strongly coloured?
a: The chronicler was an opponent of the king
It was only invented in the 19th century
It comes from an ancient poet
It was dictated by the Pope
31914.e: The chronicler Lampert of Hersfeld was critical of Henry IV and described his humiliation vividly. Many later accounts took over his picture.
31914.m: Lampert of Hersfeld created a one-sided picture of Canossa.

31915.q: How do some historians interpret the walk to Canossa differently today?
a: More as a peace agreement than a humiliation
As the king's victory in a battle
As the start of the Reformation
31915.e: In 2012 the historian Johannes Fried argued that a peace treaty between king and Pope was concluded at Canossa. His theory is disputed among historians.
31915.m: Recent research partly sees Canossa as a peace agreement.

31916.q: Why was Henry's crossing of the Alps in the winter of 1076/77 especially dangerous?
a: Blocked passes forced him to take a detour in deep winter
He had to cross an enemy Venetian army
He travelled with heavy siege engines
31916.e: Because the southern German princes blocked the passes, Henry went via Burgundy and the Mont Cenis. The crossing in winter was extremely dangerous.
31916.m: On the way to Canossa, Henry IV crossed the Mont Cenis.

31917.q: What was the result of Canossa for the dispute between Henry IV and Gregory VII?
a: The dispute soon flared up again
31917.e: The excommunication was lifted in 1077, but in 1080 Gregory excommunicated Henry again. In 1084 Henry marched on Rome and had an antipope installed. At Canossa, Abbot Hugh of Cluny had been one of the mediators.
31917.m: Canossa did not end the Investiture Controversy.

31918.q: Which conflict did the Concordat of Worms of 1122 end?
a: The schism between the Eastern and Western Churches
The dispute over the imperial crown of Byzantium
31918.e: For decades emperor and Pope argued about who could appoint bishops. At Worms they agreed on a compromise.
31918.m: The Concordat of Worms ended the Investiture Controversy in 1122.

31919.q: After the Concordat of Worms, with which symbol did the king grant bishops their worldly rights?
31919.e: The symbols of spiritual office were reserved for the Church. The king only invested bishops with the regalia, symbolised by the sceptre.
31919.m: After Worms the king invested bishops with the sceptre.

31920.q: Which order of events applied in the German part of the empire after the Concordat of Worms?
a: First investiture with the regalia, then consecration
First consecration, then investiture by the Pope
31920.e: In Germany the person elected first received the regalia, which secured influence for the king. In Italy and Burgundy investiture only came after consecration.
31920.m: In the German part of the empire, investiture came before consecration.

31921.q: Why did the king have less influence over bishops in Italy and Burgundy than in Germany after the Concordat of Worms?
a: There investiture only came after consecration
There the Byzantine emperor chose the bishops
The king was never allowed to travel there
31921.e: In Germany the person elected received the regalia before consecration, so the king had a say. In Italy and Burgundy the bishop was already consecrated when the king invested him.
31921.m: In Italy and Burgundy, investiture only followed consecration.

31922.q: Which right did the king keep in episcopal elections in the German part of the empire after the Concordat of Worms?
a: He could be present at the election
He could appoint the bishop alone
He could grant ring and staff
31922.e: The election was to be canonical and free, but the king could be present. In disputed elections he could step in to support the more reasonable side.
31922.m: The king could be present at episcopal elections.

31923.q: Who concluded the Concordat of Worms with each other in 1122?
31923.e: Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II each issued a charter. A council in Rome confirmed the agreement in 1123.
31923.m: The Concordat of Worms was a settlement between emperor and Pope.

31924.q: Which distinction did the Concordat of Worms make possible?
a: Between a bishop's spiritual office and worldly property
Between the emperor and the King of France
31924.e: The Church granted the spiritualities, the king the temporalities or regalia. This separation goes back to ideas of scholars such as Ivo of Chartres.
31924.m: The Concordat of Worms separated spiritualities and temporalities.

31925.q: In which century did Emperor Frederick Barbarossa reign?
31925.e: Frederick was elected king in 1152 and crowned emperor in 1155. He died in 1190 on the Third Crusade.

31926.q: What did Frederick Barbarossa argue about with the rich cities of northern Italy?
a: Royal rights such as tolls and minting
31926.e: At the Diet of Roncaglia in 1158, Frederick had the regalia such as tolls, minting and courts written down. The Lombard cities saw this as an attack on their freedoms.
31926.m: Barbarossa demanded the regalia back from the Italian cities.

31927.q: Why did the translation of the papal word “beneficium” as “fief” cause a dispute in 1157?
a: It sounded as if the emperor held his empire as a fief from the Pope
It meant that the Pope demanded taxes
It banned the emperor from travelling to Rome
31927.e: Chancellor Rainald of Dassel deliberately translated the word like this at the Diet of Besançon. The dispute sharpened the conflict between emperor and Pope.
31927.m: The dispute over the word beneficium showed the power struggle between emperor and Pope.

31928.q: What is the name of the legend that Emperor Frederick Barbarossa sleeps inside a mountain, waiting to return?
31928.e: According to the legend, the emperor sleeps in the Kyffhäuser in Thuringia while his beard grows through a stone table. Barbarossa drowned in 1190 on the Third Crusade.
31928.m: According to legend, Barbarossa sleeps in the Kyffhäuser.

31929.q: With which peace did Frederick Barbarossa recognise the self-government of the Lombard cities in 1183?
31929.e: In the Peace of Constance the cities kept their regalia in return for payments and an oath of loyalty. The emperor formally remained overlord.
31929.m: The Peace of Constance secured the rights of the Lombard cities in 1183.

31930.q: Which charter raised the March of Austria to an independent duchy in 1156?
31930.e: With the Privilegium minus, Frederick compensated the Babenbergs for giving up Bavaria. Austria received special privileges.
31930.m: The Privilegium minus made Austria a duchy in 1156.

31931.q: How did the long dispute between Frederick Barbarossa and the Pope end in the Peace of Venice in 1177?
a: The emperor recognised the Pope and gave up his antipopes
The Pope crowned a new emperor
31931.e: Barbarossa made peace with Pope Alexander III. This ended a schism of almost twenty years, during which the emperor had supported antipopes.
31931.m: In Venice in 1177 Barbarossa made peace with Alexander III.

31932.q: Which ruler did Frederick Barbarossa have canonised in 1165?
31932.e: The canonisation was carried out by an antipope and celebrated in Aachen. Barbarossa wanted to give the imperial office extra holiness.

31933.q: Where did the future Emperor Frederick II grow up?
31933.e: Frederick was born in 1194 in Jesi near Ancona and spent his childhood in Palermo. From there he later also ruled the Kingdom of Sicily.
31933.m: Frederick II grew up in Sicily.

31934.q: What did Frederick II promise the Pope in connection with his coronation as emperor in 1220?
31934.e: Pope Honorius III crowned Frederick on 22 November 1220. Frederick had vowed to go on crusade but kept postponing it and was excommunicated for this in 1227.
31934.m: Frederick II promised the Pope a crusade.

31935.q: In which cathedral was Frederick II buried after his death in 1250?
31935.e: Frederick died in Apulia and was buried in Palermo. His parents also rest there in magnificent porphyry sarcophagi.
31935.m: Frederick II is buried in Palermo Cathedral.

31936.q: What did Frederick II do in 1235 with his son Henry (VII), who had risen against him?
a: He deposed him and had him held prisoner
He sent him to Rome as a cardinal
He gave him the Kingdom of Sicily
31936.e: Henry (VII) had opposed his father's policies. He was deposed and died in captivity in 1242.
31936.m: In 1235 Frederick II deposed his son Henry.

31937.q: What did the Mainz Imperial Peace, issued by Frederick II in 1235, forbid?
a: Election of the king by princes
31937.e: The Mainz Imperial Peace banned unlawful feuds and regulated the courts. It was one of the first imperial laws also proclaimed in German.
31937.m: Frederick II issued the Mainz Imperial Peace in 1235.

31938.q: Which octagonal castle in Apulia did Frederick II have built around 1240?
31938.e: Castel del Monte has an octagonal ground plan with eight octagonal towers. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
31938.m: Frederick II built the octagonal Castel del Monte.

31939.q: What did Pope Innocent IV declare about Frederick II at the Council of Lyon in 1245?
a: That he was deposed as emperor
That he was the rightful King of France
That he was released from his crusade vow
31939.e: Innocent IV had fled from Frederick to Lyon. The council stripped him of all his titles, but Frederick fought on until his death in 1250.
31939.m: In 1245 the Council of Lyon declared Frederick II deposed.

31940.q: Whom did Frederick II strengthen with the Statutum in favorem principum of 1231/32?
31940.e: The Statutum in favorem principum confirmed rights of the lay princes such as minting, tolls and courts. It encouraged the growth of territorial lordships.
31940.m: The Statutum in favorem principum strengthened the lay princes.

31941.q: Which period in the Holy Roman Empire is traditionally called the Interregnum?
31941.e: After the death of Frederick II in 1250, or of Conrad IV in 1254, there was no generally recognised king. Only the election of a new king accepted by all ended this phase.
31941.m: The Interregnum lasted roughly from 1250 to 1273.

31942.q: What was special about the royal election of 1257 in the Holy Roman Empire?
a: Two foreign candidates were elected at the same time
A woman was elected for the first time
The Pope chose the king alone
31942.e: The prince-electors could not agree and elected Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso X of Castile. Neither of them could really rule in the empire.
31942.m: In 1257 the prince-electors chose two foreign kings at once.

31943.q: Which last member of the Hohenstaufen was executed in Naples in 1268?
31943.e: Conradin was defeated by Charles of Anjou at Tagliacozzo in 1268. Afterwards he was beheaded in the market square of Naples.
31943.m: With Conradin, the last Hohenstaufen was executed in 1268.

31944.q: Which poet called the Interregnum “the emperorless, the terrible time” in a ballad?
31944.e: The phrase comes from Schiller's ballad “The Count of Habsburg” of 1803. It shaped the picture of this time for a long while.
31944.m: Schiller called the Interregnum the emperorless, the terrible time.

31945.q: Which league of cities was formed in 1254 to secure the peace during the Interregnum?
31945.e: Mainz and Worms joined together in 1254 to protect trade and peace. Soon around 60 cities, including Basel, and some princes belonged to it.
31945.m: From 1254 the Rhenish League of Cities was meant to secure the peace.

31946.q: What does the Latin word “interregnum” literally mean?
31946.e: Inter means between, regnum means reign or rule. It refers to the time between the end of the Hohenstaufen and the election of Rudolf of Habsburg in 1273.

31947.q: How do historians today judge the name Interregnum for the period from 1250 to 1273?
a: As misleading, since there were elected kings
As an exact legal term from the Golden Bull
As a name for a papal vacancy
As the name of a peace treaty
31947.e: Literally, interregnum means “between reigns”. As there were in fact elected kings at this time, what was mainly missing was a central power able to assert itself.
31947.m: In the Interregnum, what was mainly missing was a king who could assert himself.

31948.q: Which group used the weak royal power during the Interregnum to expand its territorial rule?
31948.e: Princes took over imperial property and royal rights. This increased the splitting of the empire into territories.
31948.m: The princes increased their power during the Interregnum.

31949.q: Why did the prince-electors choose Count Rudolf of Habsburg as king in 1273?
a: They thought he was harmless because he had little power
He was the richest prince in the empire
The Pope had already crowned him
He was the son of the last emperor
31949.e: Rudolf was already about 55 years old and only a count. The prince-electors believed he would not be a danger to them. But he greatly expanded the power of the Habsburgs.
31949.m: The prince-electors underestimated Rudolf of Habsburg.

31950.q: Which family of counts did Rudolf of Habsburg inherit from in 1264, gaining large areas in what is now eastern and central Switzerland?
31950.e: When the male line of the Kyburgs died out, Rudolf secured their inheritance. This made him the most powerful lord in the area of today's Switzerland.
31950.m: In 1264 Rudolf of Habsburg inherited the lands of the Kyburgs.

31951.q: Which period without a generally recognised king ended in 1273 with the election of Rudolf of Habsburg?
31951.e: After the end of the Hohenstaufen there was no generally recognised king for about 20 years. This in-between time is called the Interregnum.
31951.m: Rudolf's election ended the Interregnum in 1273.

31953.q: What did Rudolf of Habsburg demand back from the princes after the time without a king?
a: Imperial property they had taken for themselves
The imperial crown of the Hohenstaufen
31953.e: Since 1245, princes had taken a lot of royal property. Rudolf demanded it back and appointed imperial bailiffs to do so. This is called the policy of revindication.
31953.m: Rudolf demanded lost imperial property back.

31954.q: Why did the prince-electors not choose Rudolf's son Albert as king in 1292?
a: They did not want hereditary Habsburg rule
31954.e: Instead the prince-electors chose Adolf of Nassau. They wanted to keep their right to elect and avoid a powerful hereditary monarchy. Albert only became king in 1298.
31954.m: In 1292 the prince-electors prevented a Habsburg hereditary monarchy.

31955.q: By what means did Rudolf of Habsburg bind several prince-electors to himself?
a: Through the marriages of his daughters
31955.e: Rudolf married several daughters to prince-electors, for example in the Palatinate, in Saxony and in Bohemia. In this way he secured their support.
31955.m: Rudolf pursued a clever marriage policy.

31956.q: Which event important for Swiss history followed only a few weeks after the death of Rudolf of Habsburg?
a: The Federal Charter of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden
31956.e: The Federal Charter is dated “early August” 1291. The king's death created uncertainty, to which the valley communities reacted with an alliance.
31956.m: The Federal Charter was made shortly after Rudolf's death in 1291.

31957.q: Under which emperor was the Golden Bull issued in 1356?
31957.e: Emperor Charles IV had the law proclaimed at court assemblies in Nuremberg and Metz. It governed the election of the king until the end of the empire in 1806.
31957.m: Charles IV issued the Golden Bull in 1356.

31958.q: How many prince-electors did the Golden Bull lay down for the election of the king?
31958.e: Three spiritual and four lay prince-electors elected the king. This number stayed the same until the 17th century.
31958.m: The Golden Bull set out seven prince-electors.

31959.q: According to the Golden Bull, which prince-elector had to invite the others to the election of the king?
a: The Count Palatine of the Rhine
31959.e: The Archbishop of Mainz was arch-chancellor for Germany and led the election. He was also the last to cast his vote.
31959.m: The Archbishop of Mainz led the election of the king.

31960.q: What were the arch-offices that the Golden Bull gave to the lay prince-electors?
a: Honorary roles in the royal court ceremony
Command of the imperial army in war
31960.e: For example, the King of Bohemia as arch-cupbearer handed the king his cup. The offices showed the high rank of the prince-electors.
31960.m: The arch-offices were ceremonial honorary roles of the prince-electors.

31961.q: Which election procedure did the Golden Bull lay down for the election of the king?
31961.e: A majority of the prince-electors was enough, that is four of seven votes. This was meant to prevent double elections like those in the Interregnum.
31961.m: Under the Golden Bull, a majority of the prince-electors was enough.

31962.q: Which rule did the Golden Bull lay down for the lay electorates?
a: Indivisibility and succession of the firstborn
Election of the prince-elector by the peasants
Yearly change of the electoral vote
31962.e: The electoral lands could not be divided, and the eldest son inherited the electoral title. This was meant to keep the number of seven votes stable.
31962.m: The lay electorates were indivisible and went to the firstborn.

31963.q: What role did the Golden Bull give the Pope in the election of the king?
a: None, the Pope is not mentioned
He had to confirm the election
He led the election in Rome
31963.e: The Golden Bull does not mention papal approval. The person elected was therefore regarded as the rightful king without any involvement of the Pope.
31963.m: The Golden Bull made the election of the king independent of the Pope.

31964.q: With which forgery did the Habsburg Rudolf IV respond to Austria not receiving an electoral vote in the Golden Bull?
31964.e: In 1358/59 Rudolf IV had the Privilegium maius made, which gave Austria special rights. Emperor Charles IV did not recognise it.
31964.m: Rudolf IV forged the Privilegium maius.

31965.q: Which monastic rule was to be strictly followed again at Cluny Abbey?
31965.e: Cluny Abbey, founded in 910, wanted to renew monastic life according to the Rule of St Benedict. Prayer, liturgy and independence from worldly lords were at its centre.
31965.m: Cluny renewed monastic life according to the Rule of Benedict.

31966.q: What was legally special about Cluny Abbey?
a: It was directly subject to the Pope
It was directly subject to the emperor
It was subject to the local bishop
It was subject to its founder's family
31966.e: From the start Cluny was placed under the Pope and was therefore free from interference by worldly lords and bishops. This independence was the basis of its great influence.
31966.m: Cluny was independent of princes and bishops and subject only to the Pope.

31967.q: Which two abuses did the 11th century Church reform, inspired partly by Cluny, fight against in particular?
a: Selling indulgences and the cult of relics
31967.e: Simony means buying and selling Church offices. The reformers also demanded that priests stay unmarried.
31967.m: The reformers fought against buying offices and for priests to stay unmarried.

31968.q: Which day of remembrance did Abbot Odilo of Cluny introduce in his monasteries around 998?
31968.e: Abbot Odilo ordered that all the dead be remembered on 2 November. The custom spread from Cluny throughout the Western Church.
31968.m: All Souls' Day on 2 November goes back to Abbot Odilo of Cluny.

31969.q: Which church was the largest church in Christendom until the new St Peter's in Rome was built?
31969.e: The third abbey church of Cluny was built from 1088 and was over 180 metres long. After the French Revolution it was mostly demolished.
31969.m: The huge abbey church Cluny III showed the power of the Cluniac network.

31970.q: Which present-day Swiss monastery church belonged to the Cluniac network as a priory in the Middle Ages?
31970.e: Romainmôtier Abbey in the canton of Vaud was given to Cluny in the 10th century and run as a priory. Its Romanesque church survives to this day.
31970.m: Romainmôtier in Vaud was a priory of Cluny.

31971.q: In which monastery was the Cistercian order founded in 1098?
31971.e: In 1098 Robert of Molesme founded the monastery of Cîteaux, in Latin Cistercium, with a few monks. The order takes its name from this place.
31971.m: The name of the Cistercians comes from the monastery of Cîteaux.

31972.q: Which Cistercian abbot preached the Second Crusade at Vézelay in 1146?
31972.e: Bernard of Clairvaux was the most influential Cistercian of his time. On behalf of the Pope, he preached the Second Crusade at Vézelay in 1146.
31972.m: Bernard of Clairvaux was the most famous preacher of the Second Crusade.

31973.q: How did the Cistercians hold their many monasteries together?
a: The abbots met every year at the General Chapter
An emperor ran all the monasteries
The monasteries obeyed the nearest prince
31973.e: The order's constitution regulated the relationship of daughter houses to their mother houses. Every year the abbots met at Cîteaux, and visitations inspected the monasteries.
31973.m: The General Chapter and visitations held the Cistercian order together.

31974.q: What were the Cistercian lay brothers called, who did a large part of the field work?
31974.e: Conversi were lay brothers who worked mainly on the farms, the granges. This allowed the monasteries to farm large estates themselves.
31974.m: The conversi did much of the manual work in Cistercian monasteries.

31975.q: How can you typically recognise a Cistercian church?
a: A small roof turret instead of a bell tower
31975.e: The Cistercians wanted to live simply and in poverty and rejected splendour in their churches. Instead of tall towers, their churches only had a small roof turret.
31975.m: Cistercian churches are plain and usually only have a roof turret.

31976.q: Which monastery in Aargau was a Cistercian abbey from 1227 to 1841?
31976.e: Wettingen Abbey was founded in 1227 and settled with monks from Salem. In 1841 the canton of Aargau dissolved the monastery.
31976.m: Wettingen Abbey on the Limmat was a Cistercian abbey.

31977.q: Which commandment was at the centre of the Franciscan Rule of 1223?
a: A life of poverty without property
31977.e: Pope Honorius III confirmed the rule in 1223 with a bull, which is why it is called the Regula bullata. The brothers were to own nothing and live from work and alms.
31977.m: The Franciscan Rule required a life of poverty.

31978.q: What is the official Latin name of the Franciscan order?
31978.e: Francis of Assisi called his community the “Lesser Brothers”. That is why Franciscans still use the letters OFM today.
31978.m: The Franciscans are officially called the Friars Minor.

31979.q: Which reform branch of the Franciscans arose in the 16th century and was very widespread in Catholic Switzerland?
31979.e: The Capuchins split from the Franciscans in 1528 as a stricter branch. They are named after their pointed hood.
31979.m: The Capuchins are a strict branch of the Franciscan family.

31980.q: Which double monastery for Franciscans and Poor Clares did Queen Elisabeth found from 1309 at the place where King Albert I was murdered?
31980.e: King Albert I was murdered near Windisch in 1308. His widow Elisabeth founded Königsfelden Abbey there, known for its stained glass windows.
31980.m: Königsfelden Abbey near Windisch recalls the murder of King Albert I.

31981.q: From which kingdom did Dominic, the founder of the Order of Preachers, come?
31981.e: Dominic de Guzmán was born around 1170 in Caleruega in Castile. As a canon he travelled to southern France, where he founded his order.

31982.q: Against which religious movement did Dominic first preach in southern France?
31982.e: In southern France Dominic wanted to win over people of other beliefs through preaching and a simple life. This led to his community of preachers in Toulouse.
31982.m: Dominic began his work by preaching in southern France.

31983.q: In which year did Pope Honorius III confirm the Dominican order?
31983.e: Pope Honorius III confirmed the order in December 1216. Dominic died as early as 1221 in Bologna.
31983.m: The Order of Preachers was confirmed by the Pope in 1216.

31984.q: Which Latin wordplay interpreted the name of the Dominicans as “hounds of the Lord”?
31984.e: “Dominicani” was playfully turned into “Domini canes”, meaning hounds of the Lord who protect the flock from false teachings. Pictures therefore often show a dog with a torch.
31984.m: The Dominicans were jokingly called the hounds of the Lord.

31985.q: Besides poverty, which tasks were especially central for the Dominicans?
31985.e: The order was meant to produce educated preachers. So the Dominicans founded their own houses of study and taught at the universities.
31985.m: The Dominicans combined poverty with preaching and learned study.

31986.q: What fundamentally set the mendicant orders apart from older orders such as the Benedictines?
a: Owning nothing and working in towns
Living as hermits in the forest
31986.e: Mendicant orders gave up property not only personally but also as a community and lived from donations. They settled in the growing towns.
31986.m: The mendicant orders lived from alms and worked in the towns.

31987.q: Which mendicant order did Martin Luther belong to as a monk?
31987.e: Luther entered the monastery of the Augustinian Friars in Erfurt in 1505. This order had formed in the 13th century from several groups of hermits.
31987.m: Martin Luther was an Augustinian monk.

31988.q: Where did the Carmelite order originally come from?
31988.e: The Carmelites arose in the 12th century from hermits on Mount Carmel near Haifa. After moving to Europe, they became a mendicant order.
31988.m: The Carmelites bear the name of Mount Carmel.

31989.q: What did the scholars of scholasticism want to bring together?
31989.e: The scholastics tried to support Christian teaching with logical thinking. Anselm of Canterbury spoke of faith seeking understanding.
31989.m: Scholasticism brought together faith and reason.

31990.q: What does the Latin title of Abelard's work “Sic et non” mean?
31990.e: Abelard collected opposing statements of the Church Fathers on theological questions. The contradictions were to be examined with reason.
31990.m: Abelard's work “Sic et non” taught people to examine contradictions with reason.

31991.q: Where was scholasticism mainly taught in the High Middle Ages?
31991.e: From about 1200, universities such as Paris, Bologna and Oxford arose. Theology using the scholastic method was a main subject there.
31991.m: Scholasticism was taught at the universities.

31992.q: Which Franciscan is known for the principle of not making unnecessary assumptions?
31992.e: William of Ockham held that explanations should not be multiplied unnecessarily. This principle is still called “Ockham's razor”.
31992.m: Ockham's razor calls for the simplest explanation that is enough.

31993.q: What is the name of Thomas Aquinas's unfinished main work?
31993.e: The Summa theologiae is a systematic account of the whole of theology in questions and answers. Thomas stopped working on it in 1273, shortly before his death.
31993.m: The Summa theologiae is Thomas Aquinas's most important work.

31994.q: Which scholar was Thomas Aquinas's most important teacher in Cologne?
31994.e: Albertus Magnus, a universal scholar, taught Thomas in Paris and Cologne. Both were members of the same order.
31994.m: Albertus Magnus was Thomas Aquinas's teacher.

31995.q: What did Thomas Aquinas want to prove with his “five ways”?
a: That the Earth is a sphere
That the emperor is above the Pope
That the soul does not exist
31995.e: The five ways reason from observations of the world, such as motion and cause, to God as the first origin. They come at the start of the Summa theologiae.
31995.m: Thomas argued for the existence of God with the five ways.

31996.q: Thomas Aquinas combined the teaching of which ancient philosopher with Christian faith?
31996.e: Thomas wanted to show that reason and faith do not contradict each other. For this he relied on the writings of Aristotle.
31996.m: Thomas Aquinas combined Aristotle with Christianity.

31997.q: Which year is traditionally regarded as the founding year of the University of Bologna?
31997.e: In 1888 the University of Bologna celebrated its 800th anniversary, thereby fixing 1088 as its founding year. It is regarded as the oldest university in Europe.
31997.m: With the year 1088, the University of Bologna is regarded as Europe's oldest university.

31998.q: Which subject was the University of Bologna especially famous for in the Middle Ages?
31998.e: In Bologna the lawyer Irnerius taught the rediscovered Roman law. Students came from all over Europe to study law.
31998.m: Bologna was the centre of legal studies in the Middle Ages.

31999.q: Which emperor protected travelling students and teachers with the privilege “Authentica Habita”?
31999.e: In the 12th century Barbarossa placed travelling scholars under imperial protection and gave them their own legal rights. The privilege strengthened the young University of Bologna.
31999.m: The Authentica Habita gave travelling students imperial protection.

32000.q: Who joined together in Bologna to form the corporation that ran the university?
32000.e: Bologna was a student university: the students elected the rector and even hired the teachers. In Paris, by contrast, the masters formed the corporation.
32000.m: In Bologna the students ran their own university.

32001.q: Which faculty had the highest rank at the University of Paris in the Middle Ages?
32001.e: Paris was the leading centre of theology in the West. Many important scholastics taught there.
32001.m: In the Middle Ages, Paris was regarded as the stronghold of theology.

32002.q: What did the University of Paris achieve in 1231 after a long strike by teachers and students?
a: The building of a new cathedral
A tax that all citizens had to pay
32002.e: Pope Gregory IX guaranteed the university self-government with a bull. This is regarded as its “Magna Carta”.
32002.m: In 1231 the University of Paris gained the right to self-government.

32003.q: Who is the Sorbonne in Paris named after?
32003.e: Robert de Sorbon, chaplain to King Louis IX, founded a college for poor theology students in 1257. Later the name came to be used for the whole university.
32003.m: The Sorbonne bears the name of its founder Robert de Sorbon.

32004.q: Which three subjects formed the trivium of the seven liberal arts at medieval universities?
32004.e: The trivium covered the language subjects, the quadrivium the mathematical ones. Only after this basic study at the arts faculty did a higher subject follow.
32004.m: The trivium consisted of grammar, rhetoric and dialectic.

32005.q: Which crusader states were founded after the First Crusade alongside the Kingdom of Jerusalem?
32005.e: After the capture of Jerusalem in 1099, four crusader states came into being. The Principality of Antioch was founded by the Norman Bohemond of Taranto.
32005.m: The First Crusade led to four crusader states in the Levant.

32006.q: Which defeat in 1071 cost Byzantium large parts of Asia Minor to the Seljuks?
32006.e: At Manzikert in eastern Anatolia, Emperor Romanos IV was taken prisoner. Afterwards the Seljuks pushed far into Asia Minor.
32006.m: After Manzikert in 1071, Byzantium lost control of Asia Minor.

32007.q: Who led the so-called People's Crusade of 1096, which set out before the armies of knights?
32007.e: The wandering preacher Peter the Hermit went east with thousands of poorly equipped people. The march was wiped out by the Seljuks in Asia Minor.
32007.m: The People's Crusade under Peter the Hermit ended in disaster.

32008.q: What did crusaders do in towns such as Speyer, Worms and Mainz in 1096?
32008.e: Bands of crusaders attacked the Jewish communities in the Rhineland and killed thousands. These pogroms are among the darkest chapters of the Crusades.
32008.m: The First Crusade began in the Rhineland with pogroms against Jews.

32009.q: Whom did the crusaders mainly fight on their way through Asia Minor in 1097?
32009.e: At Dorylaeum on 1 July 1097 the crusaders defeated the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan I. After that the way through Anatolia was open. Mongols, Ottomans and Mamluks only appeared later.
32009.m: The victory at Dorylaeum opened the way through Asia Minor for the crusaders.

32010.q: Which spiritual reward did Pope Urban II promise those who took part in the First Crusade?
a: Remission of the punishment for sins
Being made a saint after death
32010.e: Anyone who went to Jerusalem for pious reasons would not have to do any further penance for their sins. This crusade indulgence was a strong incentive.
32010.m: The crusaders were promised an indulgence for the punishment of their sins.

32011.q: Which of the four crusader states was founded last, in 1109?
32011.e: The County of Tripoli in what is now Lebanon was set up after the capture of the city of Tripoli in 1109. The other three states had existed since 1098 and 1099.
32011.m: Tripoli was the youngest of the four crusader states.

32012.q: Which Muslim ruler captured Edessa in 1144 and so set off the Second Crusade?
32012.e: Zengi, atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, took Edessa in 1144. The loss shocked Europe and led to the Second Crusade.
32012.m: With the fall of Edessa in 1144, the first crusader state was lost.

32013.q: What was the French collective name for the crusader states?
32013.e: “Outremer” means “beyond the sea”. This is what the French called the crusaders' lands on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
32013.m: In French the crusader states were called Outremer.

32014.q: Which castle of the Knights Hospitaller in Syria is regarded as the best-preserved crusader castle?
32014.e: Krak des Chevaliers was enlarged by the Hospitallers from 1142. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32014.m: Krak des Chevaliers is the most famous crusader castle.

32015.q: Which order of knights grew out of a hospital community at the siege of Acre in 1190?
32015.e: Citizens from Bremen and Lübeck set up a field hospital outside Acre. In 1198 this became the order of German knights that later ruled in the Baltic.
32015.m: The Teutonic Order has its origins outside Acre.

32016.q: Which Mamluk sultan conquered the Principality of Antioch in 1268?
32016.e: Sultan Baibars conquered Antioch in 1268, ending the principality. He took many other castles from the crusaders.
32016.m: Sultan Baibars ended the Principality of Antioch in 1268.

32017.q: How did Saladin treat the Christian inhabitants of Jerusalem in 1187?
a: They could buy their freedom with a ransom
He forced them to convert to Islam
32017.e: Saladin let the inhabitants leave in return for a ransom and did not massacre them. However, those who could not pay were often enslaved.
32017.m: Saladin allowed the Christians of Jerusalem to buy their freedom.

32018.q: Which three rulers led the Third Crusade against Saladin?
a: Louis IX, Frederick II, Henry VI
Conrad III, Louis VII, Baldwin I
Otto IV, John Lackland, Louis VIII
32018.e: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Richard the Lionheart of England and Philip II Augustus of France set out from 1189. The expedition was a response to Saladin's successes.
32018.m: The Third Crusade was the Kings' Crusade.

32019.q: What did Saladin allow the Christians in his 1192 agreement with Richard the Lionheart?
a: Christians could build churches in Mecca
32019.e: In the Treaty of Jaffa the Christians kept a strip of coast. Jerusalem stayed under Saladin's rule but was open to pilgrims.
32019.m: In 1192 Saladin guaranteed pilgrims access to Jerusalem.

32020.q: Which branch of Islam did Saladin restore in Egypt?
32020.e: In 1171 Saladin ended the Shia caliphate of the Fatimids. He had prayers said again for the Sunni caliph in Baghdad.

32021.q: Whom did Saladin decisively defeat at the Battle of Hattin in 1187?
a: The army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem
The army of Richard the Lionheart
32021.e: At Hattin Saladin destroyed the army of the crusader states. After that he was able to take Jerusalem. Richard the Lionheart only came with the Third Crusade.
32021.m: After his victory at Hattin, Saladin conquered Jerusalem.

32022.q: Which people did Saladin come from?
32022.e: Saladin, whose real name was Yusuf ibn Ayyub, came from a Kurdish family. He began his career in the service of the ruler Nur al-Din.

32023.q: Which Pope called for the Fourth Crusade in 1198?
32023.e: Shortly after his election, Innocent III called for a new crusade. He had not wanted the conquest of Constantinople.
32023.m: The Fourth Crusade was called by Pope Innocent III.

32024.q: Which country was the original target of the Fourth Crusade?
32024.e: The planners wanted to attack Egypt, the centre of Ayyubid power. Because of a lack of money and deals that were made, the army never got there.
32024.m: The Fourth Crusade was actually meant to go to Egypt.

32025.q: Which city provided the fleet for the Fourth Crusade and steered it to its own advantage?
32025.e: The aged Doge Enrico Dandolo went with the army himself. Because the crusaders could not pay for the crossing, they fought for Venice's interests.
32025.m: Venice steered the Fourth Crusade to its own advantage.

32026.q: Why did the Pope excommunicate the crusaders after the capture of Zara in 1202?
a: They had attacked a Christian city
They had taken the Pope prisoner
32026.e: Zara, today's Zadar, was a Christian city on the Adriatic. The crusaders captured it for Venice to pay off their debts for the crossing.
32026.m: At Zara in 1202 the crusaders attacked a Christian city.

32027.q: Which empire did the crusaders found in Constantinople in 1204?
32027.e: After the sack of Constantinople, the crusaders chose Baldwin of Flanders as emperor. The empire lasted until 1261.
32027.m: After 1204 the Latin Empire ruled in Constantinople.

32028.q: Which famous piece of loot from Constantinople now decorates St Mark's in Venice?
32028.e: The four ancient bronze horses stood in the Hippodrome of Constantinople. The originals are now in the St Mark's museum, with copies on the front of the church.
32028.m: The horses of St Mark's are loot from the Fourth Crusade.

32029.q: Which royal couple is known in Spain as the “Catholic Monarchs”?
32029.e: Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon married in 1469, uniting their kingdoms. Pope Alexander VI gave them the title of honour in 1496.
32029.m: Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon are called the Catholic Monarchs.

32030.q: What does the Spanish term “Reconquista” mean?
32030.e: Reconquista refers to the reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula by Christian kingdoms. According to tradition it began around 722 at Covadonga and ended in 1492.

32031.q: What did Toledo become famous for after the Christian conquest in 1085?
a: Translators who put Arabic writings into Latin
32031.e: In Toledo, Christian, Jewish and Muslim scholars worked together. They translated works of Greek and Arabic science into Latin.
32031.m: Toledo was a centre of translators in the Middle Ages.

32032.q: Which event ended the Reconquista in 1492?
32032.e: In 1492 the Catholic Monarchs conquered Granada, the last Muslim kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula. In the same year Columbus set off on his first voyage.
32032.m: With the fall of Granada in 1492, the Reconquista ended.

32033.q: By which nickname is the Castilian knight known who conquered Valencia in 1094?
32033.e: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar was called “El Cid”, from the Arabic word for “lord”. His deeds are celebrated in the epic “Cantar de mio Cid”.
32033.m: El Cid is the most famous hero of the Reconquista.

32034.q: Which palace complex is the most famous building of the Nasrids in Granada?
32034.e: The Nasrids ruled Granada until 1492 and made the Alhambra magnificent. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32034.m: The Alhambra is the palace of the Nasrids in Granada.

32035.q: What does the Latin verb “inquirere”, from which “Inquisition” comes, mean?
32035.e: The Inquisition was an investigative procedure: a judge took action against suspects on his own initiative. The aim was to track down heresy.

32036.q: Which order did the popes especially often entrust with the office of inquisitor from the 1230s onwards?
32036.e: The popes appointed inquisitors who answered directly to them. The well-trained Order of Preachers seemed especially suitable for this.

32037.q: Which controversial method did the Pope allow in Inquisition trials from 1252?
32037.e: Pope Innocent IV allowed torture to force confessions. It was not allowed to lead to death or mutilation.
32037.m: From 1252 the Inquisition was allowed to use torture.

32038.q: Who carried out the death sentences against condemned heretics?
32038.e: The Church handed unrepentant heretics over to the “secular arm”. Princes or towns then usually carried out the burning.
32038.m: Executing heretics was a matter for the secular power.

32039.q: What were handbooks for inquisitors, such as the one by Bernard Gui, used for?
a: As a guide for questioning suspects
As a prayer book for monks
As a law code for kings
32039.e: Such handbooks described how to question suspects and what features could be used to recognise different groups. Bernard Gui was an inquisitor in Toulouse.
32039.m: Inquisitors worked with handbooks for interrogations.

32040.q: Which woman was burnt in Rouen in 1431 after a Church heresy trial?
32040.e: Joan of Arc was condemned by a Church court under English influence. In 1456 the verdict was overturned, and in 1920 the Church declared her a saint.
32040.m: Joan of Arc died in 1431 after a heresy trial in Rouen.

32041.q: What does the Greek name “katharoi”, from which “Cathars” comes, mean?
32041.e: The Cathars wanted to lead a pure life, free from the material world. Their opponents mostly used the name in a negative way.

32042.q: Which view of the world did the Cathars hold?
32042.e: According to Cathar teaching, the spiritual comes from a good God, but the material world from an evil principle. That is why they rejected many of the Church's sacraments.
32042.m: The Cathars saw the world as a struggle between good spirit and evil matter.

32043.q: What were the Cathars called who lived by strict rules and acted as clergy?
32043.e: The “Perfect” lived abstinently, ate no meat and preached. Ordinary believers were called credentes.
32043.m: The Perfect formed the elite of the Cathars.

32044.q: After which town in southern France are the Cathars also called Albigensians?
32044.e: In the area around Albi in Languedoc the Cathars were especially numerous. That is why they were called Albigensians in France.
32044.m: The name Albigensians comes from the town of Albi.

32045.q: Which event in 1208 gave the reason for the Albigensian Crusade?
a: The murder of a papal legate
The removal of the Bishop of Toulouse
The theft of the Church treasure of Rome
32045.e: The papal legate Pierre de Castelnau was murdered in 1208. The Pope partly blamed the Count of Toulouse and called for a crusade.
32045.m: The murder of the legate Pierre de Castelnau set off the Albigensian Crusade.

32046.q: In which town did the crusaders massacre the whole population in 1209?
32046.e: After Béziers was stormed, Catholics and Cathars alike were killed. The massacre spread terror throughout the south.
32046.m: The massacre at Béziers in 1209 opened the Albigensian Crusade.

32047.q: Which northern French nobleman led the Albigensian Crusade militarily?
32047.e: Simon de Montfort conquered many towns in Languedoc and became lord of large areas. In 1218 he fell at the siege of Toulouse.
32047.m: Simon de Montfort was the military leader of the Albigensian Crusade.

32048.q: Which mountain fortress, a refuge of the Cathars, fell in 1244, after which over 200 people were burnt?
32048.e: After a siege of almost a year, Montségur surrendered in March 1244. Those who would not renounce their faith were killed at the stake.
32048.m: The fall of Montségur in 1244 was a heavy blow for the Cathars.

32049.q: What was the most important political consequence of the Albigensian Crusade?
a: Languedoc came under the French crown
Aragon won all of southern France
32049.e: With the Treaty of Paris in 1229, the lands of the Counts of Toulouse gradually came under the rule of the French king. The south lost its independence.
32049.m: The Albigensian Crusade strengthened the French king's power in the south.

32050.q: Which kingdom supported the Pope in Avignon during the Schism, while England backed the Pope in Rome?
32050.e: Taking sides often followed political rivalries, for example in the Hundred Years' War. France, Scotland, Naples and later Castile and Aragon were on Avignon's side.
32050.m: In the Schism, Europe split along political alliances.

32051.q: Roughly how long did the Western Schism last?
32051.e: The split began with the double election of 1378 and ended in 1417 with the election of a generally recognised Pope. That is 39 years.
32051.m: The Western Schism divided the Western Church for almost four decades.

32052.q: Which council ended the Western Schism in 1417?
32052.e: The Council of Constance deposed the rival popes or persuaded them to resign. In 1417 Martin V was elected as a generally recognised Pope.
32052.m: The Council of Constance ended the Schism.

32053.q: In which city did a second Pope reside alongside the one in Rome during the Western Schism?
32053.e: In 1378 French cardinals elected an antipope, who resided in Avignon. Now there were two popes, who condemned each other.
32053.m: In the Schism there was one Pope in Rome and one in Avignon.

32054.q: Which council of 1409 led to there even being three popes at the same time?
32054.e: The council deposed both popes and elected Alexander V. Since the others did not resign, three popes now faced each other.
32054.m: At first the Council of Pisa made the Schism even worse.

32055.q: Which doctrine, holding that a general council is above the Pope, gained importance through the Schism?
32055.e: Since the popes could not end the split themselves, a council was to decide. This view is called conciliarism.
32055.m: Conciliarism places the council above the Pope.

32056.q: Where did Pope John XXIII secretly flee from Constance in March 1415?
32056.e: The Pisan Pope wanted to break up the council and fled in disguise to Schaffhausen. Duke Frederick IV of Austria had helped him.
32056.m: Pope John XXIII fled to Schaffhausen in 1415.

32057.q: What consequence did Duke Frederick IV of Austria's help with the escape have for the Swiss Confederates?
32057.e: King Sigismund placed Frederick under the imperial ban and called on the Confederates to occupy his lands. So in 1415 Bern, Zurich, Lucerne and others conquered Aargau.
32057.m: In 1415 the Confederates conquered Habsburg Aargau.

32058.q: Which critic of the Church was burnt in 1415 during the Council of Constance?
32058.e: Jan Hus had come to Constance despite having been promised safe conduct. The council condemned him as a heretic, and he was burnt on 6 July 1415.
32058.m: Jan Hus died at the stake in Constance in 1415.

32059.q: Which of the three popes resigned voluntarily at Constance in 1415?
32059.e: Gregory XII, the Pope of the Roman line, had his resignation announced before the council in July 1415. The other two popes were deposed.
32059.m: By resigning, Gregory XII made the unity of the Church possible.

32060.q: Which office did Jan Hus hold at the University of Prague in 1409?
32060.e: After the Decree of Kutná Hora, Hus became rector of Prague University in 1409. He was one of the best-known teachers and preachers in Prague.
32060.m: Jan Hus was rector of the University of Prague.

32061.q: Which university was founded in 1409 by German masters and students who had left Prague after the Decree of Kutná Hora?
32061.e: The Decree of Kutná Hora gave the Bohemians the majority at Prague University. Many Germans then moved to Leipzig, where a university was founded that same year, 1409.
32061.m: The University of Leipzig was founded in 1409 by those who left Prague.

32062.q: What is the name of Jan Hus's most important work on the nature of the Church?
32062.e: In “De ecclesia” of 1413, Hus described the Church as the community of the chosen, with Christ as its head. He was accused of this teaching at Constance.
32062.m: Hus set out his teaching on the Church in “De ecclesia”.

32063.q: Which event in Prague in 1419 is regarded as the trigger of the Hussite Wars?
a: The burning of the Charles Bridge
32063.e: In 1419 followers of Hus threw councillors out of the window of the New Town Hall. Years of war in Bohemia followed.
32063.m: The First Defenestration of Prague in 1419 started the Hussite Wars.

32064.q: Which reformer wrote in 1520 that “we are all Hussites” without knowing it?
32064.e: When reading Hus's writings, Luther recognised many of his own ideas. So he saw Hus as a forerunner of the Reformation.
32064.m: Luther saw Jan Hus as a forerunner of the Reformation.

32065.q: In what order did the use of a field change in the three-field system?
32065.e: A year of winter grain such as rye or spelt was followed by spring grain, and then the field rested for a year as fallow. This let the soil recover without half the land lying unused.
32065.m: The three-field system rotated winter grain, spring grain and fallow.

32066.q: What share of the farmland lay fallow each year in the three-field system?
32066.e: The land was divided into three parts, one of which rested each time. In the older two-field system, by contrast, half the land lay fallow.
32066.m: Compared with the two-field system, the three-field system farmed a sixth more land.

32067.q: What is the name for the duty of all the farmers in a village to work their fields in the same way at the same time?
32067.e: Because the narrow strips of farmland lay side by side without their own paths, everyone had to sow and harvest at the same time. This shared rule is called the common field rule (in German “Flurzwang”).
32067.m: The common field rule made the village sow and harvest together.

32068.q: What were the three large fields of a village called in German-speaking Switzerland?
32068.e: In Switzerland people spoke of the Zelgen system; each Zelg carried winter crops, spring crops or lay fallow in a given year. The term lives on in many field names such as “Zelg”.
32068.m: In German-speaking Switzerland the three fields of the three-field system were called Zelgen.

32069.q: Which land did the village community use together as pasture and woodland in the Middle Ages?
32069.e: The common (in German “Allmende”) was shared property on which cattle grazed and wood was cut. In Switzerland the term still exists today, for example with corporations.
32069.m: The common belonged to the whole village community.

32070.q: Which grain was often grown in the spring field because it was important as horse feed?
32070.e: Oats were sown in spring and were the most important feed for horses. Rye, spelt and wheat were mostly sown in autumn as winter grain.
32070.m: Oats were a typical spring grain and were used as horse feed.

32071.q: Which innovation in the High Middle Ages allowed horses to pull heavy ploughs without choking?
32071.e: The padded horse collar rests on the horse's shoulders and does not press on the windpipe. This let the horse use its full pulling power.
32071.m: With the horse collar, horses could pull heavy loads.

32072.q: What was the name of the organiser who recruited settlers for a territorial lord and laid out a new village?
32072.e: The locator recruited settlers, shared out the land and often became the hereditary village headman. For this he received extra hides and income.
32072.m: A locator organised the founding of new settlements.

32073.q: Which village form, with farms in a row and long strips of land behind them, often grew up when forests were cleared in the uplands?
32073.e: In a forest strip village each farm lies along a stream or road, with its strip of land stretching behind it to the edge of the forest. In this way each settler could clear his own strip.
32073.m: In a forest strip village a long strip of land lies behind each farm.

32074.q: Which monastic order was an important driving force in clearing and settling land east of the Elbe?
32074.e: The Cistercians deliberately built their monasteries in remote areas and farmed intensively with lay brothers. Monasteries such as Lehnin or Leubus shaped the settlement of the land.
32074.m: The Cistercians pushed forward land settlement with their monasteries.

32075.q: What was the name of the military campaign of 1147 against Slavic tribes east of the Elbe?
32075.e: The Wendish Crusade took place at the same time as the Second Crusade. It was directed against the pagan Elbe Slavs, who were then called Wends.
32075.m: The Wendish Crusade of 1147 was directed against the Elbe Slavs.

32076.q: What did the Teutonic Order's Kulm Charter of 1233 regulate?
a: The rights of newly founded towns
The election of the Grand Master
32076.e: The Kulm Charter set out the rights of the towns of Kulm and Thorn. It became the model for many town and village foundations in the Order's state of Prussia.
32076.m: The Kulm Charter of 1233 became a model in the Order's state of Prussia.

32077.q: Which group of people settled high valleys in the Grisons from Valais from the 13th century?
32077.e: The Walser moved from Upper Valais to high-lying valleys, for example to Davos or the Rheinwald. In return they received special rights of freedom.
32077.m: The Walser settled high Alpine valleys in the late Middle Ages.

32078.q: Which activity do Swiss place names such as Rüti, Rüthi or Schwanden point to?
32078.e: “Rüti” comes from “reuten”, meaning to clear land, and “schwanden” from killing trees by stripping their bark. Such names are evidence of land settlement in the High Middle Ages.
32078.m: Place names with Rüti or Schwanden recall medieval forest clearing.

32079.q: After what period did a runaway serf become free under the principle “town air makes you free”?
a: After a year and a day
32079.e: Anyone who had lived in a town for a year and a day without being claimed back by his lord was regarded as free. This made towns attractive for the unfree.
32079.m: After a year and a day in the town, a serf was free.

32080.q: Which town law spread especially widely in East Central Europe, as far as Poland and Ukraine?
32080.e: Magdeburg law was granted to hundreds of towns, such as Breslau, Kraków or Kyiv. Lübeck law, by contrast, applied mainly in Baltic towns.
32080.m: Magdeburg law was the most widespread town law in East Central Europe.

32081.q: Which town law applied in many Baltic port towns such as Rostock, Stralsund or Reval?
32081.e: Lübeck law was granted from Lübeck to around a hundred towns in the Baltic region. It strengthened the legal unity of the later Hanseatic towns.
32081.m: Many Baltic towns lived by Lübeck law.

32082.q: What were citizens called who held town citizenship but lived outside the town walls?
32082.e: Outburghers (in German “Pfahlbürger”) lived outside the pales of the town fortifications but enjoyed the town's protection. Territorial lords saw this as weakening their power, which is why the Golden Bull banned them.
