32082.m: Outburghers had citizenship but lived outside the walls.

32083.q: What is the name for the elite of rich families who controlled the council in many towns?
32083.e: The patriciate mostly consisted of long-distance merchants and landowners. In the 14th century the guilds fought for seats on the council in many places against their dominance.
32083.m: For a long time the patriciate formed the town's ruling class.

32084.q: What did medieval daughter towns often do in difficult legal cases?
a: They asked the mother town with the same law for advice
They sent the case to the Byzantine emperor
32084.e: Towns of one family of town law turned to the court of the mother town. In this way Magdeburg and Lübeck gave legal advice to many towns.
32084.m: Mother towns gave their daughter towns legal advice.

32085.q: What is the privilege called, granted by the town's lord, to hold a market regularly?
32085.e: The market right was often the start of a town's growth, because a market attracted traders and craftsmen. The market peace protected everyone who visited the market.
32085.m: The market right allowed a place to hold a market regularly.

32086.q: Which family of counts inherited the Zähringen lands around Burgdorf and Thun in 1218 after the Zähringens died out?
32086.e: With Berthold V, the Dukes of Zähringen died out in 1218. Their inheritance in the eastern part went to the Counts of Kyburg, whose lands later passed to Habsburg.
32086.m: In 1218 the Kyburgs inherited from the Zähringens in the Swiss Plateau.

32087.q: What is the rule called that only members of the guild could practise a craft in the town?
32087.e: Guild compulsion protected the members from competition and secured prices and quality. It was only abolished with freedom of trade in the 19th century.
32087.m: Because of guild compulsion, only a guild member could practise a craft.

32088.q: Which piece of work did a journeyman have to present to be accepted into the guild as a master?
32088.e: With the masterpiece the journeyman proved his skill to the guild masters. Fees and proof of his own wealth were often required too.
32088.m: The masterpiece was the test to become a master.

32089.q: What is the building called in which a guild met and celebrated, in Zurich for example “zur Meisen” or “zur Saffran”?
32089.e: In the guild hall the members gathered, managed their funds and held celebrations. Many Zurich guild halls still stand on the Limmat today.
32089.m: Every guild had its own guild hall.

32090.q: Which social task did the guilds take on for their members and their families?
32090.e: Guilds were also brotherhoods with a shared fund. They helped in times of illness, ensured a dignified funeral and supported widows.
32090.m: The guild helped its members in need.

32091.q: What is a cooperative association of merchants in the Middle Ages called?
32091.e: Merchant guilds were originally communities of merchants for protection and trade. Craft guilds, by contrast, mostly brought together craftsmen.
32091.m: Merchants joined together in merchant guilds.

32092.q: Which people did the guilds exclude from membership as “dishonourable”?
32092.e: Certain jobs such as executioner, knacker or gravedigger were considered dishonourable. Even their children could hardly get into a guild craft.
32092.m: Executioners were considered dishonourable and excluded from the guilds.

32093.q: What were the craftsmen mainly fighting for in the guild struggles of the 14th century?
32093.e: The guilds paid taxes and provided the town's defence but were excluded from the council. In many towns they won a share in governing the town.
32093.m: In the guild struggles, the craftsmen demanded a say on the council.

32094.q: Which city was regarded as the head of the Hanseatic League and was where most Hanseatic Diets met?
32094.e: Lübeck was well placed between the North Sea and the Baltic and was the leading town of the league. Most Hanseatic Diets took place there.
32094.m: Lübeck was the queen of the Hanseatic League.

32095.q: Which peace treaty sealed the Hanseatic League's victory over the Danish king Valdemar IV in 1370?
32095.e: In the Peace of Stralsund the Hanseatic League received trading privileges and castles on the Øresund for 15 years. It is regarded as the high point of Hanseatic power.
32095.m: The Peace of Stralsund in 1370 marks the high point of the Hanseatic League.

32096.q: Which round-bellied type of sailing ship was the typical cargo ship of the Hanseatic League?
32096.e: The cog had a high hull and a square sail and could carry a lot of cargo. A well-preserved wreck from 1380 is the Bremen cog.
32096.m: The cog was the cargo ship of the Hanseatic League.

32097.q: Which goods were taken along the Old Salt Route from Lüneburg to Lübeck?
32097.e: Lüneburg salt was essential for preserving herring from Scania. Lübeck distributed it throughout the Baltic region.
32097.m: Lüneburg salt was one of the foundations of Hanseatic trade.

32098.q: In which Flemish city did the Hanseatic League have one of its four great kontors?
32098.e: In Bruges, Hanseatic merchants bought Flemish cloth and met traders from southern Europe. Unlike other kontors it was not a closed compound; the merchants lived spread around the city.
32098.m: Bruges was the site of the Flemish Hanseatic kontor.

a: A customs office on the imperial border
32099.e: Hanseatic merchants lived and traded in kontors such as those in Novgorod, Bergen, London and Bruges. They enjoyed special rights there.
32099.m: Kontors were the Hanseatic League's trading bases abroad.

32100.q: What was the Hanseatic kontor in London called?
32100.e: The Steelyard lay on the Thames and enjoyed privileges until the 16th century. Queen Elizabeth I closed it in 1598.
32100.m: The London kontor of the Hanseatic League was called the Steelyard.

32101.q: Which goods did Hanseatic merchants mainly export from the kontor in Bergen?
32101.e: Dried cod from northern Norway kept well and was in great demand during Lent. The harbour row Bryggen in Bergen is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32101.m: Stockfish was the main product from Bergen.

32102.q: Besides trading goods, which role did the Champagne fairs increasingly take on?
a: They were a centre for money changing and credit
They were used to elect the French king
They were the goal of great pilgrimages
They were the venue for knights' tournaments
32102.e: At the end of each fair, debts were settled and bills of exchange cashed. Italian bankers thus turned the fairs into a money market for all of Europe.
32102.m: The Champagne fairs were also an important money market.

32103.q: Why did the Champagne fairs move between several towns during the year?
a: So that there was a fair almost all year round
Each town could only sell one product
The merchants had to flee from epidemics
32103.e: Troyes and Provins each had two fairs, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube one each. So the six fairs formed a cycle covering almost the whole year.
32103.m: The Champagne fairs formed a cycle of six fairs a year.

32104.q: When were the Champagne fairs at their height?
32104.e: The fairs grew from the 12th century and reached their peak in the 13th century. In the 14th century they lost much of their importance.
32104.m: The Champagne fairs flourished in the High Middle Ages.

32105.q: Which two trading regions mainly met at the Champagne fairs?
32105.e: Flemish cloth merchants sold their fabrics, and Italian merchants brought spices, silk and capital. Champagne lay conveniently halfway between them.
32105.m: Flemings and Italians met at the Champagne fairs.

32106.q: How did the Counts of Champagne especially encourage trade at the fairs?
32106.e: The counts guaranteed merchants safe conduct and their own fair courts. This legal security attracted traders from all over Europe.
32106.m: The Counts of Champagne protected travelling merchants.

32107.q: Which development at the end of the 13th century contributed to the decline of the Champagne fairs?
a: Italian galleys sailing directly to Bruges
The discovery of the sea route to India
The founding of the Hanseatic League in Lübeck
The building of the Gotthard tunnel
32107.e: From around 1277, Genoese galleys sailed through the Strait of Gibraltar straight to Flanders. In addition, Champagne fell to the French crown, which demanded higher taxes.
32107.m: The direct sea route to Flanders weakened the Champagne fairs.

32108.q: Which unit of measurement for precious metals probably goes back to a Champagne fair town?
32108.e: The name of the troy ounce is usually traced back to Troyes, where its own system of weights was used. Gold and silver are still traded in troy ounces today.
32108.m: The troy ounce probably bears the name of the fair town of Troyes.

32109.q: Who was allowed to sit on the Great Council of Venice after the reform of 1297?
a: Only men from old patrician families
32109.e: With the Serrata, the “closing”, membership of the Great Council became practically hereditary. From then on a closed circle of noble families ruled.
32109.m: From 1297 the patrician families alone decided about Venice.

32110.q: Which body did Venice set up in 1310 after a conspiracy to watch over state security?
32110.e: The Council of Ten was created after the conspiracy of Bajamonte Tiepolo, at first as a temporary body. It became permanent and was feared for its secret procedures.
32110.m: The Council of Ten watched over the security of the Venetian state.

32111.q: Which yearly ceremony showed Venice's rule over the Adriatic?
a: The handing over of the keys
32111.e: On Ascension Day the Doge threw a golden ring into the sea from the state barge Bucintoro. In this way Venice symbolically “married” the Adriatic.
32111.m: With the Marriage of the Sea, Venice celebrated its rule of the sea.

32112.q: Which large Mediterranean island did Venice acquire after the Fourth Crusade and rule until 1669?
32112.e: Venice bought the claims to Crete in 1204 and made the island its most important colony in the eastern Mediterranean. Only in 1669 did the Ottomans capture the capital Candia.
32112.m: Crete was a Venetian colony for over four centuries.

32113.q: On which peninsula on the Black Sea was Genoa's most important trading base, Caffa?
32113.e: Caffa, today's Feodosia in Crimea, was a trading hub for grain, furs and silk. From here the plague probably reached Europe in 1347.
32113.m: Genoa's most important Black Sea port was in Crimea.

32114.q: What is the Casa di San Giorgio in Genoa, founded in 1407, known for?
a: As one of the oldest banks in Europe
As the first university in Italy
As a monastery of the crusaders
32114.e: The Casa di San Giorgio managed Genoa's public debt and received tax income and colonies in return. It acted as a bank for the state and the citizens.
32114.m: The Casa di San Giorgio in Genoa was one of the first state banks.

32115.q: Which Egyptian port was a main trading hub for pepper and other spices in the late Middle Ages?
32115.e: Spices from India came to Egypt via the Red Sea and were shipped from Alexandria to Venice. The Mamluks earned a lot from this trade.
32115.m: Venice bought spices from India mainly in Alexandria.

32116.q: In a commenda in medieval long-distance trade, how did two partners share the tasks?
a: One provided the money, the other travelled and traded
Both travelled together and shared the goods
One built ships, the other sailed them
One paid customs, the other the taxes
32116.e: In a commenda the investor bore the risk of loss, and the travelling merchant contributed his work. The profit was shared according to a fixed formula.
32116.m: The commenda combined capital and travelling work in long-distance trade.

32117.q: In which city did the powerful Medici banking family have its headquarters?
32117.e: In 1397 Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici moved the bank's headquarters to Florence. The family later also ruled the city politically.
32117.m: The Medici Bank had its headquarters in Florence.

32118.q: Who was the Medici Bank's most important and profitable customer in the 15th century?
32118.e: The Medici were bankers to the papal Curia and collected Church dues from all over Europe. A large part of the profit came from the Rome branch.
32118.m: The Medici earned most as the Pope's bankers.

32119.q: In which city, now in Switzerland, did the Medici Bank have a branch because of the fairs held there?
32119.e: The Geneva fairs were important trading places in the 15th century. When they lost importance, the Medici moved the branch to Lyon around 1465.
32119.m: The Medici had a branch in Geneva in the 15th century.

32120.q: Which Medici survived an assassination attempt in Florence Cathedral in 1478 in which his brother was killed?
32120.e: In the Pazzi conspiracy Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed to death, while Lorenzo escaped wounded. The Medici's revenge on the conspirators was bloody.
32120.m: Lorenzo the Magnificent survived the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478.

32121.q: Why did large Florentine banking houses such as the Bardi and Peruzzi collapse in the 1340s?
a: The English king did not repay his war loans
The Pope banned them from all trade
Their gold coins were exposed as fakes
Venice conquered the city of Florence
32121.e: Edward III financed the start of the Hundred Years' War with loans and did not pay them back. The collapse of the Bardi and Peruzzi shook Florence badly.
32121.m: The Bardi and Peruzzi went bankrupt in the 1340s.

32122.q: Which gold coin did Florence mint from 1252, which became the leading currency in European trade?
32122.e: The florin contained about 3.5 grams of gold and kept its value for a long time. The Venetian ducat only followed in 1284.
32122.m: The Florentine florin was minted from 1252.

32123.q: Which Church ban did bankers get round by hiding the profit in the exchange rate of a bill of exchange?
32123.e: Christians were not allowed to lend money at interest, as this was seen as usury. With a bill of exchange, the profit was recorded as a difference in rate between two currencies.
32123.m: The bill of exchange helped to get round the Church's ban on interest.

32124.q: Who published the first printed account of double-entry bookkeeping in 1494?
32124.e: The Franciscan Luca Pacioli described the Venetian method in his “Summa”. However, Italian merchants had been using double-entry bookkeeping long before that.
32124.m: Luca Pacioli made double-entry bookkeeping known in print in 1494.

32125.q: Which three cities on the Rhine formed the ShUM communities, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021?
32125.e: ShUM is made from the Hebrew initials of Shpira, Warmaisa and Magenza. The communities were centres of Jewish learning.
32125.m: Speyer, Worms and Mainz formed the ShUM communities.

32126.q: Which council ruled in 1215 that Jews had to be distinguished from Christians by their clothing?
32126.e: The Fourth Lateran Council demanded identification by clothing. This led, for example, to the Jewish hat or the yellow ring.
32126.m: The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 introduced compulsory identification.

32127.q: What did Jews in the Holy Roman Empire have to pay the emperor for?
a: For the right to own land
32127.e: Jews were regarded as “servants of the chamber” of the emperor and paid for his protection. The emperor often pledged this income to towns or princes.
32127.m: Jews paid the emperor for his protection.

32128.q: Which Jewish scholar from Troyes wrote commentaries on the Bible and Talmud in the 11th century that are still authoritative today?
32128.e: Rashi, Rabbi Shlomo ben Yitzchak, lived in Troyes and studied in Worms and Mainz. His commentaries are still printed in almost every edition of the Talmud.
32128.m: Rashi from Troyes is the best-known commentator on the Bible and Talmud.

32129.q: Which kingdom expelled all Jews from its land under Edward I in 1290?
32129.e: King Edward I issued the Edict of Expulsion in 1290. Only in the 17th century were Jews allowed to settle in England again.
32129.m: England expelled all Jews from the kingdom in 1290.

32130.q: Which false accusation led to the expulsion of the Jews from Bern in 1294?
a: A supposed ritual murder of a child
A supposed theft of the town treasure
A supposed burning of the minster
32130.e: The Jews of Bern were accused of murdering the boy Rudolf, a common ritual murder legend. The council used the mood to cancel debts to Jewish moneylenders and expelled the Jews.
32130.m: In 1294 the invented ritual murder legend served in Bern as a pretext for expelling the Jews.

32131.q: What happened to the Jewish community in Basel in January 1349?
a: It was protected by the bishop
32131.e: On the false charge of poisoning wells, the Jews of Basel were burnt on an island in the Rhine, even before the plague had reached the city. Such persecutions struck many towns at that time.
32131.m: In Basel in 1349 the Jews were murdered even before the plague arrived.

32132.q: How did the accusation of well poisoning spread from Chillon Castle on Lake Geneva in 1348?
a: Confessions extracted by torture were sent to other towns
A Pope announced it in a bull
It was handed out as a printed leaflet
An emperor had it read out in all churches
32132.e: At Chillon, Jews were tortured until they made false confessions. The records were sent to other towns and used there as supposed proof for further pogroms.
32132.m: Confessions forced under torture fuelled the pogroms of 1348.

32133.q: Which bacterium caused the Black Death?
32133.e: DNA analyses from plague graves have clearly identified Yersinia pestis. The bacterium was discovered by Alexandre Yersin in 1894.
32133.m: The Black Death was caused by Yersinia pestis.

32134.q: How did the plague reach Europe in 1347?
a: On trading ships from the Black Sea region
32134.e: Genoese ships brought the disease to Messina in Sicily in October 1347. From there it spread rapidly across Europe.
32134.m: The plague came to Europe on trading ships in 1347.

32135.q: Which animals mainly pass bubonic plague on to humans?
32135.e: Fleas suck blood from infected rodents and pass the bacteria on with their next bite. Rats were long seen as the main hosts; today human fleas and lice are also discussed.
32135.m: Bubonic plague is mainly spread by flea bites.

32136.q: Which form of plague is passed directly from person to person by droplets?
32136.e: Pneumonic plague attacks the airways and is spread by coughing. Untreated, it was almost always fatal at that time.
32136.m: Pneumonic plague spreads by droplets from person to person.

32137.q: What were the groups called who wandered around during the plague and publicly whipped themselves?
32137.e: The flagellants wanted to calm God's anger through penance. Pope Clement VI banned the movement in 1349.
32137.m: Flagellants whipped themselves as penance during the plague.

32138.q: During which period did the Black Death rage in Europe?
32138.e: The disease came to Europe in 1347 and by about 1351 had spread across almost the whole continent. After that the plague kept returning until the 18th century.
32138.m: The Black Death raged in Europe from 1347 to 1351.

32139.q: What happened to the wages of farmhands and day labourers in Europe after the Black Death?
a: They rose because workers were scarce
They fell because there were too many workers
They were only paid in gold
32139.e: The plague killed a large part of the population, so workers were scarce. The survivors could demand higher wages, which landlords tried to prevent with laws.
32139.m: After the plague, wages rose because workers were scarce.

32140.q: What are villages called that were abandoned after plague and crises in the late Middle Ages?
32140.e: Many settlements on poor soil were abandoned because the people died or moved to towns. In Germany a large share of villages disappeared in the late Middle Ages.
32140.m: Abandoned medieval settlements are called deserted villages.

32141.q: Where does the name of the French peasant revolt of 1358, the Jacquerie, come from?
a: From the mocking nickname Jacques Bonhomme for peasants
From the jackets of the rebels
32141.e: Nobles mockingly called the peasants “Jacques Bonhomme”. This became the name of the revolt in northern France.
32141.m: The Jacquerie is named after the mocking nickname Jacques Bonhomme.

32142.q: How did the Jacquerie peasant revolt of 1358 end?
a: The nobility crushed it after a few weeks
The nobility in France was abolished
32142.e: The rebels were poorly armed and divided. Their leader Guillaume Cale was captured and executed, after which the nobility took bloody revenge.
32142.m: The Jacquerie was crushed after a few weeks.

32143.q: Which event of 1356 badly damaged the reputation of the French nobility before the Jacquerie?
32143.e: At Poitiers, King John II was taken prisoner by the English. The nobility was seen as incompetent, yet the peasants still had to bear high ransoms and dues.
32143.m: The defeat at Poitiers in 1356 undermined the nobility's reputation.

32144.q: Which tax set off the great Peasants' Revolt in England in 1381?
32144.e: The poll tax charged every adult the same amount, so it hit the poor especially hard. It was used to pay for the war against France.
32144.m: The poll tax set off the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

32145.q: Which preacher asked during the revolt of 1381, “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?”
32145.e: John Ball preached the original equality of all people. After the revolt he was executed.
32145.m: John Ball questioned the order of estates with the picture of Adam and Eve.

32146.q: What role did Wat Tyler play in the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
a: He was a leader of the rebels
He was the royal tax collector
32146.e: Wat Tyler led the rebels from Kent to London. During negotiations with King Richard II at Smithfield he was fatally wounded, after which the revolt quickly collapsed.
32146.m: Wat Tyler led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

32147.q: How old was King Richard II when he faced the rebels of 1381?
32147.e: Richard II was born in 1367 and came to the throne as a child in 1377. He promised the rebels concessions, which he later withdrew.
32147.m: Richard II was only 14 during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

32148.q: Against which lord did the people of Appenzell rise up from 1401 in the Appenzell Wars?
32148.e: The people of Appenzell resisted the dues and bailiffs of the Prince-Abbot. With help from Schwyz, they won the Battle of Stoss in 1405.
32148.m: The people of Appenzell fought against the rule of the Abbot of St Gallen.

32149.q: Roughly when was the Medieval Climate Anomaly?
32149.e: During this time it was comparatively warm in the North Atlantic region. However, the warming varied by region and did not happen everywhere at the same time.
32149.m: The Medieval Climate Anomaly lasted from about 950 to 1250.

32150.q: Which island did Vikings under Erik the Red settle around 985 during the warm phase?
32150.e: Erik the Red led settlers from Iceland to south-western Greenland. As the climate cooled in the late Middle Ages, the settlements were abandoned in the 15th century.
32150.m: Erik the Red founded settlements in Greenland around 985.

32151.q: How did the warm climate of the High Middle Ages encourage population growth?
a: Through longer growing seasons and better harvests
Through the end of all epidemics
32151.e: Milder temperatures allowed farming even at higher altitudes and brought more reliable harvests. This helped land settlement and the growth of towns.
32151.m: Better harvests in the warm phase encouraged population growth.

32152.q: Which famine struck northern Europe after constant rain in the years 1315 to 1317?
32152.e: Several wet summers made the grain rot in the fields. Millions of people died, even before the Black Death came.
32152.m: The Great Famine of 1315 to 1317 followed rainy summers.

32153.q: When did the Alpine glaciers reach their last high point at the end of the Little Ice Age?
32153.e: Around the middle of the 19th century, glaciers such as the Rhône Glacier reached far down into the valley. Since then they have been melting back strongly.
32153.m: The Alpine glaciers reached their last great high point around 1850.

32154.q: What is the name for the period from about 1645 to 1715 with very few sunspots?
32154.e: The Maunder Minimum fell in a particularly cold phase of the Little Ice Age. It is named after the astronomer Edward Walter Maunder.
32154.m: During the Maunder Minimum there were hardly any sunspots.

32155.q: How can large volcanic eruptions cool the climate for a few years?
a: Fine particles in the air block sunlight
They slow down the Earth's rotation
32155.e: In strong eruptions, ash and sulphur gases rise high into the atmosphere. They reflect sunlight, as after the eruption of Samalas in 1257.
32155.m: Volcanic eruptions can cool the climate through particles in the air.

32156.q: Which flood of 1342 is regarded as the worst flooding in Central Europe in the last few thousand years?
32156.e: In July 1342, days of rain led to enormous floods on the Rhine, Main and Danube. Soil erosion was so severe that traces can still be detected today.
32156.m: St Mary Magdalene's flood of 1342 was a flood of the millennium.

32157.q: What position did Hildegard of Bingen hold in the 12th century?
a: She was abbess of a convent
She was empress of the realm
32157.e: As abbess, Hildegard led a community of nuns and founded the Rupertsberg convent near Bingen. She wrote about faith, nature and medicine and composed music.
32157.m: Hildegard of Bingen was a learned abbess.

32158.q: Besides her music, what is Hildegard of Bingen especially known for today?
32158.e: In her natural history, Hildegard describes hundreds of plants and animals and their healing effects. She is an important source on monastic medicine.
32158.m: Hildegard of Bingen wrote about the healing power of plants.

32159.q: Which title did Pope Benedict XVI give Hildegard of Bingen in 2012?
32159.e: In 2012 Hildegard was canonised and made a Doctor of the Church. She is one of only a few women with this title.
32159.m: Hildegard of Bingen has been a Doctor of the Church since 2012.

32160.q: What did Hildegard of Bingen invent with the “Lingua ignota”?
a: A secret language of her own
32160.e: The Lingua ignota consists of about a thousand invented words with its own script. Its exact purpose is still disputed today.
32160.m: With the Lingua ignota, Hildegard invented a language of her own.

32161.q: What were women called who lived and worked in religious communities without taking permanent vows?
32161.e: Beguines lived devout lives in beguinages but could leave the community again. They often earned their living with textile work or nursing.
32161.m: Beguines lived religious lives but without permanent vows.

32162.q: Which writer defended the dignity of women in 1405 in “The Book of the City of Ladies”?
32162.e: Christine de Pizan lived at the French court and earned her living as a writer. Her work contradicts the anti-women writings of her time.
32162.m: Christine de Pizan wrote “The Book of the City of Ladies”.

32163.q: In which trade could women form their own guilds in late medieval towns such as Cologne?
a: In textile making, for example silk and yarn
32163.e: In Cologne, women were allowed to form their own guilds in some textile trades and train girl apprentices. This was an exception in the empire.
32163.m: In some textile trades women had their own guilds.

32164.q: What is the “Hortus deliciarum”, created by an abbess in the 12th century?
32164.e: Herrad of Landsberg led Hohenburg Abbey in Alsace and created the work for her nuns. The original burnt in Strasbourg in 1870.
32164.m: Herrad of Landsberg created the “Hortus deliciarum”.

32165.q: Who won the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and became King of England?
32165.e: After Edward the Confessor died childless, several claimants fought over the crown. William of Normandy defeated Harold Godwinson at Hastings.
32165.m: In 1066 William the Conqueror conquered England.

32166.q: Why was the English army weakened at the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
a: It had just fought the Norwegians in the north
It had no horses and no weapons
The king was a prisoner in France
The plague had halved the army
32166.e: In September 1066 Harold Godwinson defeated the Norwegian Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge. Then his army had to march south at speed to face William.
32166.m: Before Hastings the English army was exhausted from fighting the Norwegians.

32167.q: Which survey of land ownership and taxes in England did William the Conqueror have made in 1086?
32167.e: The Domesday Book recorded the land, livestock and tax value of almost all of England. The crown used it as a basis for taxes and feudal rights.
32167.m: The Domesday Book is one of the first great land surveys in Europe.

32168.q: Which language was the language of the English nobility and court for about three centuries after 1066?
32168.e: The Normans brought a form of Old French to England, Anglo-Norman. That is why many English words come from French.
32168.m: The Norman Conquest brought many French words into English.

32169.q: Which building in London goes back to a stone keep built by William the Conqueror?
32169.e: After 1066 William had a castle built in London, whose keep is the White Tower. The Tower of London grew out of it.
32169.m: The White Tower in the Tower of London dates from the time of William the Conqueror.

32170.q: What is the name of William's campaigns of 1069 to 1070, in which he crushed revolts in northern England by destroying villages and supplies?
32170.e: The devastation known as the “Harrying of the North” led to famine in northern England. Even in the Domesday Book many places there are listed as waste.
32170.m: William secured his rule in the north with great harshness.

32171.q: What effect did the Norman Conquest have on the leading class of landowners in England?
a: The Church lost all its property
The Anglo-Saxon nobility stayed the same
32171.e: William seized the land of the defeated Anglo-Saxons and granted it as fiefs to his followers. By about 1086 the Anglo-Saxon high nobility had been almost entirely pushed out.
32171.m: After 1066 England's land belonged mainly to Norman barons.

32172.q: Which group did Simon de Montfort invite to the English Parliament in 1265 for the first time, alongside nobles and knights?
32172.e: Simon de Montfort led the barons in revolt against Henry III. His Parliament of 1265 brought in townspeople for the first time.
32172.m: In 1265 townspeople sat in the English Parliament for the first time.

32173.q: Why is the English Parliament of 1295 seen as a model for later parliaments?
a: It brought together nobility, clergy, counties and towns
It was elected by the whole people
Women could take part for the first time
32173.e: In 1295 Edward I invited all the important groups of the country. This make-up, as the “Model Parliament”, became the pattern for later parliaments.
32173.m: The Parliament of 1295 brought together all the important estates of England.

32174.q: Into which two chambers has the English Parliament been divided since the 14th century?
a: House of Lords and House of Commons
Crown Council and Council of States
32174.e: The high nobility and senior clergy met in the upper house, the representatives of the counties and towns in the lower house. This division still exists today.
32174.m: Since the Middle Ages the English Parliament has had an upper and a lower house.

32175.q: In the late Middle Ages, which right was the English Parliament's most important means of pressure on the king?
32175.e: The king needed money for wars, for example in the Hundred Years' War. Parliament often linked approving taxes to demands and complaints.
32175.m: Whoever approves the taxes can set conditions for the ruler.

32176.q: What is an “impeachment”, which arose in the English Parliament in 1376?
a: An accusation of high officials by Parliament
The coronation of a new king
32176.e: In the Good Parliament of 1376 the Commons accused close advisers of Edward III of corruption. The procedure still exists today, for example in the USA.
32176.m: With impeachment a parliament can bring charges against high officials.

32177.q: What is the office of the chairman and spokesman of the House of Commons called, recorded since the late 14th century?
32177.e: The Speaker presented the Commons' concerns to the king. Thomas Hungerford in 1377 is regarded as the first officially named Speaker.
32177.m: The Speaker still chairs the British House of Commons today.

32178.q: Which groups represented the country in the medieval House of Commons?
a: Knights of the shires and townspeople
32178.e: Each county sent two knights and many towns two burgesses to the lower house. The high nobility and senior clergy, by contrast, sat in the upper house.
32178.m: Knights from the countryside and townspeople sat in the House of Commons.

32179.q: On what did Edward III of England base his claim to the French throne?
a: On his mother, a daughter of Philip IV
On a treaty with the Pope
On his marriage to a Valois
32179.e: Edward's mother Isabella was a daughter of the Capetian Philip IV. However, the French nobles rejected succession through the female line.
32179.m: The Hundred Years' War began as a dispute over the succession to the French throne.

32180.q: Which weapon helped the English to great victories such as Crécy at the start of the Hundred Years' War?
32180.e: English longbowmen shot quickly and far. At Crécy in 1346 they smashed the attacks of the French knights.
32180.m: The longbow made the English strong in the Hundred Years' War.

32181.q: What is the great peasant revolt called that broke out in northern France in 1358 during the war?
32181.e: After the defeat at Poitiers, the peasants suffered from plundering and dues. The Jacquerie revolt was bloodily crushed by the nobility after a few weeks.
32181.m: The war also brought social unrest to France.

32182.q: Which French king was taken prisoner by the English at the Battle of Poitiers in 1356?
32182.e: In 1356 Edward the Black Prince defeated the French army at Poitiers and captured John II. A huge ransom was demanded for his release.
32182.m: At Poitiers in 1356 even the King of France was taken prisoner.

32183.q: Roughly how long did the Hundred Years' War actually last?
32183.e: The war lasted from 1337 to 1453. In between there were long truces, for example after the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360.
32183.m: The Hundred Years' War lasted from 1337 to 1453.

32184.q: What did the Treaty of Troyes lay down in 1420?
a: Henry V was to become King of France
England gave up all its mainland lands
France paid a ransom for John II
32184.e: Under the Treaty of Troyes, Henry V married a daughter of Charles VI and was declared Charles VI's heir. The Dauphin Charles was disinherited.
32184.m: In 1420 the Treaty of Troyes made the English king heir to France.

32185.q: Which battle of 1453 is regarded as the military end of the Hundred Years' War?
32185.e: At Castillon in Gascony the French army, with strong artillery, defeated the English. Shortly afterwards Bordeaux fell to France.
32185.m: At Castillon in 1453, cannons helped decide the Hundred Years' War.

32186.q: Who condemned Joan of Arc in Rouen in 1431?
a: A Church court under English influence
A court of the French king
A court of the city of Paris
32186.e: The trial was led by Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, who was on the side of the English. The court condemned Joan as a heretic.
32186.m: Joan of Arc was condemned by a Church court.

32187.q: Which behaviour did the court in 1431 treat as a relapse that led to Joan of Arc's execution?
32187.e: Joan had at first recanted and put on women's clothes. When she wore men's clothing again, she was regarded as relapsed and handed over to the secular arm.
32187.m: The charge of wearing men's clothing served as a pretext for the death sentence.

32188.q: In which castle on the Loire did Joan of Arc first meet the Dauphin Charles in 1429?
32188.e: In March 1429 Joan was received by the Dauphin at Chinon. Afterwards she was allowed to march with an army to relieve Orléans.
32188.m: At Chinon, Joan of Arc convinced the heir to the throne of her mission.

32189.q: Which pitched battle did the French army with Joan of Arc win in June 1429?
32189.e: At Patay on 18 June 1429 the French beat an English army before the archers could take up position. The victory opened the way to the coronation.
32189.m: Patay was a great French victory in the year Joan appeared.

32190.q: What happened to the verdict against Joan of Arc in 1456?
a: It was declared null and void
It was made harsher by the emperor
32190.e: At her family's request and with Charles VII's support, the Pope allowed a review. The old verdict was overturned, and in 1920 Joan was declared a saint.
32190.m: A later trial cleared Joan of Arc.

32191.q: Which side in the French civil war did Charles VII and Joan of Arc belong to?
32191.e: France was split between Armagnacs and Burgundians. The Armagnacs supported the Dauphin Charles, while the Burgundians allied with England.
32191.m: The Hundred Years' War was also a French civil war.

32192.q: How did Joan of Arc end up in English hands after she was captured?
a: She was handed over for money
She was released in an exchange
32192.e: The Burgundians handed Joan over to the English for a payment of 10,000 livres. The English wanted to have her condemned by a Church trial.
32192.m: Joan of Arc was sold by her enemies like a spoil of war.

32193.q: Which English weapon was decisive at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
32193.e: English archers shot rapidly one after another over long distances. As a result the French knights were badly hit even before the hand-to-hand fighting.
32193.m: At Agincourt the English longbow won.

32194.q: In which long war between England and France did the Battle of Agincourt take place?
a: In the Wars of the Roses
32194.e: The Hundred Years' War lasted from 1337 to 1453. Agincourt in 1415 was one of the greatest English victories.
32194.m: Agincourt was a battle in the Hundred Years' War.

32195.q: Where was the English army trying to march to when it was cornered at Agincourt?
32195.e: Calais was then in English hands and offered a safe harbour for the journey home. The French army blocked the English on the way.
32195.m: At Agincourt an English army was cornered while retreating to the coast.

32196.q: In which play by Shakespeare does the Battle of Agincourt play a central role?
32196.e: Shakespeare's “Henry V” ends with the victory at Agincourt and the making of peace. The speech about the “band of brothers” comes from this play.
32196.m: Shakespeare made Agincourt unforgettable in “Henry V”.

32197.q: What made the attack of the heavily armoured French knights at Agincourt especially difficult?
a: A wide river in front of them
32197.e: After rain, the freshly ploughed field was deeply soaked. The knights could only move slowly and were hit by arrows as they did.
32197.m: At Agincourt the mud was the knights' downfall.

32198.q: Which order given by Henry V during the Battle of Agincourt is still controversial today?
32198.e: When a new French attack threatened, Henry had many captured knights killed. He feared the prisoners might arm themselves again.
32198.m: The killing of the prisoners is seen as the dark side of the victory at Agincourt.

32199.q: Why were noble enemies in the Middle Ages often taken prisoner rather than killed?
a: A ransom could be demanded for them
They then had to work as servants
The Church banned all killing in war
They were needed as hostages for tolls
32199.e: A noble prisoner's family paid a lot of money for him. After Agincourt, Charles of Orléans, for example, stayed in England for about 25 years until he was freed.
32199.m: Noble prisoners brought in ransom money in the Middle Ages.

32200.q: Which two branches of the House of Plantagenet fought for the English crown in the Wars of the Roses?
32200.e: Both houses were descended from sons of Edward III. From 1455 to 1485 the crown changed hands between them several times.
32200.m: In the Wars of the Roses, Lancaster and York fought for England's throne.

32201.q: Which emblem is linked with the House of York in the Wars of the Roses?
32201.e: The white rose was a badge of the Yorkists, while the red rose was linked with Lancaster. The name “Wars of the Roses” only became common later.
32201.m: The white rose stands for York, the red rose for Lancaster.

32202.q: What happened to King Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485?
a: He gave up the throne voluntarily
32202.e: Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth. Richard was the last English king to fall in battle. His skeleton was found under a car park in Leicester in 2012.
32202.m: With Bosworth in 1485, the rule of the House of York ended.

32203.q: Which dynasty took the English throne after the Wars of the Roses?
32203.e: After his victory in 1485, Henry VII founded the Tudor dynasty. It ruled England until 1603.
32203.m: The Wars of the Roses ended with the rise of the Tudors.

32204.q: How did Henry VII unite the rival houses after 1485?
32204.e: Henry VII, from the Lancastrian side, married Elizabeth of York, the daughter of Edward IV, in 1486. That is why the Tudor rose combines red and white.
32204.m: The Tudor rose shows the reconciliation of Lancaster and York.

32205.q: Why did Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, get the nickname “Kingmaker” in the Wars of the Roses?
a: He helped different kings onto the throne one after another
He made the crowns for the kings
As archbishop he crowned the kings
32205.e: Warwick first helped Edward IV onto the throne and later restored Henry VI. He fell at the Battle of Barnet in 1471.
32205.m: For a time the Earl of Warwick decided who was king in England.

32206.q: What did King Philip IV of France and Pope Boniface VIII argue about around 1300?
a: Whether the king could tax the clergy
Whether France had to lead a crusade
Who owned the city of Rome
32206.e: Philip IV wanted to tax the clergy too. In 1302 Boniface VIII claimed the supremacy of spiritual power in the bull “Unam sanctam”, which Philip rejected.
32206.m: Philip IV put the king's power above the Pope's claims.

32207.q: Where did the popes move their seat in 1309 under French influence?
32207.e: After the dispute with Philip IV and the attack at Anagni in 1303, the papacy came under French influence. The popes resided in Avignon until 1377.
32207.m: From 1309 to 1377 the popes resided in Avignon.

32208.q: Which assembly did Philip IV call in 1302 to get the nobility, clergy and towns behind him?
32208.e: The Estates General brought together representatives of the three estates of France. Philip sought their backing in his dispute with the Pope.
32208.m: The Estates General first met under Philip IV in 1302.

32209.q: What was unusual about the Battle of the Golden Spurs at Kortrijk in Flanders in 1302?
a: Townspeople on foot defeated an army of knights
The battle was fought at sea
Cannons were used for the first time
The king fought a knight alone
32209.e: Flemish town militias beat the French knights of Philip IV. The golden spurs taken as booty gave the battle its name.
32209.m: At Kortrijk in 1302 townspeople on foot defeated an army of knights.

32210.q: Who founded the Capetian royal dynasty in France in 987?
32210.e: Hugh Capet was elected king in 987 after the end of the West Frankish Carolingians. His descendants ruled France in various lines until 1848.
32210.m: With Hugh Capet in 987, the rule of the Capetians began.

32211.q: Which house took over the French throne in 1328 after the direct Capetian line died out?
32211.e: Charles IV died in 1328 without a son. His cousin Philip VI from the Valois branch became king.
32211.m: From 1328 the Valois ruled as a branch of the Capetians.

32212.q: Which old law was later used in France to exclude women, and succession through women, from the throne?
32212.e: The Lex Salica was an early medieval Frankish law code. Lawyers later used it as a reason to exclude female succession.
32212.m: Salic law served as a reason against female succession to the French throne.

32213.q: Which Capetian died on a crusade outside Tunis in 1270 and was later made a saint?
32213.e: Louis IX led two crusades and died of an epidemic outside Tunis on the second. He was canonised in 1297.
32213.m: Louis IX is regarded as the saint king of France.

32214.q: Which Pope took up residence in Avignon in 1309?
32214.e: Clement V was French and under the influence of Philip IV. He stayed in southern France and settled in Avignon in 1309.
32214.m: With Clement V in 1309, the time of the popes in Avignon began.

32215.q: Which Pope moved his seat from Avignon back to Rome in 1377?
32215.e: Gregory XI returned to Rome in 1377. After his death in 1378 there was a double election and with it the Western Schism.
32215.m: Gregory XI ended the popes' stay in Avignon in 1377.

32216.q: Which Italian mystic urged the Pope in letters and visits to return to Rome?
32216.e: Catherine of Siena travelled to Avignon in 1376 and demanded the Pope's return. She was later made a saint and declared a Doctor of the Church.
32216.m: Catherine of Siena firmly campaigned for the Pope's return to Rome.

32217.q: How did the poet Petrarch critically describe the popes' stay in Avignon?
32217.e: Petrarch compared the time in Avignon with the exile of the Israelites in Babylon. He accused the papal court of luxury and dependence on France.
32217.m: Critics spoke of the Babylonian Captivity of the Church.

32218.q: How did Avignon become the property of the popes in 1348?
32218.e: Avignon belonged to Provence, which was owned by Queen Joanna I of Naples. Pope Clement VI bought the city from her for 80,000 florins.
32218.m: Avignon became papal property by purchase in 1348.

32219.q: Which building in Avignon still bears witness to the popes' stay and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
32219.e: The Papal Palace in Avignon is one of the largest Gothic buildings in Europe. Together with the old town it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.
32219.m: The Papal Palace still dominates the cityscape of Avignon.

32220.q: Which council in a city on Lake Constance ended the Church split in 1417 by electing Martin V?
32220.e: The Council of Constance met from 1414 to 1418 and deposed the rival popes or accepted their resignations. In 1417 it elected Martin V as the only Pope.
32220.m: The Council of Constance on Lake Constance ended the great schism.

32221.q: What was special about the Templars as an order?
a: They were monks and knights at the same time
They lived as hermits without weapons
32221.e: The Templars took monastic vows and at the same time fought with weapons. In 1129 they received their own rule.
32221.m: The Templars were a religious order of knights.

32222.q: Which Cistercian abbot promoted the Templar order with the work “In Praise of the New Knighthood”?
32222.e: Bernard of Clairvaux described the Templars as knights who are also monks. His work made the order known in Europe.
32222.m: Bernard of Clairvaux was an influential supporter of the Templars.

32223.q: To whom was the Templar order directly subject from 1139?
32223.e: A papal bull made the order independent of the bishops and freed it from many dues. This strengthened its position throughout Europe.
32223.m: The Templars were directly subject to the Pope.

32224.q: Which service did the Templars offer pilgrims on the way to the Holy Land?
a: Paying in money and withdrawing it elsewhere
32224.e: Pilgrims could deposit money at a house in Europe and collect it elsewhere with a letter. That way they did not have to carry large sums with them.
32224.m: The Templars developed early forms of cashless payment.

32225.q: What clothing did the knights of the Templar order wear?
a: A white cloak with a red cross
A black cloak with a white cross
A red cloak with a white cross
A blue cloak with a gold cross
32225.e: The white cloak stood for purity, and the red cross was added around 1147. A black cloak with a white cross, on the other hand, marked the Hospitallers.
32225.m: The Templars wore white with a red cross.

32226.q: To which island did the Templar order move its headquarters after the fall of Acre in 1291?
32226.e: After losing their last fortresses in the Holy Land, the Templars withdrew to Cyprus. From there they planned new crusades in vain.
32226.m: After 1291 the centre of the Templars was on Cyprus.

32227.q: Why did the French king move against the Templars from 1307?
a: He wanted their wealth and was in debt to them
The Templars had stolen his crown
The Templars refused him horses for hunting
32227.e: Philip IV had the Templars arrested and charged with heresy using forced confessions. In 1312 the Pope dissolved the order.
32227.m: The French king also crushed the Templars out of greed for money.

32228.q: From which empire did Kievan Rus adopt Christianity around 988?
32228.e: Grand Prince Vladimir was baptised in the Byzantine rite around 988 and married a sister of the emperor. This gave the Rus an Orthodox character.
32228.m: Kievan Rus adopted Christianity from Byzantium.

32229.q: According to the Primary Chronicle, which people did the first princes of the Rus around Rurik come from?
32229.e: The chronicle reports that the Eastern Slavs called on Varangians from Scandinavia to rule them. Rurik is said to have settled in Novgorod around 862.
32229.m: The ruling family of the Rus goes back to Scandinavian Varangians.

32230.q: What is the most important chronicle on the early history of Kievan Rus called?
32230.e: The Primary Chronicle was written in Kyiv in the early 12th century. It is also known as the “Tale of Bygone Years”.
32230.m: The Primary Chronicle is the most important source on the early Rus.

32231.q: Which grand prince had the first law code of the Rus, the “Russkaya Pravda”, written down?
32231.e: The Russkaya Pravda was created under Yaroslav the Wise in the 11th century. His reign is seen as the golden age of Kievan Rus.
32231.m: Yaroslav the Wise gave the Rus their first written law.

32232.q: Which cathedral in Kyiv did Yaroslav the Wise have built in the 11th century?
32232.e: St Sophia's Cathedral was named after the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32232.m: St Sophia's Cathedral is the best-known building of Kievan Rus.

32233.q: What was the important trade route from the Baltic via the Dnieper to Constantinople called?
a: The route from the Varangians to the Greeks
32233.e: On rivers and short overland stretches, traders carried furs, wax and slaves south. Kyiv on the Dnieper was well placed on this route.
32233.m: Trade between Scandinavia and Byzantium made Kyiv flourish.

32234.q: In which year did the Mongols capture and destroy Kyiv?
32234.e: In December 1240 the Mongols took Kyiv after a siege. This ended Kyiv's importance as the centre of the Rus.
32234.m: The capture of Kyiv in 1240 sealed the end of Kievan Rus.

32235.q: Whose grandson led the great Mongol campaign into Eastern Europe from 1236?
32235.e: Batu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, led the army together with the general Subutai. The campaign struck the Rus, Poland and Hungary.
32235.m: A grandson of Genghis Khan led the Mongol invasion of Europe.

32236.q: What is the roughly 240-year rule of the Mongols over the Russian principalities called in Russia?
32236.e: After the Mongol invasion, the Russian princes had to pay tribute to the Golden Horde. This dependence only ended in 1480.
32236.m: The Tatar yoke was the Mongols' rule over the Rus.

32237.q: Which city, then the old centre of the Rus, did the Mongols capture and destroy in 1240?
32237.e: Kyiv was the capital of Kievan Rus. After its destruction in 1240 the city lost its importance for a long time. Novgorod, by contrast, was spared.

32238.q: Which kingdom did the Mongols devastate especially badly in 1241 and 1242?
32238.e: After their victory at Mohi in 1241, the Mongols plundered their way through Hungary. King Béla IV fled to the Adriatic and afterwards had many stone castles built.
32238.m: Hungary suffered especially badly from the Mongol invasion in 1241.

32239.q: Whom did an army of Poles, Silesians and knights of the orders fight at Legnica in 1241?
32239.e: Duke Henry II of Silesia led the army and fell in the battle. The Mongols then moved on to Hungary.
32239.m: In 1241 the Mongols fought a European army at Legnica.

32240.q: How did the Battle of Legnica in 1241 end?
a: A draw with a peace treaty
It did not take place because of a storm
32240.e: The Mongols defeated the army of the Poles and Silesians. Even so, they did not move further west but joined their main army in Hungary.
32240.m: The Mongols won at Legnica in 1241.

32241.q: What does it show that the Mongols won at Legnica and in Hungary within two days in 1241?
a: Several parts of the army attacked at the same time according to plan
32241.e: One part of the army went through Poland, the main part to Hungary. On 11 April 1241 the Mongols won on the River Sajó at Mohi.
32241.m: The Mongols led several armies at once according to a plan.

32242.q: What is the town of Liegnitz called today, and which country is it in?
32242.e: Liegnitz in Lower Silesia has belonged to Poland since 1945 and is called Legnica. A museum near the town recalls the battle of 1241.
32242.m: The battlefield of Legnica is now in Poland.

32243.q: What was the capital of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga called?
32243.e: The Mongols founded Sarai as a residence on a side arm of the Volga. The city became an important trading centre.
32243.m: Sarai on the Volga was the capital of the Golden Horde.

32244.q: Which religion became the state religion of the Golden Horde around 1313?
32244.e: Özbeg Khan promoted Islam and made it the religion of the state. His reign is regarded as the high point of the Golden Horde.
32244.m: Under Özbeg Khan the Golden Horde became an Islamic empire.

32245.q: What does Russian history writing call the long dependence of the Rus on the Mongols?
32245.e: The Russian princes had to pay tribute and recognise the khan's overlordship. This period lasted about 240 years.
32245.m: The Tatar yoke refers to the Golden Horde's rule over the Rus.

32246.q: What did Russian princes need under the rule of the Golden Horde to be allowed to rule?
a: A charter of rule from the khan
32246.e: The charter of rule was called a yarlyk. Princes often travelled to Sarai for it and competed for the khan's favour.
32246.m: With the yarlyk the khan confirmed the Russian princes.

32247.q: Which grand prince of Moscow defeated an army of the Golden Horde on the Kulikovo Field in 1380?
32247.e: Dmitry Donskoy beat the army of the commander Mamai on the Don. The victory did not yet end the dependence but raised Moscow's standing.
32247.m: The victory on the Kulikovo Field made Moscow the leader of the Rus.

32248.q: How did the Golden Horde's rule over Moscow end in 1480?
a: The armies faced each other on the River Ugra, then the Tatars withdrew
Moscow was destroyed in a battle
32248.e: The armies of Ivan III and Khan Akhmat faced each other on the Ugra without fighting a great battle. Afterwards the Tatar army withdrew.
32248.m: With the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480, the Tatar yoke ended.

32249.q: At the siege of which city on the Black Sea is a Golden Horde army said to have hurled plague corpses over the walls in 1346?
32249.e: Caffa in Crimea was a Genoese trading city. From there the plague is said to have reached Italy and the rest of Europe by ship.
32249.m: The plague probably reached Europe along trade routes from the Black Sea.

32250.q: In which city in the Holy Land did the hospital community from which the Teutonic Order grew start in 1190?
32250.e: Citizens from Bremen and Lübeck set up a field hospital during the siege of Acre. In 1198 it became an order of knights.
32250.m: The Teutonic Order began in 1190 as a hospital outside Acre.

32251.q: Why did a Polish duke bring the Teutonic Order to the Baltic around 1226?
32251.e: Duke Conrad of Masovia offered the order the Kulm Land. From there the order conquered the land of the Prussians over about fifty years.
32251.m: A Polish duke brought the Teutonic Order in against the Prussians.

32252.q: Which rights did Emperor Frederick II give the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order in Prussia?
a: Princely rule over the conquered land
The right to elect the Pope
The title of King of Poland
Freedom from taxes throughout the empire
32252.e: The Golden Bull of Rimini, dated 1226, gave the Grand Master princely rights over the land to be conquered. The later state of the order was built on this.
32252.m: The Golden Bull of Rimini laid the foundation for the order's state in Prussia.

32253.q: Which castle on the Nogat became the seat of the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order in 1309?
32253.e: Marienburg (today Malbork in Poland) is the largest brick castle in the world. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32253.m: Marienburg was the centre of power of the order's state.

32254.q: Against which prince did an army of the order lose on the ice of Lake Peipus in 1242?
32254.e: The Prince of Novgorod defeated the knights of the Livonian branch of the order. This stopped the order's expansion to the east.
32254.m: The Battle on Lake Peipus set a limit to the order's power in the east.

32255.q: What did Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach turn the order's land of Prussia into in 1525?
32255.e: Albert converted to the Reformation and turned the order's land into the Duchy of Prussia. In return he paid homage to the King of Poland as his overlord.
32255.m: In 1525 the first Protestant duchy arose from the order's state.

32256.q: What kind of order was the Teutonic Order?
32256.e: Like the Templars and Hospitallers, the Teutonic Order combined monastic life and military service. It also had houses in Switzerland, for example the commandery of Hitzkirch in the canton of Lucerne.
32256.m: The Teutonic Order was a religious order of knights.

32257.q: How were Poland and Lithuania linked in 1385 and 1386?
a: Through a personal union under one ruler
Through a ruling by the emperor
32257.e: With the Union of Krewo, the Lithuanian grand duke also became King of Poland through marriage. Both countries remained separate but had the same ruler.
32257.m: From 1386 Poland and Lithuania had a shared ruler.

32258.q: Which dynasty did the Lithuanian Jogaila found as King of Poland?
32258.e: Jogaila was crowned Władysław II Jagiełło in 1386. The Jagiellonians later also ruled in Bohemia and Hungary.

32259.q: What did the pagan grand duke Jogaila have to do to be able to marry the Polish queen?
32259.e: Jogaila was baptised in 1386 and married Jadwiga of Anjou. Afterwards Lithuania was also Christianised.
32259.m: Jogaila was baptised for the Polish crown.

32260.q: Which country became the last in Europe to be Christianised, with the baptism of its ruler in 1386?
32260.e: Lithuania had remained pagan into the 14th century. This ended with Jogaila's baptism and the people's acceptance of Christianity.
32260.m: Lithuania was the last country in Europe to accept Christianity.

32261.q: Which two countries defeated the Teutonic Order at Tannenberg in 1410?
32261.e: King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas led the joint army. The Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen fell in the battle.
32261.m: In 1410 Poland and Lithuania defeated the Teutonic Order.

32262.q: What was the result of the defeat at Tannenberg in 1410 for the Teutonic Order?
a: Its power on the Baltic began to decline
It then conquered all of Poland
It moved to the Holy Land
32262.e: The order lost many knights and had to make large payments. After that it grew weaker and weaker in the Baltic region.
32262.m: After Tannenberg the Teutonic Order lost power.

32263.q: By what name is the Battle of Tannenberg of 1410 known in Poland?
32263.e: The Poles name the battle after the village of Grunwald. There it is seen as one of the greatest victories in their history.
32263.m: In Poland, Tannenberg 1410 is known as the Battle of Grunwald.

32264.q: Which castle, the headquarters of the Teutonic Order, withstood the siege by Poland and Lithuania in 1410?
32264.e: Heinrich von Plauen defended Marienburg for about two months. Today, as Malbork in Poland, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

32265.q: Which city was the capital of the Tang dynasty and one of the largest cities in the world at the time?
32265.e: Chang'an, today's Xi'an, was the starting point of the Silk Road. In the 8th century the city probably had around one million inhabitants.
32265.m: Chang'an was the splendid capital of the Tang.

32266.q: Who was the only woman to rule China officially as empress in her own right?
32266.e: In 690 Wu Zetian proclaimed her own Zhou dynasty and ruled until 705. After that the Tang dynasty was restored.
32266.m: Wu Zetian was China's only reigning empress.

32267.q: Which rebellion shook the Tang dynasty from 755 to 763 and permanently weakened central power?
32267.e: General An Lushan rose up against the imperial court and for a time captured both capitals. The war cost millions of lives and strengthened the regional military governors.
32267.m: The An Lushan Rebellion began the decline of the Tang.

32268.q: Against whom did a Tang army lose the Battle of Talas in Central Asia in 751?
32268.e: At the River Talas the Tang army was defeated by an army of the Abbasid Caliphate. The battle limited Chinese influence in Central Asia.
32268.m: In 751 Tang China and the Caliphate clashed at the Talas.

32269.q: Which work is considered the oldest surviving dated printed book in the world?
32269.e: The Diamond Sutra was made by woodblock printing in the Tang period and found in the caves of Dunhuang. It bears a date that corresponds to the year 868.
32269.m: The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed work.

32270.q: Which two poets are considered the greatest poets of the Tang period?
32270.e: Li Bai and Du Fu lived in the 8th century and shaped classical Chinese poetry. The Tang period is seen as the golden age of Chinese poetry.
32270.m: Li Bai and Du Fu are the great poets of the Tang period.

32271.q: Why did the Song dynasty move its court south to Hangzhou in 1127?
a: The Jurchen of the Jin dynasty conquered the north
A flood destroyed the imperial palace
32271.e: In the Jingkang Incident the Jurchen took the capital and carried off the emperor. After that the Song ruled as the Southern Song from Hangzhou.
32271.m: Losing the north to the Jin turned the Song into the Southern Song.

32272.q: Which innovation in money did the Chinese state introduce under the Song dynasty around 1024?
a: Silver bars as the only currency
32272.e: Merchants in Sichuan first used private promissory notes. Around 1024 the state took over issuing them, creating the world's first state paper money.
32272.m: The first state paper money appeared under the Song.

32273.q: Which navigation aid did Chinese scholars of the Song period describe first?
32273.e: In 1088 the scholar Shen Kuo described a magnetised needle that points south. Soon afterwards Chinese sailors used the compass on their ships.
32273.m: The magnetic compass was described in China in the Song period.

32274.q: What does a Chinese military handbook from 1044 contain the oldest known written recipes for?
32274.e: The handbook was compiled on behalf of the Song court. It describes mixtures of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal for incendiary weapons.
32274.m: The first gunpowder recipes come from China.

32275.q: Which teaching was renewed in the Song period and later became the basis of the Chinese civil service examinations?
32275.e: Scholars such as Zhu Xi combined the ethics of Confucius with new philosophical ideas. This Neo-Confucianism was examination material from 1313.
32275.m: Neo-Confucianism shaped China's civil service examinations.

32276.q: What was the assembly of Mongol princes that elected rulers and decided on military campaigns called?
32276.e: The kurultai was a council of nobles and military leaders. It confirmed every new Great Khan.
32276.m: A kurultai was the great council of the Mongols.

32277.q: What is the code of law attributed to Genghis Khan called?
32277.e: The Yassa regulated discipline, punishments and duties in the empire. Its exact wording has not survived.
32277.m: The Yassa was the law of the Mongols under Genghis Khan.

32278.q: On what principle did Genghis Khan organise his army?
a: In a decimal system of units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000
Separated by clans and family groups
32278.e: The division into arban, jagun, mingghan and tumen broke up old tribal ties. This created a tightly led, loyal army.
32278.m: The Mongol army was built on units of ten.

32279.q: Which event triggered Genghis Khan's campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219?
a: The murder of a Mongol trade caravan in Otrar
The kidnapping of his wife Börte
A refusal to pay tribute in silk
32279.e: The governor of Otrar had a caravan killed, and later an envoy was executed too. A devastating war followed that struck cities such as Bukhara and Samarkand.
32279.m: The attack at Otrar led to the war against Khwarazm.

32280.q: Which present-day city did Genghis Khan capture from the Chinese Jin dynasty in 1215?
32280.e: The city was then called Zhongdu and was the capital of the Jin. Later Kublai Khan made it the capital of his empire under the name Khanbaliq.
32280.m: The Mongols captured present-day Beijing in 1215.

32281.q: During which campaign did Genghis Khan die in 1227?
a: Against the Tangut kingdom of Western Xia
32281.e: Genghis Khan died in 1227 during the siege of the Tangut capital. His grave has still not been found.
32281.m: Genghis Khan died in the war against the Tanguts.

32282.q: Why did the Mongols withdraw from Central Europe in 1242?
a: The plague had wiped out their army
A crusader army beat them near Vienna
32282.e: After Ögedei's death in December 1241 leading princes returned to elect a successor. Europe was then spared further large campaigns.
32282.m: Ögedei's death saved Central Europe from further attacks.

32283.q: Which city, seat of the caliph, did the Mongols capture and destroy in 1258?
32283.e: The Mongol prince Hülegü had Baghdad plundered and the caliph killed. This ended the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad.

32284.q: Who inflicted one of the first great defeats on the Mongols at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260?
32284.e: At Ain Jalut in Palestine the Mamluks under Qutuz and Baibars stopped the Mongol advance. Egypt thus remained unconquered.
32284.m: The Mamluks stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260.

32285.q: What is the period of relative safety on Eurasia's trade routes under Mongol rule in the 13th and 14th centuries called?
32285.e: Under Mongol control merchants, envoys and missionaries could travel from Eastern Europe to China. Goods, techniques and ideas spread faster as a result.
32285.m: The Pax Mongolica made exchange between East and West easier.

32286.q: What was the network of relay stations in the Mongol Empire for?
a: Merchants paid their customs duties there
32286.e: In the Mongol postal system, called the Yam, couriers received fresh horses and food. This way messages covered several hundred kilometres a day.
32286.m: The Mongol postal system made messages very fast.

32287.q: Which dynasty did the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan found in China?
32287.e: Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and ruled from Beijing. In 1368 it was replaced by the Chinese Ming dynasty.
32287.m: Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China.

32288.q: What was the capital of the Yuan dynasty, located on the site of present-day Beijing, called?
32288.e: Dadu (Turkic Khanbaliq, ‘city of the khan’) was built to a plan from 1267. Shangdu served as the summer residence.
32288.m: Dadu was the capital of the Yuan.

32289.q: How did Kublai Khan's two attempts to invade Japan in 1274 and 1281 end?
a: They failed, partly because of heavy storms
32289.e: Japanese warriors resisted, and typhoons destroyed large parts of the fleets. The Japanese interpreted the storms as ‘kamikaze’, divine wind.
32289.m: Storms and resistance made Kublai's attacks on Japan fail.

32290.q: Which group was at the very bottom of the social ranking of the Yuan dynasty?
32290.e: The Yuan divided the population into Mongols, Semu, Han (northern Chinese) and Nanren (southern Chinese). The southern Chinese, conquered last, had the fewest rights.
32290.m: In the Yuan empire the southern Chinese ranked lowest.

32291.q: Which dynasty did Kublai Khan found in China?
32291.e: Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271. It was the first foreign rule over all of China and ended in 1368.
32291.m: Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty.

32292.q: Where did Marco Polo dictate his travel account to the writer Rustichello da Pisa?
a: On a ship on the way home
32292.e: After being captured in a war between Venice and Genoa, Marco Polo was in prison around 1298. There Rustichello wrote down his stories.
32292.m: Marco Polo's account was written in a Genoese prison.

32293.q: At whose court did Marco Polo serve for many years in China?
32293.e: Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, ruled China as emperor. By his own account Marco Polo was in his service for around 17 years.
32293.m: Marco Polo served at the court of Kublai Khan.

32294.q: Which later explorer owned a copy of Marco Polo's account with his own notes in it?
32294.e: Columbus read the book carefully and added notes in the margins. He hoped to reach the rich Asia it described by sailing west.
32294.m: Marco Polo's account influenced Christopher Columbus.

32295.q: Which foreign rule did the Ming dynasty end in China in 1368?
32295.e: Zhu Yuanzhang led the uprising against the Mongol Yuan dynasty. As the Hongwu Emperor he drove the Mongols out of China.
32295.m: In 1368 the Ming replaced Mongol rule.

32296.q: Which palace complex was built in Beijing at the start of the 15th century and completed in 1420?
a: The Temple of Heaven in Nanjing
32296.e: At that time the Ming imperial court moved from Nanjing to Beijing. The Forbidden City was the seat of the emperors until 1912.
32296.m: The Forbidden City was completed in 1420.

32297.q: Which policy under the Ming strongly restricted private sea trade with foreign countries?
a: The founding of colonies in Africa
Building a war fleet against Europe
32297.e: The haijin ban had been in force since the first Ming emperor and was enforced further after the end of the great fleet voyages. The court focused more on defence in the north.
32297.m: The Ming restricted sea trade with the haijin.

32298.q: What was a shogun in medieval Japan?
a: The supreme military commander who ruled in place of the emperor
32298.e: After the Genpei War Minamoto no Yoritomo received the title of shogun in 1192. He ruled the country from Kamakura, while the emperor kept mainly religious duties.
32298.m: The shogun was Japan's military ruler.

32299.q: What does the Japanese term bakufu for the shogun's government mean?
32299.e: The name recalls the field camp of a military commander. It stresses the military origin of shogunate rule.

32300.q: What role did the emperor have in Japan during the Kamakura shogunate?
a: He was mainly a religious and ceremonial head
He lived in exile in China
32300.e: Real power lay with the military government in Kamakura. The imperial court in Kyoto remained important for religion and ceremonies.
32300.m: In the Kamakura shogunate the warriors ruled, not the emperor.

32301.q: Which school of Buddhism gained especially many followers among the samurai in the Kamakura shogunate?
32301.e: Zen stresses meditation, self-discipline and calm. These values suited the ideal of the warrior.

32302.q: Which warrior class shaped the Kamakura shogunate?
32302.e: With the shogunate the warrior nobility took over the government of Japan for the first time. In 1232 a separate law code was even issued for the samurai.
32302.m: In the Kamakura shogunate the samurai ruled.

32303.q: Which famous large bronze statue in Kamakura dates from the middle of the 13th century?
32303.e: The Daibutsu of Kamakura is about 13 metres high including its base and now stands in the open air. Its hall was destroyed by tidal waves.
32303.m: The Great Buddha is the landmark of Kamakura.

32304.q: Which attacks from outside badly weakened the Kamakura shogunate in the 13th century?
32304.e: The Mongols attacked Japan in 1274 and 1281. The defence cost a lot of money, and the shogunate could hardly reward its warriors. In 1333 it was overthrown.
32304.m: The Mongol attacks weakened the Kamakura shogunate.

32305.q: Which religion did the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate follow?
32305.e: The sultanate was founded in 1206 by a Muslim military commander. Most of the population remained Hindu.
32305.m: The Delhi Sultanate was a Muslim empire in northern India.

32306.q: Which building in Delhi was begun under Qutb ud-Din Aibak and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
32306.e: The victory tower of red sandstone is about 73 metres high. His successors Iltutmish and Firuz Shah continued the building.
32306.m: The Qutb Minar is a landmark of the Delhi Sultanate.

32307.q: What was special about Razia, who ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240?
a: She was the only woman on this throne
She was the first Christian on this throne
She conquered all of southern India
32307.e: Razia was the daughter of Sultan Iltutmish, who named her as his heir. The nobles overthrew her after a few years.
32307.m: Razia was the only female sultan of Delhi.

32308.q: Which mounted armies invaded the Delhi Sultanate several times around 1300 and were driven back?
32308.e: Sultan Alauddin Khalji fought off several Mongol attacks. For this he kept a large standing army.
32308.m: The Delhi Sultanate kept the Mongols out of India.

32309.q: Why did the introduction of copper coins in place of silver money fail in the Delhi Sultanate in the 14th century?
a: The coins were forged on a huge scale
Copper was more expensive than silver
The merchants did not yet know money
32309.e: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq wanted to save silver. Because many people made copper coins themselves, the new money quickly lost its value.
32309.m: Forged copper coins made a currency reform in Delhi fail.

32310.q: Which Central Asian conqueror plundered Delhi in 1398?
32310.e: Timur marched into India with his army and carried out a massacre in Delhi. The sultanate recovered only slowly.

32311.q: Which empire followed the Delhi Sultanate in northern India in 1526?
32311.e: In 1526 Babur defeated the last sultan of Delhi at Panipat. This began the Mughal Empire, which later built the Taj Mahal.
32311.m: In 1526 the Mughal Empire replaced the Delhi Sultanate.

32312.q: Near which river does Timbuktu lie?
32312.e: Timbuktu lies a few kilometres north of the Niger on the southern edge of the Sahara. Its location linked river and caravan trade.
32312.m: Timbuktu lies near the Niger on the edge of the Sahara.

32313.q: For what kind of treasures is Timbuktu especially famous as a city of scholars?
32313.e: Libraries and families keep manuscripts on law, astronomy, medicine and theology. Many date from the 13th to the 17th century.
32313.m: Timbuktu keeps a rich collection of old manuscripts.

32314.q: Which empire captured Timbuktu in 1468 under its ruler Sonni Ali?
32314.e: Sonni Ali took the city from the Tuareg, who had controlled it before. Under the Askia rulers Timbuktu flourished further.
32314.m: Timbuktu came under Songhai rule in 1468.

32315.q: Where does the name ‘Swahili’ come from?
a: From the Arabic word for coasts
From the Persian word for traders
From the Bantu word for sea
From the Portuguese word for islands
32315.e: Sawahil means ‘coasts’ in Arabic. It referred to the people of the East African coast.

32316.q: Which language family forms the basis of the Swahili language?
32316.e: Swahili is a Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords. Today it is an important common language in East Africa.
32316.m: Swahili is a Bantu language with Arabic influences.

32317.q: Which city was one of the richest trading cities of the Swahili coast in the 14th century and minted its own coins?
32317.e: Kilwa controlled the gold trade from the interior via Sofala. Ruins of the Great Mosque and the Husuni Kubwa palace survive.
32317.m: Kilwa Kisiwani was a rich city-state of the Swahili coast.

32318.q: Which natural phenomenon made regular trade between the Swahili coast, Arabia and India possible?
a: The tides of the Red Sea
32318.e: The monsoon winds change direction with the seasons. Sailing ships used them for the outward and return journeys.
32318.m: The monsoon set the rhythm of trade in the Indian Ocean.

32319.q: What did Vasco da Gama receive on the Swahili coast in 1498 for the onward journey to India?
32319.e: The ruler of Malindi supported the Portuguese and gave them a pilot. With him da Gama crossed the Indian Ocean to Calicut.
32319.m: A pilot from the Swahili coast guided Vasco da Gama to India.

32320.q: Which trade route linked the Tang capital Chang'an with Central Asia and the Mediterranean?
32320.e: Under the Tang trade flourished on the Silk Road. Along with goods, religions such as Buddhism and foreign merchants came to China.
32320.m: Chang'an was a starting point of the Silk Road.

32321.q: Which religion did Emperor Wuzong have persecuted around 845, when thousands of monasteries were dissolved?
32321.e: In the persecution of the Huichang era monasteries were seized and monks and nuns forced back into lay life. Economic reasons also lay behind the measures.

32322.q: How were officials mainly chosen under the Song dynasty?
32322.e: The Song greatly expanded the examination system. Educated officials gained more weight than the generals.
32322.m: Under the Song officials were chosen through examinations.

32323.q: What does the famous scroll painting ‘Along the River During the Qingming Festival’ from the Song period show?
32323.e: Zhang Zeduan's handscroll, over five metres long, shows hundreds of people, shops, boats and an arched bridge. It is considered one of China's most important paintings.
32323.m: The Qingming scroll shows city life in the Song period.

32324.q: What did a Song chancellor introduce for farmers, among other things, with his ‘New Laws’ from 1069?
a: The right to vote for everyone
32324.e: Chancellor Wang Anshi wanted to protect farmers from moneylenders and strengthen the state. His reforms were fiercely disputed at court.
32324.m: The Song reforms gave farmers state loans.

32325.q: What was Genghis Khan's name before he was proclaimed ruler of all the Mongols in 1206?
32325.e: Temüjin was raised to Genghis Khan at a kurultai in 1206. His chief wife Börte was the mother of his most important heirs; Kublai and Batu were grandsons, Ögedei a son.
32325.m: Genghis Khan was originally called Temüjin.

32326.q: Which 13th-century source is the most important Mongol record of Genghis Khan's life?
a: The Secret History of the Mongols
32326.e: The work was written shortly after Genghis Khan's death and tells of the origins and rise of the ruling family. It is the oldest surviving literature in the Mongolian language.
32326.m: The Secret History of the Mongols tells of Genghis Khan's life.

32327.q: Which city in Mongolia was the capital of the Mongol Empire under Ögedei?
