32327.e: Ögedei, son and successor of Genghis Khan, had Karakorum expanded. Kublai Khan later moved the capital to Beijing.
32327.m: Karakorum was the first capital of the Mongol Empire.

32328.q: Why did the Pope and European kings send monks as envoys to the Mongols in the 13th century?
a: They hoped for conversion and an alliance against the Muslims
They wanted to buy land in Mongolia
They wanted to collect tribute from the Mongols
They were looking for the sea route to India there
32328.e: Envoys such as William of Rubruck travelled as far as Karakorum. No alliance came about, but their reports improved knowledge about Asia.
32328.m: Europe sought allies and new Christians among the Mongols.

32329.e: Kublai was a son of Tolui, the youngest son of Genghis Khan. He became Great Khan in 1260.
32329.m: Kublai Khan was a grandson of Genghis Khan.

32330.q: Which empire in southern China did Kublai Khan conquer by 1279?
32330.e: After years of fighting, the last Song resistance fell in 1279. The Mongols then ruled all of China.
32330.m: Kublai Khan conquered the Song empire.

32331.q: Which transport structure did Kublai Khan have extended to his capital in the north to supply it with grain?
a: The pontoon bridge over the Yangtze
32331.e: From 1289 and 1293 new canal sections linked the north directly with the waterway from the south. This way rice from the Yangtze region reached the capital.
32331.m: Kublai Khan extended the Grand Canal northwards.

32332.q: Why do some historians doubt that Marco Polo was really in China?
a: He mentions neither the Great Wall nor tea
He wrote his account in Chinese
32332.e: Critics point to striking gaps in his account. However, many other details, for example about the salt tax and money, match Chinese sources well.
32332.m: Marco Polo's account has gaps but is credible in many ways.

32333.q: What did Marco Polo describe in China as amazing because it was still unknown in Europe?
32333.e: Marco Polo was amazed that people in Kublai Khan's empire paid with printed paper. In Europe paper money only caught on centuries later.
32333.m: Marco Polo told Europe about Chinese paper money.

32334.q: Roughly how long was Marco Polo away before he returned to Venice?
32334.e: Marco Polo set off in 1271 with his father and uncle and came back in 1295. In Venice people hardly recognised the returning travellers at first.
32334.m: Marco Polo was away for about 24 years.

32335.q: How did many people of his time react to Marco Polo's travel account?
a: They thought much of it was exaggerated or made up
The Pope made it required reading
32335.e: The descriptions of huge cities and riches sounded unbelievable. Even so, the book was copied often and later influenced explorers such as Columbus.
32335.m: Many thought Marco Polo's account was exaggerated.

32336.q: Which religion was the Chinese admiral Zheng He born into?
32336.e: Zheng He came from a Muslim family in south-west China. His father and grandfather had made the pilgrimage to Mecca.

32337.q: Which important strait in South-East Asia did Zheng He's fleet free from pirates in 1407?
32337.e: The pirate Chen Zuyi threatened trade between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Zheng He captured him near Palembang on Sumatra.
32337.m: Zheng He secured the Strait of Malacca.

32338.q: What does the inscription in three languages that Zheng He had set up in Sri Lanka in 1409 show?
a: A declaration of war on India
A map of the Indian Ocean
32338.e: The stone tablet in Chinese, Tamil and Persian records offerings to the Buddha, to a Hindu deity and to Allah. It shows the religious openness of the Ming missions.
32338.m: Zheng He's inscription in Sri Lanka honours several religions.

32339.q: What did the third Ming emperor have over 2,000 scholars compile by 1408?
a: A world map made of silk
32339.e: The Yongle Encyclopaedia comprised over 11,000 volumes with texts from all fields of knowledge. Today only a few hundred volumes survive.
32339.m: The largest encyclopaedia of its time was created under the Ming.

32340.q: When did Zheng He die, according to the most common view?
32340.e: Zheng He probably died in 1433 on the return journey of the seventh expedition; other sources say 1435. A tomb in Nanjing commemorates him.
32340.m: Zheng He died in 1433 on his last voyage.

32341.q: How did the Jokyu War of 1221 end, in which the retired emperor Go-Toba wanted to overthrow the shogunate?
a: The shogunate won and Go-Toba was exiled
The emperor took back full power
Japan was split into two kingdoms
The Mongols stepped in and decided the war
32341.e: The troops from Kamakura quickly took Kyoto. After that the shogunate watched over the imperial court with its own office.
32341.m: After the Jokyu War of 1221 the shogunate's power was secure.

32342.q: Which scene from Hindu mythology does the most famous bas-relief in the galleries of Angkor Wat show?
a: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk
The wedding of Shiva and Parvati
32342.e: The relief, about 50 metres long, shows gods and demons pulling on a serpent to obtain the elixir of immortality. It is in the eastern gallery.
32342.m: Angkor Wat shows the Churning of the Ocean of Milk as a large relief.

32343.q: Which mythical mountain do the five towers at the centre of Angkor Wat represent?
32343.e: In Hinduism and Buddhism Meru is the centre of the world and home of the gods. The moat stands for the surrounding ocean.
32343.m: Angkor Wat recreates the world mountain Meru.

32344.q: From which source do we know most about everyday life in Angkor around 1300?
a: From the report of a Chinese envoy
32344.e: Zhou Daguan stayed in Angkor in 1296 and 1297 on behalf of the Yuan dynasty. He described markets, festivals, clothing and the Khmer king.
32344.m: A Chinese envoy described Angkor as an eyewitness.

32345.q: Which temple near Angkor is famous because huge tree roots wrap around its walls?
32345.e: Ta Prohm was built by Jayavarman VII. Part of the jungle was left standing to show how explorers once found the temples.
32345.m: At Ta Prohm trees grow on the temple walls.

32346.q: According to inscriptions, which facilities did Jayavarman VII have built throughout the Khmer Empire?
32346.e: Inscriptions name 102 hospitals with staff and medicines. There were also rest houses along the roads.
32346.m: Jayavarman VII built many hospitals in the Khmer Empire.

32347.q: In which present-day country is the temple city of Angkor?
32347.e: Angkor lies near Siem Reap in north-west Cambodia. Angkor Wat even appears on the national flag.

32348.q: Which Moroccan traveller served for several years as a judge (qadi) in Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughluq?
32348.e: He came to Delhi around 1334 and was received generously by the sultan. Later the ruler sent him as an envoy to China.
32348.m: Ibn Battuta was a judge at the court of the Sultan of Delhi.

32349.q: In which trading city on the edge of the Sahara did Mansa Musa have the famous mud-brick Djinguereber Mosque built?
32349.e: After his pilgrimage Mansa Musa had the Djinguereber Mosque built in Timbuktu around 1327. The city became a centre of trade and learning.
32349.m: Mansa Musa made Timbuktu a centre of learning.

32350.q: What did Mansa Musa become famous for on his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324?
a: He gave away so much gold that the price of gold fell in Cairo
He conquered all of Egypt on the way
He was the first to bring coffee to Europe
32350.e: Mansa Musa travelled with a huge entourage and handed out gold generously in Cairo. As a result gold lost value there for years.
32350.m: Mansa Musa's gold made the price of gold fall in Cairo.

32351.q: Which river was the most important transport route of the Mali Empire?
32351.e: Important trading cities such as Djenné, Timbuktu and Gao lay on the Niger. Gold, salt and grain were transported on the river.
32351.m: The Niger was the lifeline of the Mali Empire.

32352.q: How was the history of the Mali Empire in West Africa passed on for centuries?
a: Orally by griots, the storytellers and singers
32352.e: Griots still preserve family histories and heroic epics such as that of Sundiata Keita orally today. Written reports about Mali come mainly from Arab scholars.
32352.m: Griots pass on the history of Mali orally.

32353.q: What did Mansa Musa have to do in Cairo towards the end of his pilgrimage?
32353.e: Because he had given away so much gold, his funds were no longer enough for the journey home. Cairo merchants lent him money and made a good profit from it.
32353.m: Mansa Musa ran into debt at the end of his pilgrimage.

32354.q: Which country conquered the Songhai Empire in 1591 and carried off scholars from Timbuktu?
32354.e: A Moroccan army with firearms defeated the Songhai. The famous scholar Ahmad Baba was also taken to Marrakesh.
32354.m: Morocco ended Timbuktu's golden age in 1591.

32355.q: For what did the International Criminal Court convict an Islamist in the Timbuktu case in 2016?
a: For destroying mausoleums and a mosque
For stealing gold from the city treasury
For driving out all the inhabitants
32355.e: In 2012 Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi had led the destruction of saints' tombs. It was the court's first case centred on the destruction of cultural heritage as a war crime.
32355.m: In 2016 the destruction of cultural heritage in Timbuktu was punished as a war crime.

32356.q: Which nickname is Timbuktu given because of its many saints' tombs?
32356.e: In and around Timbuktu lie the mausoleums of many revered scholars. According to popular belief they protect the city.
32356.m: Timbuktu is called the City of 333 Saints.

32357.q: Which part of Great Zimbabwe is considered the largest pre-colonial structure south of the Sahara?
32357.e: The oval wall of the Great Enclosure is about 250 metres long. Inside are further walls and platforms.
32357.m: The Great Enclosure is the largest structure of Great Zimbabwe.

32358.q: Which area is the oldest part of Great Zimbabwe?
32358.e: Building on the rocky hill began early; the rulers probably lived there. The Great Enclosure in the valley came later.
32358.m: The Hill Complex is the oldest part of Great Zimbabwe.

32359.q: How were the walls of Great Zimbabwe built?
32359.e: The walls were stacked dry from shaped granite blocks. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.
32359.m: The walls of Great Zimbabwe were built without mortar.

32360.q: What was the wealth of the rulers of Great Zimbabwe mainly based on?
a: On cattle herds and the gold trade
On the salt trade across the Sahara
32360.e: The rulers owned large herds of cattle and controlled the gold trade to the coast of the Indian Ocean. Finds of Chinese porcelain and Persian glass beads show far-reaching trade links. A forerunner was Mapungubwe in the Limpopo valley.
32360.m: Gold and cattle made Great Zimbabwe rich.

32361.q: Which empire succeeded Great Zimbabwe in the 15th century in the north of present-day Zimbabwe?
32361.e: The Mutapa Empire controlled the gold trade to the Zambezi. Later the Portuguese traded with it.
32361.m: The Mutapa Empire followed Great Zimbabwe.

32362.q: Which traveller visited the city of Kilwa in 1331 and praised it as one of the most beautiful cities in the world?
32362.e: The Moroccan described Kilwa as splendid and well built. He travelled along the East African coast far to the south.
32362.m: Ibn Battuta admired the Swahili city of Kilwa.

32363.q: Which European power captured and plundered the Swahili city of Kilwa in 1505?
32363.e: The Portuguese under Francisco de Almeida wanted to control the gold and spice trade in the Indian Ocean. Afterwards Kilwa lost its importance.

32364.q: What building material did the Swahili cities mainly use for their mosques and stone houses?
32364.e: Coral limestone was quarried on the coast and laid with lime mortar. The Great Mosque of Kilwa and the old town of Lamu, for example, were built this way.
32364.m: The Swahili built with coral stone.

32365.q: Which ruler founded the Mughal Empire in India in 1526 after the Battle of Panipat?
32365.e: Babur, a descendant of Timur from Central Asia, defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat in 1526. With this he laid the foundation of the Mughal Empire.
32365.m: Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.

32366.q: What did the Mughal emperor Akbar abolish in 1564 to win over the Hindu majority?
a: Islam as the religion of the court
32366.e: The jizya was a poll tax on non-Muslim subjects. Akbar abolished it and followed a policy of religious tolerance.
32366.m: Akbar won over the Hindus through tolerance and by abolishing a special tax.

32367.q: What did the Mughal emperor Akbar try to do with the teaching of Din-i Ilahi, which he promoted?
a: Impose Islam throughout India by force
32367.e: Din-i Ilahi (“divine faith”) combined ideas from Islam, Hinduism and other religions. The teaching remained limited to a small circle at court.
32367.m: Akbar’s Din-i Ilahi shows his policy of religious tolerance.

32368.q: For whom did the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan have the Taj Mahal built as a tomb?
32368.e: From 1632 Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built for his late favourite wife Mumtaz Mahal. The mausoleum is regarded as the high point of Mughal architecture.
32368.m: The Taj Mahal is the tomb of Mumtaz Mahal.

32369.q: In which city is the Taj Mahal?
32369.e: The Taj Mahal stands on the bank of the Yamuna in Agra, in today’s Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32369.m: The Taj Mahal stands in Agra on the Yamuna.

32370.q: Which royal city did Akbar have newly built in the second half of the 16th century?
32370.e: From 1571 Akbar had Fatehpur Sikri near Agra built as his new capital. He left it again as early as 1585, probably partly because of problems with the water supply.
32370.m: Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar’s short-lived capital.

32371.q: Under which Mughal emperor did the empire reach its greatest extent, before it broke up after his death in 1707?
32371.e: Aurangzeb conquered large parts of the Deccan, but fought expensive wars and followed a strict religious policy. After his death the empire quickly broke up into smaller states.
32371.m: Under Aurangzeb the Mughal Empire was at its largest and then began to break up.

32372.q: After which event did the British depose the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah II, in 1858?
a: The founding of the Indian National Congress
32372.e: The rebels of 1857 had made Bahadur Shah II their symbol. After the uprising was crushed, the British exiled him to Rangoon and formally ended the Mughal Empire.
32372.m: The Mughal Empire ended with the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

32373.q: Which former slave from Ruthenia did Suleiman I marry, making her his lawful wife?
32373.e: Hürrem, called Roxelana in Europe, came to the harem as a slave. The sultan marrying her was a break with tradition.
32373.m: Hürrem Sultan was the influential wife of Suleiman I.

32374.q: Which fortress city on the Danube did Suleiman I conquer in 1521, shortly after coming to power?
32374.e: Belgrade was considered the key to Hungary. By conquering it, Suleiman opened the way for his campaigns into Central Europe.
32374.m: With Belgrade, Suleiman won the gateway to Hungary in 1521.

32375.q: Which island did Suleiman I conquer from the Knights of St John in 1522?
32375.e: After a siege lasting months, the Knights of St John had to leave Rhodes in 1522. They later settled on Malta.
32375.m: In 1522 Suleiman drove the Knights of St John out of Rhodes.

32376.q: What name is Suleiman I known by in Europe?
32376.e: Under Suleiman the Ottoman Empire reached its greatest power and splendour. In Turkey he is called Kanuni, the Lawgiver.
32376.m: In Europe Suleiman I is called “the Magnificent”.

32377.q: Which city did Suleiman I besiege without success in 1529?
32377.e: The first siege of Vienna failed because of strong resistance, supply problems and the approaching winter. It marked the westernmost point of Suleiman’s campaigns.
32377.m: In 1529 Suleiman failed at the gates of Vienna.

32378.q: Which kingdom came largely under Ottoman rule after Suleiman’s victory at Mohács in 1526?
32378.e: The Hungarian king was killed at the Battle of Mohács. In the following years the Ottomans conquered most of Hungary.
32378.m: After Mohács in 1526 most of Hungary became Ottoman.

32379.q: With which Christian ruler did Suleiman I ally himself against the Habsburgs?
32379.e: France and the Ottoman Empire had a common enemy in the Habsburgs. The alliance was seen as a scandal in Christian Europe.
32379.m: Suleiman and Francis I were united by their opposition to the Habsburgs.

32380.q: In which year did the Ottomans besiege Vienna for the second time?
32380.e: The first siege of Vienna took place in 1529, the second in 1683. Both times the Ottomans were unable to take the city.
32380.m: The second Turkish siege of Vienna was in 1683.

32381.q: Which king commanded the relief army that freed Vienna in 1683?
32381.e: The Polish king John III Sobieski was in overall command of the united Christian army. His cavalry charge decided the battle.
32381.m: John III Sobieski led the relief army at Vienna.

32382.q: Which alliance did the Emperor, Poland and Venice form against the Ottoman Empire in 1684?
32382.e: Pope Innocent XI promoted the alliance after the victory at Vienna. Russia later joined too.
32382.m: After 1683 the Holy League continued the war against the Ottomans.

32383.q: Which country were the Habsburgs and Ottomans mainly fighting over at the time of the second Turkish siege of Vienna?
32383.e: Since the 16th century Hungary had been divided between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. Some Hungarian nobles even fought on the Ottoman side against the Habsburgs.
32383.m: Hungary was fought over by the Habsburgs and the Ottomans.

32384.q: What fate befell the Ottoman commander-in-chief after the defeat at Vienna?
a: He was executed on the sultan’s orders
He was taken prisoner by the Poles
He was killed in the decisive battle
32384.e: In December 1683 the Grand Vizier was strangled in Belgrade on the sultan’s orders. He was blamed for the defeat.
32384.m: The defeat at Vienna cost the Grand Vizier his life.

32385.q: Which territory did the Ottoman Empire have to give up almost entirely to the Habsburgs in the Peace of Karlowitz in 1699?
32385.e: After the Great Turkish War, the Ottoman Empire lost almost all of Hungary and Transylvania. It was the Ottomans’ first major loss of territory in Europe.
32385.m: The Ottoman retreat from Europe began with the Peace of Karlowitz in 1699.

32386.q: Which ruling family ruled in Vienna in 1683?
32386.e: Emperor Leopold I of the House of Habsburg fled from the Ottomans to Passau in 1683. From there he organised help from his allies.
32386.m: In 1683 the Habsburgs ruled in Vienna.

32387.q: Who founded the rule of the Safavids in Tabriz in 1501?
32387.e: Ismail I had himself crowned Shah in Tabriz in 1501. He united Persia under a native dynasty for the first time in centuries.
32387.m: Ismail I founded the Safavid Empire in 1501.

32388.q: Which branch of faith did the Safavids make the state religion of Persia?
32388.e: Ismail I made Twelver Shia the state religion. This decision still shapes Iran today and separated it religiously from the Sunni Ottomans.
32388.m: Since the Safavids, Iran has been shaped by Shia Islam.

32389.q: In which battle were the Safavids defeated by the Ottomans under Selim I in 1514?
32389.e: At Chaldiran the Ottomans defeated the Safavid cavalry with firearms and artillery. Eastern Anatolia fell to the Ottoman Empire.
32389.m: At Chaldiran in 1514 the Ottomans defeated the Safavids.

32390.q: To which city did Shah Abbas I move the Safavid capital in 1598?
32390.e: Abbas I made Isfahan a splendid royal seat with a great royal square, mosques and palaces. A Persian saying called the city “half the world”.
32390.m: Abbas I made Isfahan the capital.

32391.q: What is Isfahan still famous for today from the Safavid period?
a: Splendid mosques and the great royal square
32391.e: From 1598 Shah Abbas I had Isfahan expanded with mosques, palaces and a huge square. The city was regarded as “half the world”.
32391.m: Under the Safavids Isfahan became a splendid capital.

32392.q: Who conquered Isfahan in 1722, effectively ending Safavid rule?
32392.e: Afghan Ghilzai under Mahmud Hotaki besieged and conquered Isfahan in 1722. The Shah had to abdicate.
32392.m: In 1722 Isfahan fell to Afghan conquerors.

32393.q: Which religious divide made the wars between the Safavids and Ottomans fiercer?
32393.e: The Safavids made Shia Islam the state religion, while the Ottomans were Sunni. In the peace of 1639 a border was drawn that roughly matches today’s border between Iran and Iraq.
32393.m: Between the Safavids and Ottomans there was also the divide between Shia and Sunni.

32394.q: Who became the first shogun of the Tokugawa period in 1603?
32394.e: Tokugawa Ieyasu won out in the fighting after Hideyoshi’s death and was appointed shogun in 1603. His family ruled until 1867.
32394.m: Tokugawa Ieyasu founded the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603.

32395.q: Which city was the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns?
32395.e: The shoguns ruled from Edo, while the emperor stayed in Kyōto. In the 18th century Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world.
32395.m: The Tokugawa shoguns ruled from Edo.

32396.q: What is the policy of Japan largely closing itself off during the Tokugawa period called?
32396.e: Sakoku means roughly “closed country”. From the 1630s Japanese people were no longer allowed to leave the country, and foreign trade was strictly limited.
32396.m: With sakoku Japan largely closed itself off for more than 200 years.

32397.q: Which Europeans were allowed to trade on the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki while Japan was closed off?
32397.e: The Dutch East India Company was considered harmless because it did not try to convert people. Western knowledge reached Japan via Dejima.
32397.m: Only the Dutch were allowed to trade on Dejima.

32398.q: What were the powerful regional lords in Tokugawa Japan called?
32398.e: The daimyō ruled their own territories but had to obey the shogun. The shogun forced them to live in Edo regularly so that he could control them.
32398.m: The daimyō were the regional lords under the shogun.

32399.q: Which religion did the Tokugawa shogunate ban in the 17th century, persecuting its followers?
32399.e: The shoguns saw the Christian missionaries as a threat to their power. After an uprising of Christian peasants in 1637, the Portuguese were also expelled.

32400.q: Which American commodore forced Japan to open up with his “Black Ships” in 1853/54?
32400.e: Matthew Perry appeared in Edo Bay with warships in 1853. In 1854, in the Treaty of Kanagawa, Japan had to open ports to American ships.

32401.q: Which rule ended in Japan in 1867/68 with the Meiji Restoration?
32401.e: With the Meiji Restoration, power passed from the shogun back to the emperor. In the Boshin War of 1868/69 the troops loyal to the emperor won.
32401.m: The Meiji Restoration ended the rule of the shoguns.

32402.q: What is the Japanese title of the emperor who returned to power in the Meiji Restoration?
32402.e: The Meiji Tennō, whose personal name was Mutsuhito, reigned from 1867 to 1912. Until then the shogun had been the real ruler.
32402.m: The Japanese emperor has the title Tennō.

32403.q: What new name was the city of Edo given in 1868?
32403.e: Tōkyō means “eastern capital”. Shortly afterwards the emperor moved from Kyōto into the former residence of the shoguns.
32403.m: Edo has been called Tōkyō since 1868.

32404.q: What replaced the old domains (han) of the daimyō in Japan in 1871?
32404.e: With the abolition of the han and the creation of prefectures, a centrally controlled administration was formed. The daimyō lost their rights to rule.
32404.m: Since 1871 Japan has been divided into prefectures.

32405.q: Which rebellion of dissatisfied samurai under Saigō Takamori did the Meiji government crush in 1877?
32405.e: The samurai had lost their privileges, such as the right to carry swords. The modern conscript army defeated them in 1877.
32405.m: The Satsuma Rebellion was the last big samurai uprising.

32406.q: Why did Japan send delegations and students to the USA and Europe after 1868?
a: To learn about Western technology, government and education
32406.e: The Iwakura Mission of 1871 to 1873 studied Western states, industry and schools. Its experiences shaped Japan’s modernisation.
32406.m: Japan modernised by deliberately learning from the West.

32407.q: What goal did Japan pursue in the Meiji period with industrialisation and rearmament?
a: To catch up with the Western great powers
To shut itself off completely from other countries
32407.e: The slogan “fukoku kyōhei” means “rich country, strong army”. In this way Japan wanted to avoid being dominated by Western powers.
32407.m: The Meiji period stood for prosperity and military strength on the Western model.

32408.q: Which people founded the Qing dynasty and took Beijing in 1644?
32408.e: The Manchus from the north-east took advantage of the collapse of the Ming dynasty and conquered Beijing. They ruled China until 1912.
32408.m: The Qing dynasty was rule by the Manchus.

32409.q: Which hairstyle did Han Chinese men have to wear under the Qing dynasty as a sign of submission?
a: A pigtail with a shaved forehead
32409.e: The Manchus required their own pigtail with the front of the head shaved. Anyone who refused risked the death penalty.
32409.m: Under the Qing the pigtail was a sign of submission.

32410.q: Which Qing emperor reigned the longest, for about 61 years?
32410.e: Kangxi reigned from 1661 to 1722. He strengthened the empire, had Taiwan conquered and promoted science and culture.
32410.m: Kangxi was the longest-reigning emperor of China.

32411.q: Which British embassy did Emperor Qianlong turn away with its trade requests in 1793?
32411.e: Lord Macartney wanted to achieve freer trade and a permanent embassy. Qianlong declared that China had no need for the goods of the barbarians.
32411.m: The Macartney Mission of 1793 failed because Qianlong refused.

32412.q: To which city did the Qing government restrict sea trade with Europeans from 1757?
32412.e: Under the so-called Canton System, Europeans could only trade in Canton (Guangzhou) and only through licensed merchants, the Cohong.
32412.m: The Canton System limited trade with Europe to one city.

32413.q: Which woman largely controlled the politics of the Qing court from 1861 to 1908?
32413.e: Cixi ruled first for her son, then for her nephew. She blocked many reforms and is regarded as a defining figure of the late Qing period.
32413.m: Empress Dowager Cixi dominated the Qing court for decades.

32414.q: What is the name of the reform programme begun by Emperor Guangxu in 1898 and quickly stopped?
32414.e: Guangxu wanted to modernise the administration, education and military on the Japanese model. After about a hundred days, Cixi had him placed under house arrest.
32414.m: The Hundred Days’ Reform of 1898 failed because of resistance at court.

32415.q: Which problem did British traders want to solve by selling opium to China?
a: The outflow of silver from buying tea
The high freight costs to India
The decline of the spice trade
32415.e: Britain bought a lot of Chinese tea, but China hardly wanted any British goods. With Indian opium the British reversed the flow of silver.
32415.m: Opium was meant to balance Britain’s trade deficit with China.

32416.q: Which imperial commissioner had over 1,000 tonnes of British opium destroyed in Humen in 1839?
32416.e: Lin Zexu confiscated the opium and had it broken down with lime and salt. The action was one of the triggers of the war.
32416.m: By destroying the opium, Lin Zexu became a national hero.

32417.q: Which territory did China give up to Great Britain in the Treaty of Nanking in 1842?
32417.e: The island of Hong Kong became a British colony. Only in 1997 did Hong Kong return to China.
32417.m: From the Treaty of Nanking onwards, Hong Kong was British.

32418.q: How many ports did China have to open to British trade in 1842?
32418.e: Canton, Amoy (Xiamen), Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai were opened. British people were allowed to settle there.
32418.m: In 1842 China opened five treaty ports.

32419.q: Which country fought alongside Great Britain in the Second Opium War of 1856 to 1860?
32419.e: The incident involving the ship “Arrow” served as the British pretext, while France used the murder of a missionary as its excuse. Together they forced China to make further concessions.
32419.m: In the Second Opium War Great Britain and France fought together.

32420.q: Which area opposite Hong Kong did China have to give up to Great Britain in the Convention of Peking in 1860?
32420.e: The Convention of Peking ended the Second Opium War. The southern tip of the Kowloon peninsula became part of the colony of Hong Kong.
32420.m: In 1860 Kowloon became part of the colony of Hong Kong.

32421.q: What are the treaties forced on China by Western powers after the Opium Wars called in China?
32421.e: The treaties gave the Western powers territory, trading rights and extraterritoriality, with nothing in return for China. They shaped the “century of humiliation”.
32421.m: The unequal treaties stand for China’s humiliation in the 19th century.

32422.q: Who led the Taiping Rebellion and believed he was the younger brother of Jesus?
32422.e: After failing the civil service exams, Hong Xiuquan had visions, which he interpreted in a Christian way. This gave rise to a religious and political mass movement.
32422.m: Hong Xiuquan was the leader of the Taiping.

32423.q: In which period did the Taiping Rebellion take place?
32423.e: The rebellion began in 1850 in the province of Guangxi. It ended in 1864 with the fall of the Taiping capital.
32423.m: The Taiping Rebellion lasted from 1850 to 1864.

32424.q: Which city did the Taiping make their capital in 1853?
32424.e: The Taiping called Nanking the “Heavenly Capital” (Tianjing). They ruled from there for eleven years.
32424.m: Nanking was the capital of the Taiping.

32425.q: What does the name “Taiping Tianguo” mean?
a: Land of the Three Principles of the People
32425.e: The Taiping wanted to create a kingdom based on their religious ideas, with equality and common ownership of land. The name expressed this hope.
32425.m: Taiping Tianguo means “Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace”.

32426.q: According to common estimates, how many people died in the Taiping Rebellion?
32426.e: Fighting, massacres, hunger and epidemics claimed huge numbers of victims. The Taiping Rebellion is regarded as one of the deadliest conflicts of the 19th century.
32426.m: The Taiping Rebellion cost tens of millions of people their lives.

32427.q: Which dynasty ruled China at the time of the Taiping Rebellion?
32427.e: The Qing ruled from 1644 to 1912. The Taiping Rebellion greatly weakened them, and they could only crush it with great difficulty.
32427.m: The Taiping Rebellion was directed against the Qing dynasty.

32428.q: Why did Western powers eventually support the Qing government against the Taiping?
a: They wanted to secure their trading advantages in China
They wanted to end the opium trade
They wanted to ban Christianity in China
They were allied with China against Japan
32428.e: In the Opium Wars the Western powers had forced trading rights. A weakened but stable Qing government was more useful for their business than the Taiping.
32428.m: Western powers helped the Qing to protect their trading interests.

32429.q: In which year did the Boxer Rebellion reach its climax with the siege of the legations in Beijing?
32429.e: The movement spread through northern China from 1899. In summer 1900 Boxers and government troops besieged the Legation Quarter.
32429.m: The Boxer Rebellion reached its climax in 1900.

32430.q: Why did foreigners call the rebels in China around 1900 “Boxers”?
a: Because of their martial arts exercises
Because their leader was a famous boxer
Because they destroyed boxes of opium
Because they wore gloves as a sign of recognition
32430.e: The movement called itself Yihetuan, Militia United in Righteousness. Its members practised martial arts that resembled boxing and believed this made them invulnerable.
32430.m: The Boxers got their name because of their martial arts exercises.

32431.q: Roughly how long did the siege of the Legation Quarter in Beijing last in 1900?
32431.e: The siege began in June and ended on 14 August 1900 when the international troops arrived. So it lasted about 55 days.
32431.m: In 1900 the Legation Quarter was besieged for about 55 days.

32432.q: What was the alliance called that sent troops to China against the Boxers in 1900?
32432.e: Great Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, the USA, Italy and Austria-Hungary took part. They occupied Beijing in August 1900.
32432.m: The Eight-Nation Alliance crushed the Boxer Rebellion.

32433.q: What consequence did the Boxer Protocol of 1901 have for China?
a: China had to pay huge compensation to the foreign powers
China was allowed to expel all foreigners
32433.e: China had to pay 450 million taels of silver, about one tael per inhabitant, over decades and with interest. This seriously weakened the Qing dynasty.
32433.m: The Boxer Protocol obliged China to pay huge compensation.

32434.q: Which event in June 1900 made the Boxer Rebellion dramatically worse?
a: The murder of the German envoy in Beijing
The abdication of the Chinese emperor
The burning of the Forbidden City
The landing of Japanese troops in Shanghai
32434.e: The German envoy Clemens von Ketteler was shot by a soldier on his way to the Chinese foreign office. After that the situation escalated.
32434.m: The murder of the envoy von Ketteler escalated the conflict.

32435.q: Which notorious speech did Emperor Wilhelm II give in 1900 when sending German troops off to China?
32435.e: In Bremerhaven Wilhelm II called for no mercy to be shown, referring to the Huns. Overall command of the international troops was taken over by the German field marshal Alfred von Waldersee.
32435.m: With the Hun speech in 1900, Wilhelm II called for merciless harshness in China.

32436.q: What was the most important result of the Xinhai Revolution of 1911?
a: The end of imperial rule in China
The founding of the People’s Republic of China
32436.e: The revolution began in October 1911 with an uprising in Wuchang. It overthrew the Qing dynasty, and in 1912 the Republic of China was proclaimed.
32436.m: The Xinhai Revolution ended the imperial era in China.

32437.q: Who became provisional President of the Republic of China in Nanking on 1 January 1912?
32437.e: Sun Yat-sen had campaigned for years in exile for the overthrow of the monarchy. In China and Taiwan he is regarded as the “Father of the Nation”.
32437.m: Sun Yat-sen was the first provisional President of the Republic of China.

32438.q: Which three goals make up Sun Yat-sen’s “Three Principles of the People”?
32438.e: Sun Yat-sen demanded national independence, government by the people and social justice. The principles became the basis of the Kuomintang.
32438.m: Sun Yat-sen’s Three Principles of the People are nationalism, democracy and people’s welfare.

32439.q: Which emperor abdicated in February 1912 as China’s last ruler?
32439.e: Puyi was only six years old when the abdication was announced in February 1912. This ended more than 2,000 years of imperial rule.
32439.m: Puyi was the last emperor of China.

32440.q: Which general took over the presidency of the young republic from Sun Yat-sen in 1912?
32440.e: Yuan Shikai controlled the strongest army in the north and negotiated the emperor’s abdication. Later he tried unsuccessfully to make himself emperor.
32440.m: Yuan Shikai replaced Sun Yat-sen as President.

32441.q: Which party emerged from the revolutionary movement around Sun Yat-sen in 1912?
32441.e: The Kuomintang (Guomindang), the Nationalist Party, was founded in 1912. Later, under Chiang Kai-shek, it governed large parts of China.

32442.q: From where did Sun Yat-sen mainly prepare the overthrow of Chinese imperial rule?
a: From the imperial palace in Beijing
As a general in the imperial army
32442.e: Sun Yat-sen lived in exile for many years, including in Japan. In 1905 he founded the revolutionary Tongmenghui in Tokyo.
32442.m: Sun Yat-sen organised the revolution from exile for a long time.

32443.q: In which year did the Long March of the Chinese communists begin?
32443.e: In October 1934 the troops of the Red Army broke through the Kuomintang’s encirclement. The march lasted about a year.

32445.q: What did the Long March mean for Mao Zedong?
a: He rose to become the leading figure of the communists
He was taken prisoner by the Kuomintang
He then fled into exile in the Soviet Union
32445.e: At the Zunyi Conference in January 1935 the previous leadership was criticised. Mao rose into the inner leadership and later became party leader.
32445.m: On the Long March Mao became China’s leading communist.

32446.q: How does the Chinese Communist Party still portray the Long March today?
a: As a heroic epic and founding myth
As an embarrassing defeat that is kept quiet
As a success of the Kuomintang
32446.e: Episodes such as the capture of the Luding Bridge became heroic legends. How dramatic the fighting really was is disputed among historians.
32446.m: The Long March is a myth of the Chinese communists.

32447.q: In which province did the Long March arrive in 1935, where the communists then set up their centre in Yan’an?
32447.e: After about 12,000 kilometres the main column reached northern Shaanxi. Yan’an was the party’s headquarters until 1947.
32447.m: The Long March ended in Shaanxi.

32448.q: What kind of family did Mao Zedong, born in Shaoshan in 1893, come from?
a: A family of imperial court officials
32448.e: Mao was born into a peasant family in the village of Shaoshan in Hunan province. The village later became a place of pilgrimage for the personality cult.
32448.m: Mao Zedong came from a peasant family in Hunan.

32449.q: What was the name of Mao’s campaign from 1958 that was meant to force rapid industrialisation through people’s communes and mass steel production?
32449.e: Unrealistic targets, bad harvests and false reports of success led to a devastating famine. Millions of people died.
32449.m: The Great Leap Forward ended in a catastrophic famine.

32450.q: Which campaign of 1956/57 at first invited criticism of the party and ended with the persecution of the critics?
32450.e: Mao called for letting “a hundred flowers bloom”. When the criticism turned out to be fierce, hundreds of thousands were punished in the following campaign against rightists.
32450.m: The Hundred Flowers Campaign was followed by the persecution of the critics.

32451.q: In which year did Mao Zedong proclaim the Cultural Revolution?
32451.e: With the Cultural Revolution Mao wanted to regain his power and fight supposedly bourgeois elements. It plunged China into a decade of chaos.

32452.q: What were the young activists called who attacked teachers and officials during the Cultural Revolution?
32452.e: Mainly school pupils and students joined the Red Guards. They humiliated, ill-treated and killed many people.
32452.m: The Red Guards were the shock troops of the Cultural Revolution.

32453.q: What was the group of radical leaders around Mao’s wife Jiang Qing, arrested in October 1976, called?
32453.e: Shortly after Mao’s death the four politicians were arrested and later convicted. Their fall marked the end of the Cultural Revolution.
32453.m: The Cultural Revolution ended with the arrest of the Gang of Four.

32454.q: What happened during the Cultural Revolution to many high-ranking officials such as head of state Liu Shaoqi?
a: They were overthrown as traitors and persecuted
They were sent abroad as ambassadors
They retired voluntarily with a large pension
32454.e: Liu Shaoqi was overthrown as a “capitalist roader”, publicly humiliated and died in custody in 1969 without medical care.
32454.m: Liu Shaoqi was the most prominent victim of the Cultural Revolution.

32455.q: Which book of quotations from Mao Zedong did the activists of the Cultural Revolution always carry with them?
32455.e: The “Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung” were printed in huge numbers. The book was compulsory reading and a symbol of the personality cult.
32455.m: The Little Red Book was the symbol of the Mao cult.

32456.q: Where were millions of young city people sent during the Cultural Revolution?
32456.e: Under the motto “Up to the mountains and down to the villages” they were supposed to learn from the peasants. Many lost their chance of an education as a result.
32456.m: Millions of young people had to go to the countryside in the Cultural Revolution.

32457.q: What were the Red Guards supposed to destroy in the fight against the “Four Olds”?
a: Old ideas, culture, customs and habits
Old emperors, officials, merchants and monks
Old temples, palaces, walls and tombs
Old parties, newspapers, schools and courts
32457.e: In the fight against the “Four Olds”, temples, works of art, books and cultural treasures were destroyed in great numbers.
32457.m: The campaign against the Four Olds destroyed countless cultural treasures.

32458.q: From which year did Deng Xiaoping launch China’s policy of reform and opening up?
32458.e: At the 3rd Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in December 1978, Deng pushed through his reform course. China gradually opened up to the market and to other countries.
32458.m: China’s policy of reform and opening up began in 1978.

32459.q: Which city became one of China’s first special economic zones in 1980?
32459.e: Shenzhen borders on Hong Kong and was meant to attract foreign capital. A small town turned into a metropolis of millions.
32459.m: Shenzhen is the showcase example of a special economic zone.

32460.q: Which saying is linked to Deng Xiaoping’s pragmatic economic policy?
a: It doesn’t matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice
He who does not work shall not eat
Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun
32460.e: The saying means that what counts is not ideology but economic success. It comes from a speech Deng gave in 1962.
32460.m: For Deng, success counted more than ideology.

32461.q: Which areas did the “Four Modernisations” under Deng Xiaoping cover?
a: Agriculture, industry, defence, science and technology
32461.e: The Four Modernisations had already been formulated by Zhou Enlai. From 1978 Deng made them the central programme.
32461.m: The Four Modernisations were meant to make China stronger economically and technically.

32462.q: Under which principle was the return of Hong Kong to China in 1997 arranged?
32462.e: The principle developed by Deng guaranteed Hong Kong its own economic and legal system for 50 years. It was agreed with Great Britain in 1984.
32462.m: Hong Kong returned to China under the principle “one country, two systems”.

32463.q: What happened in Tiananmen Square in Beijing on 4 June 1989?
a: The army violently crushed the democracy movement
The People’s Republic of China was proclaimed
32463.e: For weeks, mainly students had demonstrated for reforms and freedom of speech. The leadership around Deng sent in the military, and many people were killed.
32463.m: On 4 June 1989 the protest movement in Beijing was ended in bloodshed.

32464.q: With which journey did Deng Xiaoping revive the economic reforms in 1992?
32464.e: After 1989 the reforms had stalled. On his Southern Tour through Shenzhen and other cities, Deng called for the market opening to be speeded up.
32464.m: Deng’s Southern Tour of 1992 gave the reforms new momentum.

32465.q: In which year did the great slave uprising in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, which led to the Haitian Revolution, begin?
32465.e: In August 1791 the enslaved people in the north of Saint-Domingue rose up. The uprising grew into a revolution lasting more than a decade.
32465.m: The Haitian Revolution began in 1791 with a great slave uprising.

32466.q: Which night-time gathering in August 1791 is seen as the start of the slave uprising in Saint-Domingue?
32466.e: At Bois-Caïman enslaved people met for a religious ceremony and decided to rise up. A few days later the plantations in the north of the colony were burning.
32466.m: The Bois-Caïman ceremony is seen as the starting signal of the Haitian Revolution.

32467.q: What did France demand from Haiti in 1825 in return for recognising its independence?
a: The return of all ports to France
An oath of loyalty to the French king
32467.e: Under threat of a naval blockade, Haiti had to promise compensation for the former plantation owners in 1825. The sum was later reduced, but it burdened the country for decades.
32467.m: Haiti had to pay France huge compensation for its recognition.

32468.q: Who proclaimed Haiti’s independence on 1 January 1804?
32468.e: After the victory over the French troops, General Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared independence on 1 January 1804. He gave the country the indigenous name Haiti.
32468.m: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti’s independence in 1804.

32469.q: What contributed most to the failure of Napoleon’s great expedition to Saint-Domingue in 1802?
a: An attack on Paris by the British fleet
An earthquake that destroyed the ports
A mutiny of the whole army
32469.e: General Charles Leclerc landed in 1802 with several tens of thousands of soldiers. Fighting and above all yellow fever wiped out the expedition, and Leclerc himself died in 1802.
32469.m: Yellow fever destroyed Napoleon’s army in Saint-Domingue in 1802.

32470.q: Which structure did Henri Christophe, king in the north of Haiti from 1811, have built to protect against a return of the French?
a: A mighty fortress on a mountain
32470.e: After Dessalines was murdered, Haiti split into a north and a south. Henri Christophe ruled the north as King Henri I and had the Citadelle Laferrière built on a mountain top; today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32470.m: Henri Christophe built the Citadelle Laferrière in the north of Haiti.

32471.q: In which year did the French National Convention abolish slavery in all colonies, partly under pressure from the uprising in Saint-Domingue?
32471.e: On 4 February 1794 the National Convention decided to abolish slavery. Napoleon reintroduced it in several colonies in 1802; France only abolished it for good in 1848.
32471.m: France abolished slavery for the first time in 1794.

32472.q: What title of honour does Simón Bolívar still have in South America today?
32472.e: Bolívar led the struggles for independence against Spain in several countries. That is why he is honoured as “El Libertador”, the Liberator.
32472.m: Simón Bolívar is called “the Liberator” in South America.

32473.q: Which South American country is named after Simón Bolívar?
32473.e: The former Upper Peru became independent in 1825 and called itself Bolivia in Bolívar’s honour. Bolívar was also its first President.
32473.m: Bolivia bears the name of Simón Bolívar.

32474.q: Which large state was created under Bolívar in 1819 and broke up into several countries in 1830?
32474.e: Gran Colombia covered roughly today’s Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Panama. After disputes it broke up in 1830.
32474.m: Bolívar’s Gran Colombia only lasted until 1830.

32475.q: What political goal did Bolívar pursue for the liberated states of Spanish America?
a: A close union of the young republics
A monarchy under the Spanish king
As many small independent states as possible
32475.e: Bolívar wanted to unite the new republics in a strong alliance. In 1826 he invited them to a congress in Panama for this purpose, but it achieved little.
32475.m: Bolívar dreamt of a united Spanish America.

32476.q: In which present-day capital city was Simón Bolívar born in 1783?
32476.e: Bolívar came from a wealthy Creole family in Caracas, today the capital of Venezuela.
32476.m: Simón Bolívar was born in Caracas.

32477.q: What tremendous feat did Bolívar’s army achieve in 1819 on the way to Bogotá?
32477.e: Bolívar led his troops over the high, cold passes of the Andes. He then took the Spanish by surprise and liberated New Granada.
32477.m: Bolívar’s march across the Andes in 1819 is regarded as a military masterpiece.

32478.q: Which other great liberator fought mainly in the south of South America, for example in Argentina and Chile?
32478.e: José de San Martín liberated Argentina, Chile and parts of Peru. Bolívar fought in the north, and the two liberators met in 1822.
32478.m: Besides Bolívar, San Martín was the most important liberator of South America.

32479.q: Against which president, who had ruled Mexico in an authoritarian way for decades, was the revolution from 1910 directed?
32479.e: Apart from a short break, Porfirio Díaz had ruled since 1876. His time brought modernisation, but also great social inequality and land concentrated in few hands.
32479.m: The Mexican Revolution was directed against Porfirio Díaz.

32480.q: Who called for an armed uprising against the government with the Plan of San Luis Potosí in 1910?
32480.e: After a rigged election, Francisco Madero called for an uprising on 20 November 1910. He became President in 1911.
32480.m: Francisco Madero started the revolution in 1910.

32481.q: Which revolutionary leader from the state of Morelos demanded in the Plan of Ayala that land be returned to the peasants?
32481.e: Emiliano Zapata published the Plan of Ayala in 1911. His motto “Tierra y Libertad” (Land and Liberty) stands for the demand for land reform.
32481.m: Emiliano Zapata fought for land and freedom for the peasants.

32482.q: Which revolutionary leader raided the US border town of Columbus in New Mexico in 1916, triggering a US punitive expedition?
32482.e: Pancho Villa, leader of the Division of the North from Chihuahua, attacked Columbus in March 1916. The USA then sent General Pershing to Mexico, but he could not catch Villa.
32482.m: In 1916 Pancho Villa raided a town in the USA.

32483.q: In which year was the Mexican constitution that still applies today adopted?
32483.e: The Constitution of Querétaro was proclaimed on 5 February 1917 and came into force on 1 May 1917. It contained progressive rules on land reform, labour law and natural resources.
32483.m: Mexico’s constitution, still in force, dates from 1917.

32484.q: Which general overthrew President Madero in 1913, who was murdered shortly afterwards?
32484.e: During the “Ten Tragic Days” in February 1913, Victoriano Huerta staged a coup. Madero was shot a few days later, after which new resistance against Huerta formed.
32484.m: Victoriano Huerta overthrew President Madero in 1913.

32485.q: Which party that emerged from the revolution governed Mexico without a break, under its current name, until the year 2000?
32485.e: The party was founded in 1929 as the PNR and has been called the Partido Revolucionario Institucional since 1946. Only in 2000 did a candidate from another party, Vicente Fox, win the presidency.

32486.q: Which barracks in Santiago de Cuba did Fidel Castro attack without success on 26 July 1953?
32486.e: The attack on the Moncada Barracks failed, and Castro was arrested. He later named his “26th of July Movement” after the date.
32486.m: Castro’s revolution began in 1953 with the attack on the Moncada Barracks.

32487.q: Which dictator fled Cuba on New Year’s Eve 1958/59?
32487.e: Fulgencio Batista had come to power in a coup in 1952. After the rebels’ successes, he left Cuba on 1 January 1959.
32487.m: Batista fled from the revolutionaries at the beginning of 1959.

32488.q: On which yacht did Fidel Castro and just over 80 fighters land in Cuba from Mexico in December 1956?
32488.e: The overloaded yacht “Granma” reached Cuba at the beginning of December 1956. After the landing, only a few fighters survived the first battles.
32488.m: In 1956 the revolutionaries came to Cuba on the yacht “Granma”.

32489.q: Which country did the revolutionary Ernesto “Che” Guevara come from?
32489.e: Che Guevara was born in Rosario in Argentina in 1928 and met Castro in Mexico. He was killed in Bolivia in 1967.

32490.q: Which country represented US interests in Cuba as protecting power after diplomatic relations were broken off in 1961?
32490.e: Switzerland took over the protecting power mandate for the USA in Cuba in 1961. It ended in 2015, when the two states reopened embassies.
32490.m: From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland was the protecting power of the USA in Cuba.

32491.q: To whom did Fidel Castro officially hand over the office of President in 2008?
32491.e: Fidel Castro temporarily handed over his duties because of illness in 2006, and in 2008 his brother Raúl officially became head of state. Fidel Castro died in 2016.
32491.m: In 2008 Fidel Castro handed power to his brother Raúl.

32492.q: In which mountain range in eastern Cuba did the rebels wage their guerrilla war from 1956?
32492.e: The hard-to-reach Sierra Maestra served as a retreat for the rebels. From there they spread their struggle to the whole island in 1958.
32492.m: The rebels fought from the Sierra Maestra.

32493.q: On which day did the Chilean military stage a coup against the government?
32493.e: On 11 September 1973 the army, navy, air force and police took power. This ended Chile’s long democratic tradition for almost 17 years.
32493.m: The coup in Chile took place on 11 September 1973.

32494.q: Which left-wing alliance of parties did Salvador Allende, elected President in 1970, lead?
32494.e: Allende won in 1970 as the candidate of Unidad Popular, an alliance of socialists, communists and other left-wingers. He wanted to follow a democratic path to socialism.
32494.m: Allende governed with the Unidad Popular alliance.

32495.q: Which presidential palace in Santiago was bombed by fighter planes during the coup?
32495.e: The air force attacked the Palacio de La Moneda, where Allende was. Allende died in the palace on the same day.
32495.m: The La Moneda palace was bombed during the coup of 1973.

32496.q: Until which year did General Augusto Pinochet remain head of state of Chile?
32496.e: Pinochet lost a referendum on extending his rule in 1988. In March 1990 he handed over the presidency to the elected Patricio Aylwin, but remained commander-in-chief of the army until 1998.

32497.q: Which well-known Chilean singer and songwriter was murdered in a stadium in Santiago after the coup?
32497.e: Víctor Jara was held with thousands of others in the Estadio Chile, tortured and shot. The stadium now bears his name.
32497.m: The singer Víctor Jara was murdered after the coup.

32498.q: Which of Chile’s most important export raw materials did the Allende government fully nationalise in 1971?
32498.e: In July 1971 Congress unanimously decided to nationalise the large copper mines, most of which belonged to US companies. This increased tensions with the USA.
32498.m: In 1971 Allende nationalised Chilean copper mining.

32499.q: In which city was Augusto Pinochet arrested in 1998 on a Spanish arrest warrant?
32499.e: The Spanish judge Baltasar Garzón issued an arrest warrant for human rights crimes. Pinochet was under house arrest in London and was allowed to return to Chile in 2000 for health reasons.
32499.m: Pinochet was arrested in London in 1998.

32500.q: Roughly how long did the Berlin Congo Conference last?
32500.e: The conference met from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885 in the Reich Chancellery in Berlin. It ended with the General Act of the Congo.
32500.m: The Congo Conference lasted from November 1884 to February 1885.

32501.q: Which non-European state, besides the Ottoman Empire, took part in the Congo Conference?
32501.e: The USA was represented by a delegation and recognised Leopold’s claims in the Congo early on. However, it did not ratify the General Act itself.
32501.m: The USA also took part in the Congo Conference.

32502.q: Which humanitarian goal did the powers commit themselves to in the General Act of the Congo?
32502.e: The signatories promised to fight the slave trade and promote the well-being of the population. In practice this goal was often used to justify colonial rule.
32502.m: The General Act of the Congo promised to fight the slave trade.

32503.q: Which trade rule did the General Act of the Congo set for the whole Congo Basin?
a: A ban on all trade with Europe
32503.e: In the Congo Basin, merchants from all signatory states could trade without customs duties or special rights. Leopold II later undermined this rule with state monopolies.
32503.m: After 1885 free trade was supposed to apply in the Congo Basin.

32504.q: Which country claimed the mouth of the Congo on the basis of old rights, which helped lead to the calling of the Congo Conference?
32504.e: Portugal referred to its voyages since the 15th century. A British-Portuguese treaty of 1884 on the mouth of the Congo met with resistance from other powers.
32504.m: Portugal’s claims to the mouth of the Congo helped trigger the Congo Conference.

32505.q: What is the phase of very rapid division of Africa among European powers, further sped up by the Congo Conference, called?
32505.e: In the “Scramble for Africa”, almost the whole continent was colonised by about 1914. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
32505.m: The Scramble for Africa led to the almost complete colonisation of the continent.

32506.q: Which statement about the Congo Conference is correct according to current research?
a: It set rules for acquiring territory but drew hardly any actual borders.
It divided the whole of Africa among the powers with fixed borders.
It banned the colonial powers from any further conquest.
It gave African kingdoms a say.
32506.e: Above all, the conference created rules of the game for the colonial powers. Most borders were only fixed later in bilateral treaties.
32506.m: The Congo Conference regulated colonisation but drew hardly any borders.

32507.q: What was the name of the force with which the regime in the Congo Free State enforced forced labour and levies?
32507.e: The Force Publique consisted of African soldiers under European officers. It was responsible for many acts of violence against the population.
32507.m: The Force Publique enforced forced labour in the Congo Free State with violence.

32508.q: In which year did Leopold II have to hand over the Congo Free State to the Belgian state?
32508.e: After international protests, Belgium took over the territory in 1908 as the colony of the Belgian Congo. The country only became independent in 1960.
32508.m: From 1908 the Congo Free State was called the Belgian Congo.

32510.q: Which cruel practice of the troops in the Congo Free State became an international symbol of the crimes?
32510.e: Colonial soldiers had to account for the ammunition they used and often cut off hands as proof, even from living people. Photos of this shocked the public in Europe.
32510.m: Severed hands became the symbol of the Congo atrocities.

32512.q: What did the international protest movement against the atrocities in the Congo Free State achieve?
a: Leopold II had to give the Congo to Belgium in 1908
Leopold II was convicted in court
The Congo came under British rule
32512.e: Journalists such as Edmund Dene Morel and the consul Roger Casement made the crimes known. Under this pressure, Leopold II had to hand over his private colony to the Belgian state in 1908.
32512.m: International protest ended Leopold’s private colony in 1908.

32513.q: Which story by Joseph Conrad, published in 1899, is set on the Congo and draws on his experiences there?
32513.e: In 1890 Joseph Conrad worked as captain of a river steamer on the Congo. In “Heart of Darkness” he describes the violence and greed of the colonial system.
32513.m: Joseph Conrad’s “Heart of Darkness” is set on the Congo.

32514.q: In which German colony did the genocide of the Herero and Nama take place?
32514.e: German South West Africa largely corresponds to today’s Namibia. The colony existed from 1884 to 1915.
32514.m: The genocide of the Herero and Nama happened in what is now Namibia.

32515.q: In which year did the Herero uprising against German colonial rule begin?
32515.e: In January 1904 the Herero rose up against land theft, the loss of their cattle and their lack of rights. The German conduct of the war then turned into genocide.

32516.q: Which paramount chief led the Herero uprising in 1904?
32516.e: Samuel Maharero called the Herero to rise up in January 1904. After the defeat, he fled with part of his people to British Bechuanaland.
32516.m: Samuel Maharero led the Herero uprising in 1904.

32517.q: How did thousands of Herero die after the Battle of Waterberg in 1904?
a: They died of thirst in the desert because the Germans sealed off the waterholes
They died in a volcanic eruption
They drowned while fleeing across the sea
They died in a flu epidemic from Europe
32517.e: The German troops drove the Herero into the arid Omaheke and sealed off the waterholes. Many people, including women and children, died of thirst.
32517.m: In 1904 many Herero died of thirst in the Omaheke.

32518.q: What did the Charité in Berlin return to Namibia in 2011?
32518.e: Skulls of victims had been taken to Germany, where they were misused for racist research. In 2011, 20 skulls were formally handed over to a Namibian delegation.
32518.m: In 2011 the Charité returned skulls of Herero and Nama to Namibia.

32519.q: What was on Shark Island near Lüderitz in German South West Africa from 1905?
a: A concentration camp for captured Nama and Herero
32519.e: On Shark Island there was cold, hunger and forced labour. A large proportion of the Nama and Herero held there died.
32519.m: The camp on Shark Island was a place of mass death.

32520.q: In which year did the German federal government officially call the crimes genocide in an agreement with Namibia?
32520.e: In May 2021 the federal government stated that, from today’s perspective, the acts were genocide, and promised support of 1.1 billion euros. Many representatives of the Herero and Nama criticised the agreement as inadequate.
32520.m: In 2021 Germany officially recognised the genocide of the Herero and Nama.

32521.q: In which year did the Battle of Adwa take place?
32521.e: The battle was fought on 1 March 1896 in northern Ethiopia. It was one of the heaviest defeats of a colonial army in Africa.
32521.m: The Battle of Adwa took place in 1896.

32522.q: Which Ethiopian emperor led his army to victory at the Battle of Adwa?
32522.e: Emperor Menelik II had gathered a large, well-armed army from all parts of the country. Its victory strengthened his rule and the unity of the empire.
32522.m: Emperor Menelik II won at Adwa in 1896.

32523.q: In which year did Italy under Mussolini attack Ethiopia again, partly to avenge the defeat at Adwa?
32523.e: In October 1935 the Abyssinian War began, in which Italy also used poison gas. Ethiopia was occupied in 1936 but liberated with British help in 1941.
32523.m: Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935 to wipe out the disgrace of Adwa.

32524.q: Over which treaty of 1889 did the dispute that led to war arise, because the Amharic and Italian versions said different things?
32524.e: According to the Italian version of Article 17, Ethiopia had to conduct its foreign policy through Italy, which would have meant a protectorate. In the Amharic version this was only an option, which is why Menelik cancelled the treaty.
32524.m: The dispute over the Treaty of Wuchale led to the war over Ethiopia.

32525.q: What consequence did the Ethiopian victory at Adwa have in the peace settlement of 1896?
a: Ethiopia had to give Eritrea to Great Britain.
Italy and Ethiopia formed a joint state.
32525.e: In the Peace of Addis Ababa in October 1896, Italy recognised Ethiopia’s full independence. Adwa became a symbol of resistance to colonialism throughout Africa.
32525.m: After Adwa, Italy had to recognise Ethiopia’s independence.

32526.q: Which other African country, besides Ethiopia, remained independent during the colonial period around 1900?
32526.e: Around 1900 almost all of Africa was occupied by European powers. Only Ethiopia, which had defended itself at Adwa, and Liberia remained independent.
32526.m: Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent around 1900.

32527.q: Which Swiss engineer from Thurgau was a close adviser to Emperor Menelik II and later an Ethiopian minister of state?
32527.e: Alfred Ilg came to Ethiopia in 1879 and advised Menelik II on technology and foreign policy. Among other things, he pushed ahead the building of the railway from Djibouti to Addis Ababa.
32527.m: Alfred Ilg from Thurgau was an adviser to Emperor Menelik II.

32528.q: In which city was Mustafa Kemal Atatürk born in 1881?
32528.e: Thessaloniki, then Salonica, belonged to the Ottoman Empire until 1912. Today the city is in Greece.
32528.m: Atatürk was born in Thessaloniki in 1881.

32529.q: In which battle of the First World War did Mustafa Kemal become known as a successful officer?
32529.e: In 1915, as a divisional commander on the Gallipoli peninsula, Mustafa Kemal fought off British and Australian landing troops. The success made him famous throughout the empire.
32529.m: Mustafa Kemal became known in 1915 at the Battle of Gallipoli.

32530.q: On which date was the Republic of Turkey proclaimed?
32530.e: The Grand National Assembly proclaimed the republic on 29 October 1923 and elected Mustafa Kemal as the first President. The day is now a Turkish national holiday.
32530.m: The Republic of Turkey was founded on 29 October 1923.

32531.q: In which Swiss city was the peace treaty signed in 1923 that internationally recognised the borders of the new Turkey?
32531.e: The Treaty of Lausanne replaced the harsh Treaty of Sèvres of 1920. It largely fixed Turkey’s borders and set out a population exchange with Greece.
32531.m: The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 established the borders of modern Turkey.

32532.q: Which city did Mustafa Kemal make the new capital of Turkey in 1923?
32532.e: Ankara had been the centre of the national liberation struggle and lay safely inland. Istanbul thus lost its role as capital.
32532.m: Atatürk made Ankara the capital in 1923.

32533.q: Which code of law served almost word for word as the model for the new Turkish Civil Code in 1926?
32533.e: In 1926 Turkey largely adopted the Swiss Civil Code. Among other things, this introduced monogamy and civil marriage.
32533.m: Turkish civil law is based on the Swiss Civil Code.

32534.q: In which year did Turkey replace the Arabic script with a Latin alphabet?
32534.e: The script reform came into force in November 1928. It was meant to make learning to read and write easier and to orient Turkey towards Europe.
32534.m: Turkey introduced the Latin script in 1928.

32535.q: Which day is the day of remembrance for the Armenian genocide, because hundreds of Armenian intellectuals were arrested in Constantinople on that day?
32535.e: On 24 April 1915 the Ottoman government had Armenian politicians, clergy and scholars arrested in Constantinople. Most of them were murdered.
32535.m: The Armenian genocide is remembered on 24 April.

32536.q: Which political movement governed the Ottoman Empire at the time of the Armenian genocide?
32536.e: The Young Turks, officially the Committee of Union and Progress, had ruled as a dictatorship since 1913. Their leadership planned and organised the deportations.
32536.m: The Young Turks organised the Armenian genocide.

32537.q: Which Ottoman interior minister is regarded as chiefly responsible for the deportations of the Armenians?
32537.e: As interior minister, Talat Pasha ordered the deportations. He was shot in Berlin in 1921 by an Armenian survivor.
32537.m: Talat Pasha was chiefly responsible for the Armenian genocide.

32538.q: Where did many death marches of the deported Armenians lead from 1915?
32538.e: The deportations led through Anatolia into the Syrian desert, for example to the area around Deir ez-Zor. Many died there of hunger, thirst and in massacres.
32538.m: The Armenian death marches led into the Syrian desert.

32539.q: Which lawyer coined the term “genocide” in 1944, partly influenced by the fate of the Armenians?
32539.e: Raphael Lemkin formed the word from the Greek “genos” and the Latin “caedere”. He then campaigned for the UN Genocide Convention of 1948.
32539.m: Raphael Lemkin created the term genocide.

32540.q: Which chamber of the Swiss parliament recognised the Armenian genocide in 2003?
32540.e: The National Council adopted a corresponding postulate in December 2003. Before that, the cantons of Vaud and Geneva had already recognised the genocide.
32540.m: The National Council recognised the Armenian genocide in 2003.

32541.q: Which novel by Franz Werfel from 1933 describes the resistance of Armenian villages to deportation?
a: The Forty Days of Musa Dagh
All Quiet on the Western Front
32541.e: Werfel tells how Armenians escaped to the mountain Musa Dagh in 1915 and defended themselves for weeks. The novel made the genocide known to a wide audience.
32541.m: Franz Werfel wrote about Musa Dagh.

32542.q: In which year was the Sykes-Picot Agreement concluded?
32542.e: The secret agreement was made in May 1916, in the middle of the First World War. It planned the division of the Ottoman Middle East after the war.

32543.q: Which two powers divided the Middle East into zones of influence in the Sykes-Picot Agreement?
32543.e: The agreement is named after the Briton Mark Sykes and the Frenchman François Georges-Picot. Russia agreed to the division.
32543.m: In 1916 Great Britain and France divided up the Middle East.

32544.q: Who made the secret Sykes-Picot Agreement public at the end of 1917?
32544.e: After the October Revolution, the Bolsheviks published secret treaties of the Tsarist empire. That is how the Arabs also learnt of the plans to divide the region.
32544.m: The Bolsheviks revealed the Sykes-Picot Agreement in 1917.

32545.q: Which present-day areas fell into the French zone of influence under the Sykes-Picot Agreement?
32545.e: France received the coast of Syria and Lebanon as well as influence in the interior. After the war it became the mandate power there.
32545.m: After Sykes-Picot, Syria and Lebanon came under French influence.

32546.q: What did the Sykes-Picot Agreement plan for a large part of Palestine?
32546.e: Because of the holy places, part of Palestine was to be administered internationally. In fact, Great Britain later took over the mandate.
32546.m: Sykes-Picot planned an international administration for Palestine.

32547.q: Why did many Arabs feel betrayed by Great Britain because of the Sykes-Picot Agreement?
a: The British had promised them an independent Arab state
The British had promised them large payments for oil
The British had secretly supported the Ottomans
The British wanted to occupy Mecca
32547.e: In 1915 and 1916 Great Britain held out the prospect of an independent kingdom to the Arabs if they fought against the Ottomans. At the same time it secretly divided the region with France.
32547.m: Sykes-Picot contradicted Britain’s promises to the Arabs.

32548.q: In what form did Great Britain and France rule areas such as Syria, Palestine and Iraq from 1920?
a: As mandate powers on behalf of the League of Nations
As trustees on behalf of the UN
As occupiers together with the USA
As protecting powers of the Ottoman Empire
32548.e: The League of Nations handed the former Ottoman territories to the victorious powers as mandates. In this way the plans of Sykes-Picot were carried out in a changed form.
32548.m: After 1920 the Middle East was administered as League of Nations mandates.

32549.q: Which work did Theodor Herzl publish in 1896 as the basis of political Zionism?
32549.e: In “The Jewish State” Herzl called for a state of their own as the answer to antisemitism. The work made him leader of the Zionist movement.
32549.m: With “The Jewish State” in 1896, Theodor Herzl founded political Zionism.

32550.q: What did the UN General Assembly recommend for Palestine in November 1947?
a: Division into a Jewish and an Arab state
A joint state under British rule
32550.e: Resolution 181 of 29 November 1947 provided for two states, with Jerusalem to be administered internationally. The Jewish side agreed, the Arab side rejected it.
32550.m: In 1947 the UN recommended the partition of Palestine.

32551.q: Which two states launched a surprise attack on Israel on the holiest Jewish holiday in October 1973?
32551.e: The attack on the Day of Atonement gave the Yom Kippur War its name. After initial losses, Israel was able to turn the situation around militarily.
32551.m: Egypt and Syria started the Yom Kippur War in 1973.

32552.q: Which British declaration of 1917 supported the establishment of a “national home” for the Jewish people in Palestine?
32552.e: Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour promised British support in a letter to Lord Rothschild. At the same time, the rights of the non-Jewish population were to be protected.
32552.m: The Balfour Declaration of 1917 promised a Jewish national home in Palestine.

32553.q: What do Palestinians call the flight and expulsion of about 700,000 people in connection with the war of 1948?
32553.e: Nakba means “catastrophe” in Arabic. The refugee question is still one of the core issues of the Middle East conflict.
32553.m: Palestinians call the expulsion of 1948 the Nakba.

32554.q: In which war did Israel occupy the West Bank, the Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem?
32554.e: In June 1967 Israel also conquered the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights. The occupation of the Palestinian territories still shapes the conflict today.
32554.m: In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank and Gaza.

32555.q: Which two politicians sealed the Oslo Accords in 1993 with a famous handshake in front of the White House?
a: David Ben-Gurion and Gamal Abdel Nasser
32555.e: The accords brought mutual recognition of Israel and the PLO and limited Palestinian self-government. Rabin was murdered by an Israeli extremist in 1995.
32555.m: Rabin and Arafat shook hands at the Oslo Accords in 1993.

32556.q: Which Arab state was the first to sign a peace treaty with Israel, in 1979?
32556.e: After the Camp David negotiations, Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in 1979, and Israel returned the Sinai. Jordan only followed in 1994.
32556.m: In 1979 Egypt was the first Arab country to make peace with Israel.

32557.q: In which year did the genocide in Rwanda take place?
32557.e: The genocide lasted from April to July 1994, about 100 days. In this short time hundreds of thousands of people were killed.
32557.m: The genocide in Rwanda happened in 1994.

32558.q: Which event on 6 April 1994 directly triggered the genocide in Rwanda?
a: The shooting down of the Rwandan President’s plane
An earthquake in the capital Kigali
The withdrawal of all UN soldiers
32558.e: When the plane was shot down over Kigali, Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana and the President of Burundi died. Extremist militias began the killings that same night.
32558.m: The shooting down of the President’s plane triggered the genocide.

32559.q: Against which population group was the genocide in Rwanda mainly directed?
32559.e: Hutu extremists deliberately murdered Tutsi, as well as moderate Hutu who resisted. The division into Hutu and Tutsi had been fixed during the colonial period through identity cards.
32559.m: The genocide in Rwanda was mainly directed against the Tutsi.

32560.q: According to common estimates, how many people were killed in the genocide in Rwanda?
32560.e: Most estimates put the number of dead at between 800,000 and one million. That was a large part of the country’s Tutsi population.
32560.m: An estimated 800,000 to one million people died in the genocide in Rwanda.

32561.q: Which radio station stirred up hatred against the Tutsi before and during the genocide in Rwanda?
32561.e: The station RTLM called Tutsi “cockroaches” and openly called for killing. Those responsible were later convicted of incitement to genocide.
32561.m: The radio station RTLM called for genocide in Rwanda.

32562.q: Which Canadian general commanded the UN troops in Rwanda and warned of the genocide in vain?
32562.e: Roméo Dallaire led the UNAMIR mission and reported signs of planned massacres to New York in January 1994. Instead of reinforcements, he was given hardly any room to act, and the troops were even reduced.
32562.m: General Roméo Dallaire warned the UN of the genocide in vain.

32563.q: Which rebel army ended the genocide in July 1994 by conquering Rwanda militarily?
32563.e: The Rwandan Patriotic Front under Paul Kagame took Kigali in July 1994. The Interahamwe, by contrast, were the Hutu militias that committed a large part of the killings.
32563.m: The Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide in 1994.

32564.q: In which city was the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda based?
32564.e: The UN set up the tribunal in 1994, and it sat in Arusha in Tanzania. In 1998 it handed down the first verdict of an international court for genocide.
32564.m: The Rwanda tribunal sat in Arusha in Tanzania.

32565.q: In which year was the Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded?
32565.e: The VOC was founded on 20 March 1602 by merging several trading companies. The States General granted it a trade monopoly for Asia.

32566.q: Why is the VOC regarded as a milestone in economic history?
a: It issued freely tradable shares to the general public
It was the first bank with paper money
It was the first to introduce income tax
It was the first state postal company
32566.e: Every citizen could buy shares in the VOC, which could then be sold on. That is why it is often regarded as the first joint-stock company in the modern sense.
32566.m: The VOC is seen as an early joint-stock company with tradable shares.

32567.q: With which goods did the VOC make its biggest profits in Asia?
a: Spices such as pepper, nutmeg and cloves
32567.e: Spices were very expensive in Europe. The VOC secured monopolies on the Moluccas and the Banda Islands, often with great violence.
32567.m: The VOC became rich above all through the spice trade.

32568.q: Which city did the VOC found in 1619 as its main base in Asia?
32568.e: In 1619 Jan Pieterszoon Coen conquered Jayakarta and founded Batavia there. The city is now called Jakarta.
32568.m: Batavia, today’s Jakarta, was the centre of the VOC in Asia.

32569.q: Which artificial island near Nagasaki was for a long time the only European trading post in Japan?
32569.e: During Japan’s policy of isolation, only the Dutch were allowed to trade on Dejima. The VOC ran the post from 1641.
32569.m: On Dejima the VOC was the only European power to trade with Japan.

32570.q: Which settlement did Jan van Riebeeck set up on behalf of the VOC in 1652?
a: A supply station at the Cape of Good Hope
A port at the mouth of the Hudson
32570.e: The station at the Cape supplied the ships on the long voyage to Asia with water and food. It grew into the Cape Colony with Cape Town.
32570.m: Cape Town began in 1652 as a VOC supply station.

32571.q: Over which valuable spices did the VOC wage a brutal war of conquest on the Banda Islands?
32571.e: The Banda Islands were then the only source of nutmeg. In 1621 the VOC under Coen conquered the islands and killed or drove out most of the population.
32571.m: The VOC secured the nutmeg monopoly on the Banda Islands with great violence.

32572.q: When was the VOC finally dissolved?
